| **Guru** | Broad categories, workrooms |
| **Toptal**, **Arc**, **Turing** | Selective networks for experienced developers/designers (rigorous screening, higher pay) |
| **99designs** | Design contests and direct projects |
| **ProBlogger**, **ProZ** | Writing jobs; translation |
| **Preply/italki** | Tutoring and language teaching |
| **Contra**, **Malt**, others | Newer/independent platforms (check country availability) |

## LinkedIn and direct clients

- **LinkedIn:** optimise your profile (headline with your service, About, Featured portfolio), post useful content, connect with potential clients, use the "Services" page feature, and search for "freelance" and "contract" roles.
- **Direct clients:** local businesses, referrals, past employers, communities. No platform fees, but you handle contracts, invoicing and payment collection yourself (use deposits and written agreements).
- **Social media:** show your work (before/after, tutorials) on TikTok, Instagram, Facebook groups.

Many successful freelancers start on platforms for reviews, then gradually add direct clients.

## Local and Kenyan options

- **Ajira Digital** and **Jitume** programmes provide training, mentorship and sometimes connections to work.
- Kenyan businesses (SMEs, schools, churches, NGOs) hire freelancers directly: approach them with specific offers.
- Kenyan job boards and agencies post contract and remote roles.

## Getting paid from platforms

| Method | How it works for Kenya |
|---|---|
| **Payoneer** | Commonly used with Upwork and Fiverr; withdraw to a Kenyan bank account |
| **PayPal** | Withdraw to M-Pesa via the PayPal option in M-Pesa, or to a bank |
| **Direct bank transfer** | Some platforms pay to Kenyan banks (fees apply) |
| **Wise** | For direct clients abroad |

Use accounts in **your own name**, matching your ID. See the "Getting paid in Kenya" lesson for step-by-step setup.

## Rules that get accounts banned

| Violation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Taking communication/payment **off the platform** before a contract (with platform-introduced clients) | Account suspension |
| **Multiple accounts** or using someone else's account | Permanent ban, frozen funds |
| **Fake identity** or VPN to pretend to be in another country | Ban |
| Fake reviews | Ban |
| Plagiarism or unoriginal work | Disputes, bans |
| Missing deadlines repeatedly | Low ratings, lower visibility |

:::think A client on Upwork offers to pay you directly through M-Pesa to "avoid fees" before you've done any work together. What are the risks?
It breaks Upwork's terms (you could lose your account), and you lose payment protection: the client could disappear without paying, or it could be a scam. Keep the work and payments on the platform, especially with new clients.
:::

## Choosing your first platform

| You are... | Start with |
|---|---|
| A specialist with a clear service (design, writing, video) | Fiverr (gigs) + Upwork |
| Good at writing proposals, want bigger projects | Upwork |
| A tutor/language teacher | Preply/italki |
| An experienced developer | Upwork, then selective networks (Toptal etc.) |
| Focused on local clients | Direct outreach + LinkedIn + WhatsApp Business |

## Summary

- Marketplaces provide clients, contracts and payment protection, at the cost of fees and competition.
- Upwork: proposals with connects, fixed-price or hourly contracts, JSS; Fiverr: packaged gigs, levels, ranking factors.
- Other platforms: Freelancer, PeopleperHour, Guru, selective networks, niche sites; plus LinkedIn and direct clients.
- Withdraw via Payoneer, PayPal (to M-Pesa), bank transfer or Wise, using accounts in your own name.
- Follow platform rules: no off-platform payments with platform clients, no multiple or borrowed accounts, no fake identities.

```quiz
Q: On Upwork, what credits do you spend to send proposals?
A: Connects | connects
Q: On Fiverr, what are your packaged services called?
A: gigs | gig
Q: What is Upwork's reputation score called? (three words)
A: Job Success Score | JSS
Q: Which payment service is commonly used to withdraw Upwork/Fiverr earnings to a Kenyan bank?
A: Payoneer
Q: Should you accept payment outside the platform from a client you met there? (yes or no)
A: no
```

lessons.title: Freelance marketplaces directory (with links)
lessons.body:
# Freelance marketplaces directory (with links)

A **freelance marketplace** connects you with clients who need work done, holds the client's money safely and pays you when the work is approved. This is a directory of the main ones: what each is for, how it charges, and who it suits. Use it with [Freelancing platforms compared](./?track=make-money-online&lesson=freelancing-platforms) and [A winning profile and proposals](./?track=make-money-online&lesson=profile-and-proposals).

> Fees and rules change: check each site's current fee page before you join.

## General marketplaces (all skills)

| Marketplace | How it works | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| [Upwork](https://www.upwork.com) | Clients post jobs; you send proposals using "Connects" (some free, more can be bought). Hourly or fixed-price contracts with payment protection. | Long-term clients in writing, design, coding, VA, marketing |
| [Fiverr](https://www.fiverr.com) | You create "gigs" (packaged services with prices); clients buy them. | Clear, packaged services (logo, video edit, website fix) |
| [Freelancer.com](https://www.freelancer.com) | Bid on projects and contests. | Many small projects; competitive on price |
| [PeoplePerHour](https://www.peopleperhour.com) | Proposals and fixed-price "offers"; UK-based clients. | Design, writing, web |
| [Guru](https://www.guru.com) | Profiles, quotes and workrooms. | Programming, design, admin |
| [Contra](https://contra.com) | Commission-free: a portfolio profile you share; clients pay you through it. | Freelancers who bring their own clients |
| [LinkedIn Services](https://www.linkedin.com/services/) | Add services to your LinkedIn profile; clients request proposals. | Professionals with a network |
| [Workana](https://www.workana.com) | Marketplace focused on Latin America. | Spanish/Portuguese speakers |
| [Malt](https://www.malt.com) | European freelance marketplace. | Developers and consultants serving Europe |

## Specialist and vetted networks

| Network | Skill | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [Toptal](https://www.toptal.com) | Developers, designers, finance experts | Very strict screening; high rates |
| [Arc](https://arc.dev) | Developers | Remote jobs and freelance work after vetting |
| [Turing](https://www.turing.com) | Developers | Long-term remote roles with US companies |
| [Andela](https://andela.com) | Engineers in Africa and beyond | Matches vetted engineers with companies |
| [99designs](https://99designs.com) | Designers | Contests and 1-to-1 projects |
| [Codeable](https://www.codeable.io) | WordPress developers | Vetted WordPress-only marketplace |
| [Preply](https://preply.com) / [italki](https://www.italki.com) | Tutors and language teachers | See [Online teaching platforms](./?track=make-money-online&lesson=online-teaching-platforms) |
| [Outlier](https://outlier.ai) / [DataAnnotation](https://www.dataannotation.tech) | AI training | See [AI training & data annotation](./?track=make-money-online&lesson=ai-training-data-annotation) |

## Kenyan and African sources of work

| Source | What it offers |
|---|---|
| [Ajira Digital](https://ajiradigital.go.ke) | Government programme: training, mentorship and links to digital work |
| [BrighterMonday](https://www.brightermonday.co.ke) | Kenyan job board, including remote and contract roles |
| [Fuzu](https://www.fuzu.com) | Jobs and career courses in East Africa |
| [MyJobMag Kenya](https://www.myjobmag.co.ke) | Kenyan job listings |
| County and national government tenders ([tenders.go.ke](https://tenders.go.ke)) | Larger contracts for registered businesses (AGPO for youth, women and PWDs) |
| WhatsApp/Facebook business groups, chambers of commerce | Local clients who prefer someone they can meet |

## Getting paid from marketplaces in Kenya

| Method | Notes |
|---|---|
| **PayPal → M-Pesa** | Link PayPal to M-Pesa and withdraw directly to your phone (search "PayPal M-Pesa" on Safaricom's site). |
| [Payoneer](https://www.payoneer.com) | Receive from Upwork, Fiverr, Amazon and others; withdraw to a Kenyan bank. |
| **Direct bank transfer** | Many platforms pay straight to Kenyan bank accounts. |
| [Wise](https://wise.com) | Useful for international transfers; check what's supported for Kenyan residents. |

Full details: [Getting paid in Kenya](./?track=make-money-online&lesson=getting-paid-kenya).

## Choosing your first marketplace

| If you... | Start on |
|---|---|
| Have a clear service you can package | Fiverr |
| Want long-term clients and are willing to write proposals | Upwork |
| Are an experienced developer | Toptal, Arc, Turing, Andela (alongside Upwork) |
| Teach a language or subject | Preply or italki |
| Already have clients from your network | Contra or LinkedIn Services |

**Focus on one or two** at first. A complete profile, 3 portfolio samples and daily proposals on one platform beat a half-empty profile on ten.

## Staying safe on marketplaces

- **Keep communication and payment on the platform** until you trust the client. Moving off-platform early loses your payment protection (and breaks most platforms' rules).
- **Never pay a "client" to receive work**, buy "training materials" from them, or deposit cheques for them.
- **Don't rent or buy accounts.** Use your own identity: verified accounts in your name protect your earnings.
- **Watch for fake job posts** asking you to install apps, share passwords or contact them on Telegram immediately.

```quiz
Q: On which marketplace do you create "gigs" (packaged services)?
A: Fiverr
Q: On Upwork, what do you spend to send proposals?
A: Connects
Q: Which marketplace lets you take your own clients without commission?
A: Contra
Q: Which Kenyan government programme links youth to digital work?
A: Ajira Digital | Ajira
Q: Which service can receive marketplace payments and withdraw to a Kenyan bank?
A: Payoneer | PayPal
Q: Should you move a new client off the platform to get paid faster?
A: no
```

lessons.title: A winning profile and proposals: templates, examples and what clients look for
lessons.body:
# A winning profile and proposals: templates, examples and what clients look for

On freelance platforms and LinkedIn, your profile and proposals are your shop window and your sales pitch. Clients scan dozens of applicants in minutes; most proposals are generic copy-paste messages they ignore. This unit shows exactly how to build a profile that attracts the right clients and write proposals that get replies, with templates and before/after examples.

:::note What you will learn
- How clients choose freelancers
- Profile photo, title, overview, portfolio, skills and rates
- Writing a specialised headline that ranks in search
- The proposal formula, with templates for different jobs
- Before/after proposal examples
- Interviews and follow-ups
- Tracking and improving your win rate
:::

## How clients choose

Clients ask: *Does this person understand my need? Can they do it well? Can I trust them? Is the price reasonable?* They look at:
1. **Relevance:** your title and first lines match their job.
2. **Proof:** portfolio samples and reviews in the same type of work.
3. **Communication:** clear, correct, specific writing.
4. **Reliability signals:** verified identity, complete profile, response time, job success.
5. **Price and value.**

## Building your profile

### Photo
Clear, friendly, professional headshot: good light (face a window), plain background, your face filling most of the frame, smiling, no sunglasses or group photos. It builds trust immediately.

### Title / headline
Specific titles beat general ones and match what clients search for.

| Weak | Strong |
|---|---|
| "Freelancer" | "Shopify & WooCommerce Developer: Fast, Mobile-Ready Online Stores" |
| "Writer" | "SEO Blog Writer for Fintech & Personal Finance Brands" |
| "Graphic designer" | "Brand Identity Designer: Logos & Brand Kits for Restaurants and Cafés" |
| "Virtual assistant" | "Executive Virtual Assistant: Inbox, Calendar & Travel Management" |

### Overview (About)

Structure:
1. **Hook:** who you help and the result ("I help small e-commerce brands turn browsers into buyers with clear, persuasive product pages.").
2. **What you offer:** 3–5 services.
3. **Proof:** experience, results, notable clients or projects (numbers where possible).
4. **Process/why you:** how you work (communication, deadlines, revisions).
5. **Call to action:** "Message me with your project details and I'll reply within a few hours."

Keep paragraphs short; the first 2 lines matter most (they show in search previews).

**Example:**
> I build fast, mobile-friendly WordPress and WooCommerce websites for small businesses, with M-Pesa and card payments, SEO basics and easy content editing.
>
> What I do: business websites · online shops · speed optimisation · bug fixes · website maintenance
>
> Recent work: an online shop for a Nairobi cosmetics brand (300+ products, M-Pesa checkout); a booking site for a Mombasa tour company that cut phone enquiries in half.
>
> How I work: clear milestones, daily updates, and 30 days of free fixes after launch.
>
> Send me your project details and I'll reply with ideas and a timeline.

### Portfolio
- 3–6 **best, relevant** pieces (not everything you've ever done).
- Each with a title, the problem, what you did, tools used and results.
- Concept/practice work is fine if labelled honestly.

### Skills, rates and other sections
- Add relevant skills/tags (they affect search).
- Set a reasonable rate (see the pricing lesson); you can adjust per project.
- Complete education, certifications, languages (Kiswahili and others can be an advantage), and **verify your identity**.

## The proposal formula

Clients receive many proposals; yours must show **you read their job** in the first two lines.

```
1. Personal opening: their goal/problem in your words (1–2 lines)
2. Relevant proof: a similar project + result + link (1–2 lines)
3. Your approach: 2–4 specific steps or ideas for their project
4. Timeline/price (if appropriate) and availability
5. A smart question to start a conversation
6. Short sign-off
```

Keep it **short** (100–200 words), specific and free of errors.

### Template: web development

> Hi [Name], you need a WooCommerce shop for your skincare products with M-Pesa payments and a clean, mobile-first design.
>
> I recently built a similar store for a Nairobi beauty brand (link): 120 products, M-Pesa checkout, and page speed under 2 seconds on mobile.
>
> For your shop I'd:
> 1. Set up WooCommerce with your products, categories and variations
> 2. Integrate M-Pesa (STK push) and card payments
> 3. Optimise images and speed for mobile users
> 4. Train you to add products yourself
>
> I can deliver in about 2–3 weeks. Do you already have product photos and descriptions, or will you need help with those?
>
> Best regards, [Your name]

### Template: writing

> Hi [Name], you're looking for weekly SEO articles on personal finance for a Kenyan audience.
>
> I write for [publication/blog] on saving, SACCOs and money market funds; one of my articles ranks on page one for "best money market funds in Kenya" (sample link).
>
> My process: keyword research, an outline for your approval, a well-sourced draft with headings and meta description, and one revision.
>
> Which keywords or topics are your priority for the first month?
>
> Thanks, [Your name]

### Template: virtual assistance

> Hi [Name], managing your inbox and calendar while travelling between clients sounds overwhelming; I can take that off your plate.
>
> I currently support a real estate agent with inbox management, scheduling and CRM updates, saving her about 10 hours a week.
>
> I'm available 9am–5pm EAT, which overlaps with your UK mornings. I'm comfortable with Google Workspace, Calendly and HubSpot.
>
> Would you like me to start with a short paid trial week?
>
> Kind regards, [Your name]

## Before and after

**Before (generic, ignored):**
> Dear Sir/Madam, I am a hardworking and experienced freelancer with many skills. I have read your job and I can do it perfectly. Please give me a chance. I am available 24/7. Thank you.

Problems: no evidence of reading the job, no proof, no specifics, sounds desperate, generic greeting.

**After (specific, gets replies):**
> Hi Sarah, you need 10 Instagram carousel designs to launch your new juice brand next month, matching your green and orange branding.
>
> Here are carousels I designed for a Nairobi café's launch (link); their posts got 3× more saves than usual.
>
> I'd create a template set first for your approval, then the 10 carousels with your copy, delivered as PNG and editable Canva links.
>
> Could you share your brand guidelines or logo files?
>
> Thanks, Achieng

## Interviews and follow-ups

- **Reply fast** when a client messages: speed matters.
- **Prepare:** reread the job, prepare questions, have portfolio links ready.
- **Video calls:** good light, quiet room, test internet; be professional and friendly.
- **Clarify scope:** deliverables, deadlines, revisions, communication, payment milestones.
- **Follow up once** politely if no reply after a few days, adding value ("I had another idea for your homepage...").

## Track and improve

Keep a simple spreadsheet: date, job, platform, proposal version, reply (yes/no), hired (yes/no). After 20–30 proposals, review:
- Which job types reply most? Focus there.
- Which openings work? Reuse the structure (not the exact text).
- Are you applying too late? Apply early to fresh jobs.
- Is your price wildly off?

:::think You've sent 40 proposals in two weeks with no replies. What would you check and change?
Check relevance (are you applying to jobs that match your specialisation and portfolio?), the first two lines (personalised to the client's need?), proof (relevant samples linked?), profile completeness and photo, timing (applying early?), and length (short and specific?). Improve, then track results on the next 20 proposals.
:::

## Summary

- Clients choose based on relevance, proof, communication, reliability and value.
- Profile: professional photo, specialised searchable title, results-focused overview, 3–6 relevant portfolio pieces, verified details.
- Proposals: personal opening about their need, relevant proof, specific approach, timeline, a smart question, short sign-off.
- Avoid generic, desperate messages; reply fast; clarify scope in interviews; follow up once.
- Track proposals and improve based on data.

```quiz
Q: What should the first two lines of a proposal show? (that you read their ...)
A: job | job post | need
Q: Roughly how long should a proposal be? Write a range like 100-200 words.
A: 100-200 | 100 to 200
Q: How many portfolio pieces should a profile highlight? Write a range like 3-6.
A: 3-6 | 3 to 6
Q: What should end a proposal to start a conversation? (two words)
A: a question | question | smart question
Q: Is "I am available 24/7, please give me a chance" a strong proposal opening? (yes or no)
A: no
```

lessons.title: Pricing your work: hourly vs project rates, packages, deposits and raising your prices
lessons.body:
# Pricing your work: hourly vs project rates, packages, deposits and raising your prices

Pricing is where many freelancers lose money: charging too little out of fear, underestimating time, giving unlimited revisions, or starting work without a deposit. This unit gives you practical methods to set prices that cover your costs and grow with your skills, plus packages, quotes, contracts and how to raise rates confidently.

:::note What you will learn
- What a price must cover
- Calculating your minimum hourly rate
- Hourly vs fixed-price vs value-based vs retainer pricing
- Researching market rates (local and international)
- Building packages (good, better, best)
- Writing quotes and simple contracts; deposits and milestones
- Handling discounts, scope creep and late payments
- When and how to raise your prices
:::

## What your price must cover

Your price isn't just "time spent". It must cover:
- Your **living costs** and savings
- **Business costs:** data/internet, electricity, equipment (laptop wear), software subscriptions, platform fees, M-Pesa/transfer fees
- **Non-billable time:** finding clients, proposals, admin, learning (often 30–50% of a freelancer's time)
- **Taxes**
- **Risk:** months with less work

## Calculating your minimum hourly rate

```
Minimum hourly rate = (monthly living costs + monthly business costs + savings + tax allowance)
                      ÷ billable hours per month
```

Example:
| Item | KSh per month |
|---|---|
| Living costs | 40,000 |
| Business costs (data, power, tools, equipment fund) | 8,000 |
| Savings | 7,000 |
| Tax allowance | 5,000 |
| **Total needed** | **60,000** |

If you can bill **80 hours** a month (about 4 hours a day, 20 days, because the rest goes to admin and finding work):

`60,000 ÷ 80 = KSh 750 per hour minimum`

This is your **floor**: below it you're losing money. Charge more when the market, your skill and the value allow.

## Pricing models

| Model | How it works | Best for | Watch out |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hourly** | Paid per hour worked (tracked) | Ongoing support, unclear scope, VA work | Income capped by hours; clients may watch the clock |
| **Fixed-price (project)** | One price for defined deliverables | Websites, logos, articles, videos | Must define scope precisely; estimate time carefully |
| **Per unit** | Per word, per audio minute, per product listing, per page | Writing, transcription, data entry | Make sure unit price covers effort |
| **Value-based** | Priced on the value to the client | Copywriting, marketing, systems that save/make money | Needs confidence and understanding of client's business |
| **Retainer** | Monthly fee for ongoing work | Social media management, maintenance, bookkeeping | Define what's included each month |

**Fixed-price** is often better for skilled freelancers: as you get faster, you earn more per hour, and clients prefer knowing the total cost.

## Researching market rates

- **Platforms:** look at profiles similar to yours (experience, reviews, location) on Upwork/Fiverr.
- **Local market:** ask peers, check what agencies charge, see price lists of competitors.
- **Job posts:** budgets in posts show what clients expect (though many lowball).
- **Communities:** freelancer groups often discuss rates.

International clients often pay more than local ones for the same skill, but competition is global. Local clients value proximity, local knowledge (M-Pesa, KRA, Kiswahili) and in-person meetings.

## Packages: good, better, best

Packages make choosing easy and increase average order value.

| | Starter | Business (most popular) | Premium |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pages | Up to 5 | Up to 10 | Up to 20 |
| Design | Template-based | Custom design | Custom + brand refresh |
| Features | Contact form, WhatsApp button | + blog, Google Maps, SEO basics | + online payments (M-Pesa), booking |
| Revisions | 2 rounds | 3 rounds | 4 rounds |
| Support | 14 days | 30 days | 60 days |
| Price | KSh 15,000 | KSh 35,000 | KSh 60,000 |

(Example figures for illustration.)

Tips:
- Most clients choose the **middle** option; make it the best value.
- Clearly list what's **included** and **not included**.
- Add **upsells**: extra pages, express delivery, content writing, logo design, hosting.

## Quotes, contracts, deposits and milestones

### A good quote includes
1. Client and project name, date, quote number, validity (e.g. 14 days)
2. **Scope:** exact deliverables
3. **Exclusions:** what's not included (content writing, hosting, extra pages)
4. **Timeline** and what you need from the client (content, photos, access) and by when
5. **Price** and **payment terms**: deposit, milestones, final payment, methods (M-Pesa till/paybill, bank)
6. **Revisions** included and the cost of extra revisions
7. **Ownership:** rights transfer on full payment

### Deposits and milestones

- New clients: **deposit before starting** (e.g. 40–50%).
- Larger projects: **milestones** (e.g. 40% start, 30% design approval, 30% launch).
- Platforms: use **escrow** milestones.
- Never deliver final files (source files, full website access) before final payment from unknown clients; share previews/watermarked versions instead.

## Scope creep, discounts and late payments

### Scope creep
Clients often ask for "one small extra thing" repeatedly. Protect yourself:
- Refer back to the agreed scope politely: "That's a great idea; it's outside the current scope. I can add it for KSh X and 2 extra days."
- Use a **change request** for additions.

### Discounts
- Prefer **adding value** over cutting price ("I can't reduce the price, but I can include an extra revision").
- If you discount, reduce scope too, or offer discounts for prepayment or longer retainers.
- Avoid very cheap prices to "get started": they attract difficult clients and are hard to raise later.

### Late payments
- Clear due dates on invoices; reminders before and after the due date.
- Pause work if payments are overdue (state this in your terms).
- For platform work, use the platform's dispute processes.

## Raising your prices

Raise prices when:
- You're consistently busy (more demand than time).
- You've gained skills, results and reviews.
- Your costs increased.

How:
- New clients get new prices immediately.
- Existing clients: give notice (e.g. 30 days) and explain the value you provide.
- Increase in steps (e.g. 10–25%), and watch the response.

:::think A designer charges KSh 2,000 per logo, spends about 10 hours on each including revisions, and wonders why they're always broke. What's wrong, and what would you suggest?
They earn about KSh 200 per hour before costs, far below a sustainable rate. Suggest calculating a minimum hourly rate, limiting revisions in packages, raising prices (or offering packages like logo + brand kit), improving the portfolio to target better-paying clients, and taking deposits.
:::

## Summary

- Prices must cover living costs, business costs, non-billable time, taxes and risk.
- Minimum hourly rate = total monthly needs ÷ realistic billable hours.
- Choose models wisely: hourly, fixed-price, per unit, value-based or retainers.
- Research market rates; build good/better/best packages with clear inclusions and upsells.
- Use written quotes with scope, exclusions, timeline, payment terms and revisions; take deposits and use milestones.
- Manage scope creep with change requests, add value instead of discounting, and raise prices as demand and skills grow.

```quiz
Q: If you need KSh 60,000 a month and can bill 80 hours, what is your minimum hourly rate in KSh?
A: 750
Q: Which package do most clients choose: starter, middle or premium?
A: middle
Q: What should new clients pay before work starts? (one word)
A: deposit | a deposit
Q: When clients keep adding small extra tasks beyond the agreement, what is it called? (two words)
A: scope creep
Q: Which pricing model charges a monthly fee for ongoing work?
A: retainer
```

lessons.title: Getting paid in Kenya: M-Pesa, PayPal, Payoneer, Wise, bank transfers and invoices step by step
lessons.body:
# Getting paid in Kenya: M-Pesa, PayPal, Payoneer, Wise, bank transfers and invoices step by step

Earning online is only half the job; you also need to **receive** money safely, cheaply and in your own name. Kenyans have more options than many countries thanks to M-Pesa, but each method has fees, limits and rules. This unit explains how each payment method works, how to set them up, how to move money to M-Pesa or your bank, how to invoice clients professionally, and how to avoid payment scams.

:::warning Fees and features change
Payment providers change fees, limits and features often. Check each provider's current fee pages and the M-Pesa/PayPal terms before relying on specific numbers.
:::

:::note What you will learn
- Choosing payment methods for local and international clients
- M-Pesa for business: Till, Paybill, Pochi la Biashara
- PayPal: account setup, verification and withdrawing to M-Pesa
- Payoneer: receiving from platforms and withdrawing to banks
- Wise and bank (SWIFT) transfers
- Invoicing: what to include and tools to use
- Exchange rates, fees and record keeping
- Payment scams to avoid
:::

## Which method for which client?

| Client / source | Best methods |
|---|---|
| Local individuals and businesses | M-Pesa (Till/Paybill/Pochi), bank transfer |
| Upwork, Fiverr, other marketplaces | Payoneer, PayPal, direct bank transfer (as offered) |
| International direct clients | PayPal, Wise, Payoneer, bank transfer |
| YouTube AdSense | Bank transfer (wire) to your bank account |
| Digital product sales | Platform payouts (Selar, Gumroad, Payhip) to bank/PayPal/M-Pesa options |

Always use accounts in **your own legal name**, matching your ID. Mismatched names cause frozen accounts and failed withdrawals.

## M-Pesa for business

| Option | What it is | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **Personal M-Pesa** | Normal "Send Money" to your number | Very small side hustles (looks less professional; mixes personal and business money) |
| **Pochi la Biashara** | A business "pocket" on your personal line; customers pay your phone number via a separate menu | Small traders and freelancers starting out |
| **Buy Goods Till** (Lipa na M-Pesa) | A till number for receiving payments | Shops, service businesses |
| **Paybill** | Business number + account number | Organisations, schools, larger businesses, invoices with references |

How to get a Till or Paybill: apply through Safaricom's official business channels (agent/shop or online application) with the required documents (ID, KRA PIN, business registration for some options). Requirements differ by product.

Benefits: customers trust business numbers, records are separate, and statements help with bookkeeping and taxes.

## PayPal

### Setting up
1. Create an account at **paypal.com** (choose personal or business) with your real name and email.
2. Link and **verify** your M-Pesa/phone and card (if requested) following PayPal's steps.
3. Complete your profile and enable security (2-step verification).

### Receiving money
- Share your PayPal email or a PayPal.Me link with clients.
- For work, request payment as "goods and services" style (with fees) rather than "friends and family", which removes protections and may break terms when used for business.

### Withdrawing to M-Pesa
Safaricom and PayPal offer a service to move money from PayPal to M-Pesa (and to top up PayPal from M-Pesa):
1. Use the PayPal option in the **M-Pesa menu or M-Pesa app** (or the official M-Pesa PayPal portal).
2. Link your PayPal account (same name and verified details).
3. Choose **withdraw**, enter the amount (in USD) and confirm; money arrives in M-Pesa in KES (exchange rate applied).

You can also withdraw PayPal funds to a linked Kenyan bank account.

### PayPal cautions
- Accounts can be limited for unusual activity or mismatched details: keep your information consistent and verified.
- Beware **chargebacks** (buyers reversing payments) and overpayment scams.

## Payoneer

Commonly used to receive payments from **Upwork**, **Fiverr** and many marketplaces and companies.

1. Sign up at **payoneer.com** (often via a link from the platform, which can make approval smoother).
2. Provide your details and ID for verification.
3. Connect it to the platform as your withdrawal method.
4. Receive funds in your Payoneer balance (USD).
5. Withdraw to a **Kenyan bank account** (KES or USD accounts) via Payoneer's withdrawal option. Fees and exchange rates apply.

Payoneer also offers receiving accounts (e.g. USD account details) for direct clients in some cases.

## Wise

**Wise** (wise.com) lets international clients pay you at the real exchange rate with transparent fees. Clients can send money from their country; you receive into your Wise balance (if available to you) or directly to your Kenyan bank/M-Pesa where supported. Check current availability for Kenyan recipients.

## Bank transfers (SWIFT)

- International clients and AdSense can pay directly into your Kenyan bank account via **SWIFT** (they need your bank's SWIFT/BIC code, account name and number, bank address).
- Consider a **USD account** to avoid double currency conversion if you hold dollars.
- Fees: sending bank fees, intermediary fees, and receiving fees can reduce the amount.

## Invoicing professionally

An invoice is a formal request for payment and a record for both sides.

### What to include

```
INVOICE                         Invoice No: INV-2026-042
Date: 2 October 2026            Due date: 16 October 2026

From: Wanjiku Kamau Designs, Nairobi · 0712 345 678 · KRA PIN: A012345678Z
To:   Juma Electronics Ltd, Kisumu

| Description                         | Qty | Rate (KSh) | Amount (KSh) |
| Logo design (3 concepts, 2 revisions)| 1   | 15,000     | 15,000       |
| Brand kit (colours, fonts, guide)    | 1   | 10,000     | 10,000       |
|                                      |     | Subtotal   | 25,000       |
|                                      |     | Deposit paid | (10,000)   |
|                                      |     | Balance due | 15,000      |

Payment: M-Pesa Till 123456 · or Bank: ABC Bank, Acc. 0123456789
Thank you for your business!
```

### Tools
- Excel/Google Sheets or Word templates (see the Excel projects lesson)
- Free invoicing apps (e.g. Wave, Zoho Invoice) and accounting software
- Platforms generate invoices automatically for platform work
- VAT-registered businesses must issue invoices compliant with KRA's **eTIMS** requirements

### Getting paid on time
- Agree payment terms in advance (deposit, milestones, due dates).
- Send invoices promptly; follow up politely on the due date.
- Offer convenient methods (M-Pesa for locals; PayPal/Wise for international).

## Exchange rates, fees and records

- Compare total costs: platform fee + withdrawal fee + exchange rate margin.
- Withdraw in larger, less frequent amounts if fees are per transaction (check fee structures).
- **Record every payment:** date, client, gross amount, fees, net received, method. This helps with taxes (see the taxes lesson) and spotting problems.
- Keep business and personal money separate (a separate line, Pochi/Till, or bank account).

## Payment scams to avoid

| Scam | How it works | Protection |
|---|---|---|
| **Overpayment** | "I sent extra by mistake, refund the difference" (the original payment later reverses) | Never refund until funds are fully cleared and verified; return through the same channel |
| **Fake payment screenshots/SMS** | Fake M-Pesa SMS or PayPal emails | Check your actual balance/app, not screenshots or emails |
| **"Pay a fee to release your funds"** | Fake platforms or "agents" ask for fees to unlock earnings | Real platforms deduct fees from earnings, they don't ask you to send money |
| **Account renting/selling** | Using others' PayPal/Payoneer accounts | Use only your own verified accounts |
| **Chargebacks** | Client pays, receives work, then disputes the payment | Use escrow/milestones; keep records of delivery and communication |

:::think A new overseas client sends you USD 1,500 via PayPal for a USD 500 job, then asks you to refund USD 1,000 by M-Pesa to "their assistant in Nairobi". What's happening?
This is a classic overpayment scam. The PayPal payment may be from a stolen account and will likely be reversed, leaving you out of pocket for the USD 1,000 you sent. Don't send any money; contact PayPal support, and refund (if at all) only through PayPal after funds are fully cleared.
:::

## Summary

- Match payment methods to clients: M-Pesa for local, Payoneer/PayPal/Wise/bank for international and platforms.
- Use M-Pesa business options (Pochi, Till, Paybill) to look professional and keep records separate.
- PayPal can be withdrawn to M-Pesa via the official M-Pesa PayPal service; Payoneer withdraws to Kenyan banks; Wise and SWIFT handle direct international payments.
- Invoice professionally with numbers, dates, items, totals and payment details; take deposits and follow up.
- Track fees and exchange rates, keep records, separate business money, and avoid overpayment and fake-payment scams.

```quiz
Q: Which M-Pesa option gives small businesses a separate pocket on a personal line? (three words)
A: Pochi la Biashara
Q: Which payment service is commonly used for Upwork and Fiverr withdrawals to Kenyan banks?
A: Payoneer
Q: Through which service can you move PayPal money to M-Pesa? (the mobile money service)
A: M-Pesa | M-Pesa PayPal
Q: What code does a foreign client need to send money to your bank by international transfer? (two words or one: SWIFT ...)
A: SWIFT | SWIFT code | BIC
Q: A client overpays and asks you to refund the difference by M-Pesa. What scam is this?
A: overpayment | overpayment scam
Q: Should business and personal money be kept separate? (yes or no)
A: yes
```

lessons.title: Start a web design business: skills, services, pricing, finding clients and delivering projects
lessons.body:
# Start a web design business: skills, services, pricing, finding clients and delivering projects

Many Kenyan businesses still have no website, or have an old, slow one that doesn't work on phones. Others need online shops, booking systems, M-Pesa payments, Google visibility and maintenance. A web design business can start with one laptop and grow into an agency. This unit covers everything: the skills, services to offer, tools, pricing, finding clients, the project process, contracts, hosting, maintenance income and scaling.

:::note What you will learn
- Skills needed and how to learn them (this hub's web subjects)
- Services to offer and recurring income streams
- Tools: code, WordPress, hosting, design
- Building a portfolio before your first client
- Pricing websites and care plans
- Finding clients locally and online
- The project process from enquiry to launch
- Contracts, domains in the client's name, and ethics
- Growing from freelancer to agency
:::

## Skills you need

| Skill | Learn on this hub |
|---|---|
| HTML and CSS (structure, responsive design) | HTML, CSS subjects |
| JavaScript basics (interactivity) | JavaScript subject |
| WordPress (themes, plugins, WooCommerce) | Tech lesson in 130+ ways; WordPress tutorials |
| Hosting, domains, email, SSL | Hosting subject |
| Basic design and UX | Web design, Graphic design subjects |
| SEO basics | Marketing subject; HTML SEO lesson |
| M-Pesa integration (optional, valuable) | APIs & backends subject (Daraja) |
| Communication, sales, project management | This subject |

You don't need everything on day one. A strong beginner offer is: responsive business websites (HTML/CSS or WordPress) + hosting setup + basic SEO.

## Services to offer

| Service | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Business websites** (5–10 pages) | The core offer for SMEs, schools, churches, NGOs, professionals |
| **Landing pages** | Single pages for campaigns, events, products |
| **Online shops** (WooCommerce/Shopify) | With M-Pesa and card payments, delivery options |
| **Booking/appointment sites** | Salons, clinics, tours, consultants |
| **Website redesigns** | Old/slow sites → modern, mobile-friendly |
| **Domain, hosting and business email setup** | `.co.ke` domains, cPanel, SSL, professional email |
| **SEO and Google Business Profile** | Local visibility |
| **Maintenance/care plans** (recurring) | Updates, backups, security, small edits, monthly reports |
| **Custom systems** (later) | School portals, inventory, M-Pesa-integrated systems |

**Recurring income** is the secret to a stable business: hosting renewals, maintenance plans, SEO retainers.

## Tools

| Purpose | Tools |
|---|---|
| Code editor | VS Code |
| Design/mockups | Figma, Canva |
| CMS | WordPress (+ Elementor or block themes), WooCommerce |
| Hosting | cPanel shared hosting (local and international providers), static hosting (Netlify, GitHub Pages) |
| Images | Squoosh/TinyPNG (compression), free stock photos (Unsplash/Pexels), client photos |
| Testing | Chrome DevTools, PageSpeed Insights, real phones |
| Project management | Trello, Notion, Google Sheets |
| Communication | WhatsApp Business, email, Google Meet |

## Build a portfolio first

1. Build **3–5 sample sites** for different industries (salon, restaurant, school, hardware shop, consultant), using realistic content.
2. Deploy them online (free static hosting or cheap hosting) so clients can open them on their phones.
3. Offer 1–2 **discounted or free** sites to real businesses (a relative's shop, your church) in exchange for a testimonial and permission to show the work.
4. Create a simple portfolio website with your services, samples, testimonials and contacts (WhatsApp button).

## Pricing

Prices vary widely by complexity and market. Illustrative local packages:

| Package | Typical inclusions | Example price range |
|---|---|---|
| Landing page | 1 page, WhatsApp/call buttons, map | Lower range |
| Starter business site | Up to 5 pages, mobile-friendly, contact form, basic SEO | Around KSh 15,000–30,000 |
| Business site | Up to 10–12 pages, custom design, blog, SEO setup | Higher |
| Online shop | Products, cart, M-Pesa/card checkout, delivery options, training | Higher, depends on product count and integrations |
| Care plan | Updates, backups, security, small edits monthly | Monthly fee |
| Domain + hosting | Yearly renewal | Pass-through cost + margin/service |

Use the pricing lesson to calculate your minimum rate, define scope precisely, and take deposits (e.g. 50%).

## Finding clients

### Local
- **Walk-in visits:** businesses near you (show a sample on your phone; offer a free quick audit of their Google presence).
- **Google Maps research:** businesses with no website or old sites; call or WhatsApp them with a specific offer.
- **Networks:** church, chama, alumni, family businesses; ask for referrals.
- **Partnerships:** printers, graphic designers, accountants, business consultants who meet businesses needing websites.
- **Social media:** before/after showcases, tips videos (TikTok/Instagram), WhatsApp Status.

### Online
- Upwork/Fiverr (website and WordPress jobs), LinkedIn, Facebook business groups.

### A simple outreach message

> Hello [Name], I came across [Business] on Google Maps; your reviews are great! I noticed you don't have a website yet, so customers searching "[service] in [town]" may not find your prices and location. I build fast, mobile-friendly websites with WhatsApp and call buttons for local businesses (example: [link]). Would you like a free 10-minute chat about what a website could do for you? [Your name], [phone]

## The project process

1. **Enquiry and discovery:** goals, audience, pages, features, examples they like, budget, deadline.
2. **Proposal/quote:** scope, timeline, price, payment terms, what you need from them (logo, photos, text).
3. **Agreement and deposit.**
4. **Content collection:** often the slowest part; provide a content checklist and deadline.
5. **Design:** wireframe/mockup or homepage draft for approval.
6. **Build:** pages, responsive design, forms, integrations, SEO basics.
7. **Review:** client feedback within the agreed revision rounds.
8. **Launch:** domain/DNS, SSL, final testing (phones, forms, speed), Google Search Console, Google Business Profile link.
9. **Handover and training:** how to edit content; logins; documentation.
10. **Final payment** and ongoing **care plan** offer.

## Contracts and ethics

- **Written agreement:** scope, timeline, payment schedule, revisions, ownership, hosting responsibilities, support period.
- **Register domains in the client's name** (with you as technical contact); give them access to hosting. Holding domains hostage damages trust and can be legally risky.
- **Licensed assets only:** themes, plugins, fonts and images must be properly licensed (no nulled/pirated themes: they often contain malware).
- **Security:** strong passwords, updates, backups; never store client passwords insecurely.
- **Data protection:** forms collecting personal data need privacy notices and secure handling.
- **Honesty:** don't promise "number one on Google".

## Maintenance and growth

- Offer **care plans** at launch (updates, backups, uptime monitoring, small changes, monthly report).
- **Hosting reselling** (if you can provide reliable support).
- **Upsells:** SEO, content writing, social media, Google Ads, M-Pesa integration, booking systems.
- **Scale:** templates and checklists, then hire or partner with designers, writers and developers; register a business name or company; use project management tools.

:::think A client asks you to register their domain under your own name "to make things easier". Why should you register it in the client's name instead?
The domain is the client's business asset. If it's in your name and you become unavailable or the relationship ends, the client could lose access to their website and email, causing disputes. Registering in the client's name (with you as technical contact) protects them and your reputation.
:::

## Summary

- Core skills: HTML/CSS, WordPress, hosting, design basics, SEO; add JavaScript and M-Pesa integration to grow.
- Offer business sites, landing pages, shops, booking sites, redesigns, hosting/email setup, SEO and care plans; recurring income stabilises the business.
- Build 3–5 samples and get testimonials before charging full prices.
- Price with packages, clear scope and deposits; follow a structured project process.
- Find clients locally (walk-ins, Google Maps research, referrals, partnerships) and online.
- Use contracts, client-owned domains, licensed assets, good security and honesty; grow with care plans, upsells and partners.

```quiz
Q: Whose name should a client's domain be registered in?
A: client | the client | the client's
Q: What recurring service provides stable monthly income for web designers? (two words)
A: care plans | care plan | maintenance
Q: Which stage is often the slowest part of a website project? (two words: content ...)
A: content collection | content
Q: Should you use nulled (pirated) WordPress themes? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: How many sample sites should you build for a starting portfolio? Write a range like 3-5.
A: 3-5 | 3 to 5
```

lessons.title: Content creation step by step: plan, film, edit, publish and grow on YouTube, TikTok and Facebook
lessons.body:
# Content creation step by step: plan, film, edit, publish and grow on YouTube, TikTok and Facebook

The **Content creation** lesson in "130+ ways to earn online" explains how each platform pays. This unit is the hands-on production guide: how to plan content people want, film good videos with just a phone, edit them, publish with titles and thumbnails that get clicks, analyse results and stay consistent without burning out.

:::note What you will learn
- Finding your niche and content pillars
- Researching ideas people actually search for
- Scripting hooks and structure
- Filming with a phone: light, sound, framing
- Editing with CapCut and DaVinci Resolve
- Titles, thumbnails, captions and hashtags
- Posting schedules and repurposing one video into many
- Reading analytics and improving
- Copyright, ethics and safety
:::

## Step 1: Niche and content pillars

Choose a niche at the intersection of **what you know/love**, **what people want**, and **what brands or customers pay for** (see the niche table in 130+ ways). Then define 3–4 **content pillars** (recurring themes):

Example niche: "Tech for Kenyan students and small businesses"
- Pillar 1: Budget phone and laptop reviews
- Pillar 2: How-to tutorials (Excel, Canva, KRA iTax)
- Pillar 3: Side hustles and digital skills
- Pillar 4: Tech news explained simply

Pillars keep you consistent and help viewers know what to expect.

## Step 2: Research ideas

- **YouTube/TikTok search suggestions:** type a topic and note autocomplete phrases.
- **Comments:** questions on your and competitors' videos are free ideas.
- **Google Trends:** compare interest over time (set to Kenya).
- **Competitor analysis:** which videos in your niche got unusually high views? Why (topic, title, thumbnail)?
- **Seasonal calendar:** KCSE results, back to school, KRA deadline (June), Black Friday, Christmas, budget day.

Keep an **ideas list** (Google Sheets/Notion) with columns: idea, pillar, format, priority.

## Step 3: Script and structure

### The hook (first 3 seconds on TikTok, first 15 seconds on YouTube)
- Ask a question: "Why is your phone battery dying so fast?"
- Bold statement: "This free tool replaced my KSh 3,000 monthly subscription."
- Show the result first: the finished design, the before/after.

### Structure
- **Short videos (15–60 s):** hook → 1 clear point/steps → payoff → call to action (follow, comment).
- **Long videos (6–15 min):** hook → promise ("by the end you'll know...") → content in clear sections → recap → call to action.

Write bullet-point scripts; read them a few times; speak naturally rather than reading word for word.

## Step 4: Filming with a phone

| Area | Tips |
|---|---|
| **Light** | Face a window (natural light); avoid bright light behind you; a cheap ring light helps at night |
| **Sound** | The most important quality factor: record in a quiet room with soft furnishings; use a clip-on (lavalier) mic; avoid echoey rooms and wind |
| **Framing** | Vertical (9:16) for TikTok/Reels/Shorts; horizontal (16:9) for YouTube long videos; eyes about one-third from the top; clean background |
| **Stability** | Phone tripod or stack of books; avoid shaky footage |
| **Camera** | Use the rear camera for better quality when possible; clean the lens; lock focus/exposure |
| **Settings** | 1080p at 30 fps is plenty; check storage space |
| **B-roll** | Extra footage (hands typing, product close-ups, location shots) to cut into talking segments |

## Step 5: Editing

### Tools
- **CapCut** (free, phone and PC): templates, auto-captions, effects; great for short videos.
- **DaVinci Resolve** (free, PC): professional editing for long videos.
- **Canva** video editor: simple edits and templates.

### Editing workflow
1. Import clips; **cut** mistakes, pauses and filler ("eh", "umm").
2. Add **B-roll**, screenshots, zooms to keep visual interest.
3. Add **captions** (auto-generate, then correct spelling).
4. **Music:** royalty-free/licensed only, at low volume under speech.
5. **Colour and audio:** basic brightness/contrast; normalise and denoise audio.
6. **Export** at the correct aspect ratio and resolution.

Pacing tip: change something on screen every few seconds in short videos (cut, zoom, text, B-roll).

## Step 6: Titles, thumbnails, captions and hashtags

- **Titles:** clear benefit + keyword: "How to File KRA Nil Returns in 2026 (Step by Step on Phone)". Avoid clickbait that doesn't deliver.
- **Thumbnails (YouTube):** a face with emotion or the result, 3–4 big words, high contrast, readable on a phone (1280×720).
- **Descriptions:** summarise, add timestamps (chapters), links and keywords.
- **TikTok/Reels captions:** short, a question to prompt comments; 3–5 relevant hashtags (not 30 random ones).
- **Accessibility:** captions on all videos.

## Step 7: Posting schedule and repurposing

- Choose a **realistic schedule** you can sustain (e.g. 1 YouTube video + 3 shorts per week).
- **Batch** work: script on Monday, film 3 videos on Tuesday, edit Wednesday–Thursday.
- **Repurpose:** one long video → 3–5 short clips (Shorts, TikTok, Reels, Facebook) + a blog post + a carousel + a WhatsApp Channel update.
- **Engage:** reply to comments in the first hour; pin a good comment; reply with video replies on TikTok.

## Step 8: Analytics and improvement

| Metric | Meaning | If low, try |
|---|---|---|
| **Impressions / reach** | How many saw your thumbnail/video in feeds | Better topics, consistency |
| **Click-through rate (CTR)** | % who clicked after seeing the thumbnail | Better thumbnails and titles |
| **Average view duration / retention** | How long people watched | Stronger hook, tighter editing, deliver the promise faster |
| **Watch time** | Total minutes watched | Longer valuable videos, playlists |
| **Engagement** | Likes, comments, shares, saves | Ask questions, create share-worthy content |
| **Followers gained** | Growth | Consistent pillars, clear niche |

Review monthly: double down on topics and formats that perform; drop what doesn't.

## Step 9: Copyright, ethics and safety

- **Copyright:** don't upload others' videos, movies, TV clips or popular music without rights; you'll get claims, strikes or demonetisation. Use your own footage and licensed/royalty-free music (YouTube Audio Library, CapCut commercial library).
- **Disclose sponsorships** (#ad, paid partnership labels).
- **Fact-check** health, money and news claims; avoid promoting scams, unlicensed investments or betting to minors.
- **Privacy:** get permission before filming people; don't reveal your home location or children's details carelessly.
- **Mental health:** handle negative comments calmly; use filters, block abusers; take breaks.

:::think A creator's videos get many impressions but very few clicks (low CTR), and those who click watch most of the video. What should they improve?
The content is good (people who click keep watching), but the **packaging** isn't attracting clicks. Improve thumbnails (clear face/result, few bold words, contrast) and titles (clear benefit, curiosity, keywords). Test variations and compare CTR.
:::

## Summary

- Choose a niche with 3–4 content pillars; research ideas from search suggestions, comments, trends and competitors.
- Script strong hooks and clear structures for short and long videos.
- Film with good light, clean sound (clip-on mic), stable framing and B-roll.
- Edit with CapCut or DaVinci Resolve: cut, B-roll, captions, licensed music, good audio.
- Package with clear titles, strong thumbnails, captions and a few relevant hashtags.
- Post consistently, batch and repurpose, read analytics (CTR, retention) and improve.
- Respect copyright, disclose sponsorships, fact-check and protect privacy.

```quiz
Q: What is the most important quality factor to improve first when filming? (one word)
A: sound | audio
Q: Which aspect ratio is used for TikTok and Reels? Write like 9:16.
A: 9:16
Q: What does CTR measure? (two words: click-through ...)
A: click-through rate | rate | clicks
Q: Turning one long video into several shorts, a blog post and carousels is called what?
A: repurposing
Q: Which free editor is popular for short videos on phones?
A: CapCut
```

lessons.title: Content creation platforms: how each one pays
lessons.body:
# Content creation platforms: how each one pays

Content creators earn in five main ways: **platform payouts** (ad revenue, creator funds), **brand deals**, **selling their own products**, **fan support** (tips, memberships) and **affiliate links**. Each platform pays differently, and some programmes aren't open in every country. This lesson explains each one so you choose where to put your effort.

> Requirements and country lists change. Check each platform's official help page before planning around a programme.

## The platforms

| Platform | How creators earn | Typical entry requirement | Notes for Kenya |
|---|---|---|---|
| [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/creators/) | Ad revenue share, channel memberships, Super Thanks, Shopping | YouTube Partner Program: 1,000 subscribers plus 4,000 public watch hours in a year, or 10 million Shorts views in 90 days (lower tier for fan funding) | Available in Kenya. Paid through Google AdSense to your bank. The most reliable long-term video income. |
| [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/business/creators) | Ads on videos and reels, Stars (fan tips), subscriptions | Followers, watch-minutes and compliance with monetisation policies | Monetisation tools are rolled out by country; check Professional Dashboard → Monetisation. |
| [TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/creators/) | Creator Rewards Program, LIVE gifts, Subscriptions, TikTok Shop | Follower and view thresholds; country restrictions | Many payout programmes are limited by country; brand deals and LIVE gifts are common for Kenyan creators. Verify current eligibility. |
| [Instagram](https://creators.instagram.com) | Brand partnerships, subscriptions, gifts | Professional account; feature availability by country | Mostly brand deals and selling your own products/services. |
| [X (Twitter)](https://x.com) | Ads revenue sharing, subscriptions | Premium subscription and impression thresholds | Check eligibility; popular for influencer campaigns in Kenya. |
| [Spotify for Creators](https://creators.spotify.com) | Podcast hosting; partner programme and ads in some markets | Depends on market | Free hosting to grow a podcast; earn via sponsors. |
| [Patreon](https://www.patreon.com) | Monthly memberships from fans | None, but you need loyal fans | Paid out via PayPal or Payoneer. |
| [Ko-fi](https://ko-fi.com) | Tips, memberships, digital product sales | None | Payouts via PayPal. |
| [Medium](https://medium.com) | Written articles | Partner programme eligibility by country | Good for building a writing portfolio. |
| [Twitch](https://www.twitch.tv) | Gaming live streams: subs, bits, ads | Affiliate: followers and stream hours | Gaming audience; needs strong internet. |

## Brand deals: where most Kenyan creators earn

Brands pay creators to mention or show their product. In Kenya, banks, telcos, betting firms (think carefully about promoting gambling), beauty brands, restaurants and tech companies all run influencer campaigns.

How to get them:

1. **Pick a clear niche** (tech reviews, Kenyan food, farming, fashion, comedy, personal finance). Brands buy audiences, not just numbers.
2. **Make a media kit** (one page, Canva): who you are, your audience (age, location from your analytics), average views, past work, contact.
3. **Pitch** local businesses and agencies by email or DM with a specific idea.
4. **Price**: start with what a business would pay for a small ad; raise prices as results prove your value. Ask for **50% upfront**.
5. **Disclose** sponsored posts (#ad, "paid partnership"). It's honest and required by platform rules.

## Sell your own things (the biggest earners do this)

- **Services**: photography, video editing, consulting, coaching, training.
- **Digital products**: e-books, Lightroom presets, Canva templates, courses (see [Sell digital products](./?track=make-money-online&lesson=digital-products)).
- **Physical products**: merchandise, beauty products, books.
- Use your content as free marketing and send people to a WhatsApp Business catalogue or your website with M-Pesa checkout.

## Affiliate links

Earn a commission when people buy through your link. Examples: [Amazon Associates](https://affiliate-program.amazon.com) (for international audiences), [Jumia affiliate (KOL) programme](https://www.jumia.co.ke) (Kenya), hosting and software affiliate programmes. See [Affiliate marketing](./?track=make-money-online&lesson=affiliate-marketing).

## A simple content plan that works

| Day | Do |
|---|---|
| Monday | Plan 3 videos/posts: one teaching, one story, one trending format |
| Tuesday to Thursday | Film and edit (CapCut is free and enough to start) |
| Friday | Post, reply to every comment in the first hour |
| Weekend | Study analytics: which video kept people watching longest? Make more like it. |

**Consistency beats perfection**: 3 good posts a week for a year beats 30 posts in one week then nothing.

## What platforms reward

- **Watch time and retention**: people watching to the end.
- **Engagement**: comments, shares and saves (more than likes).
- **Originality**: re-uploading other people's content gets no payouts and can get your account banned.
- **Following the rules**: no copyrighted music in monetised videos without a licence, no misleading thumbnails, no hate or dangerous content.

```quiz
Q: How many subscribers does the YouTube Partner Program require (standard tier)?
A: 1000 | 1,000
Q: How many public watch hours in 12 months does YouTube require alongside the subscribers?
A: 4000 | 4,000
Q: Which platform is built for monthly memberships from fans?
A: Patreon
Q: What should you add to a sponsored post to disclose it? Write the hashtag.
A: #ad | ad
Q: What free app is suggested for editing videos on a phone?
A: CapCut
Q: Which engagement signals matter more than likes: comments, shares and ...?
A: saves
```

lessons.title: Graphic design: where and how to earn
lessons.body:
# Graphic design: where and how to earn

Every business needs a logo, posters, menus, social media graphics, business cards, banners and packaging. In Kenya alone there are hundreds of thousands of small businesses, churches, schools, events and politicians who pay designers every week. Online, you can also sell designs to the whole world.

> Learn the skills free in this hub: **Graphic design with Canva** and **Web design & UI/UX**.

## Ways designers earn

| Way | What you sell | Pay style |
|---|---|---|
| **Client work** | Logos, flyers, brand kits, social posts | Per project or monthly retainer |
| **Freelance marketplaces** | Packaged design services to international clients | Per order |
| **Design contests** | Many designers submit; the client picks one winner | Winner takes the prize |
| **Templates** | Canva templates, PowerPoint decks, CV templates, social media kits | Many small sales (passive) |
| **Print on demand** | Designs printed on T-shirts, mugs, posters by a platform | Royalty per item sold |
| **Stock graphics** | Icons, illustrations, vectors licensed to many buyers | Per download |
| **UI/UX design** | App and website screens in Figma | Per project; pays very well |

## Platforms

| Platform | What you do there | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [Fiverr](https://www.fiverr.com) | Sell packages ("Logo + 3 revisions", "10 Instagram posts") | Huge demand; the first orders are the hardest. Use clear gig images. |
| [Upwork](https://www.upwork.com) | Apply for design jobs and long-term clients | Better for ongoing brand and marketing design work. |
| [99designs](https://99designs.com) | Design contests and 1-to-1 projects | Strict quality vetting; good for strong portfolios. |
| [Dribbble](https://dribbble.com) | Show UI/brand work; clients and companies hire from it | Your portfolio + job board. |
| [Behance](https://www.behance.net) | Free portfolio by Adobe; job listings | Show full case studies of projects. |
| [Canva Creators](https://www.canva.com/creators/) | Publish templates and elements used by Canva users | Application required; paid per use. |
| [Creative Market](https://creativemarket.com) | Sell fonts, templates, graphics | Premium marketplace. |
| [Envato Elements / Market](https://author.envato.com) | Sell templates, graphics, presentations | Large buyer base. |
| [Etsy](https://www.etsy.com) | Sell printable and digital designs (planners, wall art, invitations) | Check seller country support and payout options. |
| [Adobe Stock](https://contributor.stock.adobe.com) | Sell vectors, illustrations, photos | Royalty per download. |
| [Shutterstock](https://submit.shutterstock.com) | Sell vectors and photos | Royalty per download. |
| [Freepik Contributor](https://contributor.freepik.com) | Sell vectors, icons, PSDs | Popular with designers worldwide. |
| [Redbubble](https://www.redbubble.com) / [TeePublic](https://www.teepublic.com) | Print on demand: upload designs, they print and ship | You earn a margin per sale; no stock needed. |

## The local market (often faster money)

- **Visit or message 20 businesses near you** (salons, restaurants, schools, churches, hardware shops) with a sample poster made for *them*.
- **Offer packages in KSh**: Logo (KSh 3,000 to 15,000), 10 social media posts a month (KSh 5,000 to 20,000), business cards and flyers (per design). Prices vary with quality and client size.
- **Partner with printers** in your town: they get customers who need designs; you get referrals.
- **Events**: weddings, funerals, graduations, fundraisers (harambee) and campaigns all need posters and programmes.

## Build a portfolio that sells

1. Make **10 to 15 strong pieces**, even for imaginary or practice clients ("rebrand of a Nyeri coffee shop").
2. Show **the problem and the result**, not just the image.
3. Put it on **Behance or a simple website** and pin your best 3 pieces on WhatsApp status and LinkedIn.
4. Only show work you have the right to show. **Never use others' designs or stolen fonts/images.**

## Tools

| Tool | Cost | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Canva | Free / Pro | Fast social graphics, posters, templates |
| Figma | Free plan | UI design, collaboration |
| Adobe Illustrator / Photoshop | Paid | Professional logos, print, photo editing |
| Inkscape / GIMP / Krita | Free | Open-source alternatives to Adobe |
| Affinity Designer | One-time payment | Affordable professional alternative |

## Contracts and payment

- Agree in writing (WhatsApp/email is fine): what you'll deliver, number of revisions, deadline and price.
- Take **50% deposit** before starting for new clients.
- Send low-resolution, watermarked previews; deliver final files after payment.
- Deliver properly: logo in **PNG, SVG and PDF**, colour codes, and fonts used.

```quiz
Q: Which platform runs design contests where clients pick a winner?
A: 99designs
Q: Which free Adobe platform is used as a design portfolio?
A: Behance
Q: Print-on-demand platforms like Redbubble pay you a margin per ...?
A: sale | item sold | item
Q: What deposit is recommended for new clients? Write a percentage.
A: 50% | 50 | fifty percent
Q: Name a free open-source alternative to Adobe Illustrator.
A: Inkscape
Q: Which three file formats should a final logo be delivered in? Name one vector format.
A: SVG | PDF | svg
```

lessons.title: Programming and web development: where to earn
lessons.body:
# Programming and web development: where to earn

Coding is one of the **best-paid** online skills, and one of the few where a developer in Nyeri or Kisumu can earn the same as one in London. It takes longer to learn (months, not days), but the demand never stops: every business wants a website, every SACCO wants a system, every startup wants an app.

> Learn it free here: **HTML → CSS → JavaScript → PHP & MySQL** for websites, **Flutter** or **React Native** for apps, **Python** and **SQL** for data and automation.

## What you can sell

| Service | Typical clients | Skills |
|---|---|---|
| Business websites | Small businesses, schools, churches, NGOs | HTML, CSS, JavaScript, WordPress or PHP |
| E-commerce shops with M-Pesa | Retailers, Instagram sellers | WooCommerce/Shopify or custom PHP + Daraja API |
| Systems (school, hospital, POS, SACCO, HR) | Institutions, companies | PHP/Laravel or Python/Django, SQL, security |
| Mobile apps | Startups, businesses, NGOs | Flutter, Kotlin, React Native, APIs |
| WordPress fixes and speed-ups | Website owners worldwide | WordPress, PHP, hosting |
| Automation scripts and data work | Offices, analysts | Python, Excel, SQL |
| Bug fixing and maintenance | Anyone with software | Debugging, reading other people's code |
| Website care plans (monthly) | Your past clients | Hosting, backups, updates |

## Platforms for developers

| Platform | How it works | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [Upwork](https://www.upwork.com) | Apply for projects and long-term contracts | The biggest general marketplace. Specialise ("Laravel + M-Pesa developer") to stand out. |
| [Fiverr](https://www.fiverr.com) | Sell packages ("WordPress site in 5 days") | Good for small fixed-scope jobs. |
| [Freelancer.com](https://www.freelancer.com) | Bid on projects and contests | Very competitive on price. |
| [Toptal](https://www.toptal.com) | Elite network; strict screening | Top rates if you pass; for experienced developers. |
| [Arc](https://arc.dev) | Remote jobs and freelance roles for vetted developers | Screening tests. |
| [Turing](https://www.turing.com) | Long-term remote jobs with US companies | Vetting by coding tests. |
| [Andela](https://andela.com) | Talent network matching African engineers with global companies | Founded in Lagos with a large Kenyan community. |
| [Contra](https://contra.com) | Commission-free freelance profile | Share your own link with clients. |
| [Codeable](https://www.codeable.io) | WordPress experts only | High-quality WordPress work after vetting. |
| [Envato ThemeForest / CodeCanyon](https://author.envato.com) | Sell website themes, plugins and scripts | Passive income once approved. |
| [Google Play](https://play.google.com/console) / [Apple App Store](https://developer.apple.com) | Publish your own apps; earn from ads, sales and subscriptions | Play Console costs US$25 once. |
| [GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors) | Get sponsored for open-source work | Build a reputation first. |
| [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com) | Jobs and direct client messages | Post your projects regularly. |
| [We Work Remotely](https://weworkremotely.com) / [Remote OK](https://remoteok.com) | Remote developer jobs | Check each job's location rules ("worldwide" vs one country). |
| [BrighterMonday](https://www.brightermonday.co.ke) / [Fuzu](https://www.fuzu.com) | Kenyan job boards | Local developer jobs and internships. |

## Local clients: the most underrated market

Kenyan businesses pay well for software that saves them time or makes them money:

- **Schools**: fee management, results, SMS to parents.
- **Hospitals and pharmacies**: patients, billing, stock, NHIF/SHA claims workflows.
- **SACCOs and chamas**: contributions, loans, statements.
- **Shops and supermarkets**: POS with M-Pesa, stock and reports.
- **TVETs and colleges**: student portals, CBET documentation (see the [CBET Planner](../what-is-cbet-planner) story).

Find them through people you know, LinkedIn, local business groups, county events and by showing a working demo. A real demo beats any CV.

## Build a portfolio that gets hired

1. **3 real projects** beat 20 tutorials: a business website, a system with login and a database, and an app or API.
2. Put the code on **GitHub** with a clear README (what it does, screenshots, how to run it).
3. **Deploy** them so people can click and try (cheap cPanel hosting, or free tiers).
4. Write a short **case study** for each: the problem, what you built, the result.
5. Get **testimonials** from your first clients (even if you gave a discount).

## Pricing (Kenya)

| Project | Common range (KSh) |
|---|---|
| Simple 5-page business website | 15,000 to 60,000 |
| E-commerce with M-Pesa | 40,000 to 200,000 |
| Custom system (school, POS, SACCO) | 80,000 to 500,000+ |
| Mobile app (simple to medium) | 100,000 to 600,000+ |
| Monthly care plan | 1,500 to 10,000 per month |

Ranges depend on features, quality and the client. Always quote **by scope** (a written list of features), take a **deposit** (usually 40 to 50%), and charge for changes outside the scope. See [How much does a website cost in Kenya?](../how-much-does-a-website-cost-in-kenya).

## Mistakes that cost developers money

- **No written scope**: the project never ends.
- **Handing over all code before final payment.**
- **No backups or security**: one hacked site ruins your reputation.
- **Competing only on price**: compete on reliability, speed and support instead.
- **Stopping learning**: frameworks change; spend a few hours every week learning.

```quiz
Q: Which platform is an elite network with strict screening for top developers?
A: Toptal
Q: Which marketplace is only for WordPress experts?
A: Codeable
Q: How much does a Google Play developer account cost, in US dollars, once?
A: 25 | $25 | US$25
Q: Where should you put your project code with a clear README?
A: GitHub
Q: What should you always agree in writing before starting a project?
A: scope | the scope | a written scope
Q: What part of the price do developers usually take before starting? Give a percentage range start, like 40.
A: 40 | 50 | 40% | 50% | 40 to 50%
```

lessons.title: Starting a YouTube channel that grows
lessons.body:
# Starting a YouTube channel that grows

YouTube is the world's second-biggest search engine. A channel can build an audience, promote a business, and eventually earn through ads, sponsorships and your own products. It's a long game: most successful creators uploaded consistently for a year or more before it paid. Here's how to start right.

## 1. Pick a niche you can sustain

Choose a topic where you can make **50+ videos** and that people actively search for. Good niches combine what you know, what you enjoy, and what people need:

- Tech tutorials (Excel, phone tips, coding, KRA iTax guides)
- Farming and agribusiness (poultry, dairy, greenhouse)
- Cooking Kenyan meals, budget recipes
- Education (KCSE revision, CBC projects)
- Small business and money (M-Pesa tips, side hustles, saving)
- Local reviews (phones under KSh 20,000, travel spots)

> A clear niche helps YouTube know who to recommend your videos to. "Excel tutorials for Kenyan offices" beats "a bit of everything".

## 2. Gear: start with your phone

| Priority | Item | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Audio**: a clip-on lavalier mic (a few hundred to a couple of thousand shillings) | Viewers forgive average video, not bad sound |
| 2 | **Light**: face a window, or a ring light | Clear, bright image |
| 3 | **Stability**: a cheap tripod | No shaky footage |
| 4 | Editing app | CapCut, VN, DaVinci Resolve (free) |
| Later | Better camera | Only when you've proven you'll keep going |

Screen tutorials: record with OBS Studio (free) or your phone's screen recorder.

## 3. Plan videos people search for

- Use YouTube's **search suggestions**: type "how to" + your topic and note what appears.
- Look at the most-viewed videos in your niche: what questions do the comments ask?
- Make videos that answer a specific question: "How to file KRA nil returns in 2026 (step by step)".

A simple video structure:

1. **Hook** (first 10–15 seconds): the result or the problem. "In 5 minutes you'll file your nil returns without going to a cyber."
2. **Content**: clear steps, no long intros.
3. **Call to action**: subscribe, a related video, or your WhatsApp for services.

## 4. Titles, thumbnails and descriptions

- **Title**: clear benefit plus keywords, under ~60 characters.
- **Thumbnail**: a close-up face or the result, 3–5 big words, high contrast (design in Canva, 1280 × 720).
- **Description**: first two lines summarise the video with keywords; add timestamps (chapters), links and contacts.
- **Tags** matter much less than the title, thumbnail and how long people keep watching.

## 5. Consistency and analytics

- Upload on a regular schedule you can keep (e.g. one video a week).
- In **YouTube Studio → Analytics**, watch:
  - **Click-through rate (CTR)**: are thumbnails/titles attracting clicks?
  - **Average view duration / retention**: where do people leave? Improve the hook and pacing.
  - **Traffic sources**: search, suggested videos, external (WhatsApp shares).
- Reply to comments: it builds community and gives you new video ideas.

## 6. Ways to earn

| Income | When |
|---|---|
| **YouTube Partner Program** (ads, memberships) | After meeting YouTube's eligibility thresholds (subscribers and watch hours; check current requirements) |
| **Sponsorships** | Brands pay for mentions once you have an engaged audience in a niche |
| **Affiliate links** | Commission on products you recommend (e.g. Jumia, Amazon, software) |
| **Your own products/services** | Courses, consultancy, design or web services, farm products |
| **Paid training** | Turn your best tutorials into a paid class |

In a niche channel, your own services often earn more than ads.

## Rules and safety

- Use only music and clips you have rights to (YouTube Audio Library is free).
- Don't use misleading thumbnails or titles (clickbait loses trust and viewers).
- Follow YouTube's community guidelines; protect your account with 2-step verification.
- Declare sponsored content.
- Income from YouTube is taxable: keep records.

```quiz
Q: What matters more to viewers at first: great video or clear audio?
A: clear audio | audio | sound
Q: What size in pixels is a YouTube thumbnail? (width x height)
A: 1280 x 720 | 1280x720 | 1280 × 720
Q: What is the opening 10–15 seconds of a video that grabs attention called?
A: hook | the hook
Q: Which YouTube Studio metric shows how many people click after seeing your thumbnail? (three letters)
A: CTR | click-through rate
Q: Which free source provides music you can safely use in videos? (three words)
A: YouTube Audio Library | audio library
```

lessons.title: Blogging and ad income: setting up a blog, writing posts that rank, and monetising
lessons.body:
# Blogging and ad income: setting up a blog, writing posts that rank, and monetising

A blog is a website where you publish helpful articles regularly. Blogs earn through **display ads**, **affiliate links**, **sponsored posts** and selling your own **products and services**. Blogging also builds credibility that wins freelance clients and jobs. It's slow (often 6–12 months before meaningful traffic), and AI-generated search answers are changing how people find content, so success comes from genuinely useful, experience-based writing. This unit covers the full process.

:::note What you will learn
- Is blogging still worth it? Honest pros and cons
- Choosing a niche and blog name
- Platform choices: WordPress (self-hosted), WordPress.com, Blogger, Medium, Substack
- Setting up a self-hosted WordPress blog step by step
- Keyword research and writing posts that rank
- On-page SEO, internal links and images
- Getting traffic beyond Google
- Monetisation: AdSense, affiliates, sponsorships, products
- Legal pages and ethics
:::

## Is blogging worth it?

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Low cost to start | Slow growth (months to years) |
| Builds a long-term asset and authority | Requires consistent writing |
| Multiple income streams | Google algorithm and AI answer changes affect traffic |
| Supports your freelance/business brand | Ad income per visitor can be low for mostly local audiences |

Blogging works best when combined with other income (services, products, YouTube) and when you have real knowledge or experience to share.

## Niche and name

Choose a niche you can write **50+ articles** about, where people search for answers and there's monetisation potential:
- Personal finance in Kenya (SACCOs, MMFs, budgeting)
- Agribusiness and farming guides
- Tech how-tos and reviews
- Education and career guidance (KUCCPS, courses, CVs)
- Travel in Kenya and East Africa
- Health and fitness (with accurate, sourced information)

Name: short, memorable, relevant; check domain availability (`.co.ke`, `.com`, `.ke`).

## Platform choices

| Platform | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **Self-hosted WordPress** (your domain + hosting) | Full control, monetisation freedom, professional | Costs (domain/hosting), you manage updates/security |
| **WordPress.com** | Easy, hosted | Free plan limits; ads/plugins need paid plans |
| **Blogger** | Free, simple, AdSense-friendly | Limited design and features |
| **Medium** | Built-in audience | You don't own the platform; limited monetisation from Kenya |
| **Substack** | Newsletters + blog, paid subscriptions | Platform-dependent |

For a serious blog, **self-hosted WordPress** is the common choice.

## Setting up a WordPress blog (overview)
