1. **Buy a domain** from a registrar and **hosting** (cPanel shared hosting is fine to start).
2. In cPanel, use **Softaculous/WordPress installer** to install WordPress on your domain.
3. Turn on **SSL** (AutoSSL/Let's Encrypt) so the site uses HTTPS.
4. Choose a **lightweight theme** (e.g. GeneratePress, Astra, Kadence, or a block theme).
5. Install essential **plugins**: an SEO plugin (Yoast or Rank Math), caching/speed, security, backups, contact form, Site Kit by Google (connects Search Console and Analytics).
6. Create pages: Home, About, Contact, Privacy Policy, Disclaimer.
7. Set permalinks to **post name** (Settings → Permalinks).
8. Connect **Google Search Console** and submit your sitemap.

(The Hosting subject explains domains, DNS and cPanel in detail.)

## Keyword research

Write what people search for:
1. Brainstorm questions your audience asks.
2. Use Google autocomplete, "People also ask", related searches.
3. Free tools: Google Trends, Ubersuggest/AnswerThePublic free tiers, Search Console (once you have traffic).
4. Target **specific long-tail keywords** ("how to start a poultry business in Kenya with KSh 50,000") rather than broad ones ("poultry").
5. Check **search intent**: do results show guides, lists, product pages? Match the format.

## Writing posts that rank (and help)

- **Answer the question early**, then go deeper.
- **Show experience:** your own photos, examples, costs you actually paid, mistakes you made. Google's guidelines emphasise experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness (E-E-A-T).
- **Structure:** clear H2/H3 headings, short paragraphs, bullets, tables, FAQs.
- **Accuracy:** cite sources (official sites for fees, laws, health information); update posts when things change.
- **Length:** as long as needed to fully answer, without padding.
- **AI tools:** fine for outlines and editing, but unedited AI content without original value tends to perform poorly and can damage trust.

## On-page SEO checklist

- [ ] Keyword in the title, first paragraph, a heading and the URL slug
- [ ] Compelling meta description (150–160 characters)
- [ ] Descriptive headings (H2/H3)
- [ ] Images compressed, with descriptive file names and alt text
- [ ] **Internal links** to related posts; external links to reputable sources
- [ ] Mobile-friendly, fast-loading pages
- [ ] Schema (FAQ/How-to) via the SEO plugin where appropriate

## Traffic beyond Google

- **Pinterest** (for visual niches like food, decor, travel)
- **Facebook groups and pages**, **WhatsApp Channels**, LinkedIn articles
- **Email newsletter** (MailerLite, Brevo): your most reliable audience
- **YouTube** videos linking to detailed blog guides
- Collaborations and guest posts on related blogs

## Monetisation

| Method | How |
|---|---|
| **Google AdSense** | Apply once you have quality content (original, useful posts), clear navigation and required pages; ads earn per view/click; income depends on traffic, niche and audience location |
| **Ad networks** | Premium networks need higher traffic thresholds |
| **Affiliate marketing** | Recommend products with affiliate links (see the affiliate lesson); disclose clearly |
| **Sponsored posts** | Brands pay for reviews/features; label as sponsored |
| **Your products/services** | E-books, templates, courses, consulting, freelance services: often the best earners |

## Legal pages and ethics

- **Privacy policy** (cookies, analytics, ads, email signups; Kenya's Data Protection Act applies to personal data).
- **Affiliate disclosure** and **disclaimer** (especially finance/health).
- Don't copy others' articles or images; respect copyright.
- Don't write misleading reviews for commissions.

:::think A new blogger publishes 50 AI-generated articles in one week on random topics and applies for AdSense. Why might this fail, and what would work better?
Thin, unfocused, unoriginal content offers little value, so it may be rejected by AdSense and rank poorly. Better: choose a niche, publish fewer but genuinely helpful articles with original experience, accurate sources, good structure and internal links, and build traffic gradually.
:::

## Summary

- Blogging is slow but builds a long-term asset; combine it with other income.
- Choose a niche you can write 50+ helpful posts about; self-hosted WordPress gives the most control.
- Set up WordPress with SSL, a light theme, SEO, speed, security and backup plugins, and Search Console.
- Research long-tail keywords and search intent; write experience-rich, accurate, well-structured posts.
- Follow an on-page SEO checklist; build traffic from Pinterest, social media, email and YouTube.
- Monetise with AdSense, affiliates, sponsorships and especially your own products/services; publish legal pages and disclose.

```quiz
Q: Which platform is the common choice for a serious self-hosted blog?
A: WordPress | self-hosted WordPress
Q: Which Google tool should you connect to submit your sitemap? (two words)
A: Search Console | Google Search Console
Q: Are specific long-tail keywords or broad keywords easier for new blogs to rank for?
A: long-tail | long tail
Q: What does the first E in E-E-A-T stand for?
A: Experience
Q: Which Google programme shows display ads on blogs?
A: AdSense | Google AdSense
```

lessons.title: Affiliate marketing step by step: programmes, content that converts, tracking and honest disclosure
lessons.body:
# Affiliate marketing step by step: programmes, content that converts, tracking and honest disclosure

**Affiliate marketing** means recommending someone else's product with a special tracking link. When a person clicks your link and buys (or signs up), the company pays you a **commission**. You don't stock products, deliver anything or handle customer service. Your job is to help people make a good buying decision.

It sounds easy, and that is exactly why most people fail at it: they spam links with no audience and no trust. This unit shows how affiliate marketing actually works, who earns from it, where to find programmes that pay people in Kenya, and the exact process from your first link to steady commissions.

:::note What you will learn
- How affiliate links, cookies and commissions work
- Who uses affiliate marketing and why companies pay for it
- Affiliate programmes available to people in Kenya
- Choosing a niche and the platform for your content
- Content types that convert: reviews, comparisons, tutorials, "best of" lists
- Tracking clicks and calculating earnings
- Disclosure, ethics and mistakes that get accounts banned
:::

## Why companies pay affiliates

Advertising is expensive and uncertain: a company can pay for a billboard and sell nothing. With affiliates, the company pays **only when a sale happens**. That makes affiliates one of the lowest-risk marketing channels, so businesses from global giants to Kenyan online shops run programmes.

| Who | Why they use affiliates |
|---|---|
| **Online stores** (electronics, fashion, books) | Pay per sale, reach new audiences |
| **Software and web hosting companies** | Pay high commissions because a customer stays for years |
| **Online courses and digital products** | No stock cost, so they can share 30–50% |
| **Banks, insurance and investment apps** | Pay per sign-up or funded account (check regulations) |
| **Travel and booking sites** | Pay per booking |

## How it works, step by step

1. You join a programme and get a unique link, e.g. `https://shop.example/product?ref=kelvin123`.
2. A visitor clicks your link. The shop saves a **cookie** (a small note in the browser) with your ID.
3. If the visitor buys within the **cookie window** (often 1–90 days), the sale is credited to you.
4. After the **return/refund period**, the commission is approved.
5. Once you pass the **payment threshold**, the company pays you (bank, PayPal, Payoneer or M-Pesa depending on the programme).

:::define Key terms
- **Commission rate**: percentage or fixed amount you earn per sale (e.g. 5%, or KSh 500 per sign-up).
- **Cookie window**: how long after the click a purchase still counts.
- **Conversion rate**: the share of clickers who buy.
- **EPC (earnings per click)**: total earnings ÷ total clicks. Useful to compare programmes.
- **Payout threshold**: the minimum balance before you are paid.
:::

## Programmes you can join from Kenya

Availability and terms change, so always read the current terms page before you build content around a programme.

| Type | Examples to look up | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Kenyan online shops | Jumia affiliate programme (KOL), other local e-commerce sites | Local products, local payment; commissions vary by category |
| Global marketplaces | Amazon Associates and similar | Best for international audiences; check payment options for your country |
| Web hosting and software | Hosting companies, website builders, VPNs, email tools | Often high one-off or recurring commissions |
| Digital product networks | Selar, Gumroad creators, ClickBank, Digistore24 | Courses and e-books; judge quality before promoting |
| Affiliate networks | Impact, CJ, ShareASale/Awin, PartnerStack | One account, many brands; approval needed |
| Freelance and fintech platforms | Referral programmes of tools you already use | Sometimes pay per sign-up; check the rules |

:::warning Check before you promote
Avoid "affiliate" schemes where you earn mainly by recruiting people who pay to join. That is a pyramid structure, not affiliate marketing. Real programmes are free to join and pay you for customers' purchases.
:::

## Step 1: Pick a niche and an audience

Affiliate income follows **buying intent**. Someone searching "best laptop for campus students under KSh 50,000" is ready to buy; someone watching a dance video is not. Pick a niche where people research purchases:

- Phones, laptops and gadgets for students
- Home and kitchen appliances
- Farming equipment and inputs
- Web hosting, website tools and online business software
- Books, courses and learning resources
- Baby products, fitness gear, beauty products

Choose something you understand or will genuinely test. Your experience is what makes people trust your recommendation over a random list.

## Step 2: Choose where your audience lives

| Platform | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| **Blog/website** | Ranks on Google for buying searches for years | Slow to grow |
| **YouTube** | Reviews and comparisons are watched by buyers; links in description | Needs consistent video work |
| **TikTok/Instagram** | Fast reach; "TikTok made me buy it" effect | Short attention, links harder to place |
| **WhatsApp channel / Telegram** | Direct, high trust with local audiences | Easy to become spammy |
| **Email newsletter** | You own the list; strong conversions | Must build the list first |

Start with **one** platform. Most successful affiliates pair a searchable platform (blog or YouTube) with one social platform for reach.

## Step 3: Create content that converts

These formats consistently earn because they answer a buyer's question:

1. **Single product review**: what it is, who it's for, pros, cons, real photos or test results, price, your verdict.
2. **Comparison**: "Tecno vs Infinix vs Samsung under KSh 20,000", with a clear table.
3. **Best-of list**: "7 best budget laptops for programming students in 2026", grouped by need.
4. **Tutorial**: "How to start a blog with [hosting]", where the tool is naturally needed.
5. **Problem → solution**: "My phone storage is always full: 5 fixes", recommending a memory card or cloud plan as one fix.

A review structure that works:

```
Title: [Product] review after 3 months: is it worth KSh X?
1. Quick verdict (2–3 lines + who should buy / who should skip)
2. Key specs table
3. What I liked (with real examples)
4. What I didn't like (be honest)
5. Alternatives (cheaper and better options)
6. Final verdict + link ("Check the current price on ...")
Disclosure line near the top
```

:::tip Honesty sells
Listing real cons and recommending a cheaper alternative when it suits the reader makes your audience trust you. Trusted creators get far more clicks over time than those who praise everything.
:::

## Step 4: Place links well

- Put the link where the decision happens: after the verdict, in comparison tables, and in the first lines of a YouTube description.
- Use clear call-to-action text: "Check today's price on Jumia".
- Use a link shortener or your own redirect (e.g. `yoursite.com/go/laptop-x`) so links are tidy and easy to update when a programme changes.
- Don't hide links behind misleading buttons.

## Step 5: Track and calculate

Most dashboards show clicks, orders and commission. Keep your own simple sheet too:

| Content | Clicks | Sales | Commission (KSh) | EPC (KSh) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Budget phones video | 400 | 12 | 8,640 | 21.6 |
| Laptop blog post | 150 | 3 | 4,500 | 30.0 |

Example calculation: a video gets 20,000 views. 2% click (400 clicks). 3% of clickers buy (12 sales). Average price KSh 18,000, commission 4%:

12 × 18,000 × 0.04 = **KSh 8,640**.

The same formula tells you what to improve: more views, a better click rate (clearer call to action) or a better conversion rate (better-matched products).

:::think You have 1,000 clicks on a link. Programme A pays 3% on a KSh 30,000 product with a 2% conversion rate. Programme B pays 30% on a KSh 2,000 e-book with a 5% conversion rate. Which earns more?
A: 1,000 × 0.02 = 20 sales × 30,000 × 0.03 = KSh 18,000. B: 1,000 × 0.05 = 50 sales × 2,000 × 0.30 = KSh 30,000. B earns more here, which is why you compare EPC, not just commission rate.
:::

## Disclosure and the rules

- **Always disclose**: "Some links on this page are affiliate links. If you buy through them I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you." Put it near the top, not hidden at the bottom.
- Follow each programme's rules: many forbid using their brand name in paid ads, self-purchases, cookie stuffing or posting links in private messages to strangers.
- Platforms (YouTube, Instagram) have "paid partnership" or disclosure settings; use them.
- Never invent results, fake reviews or fake scarcity ("only 2 left!") you can't verify.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Posting bare links in Facebook groups | Build content people seek out; groups often ban spam |
| Promoting 50 random products | Focus on one niche and a few products you trust |
| No disclosure | Disclose clearly every time |
| Ignoring refunds and cookie windows | Read terms; expect pending earnings to drop slightly |
| Only one programme | Diversify so one policy change doesn't wipe out income |

## Summary

- Affiliates earn a commission when their referral buys; companies like it because they pay only for results.
- The process: join → get link → visitor clicks (cookie) → buys within the window → commission approved → paid at threshold.
- Pick a buying-intent niche and one main platform; reviews, comparisons, best-of lists and tutorials convert best.
- Track clicks, sales and EPC; compare programmes by EPC, not just rate.
- Disclose every time, follow programme rules, and avoid pay-to-join recruitment schemes.

```quiz
Q: What do you earn when someone buys through your affiliate link?
A: commission | a commission
Q: Should you tell your audience that a link is an affiliate link? (yes/no)
A: yes
Q: 1,000 clicks, 2% buy a KSh 10,000 product at 5% commission. How much do you earn (KSh)?
A: 1000 | 1,000 | ksh 1000
H: 1,000 × 0.02 = 20 sales; 20 × 10,000 × 0.05.
Q: What is the name for how long after a click a purchase still counts? (two words)
A: cookie window | cookie duration | cookie period
Q: What does EPC stand for?
A: earnings per click
Q: A scheme pays you mainly for recruiting people who pay to join. Is that real affiliate marketing? (yes/no)
A: no
```

lessons.title: Sell digital products: e-books, templates, courses and printables, from idea to M-Pesa payment
lessons.body:
# Sell digital products: e-books, templates, courses and printables, from idea to M-Pesa payment

A **digital product** is something you create once and sell many times as a file or online access: an e-book, a CV template, an Excel budget planner, a course, a set of design assets, a revision pack. There's no stock, no delivery rider and no limit on how many copies you can sell. That is why creators love them.

The catch: making the product is the easy part. Finding buyers who trust you enough to pay is the real work. This unit walks you through the whole process, from validating an idea to getting paid by M-Pesa and card.

:::note What you will learn
- Types of digital products and who buys them
- Finding and validating an idea before you build it
- Creating the product with free tools
- Pricing, bundles and launch offers
- Platforms to sell on from Kenya (Selar, Gumroad, Payhip, your own site)
- Delivering files securely and handling refunds
- Marketing: audience first, then sales
- Copyright, honesty and legal basics
:::

## Types of digital products

| Product | Example | Tools to make it |
|---|---|---|
| **E-book / guide** | "How to start poultry farming in Kenya with KSh 50,000" | Google Docs, Canva, Word → PDF |
| **Templates** | CV and cover letter templates, invoice templates, social media templates | Canva, Word, Google Docs |
| **Spreadsheets** | Budget planner, chama tracker, school fees tracker, inventory | Excel, Google Sheets |
| **Printables** | Kids' worksheets, planners, wall art, wedding cards | Canva, Inkscape |
| **Online course** | "Excel for office jobs" video course | Phone/screen recorder, OBS, CapCut |
| **Revision materials** | KCSE/CBC notes, past paper solutions you wrote | Word, Canva, scanner |
| **Design assets** | Logo packs, Lightroom presets, fonts, icons, mockups | Figma, Photoshop/Photopea |
| **Code** | Website templates, WordPress themes, scripts | Your code editor |
| **Audio/music** | Beats, sound effects, meditation audio | Audacity, DAWs |

## Who buys digital products?

People pay to **save time**, **avoid mistakes** or **get a result faster**:
- Job seekers (CV templates, interview guides)
- Small business owners (invoice templates, marketing calendars, stock trackers)
- Students and parents (revision notes, worksheets)
- Farmers and aspiring entrepreneurs (business plans, step-by-step guides)
- Designers and creators (presets, templates, mockups)

## Step 1: Find and validate an idea

Never spend two months building something nobody wants. Validate first:

1. **List problems you can solve.** What do people ask you for help with? What have you learned the hard way?
2. **Look for demand signals**: questions repeated in Facebook groups, TikTok comments, Reddit, Google "People also ask", and products already selling on Etsy, Gumroad or Selar (competition proves demand).
3. **Make a small test**: post a free tip or a mini-version and see who engages.
4. **Pre-sell**: "I'm making a complete Excel chama tracker. Early price KSh 300 until Friday." If people pay, build it. If nobody does, you saved weeks.

:::tip The "one painful problem" rule
"How to cook" is too broad. "30 cheap healthy lunches for campus students under KSh 150 each" is a specific problem with a clear buyer.
:::

## Step 2: Create the product

- **Outline first**: list the outcome, then the steps to get there. Each step becomes a chapter, module or sheet.
- **Make it practical**: checklists, examples, screenshots, worked numbers, templates the buyer fills in.
- **Design for readability**: big headings, short paragraphs, consistent fonts and colours. Canva has free e-book and workbook layouts.
- **Test it**: give it to 2–3 people from your audience and fix anything confusing.
- **Export properly**: PDF for e-books, `.xlsx` with locked formula cells for spreadsheets, editable Canva template links for templates, MP4 for videos.

For a course, keep videos short (5–12 minutes), show the screen, and give a downloadable workbook. Good audio matters more than camera quality: a cheap clip-on microphone makes a huge difference.

## Step 3: Price it

| Product | Typical Kenyan audience price | International audience |
|---|---|---|
| Single template | KSh 100–500 | $5–15 |
| E-book / guide | KSh 300–1,500 | $10–30 |
| Spreadsheet system | KSh 500–2,000 | $15–40 |
| Video course | KSh 1,500–10,000 | $30–200+ |

These are rough ranges, not rules. Pricing tactics:
- **Bundles**: CV template + cover letter + interview guide for less than separately.
- **Tiers**: Basic (e-book), Standard (+ templates), Premium (+ a 30-minute call).
- **Launch discount** with a real deadline.
- Price by **value of the result**, not by page count.

## Step 4: Choose where to sell

| Platform | Payments | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **Selar** | Card, mobile money including M-Pesa (check current options), payouts to local accounts | African creators selling to local and global buyers |
| **Gumroad / Payhip / Lemon Squeezy** | Cards, PayPal; payouts depend on country support | Global audiences |
| **Etsy** | Cards; check seller country support | Printables and templates for international buyers |
| **Your own website** | M-Pesa (Daraja API / payment gateway), card gateways | Full control, no marketplace fee |
| **WhatsApp + manual M-Pesa** | Buyer pays Till/Paybill, you send the file | Starting out with very small volumes |

:::warning Manual selling doesn't scale
Sending files by hand after confirming each M-Pesa message works for your first 20 sales, but it's slow and error-prone. Move to a platform that delivers automatically once you have regular sales.
:::

## Step 5: Deliver and protect

- Platforms deliver a download link automatically after payment.
- Add your name/website on every page so shared copies still advertise you.
- Expect some piracy; don't waste energy fighting it. Focus on updates, support and community, which pirates don't get.
- Write a clear refund policy (e.g. refunds within 7 days if the file is faulty or not as described).

## Step 6: Market it

The best digital product sellers **build an audience first**:
- Post free, useful content daily on one platform (TikTok, YouTube, LinkedIn, X or Facebook).
- Give away a **free lead magnet** (a mini checklist) in exchange for an email or WhatsApp channel follow.
- Share testimonials and results from buyers (with permission).
- Write a sales page: problem → promise → what's inside → who it's for → price → guarantee → FAQ → buy button.
- Run affiliate deals: let others promote your product for a commission.

A simple sales page outline:

```
Headline: Track your chama's contributions, loans and fines in 10 minutes a month
Problem: Lost notebooks, arguments over who paid
What's inside: 5 sheets, auto-calculated balances, loan interest, printable statements
Who it's for: chama treasurers and members
Bonus: video walkthrough
Price: KSh 800 (launch price until 15th)
Guarantee: 7-day refund if it doesn't work for you
FAQ: Does it work on phone? (Yes, Google Sheets)
[Buy now]
```

## Legal and ethical basics

- Only sell what **you created** or have rights to. Reselling KNEC papers, copyrighted textbooks or "PLR" content you didn't check can get you banned or sued.
- Don't promise income results you can't back up ("make KSh 100k in a week").
- Keep records of sales for tax (see the taxes lesson).

:::think A creator spends three months recording a 40-video course on "everything about computers", launches it, and sells two copies. What went wrong, and what should they have done?
The topic was too broad, it wasn't validated, and there was no audience. They should have picked one specific problem (e.g. "Excel for office job interviews"), tested demand with free content, pre-sold to a small group, then built the course with buyers' feedback.
:::

## Summary

- Digital products are made once and sold many times: e-books, templates, spreadsheets, courses, printables, assets.
- Validate before building: find a specific painful problem, look for demand, pre-sell.
- Create practical, well-designed products with free tools, and test them on real users.
- Price by the value of the result, use bundles and tiers, and sell on Selar, Gumroad, Etsy or your own site.
- Build an audience with free content and lead magnets; sell only what you own the rights to.

```quiz
Q: What is selling a product to buyers before you finish making it called? (one word, hyphenated)
A: pre-selling | presell | pre-sell | preselling
Q: What free item do you give away to collect emails or followers? (two words)
A: lead magnet | a lead magnet
Q: Should you price a digital product by page count or by the value of the result?
A: value | the value of the result | value of the result
Q: Can you legally sell copies of a copyrighted textbook you bought? (yes/no)
A: no
Q: Name a platform popular with African creators that supports local payment options.
A: Selar
```

lessons.title: Sell physical products online: sourcing, pricing, shop setup, payments and delivery in Kenya
lessons.body:
# Sell physical products online: sourcing, pricing, shop setup, payments and delivery in Kenya

Selling physical products online is the most familiar kind of online business in Kenya: clothes on Instagram, phone accessories on TikTok, cosmetics on WhatsApp, electronics on Jumia. It works because people already buy this way. It is also a real business with stock, cash flow, delivery and returns, so this unit treats it seriously: from choosing a product to getting it to the customer's door.

:::note What you will learn
- Business models: own stock, made-to-order, marketplace selling, dropshipping
- Choosing products that sell and make a profit
- Sourcing locally (Gikomba, Eastleigh, wholesalers) and importing
- Calculating cost, margin and price correctly
- Where to sell: social media, WhatsApp Business, marketplaces, your own store
- Payments: M-Pesa Till/Paybill, pay on delivery, cards
- Delivery and logistics across Kenya
- Customer service, returns, legal registration and records
:::

## Business models

| Model | How it works | Capital | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Own stock** | Buy goods, store them, sell | Medium–high | Unsold stock |
| **Made-to-order** | You make items after an order (tailoring, baking, crafts, printing) | Low | Time and skill |
| **Marketplace seller** | List on Jumia, Kilimall and similar; they handle traffic (and sometimes delivery) | Medium | Fees, competition |
| **Dropshipping / supplier delivery** | Supplier holds stock and ships when you sell | Low | Little control over quality and speed |
| **Pre-orders / group buying** | Collect orders and deposits, then import in bulk | Low–medium | Delays upset customers |

## Step 1: Choose a product

A good product to sell online:
- Solves a problem or fits a clear desire (looks, convenience, status, gifts)
- Is **light and hard to break** (cheaper delivery, fewer returns)
- Has a margin of at least **30–50%** after all costs
- Isn't sold everywhere at the same price
- Photographs and films well

Examples that often work: phone accessories, fashion for a specific style or size, beauty and hair products, baby items, home organisers, kitchen gadgets, fitness gear, branded merchandise, school supplies before term opens.

:::warning Avoid regulated or risky products at the start
Medicines, supplements with health claims, alcohol, counterfeit brands, cosmetics with banned ingredients and electrical goods without standards marks can bring KEBS/PPB/county problems. Start with simple, legal goods.
:::

## Step 2: Source your stock

| Source | Good for | Tips |
|---|---|---|
| **Gikomba, Eastleigh, Nairobi CBD wholesalers** | Clothes, shoes, accessories, household goods | Compare 3+ suppliers, buy samples, build relationships |
| **Local manufacturers and artisans** | Bags, sandals, soaps, crafts | Unique products, made-in-Kenya story |
| **Importing (China, Turkey, Dubai)** | Electronics accessories, gadgets, fashion | Use reputable shipping agents; include duty and VAT in cost; start small |
| **Farmers and producers** | Food products (honey, nuts, spices) | Packaging, labelling and standards matter |

Order a **small test batch** first. Sell it, learn what customers ask for, then reorder.

## Step 3: Price correctly

Most beginners lose money because they forget costs. Calculate the **landed cost** of one unit:

| Cost item | Example (KSh) |
|---|---|
| Buying price | 400 |
| Transport/shipping to you (share per unit) | 50 |
| Packaging | 20 |
| Marketing (ads ÷ units sold) | 80 |
| Payment fees and losses | 10 |
| **Total cost per unit** | **560** |

If you sell at KSh 1,000, your profit is 1,000 − 560 = KSh 440, a margin of 44%.

```try-python
cost = 400 + 50 + 20 + 80 + 10
price = 1000
profit = price - cost
margin = profit / price * 100
print("Cost per unit:", cost)
print("Profit per unit:", profit)
print("Margin: %.0f%%" % margin)
# How many units to sell to earn KSh 30,000 profit a month?
print("Units needed for 30,000 profit:", -(-30000 // profit))
```

Delivery is usually charged separately to the customer, but if you offer "free delivery", add it to your costs.

## Step 4: Set up where you sell

1. **WhatsApp Business**: business profile, catalogue with prices and photos, quick replies, labels for "new order", "paid", "delivered".
2. **Instagram / TikTok / Facebook**: post products in use, behind the scenes, customer reviews, short videos; link to WhatsApp or your store. TikTok Shop and Facebook/Instagram shops have country restrictions, so check what is available in Kenya.
3. **Marketplaces (Jumia, Kilimall and others)**: register as a seller, upload products with good photos and descriptions; you pay commissions but get ready-made traffic.
4. **Your own online store**: WordPress + WooCommerce, Shopify, or a custom site with M-Pesa checkout. This builds your brand and you own the customer relationship.

Product photo checklist: natural daylight, plain background, several angles, the product in use, size comparison, and a short video.

A product description that sells:

```
Title: Women's leather-look tote bag (large, laptop fits) – Black
- Fits a 15.6" laptop, files and lunch box
- Strong zip, inner pocket for phone and keys
- Size: 40 × 30 × 12 cm
- Price: KSh 2,500 | Nairobi delivery KSh 200 | Countrywide via courier
- Pay: M-Pesa Till 123456 or pay on delivery (Nairobi)
- Exchange within 3 days if faulty
```

## Step 5: Take payments

| Method | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **M-Pesa Till (Buy Goods)** | Customers trust it, instant | Must confirm each payment |
| **M-Pesa Paybill** | Account numbers help track orders | Setup paperwork |
| **Pay on delivery** | Builds trust with new customers | Fake orders, rider waiting time |
| **Card/online checkout** | Automatic, works on websites | Gateway fees, setup |

:::tip Reduce fake orders
For pay-on-delivery, confirm orders by phone, ask for a small delivery deposit for far locations, and keep a list of numbers that refused deliveries.
:::

## Step 6: Deliver

- **Nairobi**: boda-boda riders, delivery apps and courier companies; agree a fixed price per zone.
- **Countrywide**: bus/shuttle parcel services, courier companies and pick-up point networks; share the tracking or receipt photo with the customer.
- Package well: waterproof bag, the item wrapped, a thank-you note and your social handles.

## Step 7: Customer service and returns

- Reply quickly (within an hour during business hours).
- Have a clear exchange/return policy and stick to it.
- Ask happy customers for a review or photo; it's your best marketing.
- Track repeat customers and offer them early access to new stock.

## Legal and records

- Register a **business name** on eCitizen (Business Registration Service) when you grow; get a **KRA PIN** and check whether you need a county **business permit**.
- Keep a sales and expenses record (a simple Excel or Google Sheet): date, item, quantity, price, cost, customer, payment reference.
- Learn about turnover tax and eTIMS invoicing requirements in the taxes lesson.

:::think You sell a phone case at KSh 500. It costs you KSh 250 to buy, KSh 30 packaging, and you spend KSh 3,000 on ads that bring 20 sales. Are you making money?
Ads per unit = 3,000 ÷ 20 = KSh 150. Total cost = 250 + 30 + 150 = KSh 430. Profit = 500 − 430 = KSh 70 per case (14%). It's barely profitable: raise the price, bundle (case + screen protector), or improve ads so they bring more sales per shilling.
:::

## Summary

- Choose a model (own stock, made-to-order, marketplace, supplier delivery, pre-orders) that fits your capital and risk.
- Pick light, legal products with 30–50% margin; test with small batches.
- Always calculate total cost per unit (buying, transport, packaging, ads, fees) before pricing.
- Sell through WhatsApp Business, social media, marketplaces and eventually your own store.
- Offer trusted payments (M-Pesa, pay on delivery), reliable delivery, great service and clear returns; register and keep records as you grow.

```quiz
Q: A product costs KSh 600 in total and sells for KSh 1,000. What is the profit margin in percent?
A: 40 | 40% | 40 percent
H: Profit 400 ÷ price 1,000 × 100.
Q: Which free app lets you add a product catalogue and quick replies for your shop? (two words)
A: WhatsApp Business
Q: Before a big order, should you buy a small test batch? (yes/no)
A: yes
Q: Where do you register a business name in Kenya online?
A: eCitizen | ecitizen | business registration service | BRS
Q: You spend KSh 2,000 on ads and get 10 sales. What is the ad cost per sale (KSh)?
A: 200 | ksh 200
```

lessons.title: E-commerce and dropshipping in Kenya
lessons.body:
# E-commerce and dropshipping in Kenya

Selling online in Kenya has never been easier: customers already pay with **M-Pesa**, order on **WhatsApp** and **Instagram**, and couriers deliver countrywide. This lesson lists the platforms, explains dropshipping honestly, and walks you through delivery, payment and the numbers.

## Where to sell

| Channel | What it is | Good for | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| [WhatsApp Business](https://business.whatsapp.com) | Free app with a product catalogue, quick replies and labels | Every seller, especially to start | Free |
| [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com) and [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com) shops | Product posts, reels and shop tabs | Fashion, beauty, food, décor | Free (ads optional) |
| [TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com) | Short videos that sell products | Trendy, visual products | Free (ads optional) |
| [Jumia Kenya](https://www.jumia.co.ke) | Kenya's largest online marketplace: list products, Jumia handles checkout and delivery | Electronics, fashion, home goods | Commission per sale + fees |
| [Kilimall](https://www.kilimall.co.ke) | Online marketplace in Kenya | Similar to Jumia | Commission per sale |
| [Jiji Kenya](https://jiji.co.ke) | Classified ads (like an online market) | Second-hand, cars, phones, property, furniture | Free listings; paid boosts |
| Your own website | Your brand and your rules: WooCommerce, Shopify or custom with M-Pesa | Growing brands | Hosting + domain (+ app fees) |
| [Shopify](https://www.shopify.com) | Hosted online shop builder | Brands that want a quick professional shop | Monthly subscription |
| [WooCommerce](https://woocommerce.com) | Free shop plugin for WordPress | Full control, low monthly cost | Hosting + plugins |

**Start where your customers already are** (WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok), then add a website when you have steady sales and want to look bigger and take payments automatically.

## Payments

| Method | How |
|---|---|
| **M-Pesa Till (Buy Goods)** | Apply through Safaricom (Lipa na M-Pesa). Customers pay your till number. |
| **M-Pesa Paybill** | Account numbers per order; good for businesses and websites. |
| **STK push on your website** | The customer gets a PIN prompt on their phone; needs the Daraja API. See [How to add M-Pesa payments to your website](../how-to-add-mpesa-payments-to-your-website). |
| [Paystack](https://paystack.com/ke) | Cards and M-Pesa through one checkout for websites |
| Cash on delivery | Builds trust with new customers, but risk of fake orders; ask for a small deposit for far deliveries |

Never send goods before confirming the money **in your own M-Pesa messages** (fake "payment confirmation" SMS are a common scam).

## Delivery options

| Option | Use |
|---|---|
| **Boda riders** you trust | Same-day delivery in town |
| [Pickup Mtaani](https://pickupmtaani.com) | Cheap pickup points and agents around Kenya |
| [G4S Courier](https://www.g4s.com) / Fargo Courier | Countrywide parcels |
| Bus and shuttle parcels (Easy Coach, Modern Coast, matatu saccos) | Cheap upcountry delivery |
| [Posta Kenya](https://www.posta.co.ke) | Countrywide postal and EMS services |
| Marketplace logistics | Jumia and Kilimall deliver for their sellers |

## Dropshipping, explained honestly

**Dropshipping** means you sell products you don't keep in stock: when a customer orders, your supplier sends it directly to them. You earn the difference between your price and the supplier's price.

| Type | How it works in Kenya | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **International** (AliExpress, Alibaba, CJ Dropshipping) | Supplier in China ships to the customer | Long delivery (weeks), customs duties and delays, returns are hard. Kenyan customers rarely accept waiting. |
| **Local dropshipping** | Partner with a wholesaler in Nairobi (Luthuli Avenue, Eastleigh, Gikomba, Industrial Area) who packs and sends orders you bring | You need a reliable supplier and clear agreement on stock, prices and who pays for returns. |
| **Import and hold small stock** | Buy small quantities (from local wholesalers or import via consolidators) and deliver yourself | Needs capital, but delivery is fast and you control quality. |

Most successful Kenyan "dropshippers" actually do **local dropshipping or small-stock selling**: they market on TikTok/Instagram, collect orders and payment, and a nearby supplier or rider delivers the same or next day.

## Know your numbers (example)

| Item | KSh |
|---|---|
| Selling price of a phone holder | 1,200 |
| Supplier cost | − 450 |
| Delivery you pay (free delivery offer) | − 250 |
| Ads spent per sale (TikTok/Facebook) | − 200 |
| M-Pesa and packaging | − 50 |
| **Profit per sale** | **250** |

If ads cost more than KSh 450 per sale, you lose money even though "sales are coming in". Track **cost per sale** every week. (Practise these sums in the **Excel** subject.)

## Legal and trust basics

- **Register a business name** on eCitizen (Business Registration Service) when you grow; get a **KRA PIN** and understand Turnover Tax.
- **Clear return policy** (for example, 7 days for faulty items) builds trust.
- **Real photos and videos** of your actual products beat stock images.
- **Don't sell counterfeits** or restricted goods: marketplaces ban sellers, and it's illegal.
- **Respond fast**: WhatsApp quick replies, opening hours, and delivery updates.

## Your first 30 days

1. Pick **one product category** you understand and can source reliably.
2. Set up **WhatsApp Business** (catalogue, greeting message, labels) and one social account.
3. Post **daily**: product videos, customer reviews, how-to-use clips.
4. Get your first 10 sales from friends, family and local groups; ask each for a review.
5. Track every sale, cost and profit in a spreadsheet. Only then try paid ads.

```quiz
Q: What is selling products you don't keep, where the supplier sends directly to the customer, called?
A: dropshipping
Q: Which is Kenya's largest online marketplace for vendors?
A: Jumia | Jumia Kenya
Q: Which free app gives you a product catalogue and quick replies for selling?
A: WhatsApp Business
Q: A product sells for 1,000. Supplier 400, delivery 200, ads 150, packaging 50. What is the profit in KSh?
A: 200
Q: Before sending goods, where should you confirm the payment?
A: in your own M-Pesa messages | your M-Pesa | own M-Pesa messages | M-Pesa statement
Q: Where do you register a business name in Kenya online?
A: eCitizen | BRS | Business Registration Service
```

lessons.title: Social media management as a service: skills, packages, content calendars, clients and reports
lessons.body:
# Social media management as a service: skills, packages, content calendars, clients and reports

Almost every business in Kenya knows it should be on social media: the salon, the school, the hardware shop, the restaurant, the law firm, the church. Most owners don't have time to post consistently, design graphics, reply to comments or understand what's working. A **social media manager** does this for them for a monthly fee. It's one of the most accessible online services to start: you need a smartphone, a laptop helps, and the skills can be learned free.

:::note What you will learn
- What a social media manager actually does each week
- Skills and free tools you need
- Building a portfolio before your first client
- Packages and pricing (with examples)
- Finding clients locally and online
- Onboarding a client and planning a content calendar
- Creating, scheduling and engaging
- Running basic paid ads
- Monthly reports that keep clients paying
:::

## What the job involves

| Task | Example |
|---|---|
| **Strategy** | Decide goals (more bookings, more WhatsApp enquiries), audience, platforms and content themes |
| **Content creation** | Graphics in Canva, short videos, captions, carousels, stories |
| **Scheduling** | Plan a month of posts and schedule them in Meta Business Suite or other tools |
| **Community management** | Reply to comments and DMs, hide spam, pass leads to the client |
| **Paid ads** | Run boosts or Ads Manager campaigns with the client's budget |
| **Reporting** | Monthly results: reach, followers, engagement, messages, sales leads |

## Skills and tools

- **Writing** short, clear captions in English, Swahili or Sheng depending on the audience.
- **Basic design**: Canva (templates, brand kit, resizing), CapCut for video editing.
- **Platform knowledge**: Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, X, YouTube Shorts; each has different formats.
- **Planning**: Google Sheets or Notion for a content calendar.
- **Scheduling**: Meta Business Suite (free for Facebook and Instagram), TikTok's built-in scheduler, other tools with free tiers.
- **Analytics**: platform insights, Google Analytics if the client has a website.
- **Free learning**: Meta Blueprint, Google Digital Garage, HubSpot Academy social media courses, Ajira Digital training.

## Step 1: Build a portfolio before clients

Clients want proof. Create it:
1. Run your own page about a topic and grow it for 30 days.
2. Create **3 sample content packs** for imaginary or real local businesses (a café, a salon, a school): 9 posts each with captions.
3. Offer one or two businesses a **2-week free or discounted trial** in return for a testimonial and permission to show results.
4. Put everything in a simple portfolio: a Canva PDF, a Behance page or a page on your website.

## Step 2: Packages and pricing

Sell monthly **packages**, not "per post", so income is predictable.

| Package | Includes | Example price (Kenyan SMEs) |
|---|---|---|
| **Starter** | 1 platform, 12 posts/month, captions, scheduling | KSh 8,000–15,000 |
| **Growth** | 2 platforms, 16–20 posts, 4 short videos, comment replies | KSh 15,000–35,000 |
| **Premium** | 3 platforms, daily posting, videos, DM handling, ads management, report | KSh 35,000–80,000+ |

Prices vary hugely by client size and city; international clients often pay more. **Ad spend is separate** from your fee: the client pays Meta/TikTok directly or gives you a budget.

:::tip Always write a scope
List exactly what's included (number of posts, platforms, revisions, response hours). Extra requests ("can you also design our menu?") are charged separately.
:::

## Step 3: Find clients

- **Walk in locally**: businesses near you with inactive or messy pages. Show them a mock-up of 3 posts for their brand.
- **Your network**: tell friends, family, church and chama members what you do.
- **LinkedIn and Facebook groups** for business owners.
- **Freelance platforms**: Upwork, Fiverr ("social media manager", "Instagram content"), and local job boards.
- **Partner** with web designers, photographers and branding agencies who need someone for social media.

A cold message template:

```
Hi [Name], I came across [Business] on Instagram – your [product/service] looks great.
I noticed the page hasn't posted since [month]. I help local businesses post consistently
and turn followers into WhatsApp enquiries. I made 3 sample posts for you (attached).
Would you be open to a 10-minute call this week to see if a monthly plan would help?
– [Your name], [portfolio link]
```

## Step 4: Onboard a new client

1. **Contract and deposit**: sign a simple agreement; take the first month's fee upfront.
2. **Access**: ask to be added as a partner/admin in Meta Business Suite rather than getting passwords. Never ask for or store their personal passwords if a role-based option exists.
3. **Brand kit**: logo, colours, fonts, tone of voice, photos, products and prices, FAQs.
4. **Goals**: what does success look like? More calls? More visits? Choose 2–3 measurable goals.
5. **Audit**: current followers, best and worst posts, competitors, what's missing.

## Step 5: Plan the content calendar

Use content **pillars** (repeating themes) so you never run out of ideas. For a salon:

| Pillar | Example posts |
|---|---|
| Showcase | Before/after hairstyles, new braids styles |
| Education | How to care for locs, best products for natural hair |
| Social proof | Client reviews, stylist of the month |
| Offers | Tuesday discount, back-to-school package |
| Behind the scenes | Team, setup, day in the salon |

A monthly calendar in a sheet: Date | Platform | Pillar | Format (reel, carousel, image, story) | Caption | Visual link | Status (draft, approved, scheduled, posted).

Send the month's plan for **approval** a week before it starts.

## Step 6: Create, schedule and engage

- Batch-create content: shoot videos on one day, design graphics on another.
- Write captions with a hook, value, and a call to action: "Book on WhatsApp: 07xx…".
- Schedule in Meta Business Suite; post TikToks natively.
- Check comments and messages daily (agree response hours in the contract). Pass enquiries to the client quickly; leads are what they pay for.

## Step 7: Basic paid ads

- Start with a clear goal: messages, website visits or calls.
- Target by location (e.g. 5 km around the shop), age and interests.
- Test 2–3 creatives with a small daily budget, keep the best performer.
- Track cost per message or cost per lead, not just likes.

## Step 8: Report monthly

A one-page report keeps clients renewing:
- Posts published vs planned
- Reach and impressions, follower growth
- Engagement (likes, comments, shares, saves)
- Messages/enquiries and, if known, sales
- Top 3 posts and why they worked
- Plan for next month

:::think A client says "we're paying you but sales haven't increased" after two months. What should you have done from the start, and what do you do now?
Agree measurable goals and how leads are tracked (e.g. a WhatsApp link, "mention this post" offers). Now: review the report together, show enquiries generated, check whether the client is responding to leads quickly, and adjust content and ads toward offers and calls to action.
:::

## Summary

- Social media managers plan, create, schedule, engage, run ads and report for businesses.
- Learn Canva, CapCut, Meta Business Suite and platform insights; free courses exist.
- Build a portfolio with your own page, sample packs and trial clients.
- Sell monthly packages with a written scope; ad spend is separate.
- Onboard with a contract, deposit and role-based access; plan with content pillars and a calendar; report results monthly.

```quiz
Q: What free Meta tool schedules posts for Facebook and Instagram? (three words)
A: Meta Business Suite | business suite
Q: What are the repeating content themes in a calendar called? (two words)
A: content pillars | pillars
Q: Is ad spend usually included in your management fee or separate?
A: separate
Q: Should you get client access through roles or by asking for their personal password?
A: roles | role | partner access | admin role
Q: What should you take before starting a client's first month?
A: deposit | a deposit | payment | upfront payment
```

lessons.title: Remote jobs from Kenya: roles, job boards, CVs, interviews, contracts and working well remotely
lessons.body:
# Remote jobs from Kenya: roles, job boards, CVs, interviews, contracts and working well remotely

Freelancing means many short projects for different clients. A **remote job** is different: one employer, regular hours or tasks, and a monthly salary or contract fee, but you work from home or a co-working space instead of an office. Kenyans work remotely for local companies, regional firms and international companies in support, sales, tech, content, finance and operations.

Remote jobs are competitive because one posting can receive thousands of applicants from around the world. This unit shows what roles exist, where to find them, how to apply so you stand out, and how to avoid fake "remote job" scams.

:::note What you will learn
- Types of remote roles and the skills each needs
- Fully remote vs hybrid; employee vs contractor
- Where to find legitimate remote jobs
- A remote-ready CV, LinkedIn and portfolio
- Applications and interviews (including video and tests)
- Contracts, payment and tax basics
- Your home setup: internet, power backup and tools
- Remote work habits that get you promoted
- Spotting fake job offers
:::

## Common remote roles

| Field | Roles | Key skills |
|---|---|---|
| **Customer support** | Chat/email support agent, help desk, customer success | Clear writing, patience, typing speed, CRM tools |
| **Sales and marketing** | SDR (sales development), social media, SEO, email marketing | Communication, persuasion, analytics |
| **Admin and operations** | Virtual assistant, executive assistant, project coordinator | Organisation, Google Workspace, scheduling |
| **Content** | Writer, editor, video editor, designer | Portfolio, tools (Canva, Adobe, CapCut) |
| **Tech** | Developer, QA tester, data analyst, IT support, DevOps | Technical skills, GitHub, problem solving |
| **Finance** | Bookkeeper, accounts assistant | Excel, QuickBooks/Xero, accuracy |
| **AI and data** | Data annotation, AI trainer, content evaluator | Attention to detail, subject knowledge |
| **Education** | Online tutor, curriculum writer | Subject expertise, teaching skills |

## Employee vs contractor

| | Employee (local or via an employer of record) | Contractor |
|---|---|---|
| Pay | Salary, often with PAYE deducted | Invoice the company; you handle tax |
| Benefits | May include leave, health cover, pension | Usually none; build your own |
| Stability | Notice periods, labour protections | Can end quickly |
| Paperwork | Employment contract | Contractor agreement |

Many international companies hire Kenyans as contractors or through **employer-of-record** services (companies like Deel or Remote that legally employ you on their behalf). Read the contract carefully either way.

## Where to find remote jobs

- **LinkedIn Jobs**: filter by "Remote" and location "Kenya" or "Africa"; follow companies that hire in Africa.
- **Remote job boards**: We Work Remotely, Remote OK, Remotive, Working Nomads, JustRemote, FlexJobs (paid). Check whether a posting says "worldwide" or limits countries.
- **Africa-focused**: companies and boards that hire across Africa; Kenyan job sites (BrighterMonday, MyJobMag, Fuzu) with remote filters.
- **Company career pages**: many remote-first companies list "work from anywhere" roles.
- **Communities**: Twitter/X, Slack and Discord tech communities, Ajira Digital clubs, alumni networks.
- **Referrals**: most hires still come through people. Tell your network exactly what role you want.

:::tip Search smarter
Use searches like `"remote" "Africa" customer support` or `"EMEA" remote support Kenya`. "EMEA" roles (Europe, Middle East, Africa) often accept Kenyan applicants because the time zone matches Europe.
:::

## Step 1: A remote-ready CV

- **One to two pages**, clean layout, no photo needed for most international roles.
- At the top: name, role title ("Customer Support Specialist"), email, phone, LinkedIn, portfolio, "Nairobi, Kenya (EAT, UTC+3)".
- Bullet achievements with numbers: "Resolved 60+ chats daily with 95% satisfaction" beats "Responsible for customer care".
- Mention remote skills: Slack, Zoom, Google Workspace, Notion, Trello/Asana, Zendesk/Freshdesk, async communication.
- Tailor keywords to each job description; many companies use applicant tracking systems (ATS) that scan for them.

## Step 2: LinkedIn and portfolio

- Professional photo, headline that states the role you want and your key skill.
- An "About" section in first person: what you do, results, tools, availability.
- Turn on **Open to work** (visible to recruiters only if you prefer).
- Post occasionally about what you're learning or building.
- A portfolio for creative and tech roles (website, GitHub, Behance, Google Drive folder with samples).

## Step 3: Apply well

- Apply within the first few days of a posting.
- Write a short, specific cover letter: why this company, what you'll bring, one relevant result.
- Complete skills tests carefully (typing tests, writing samples, coding tasks). They often decide the shortlist.
- Keep a tracker sheet: company, role, link, date applied, status, follow-up date.

## Step 4: Interviews

- **Test your setup**: stable internet, charged laptop, quiet room, good light facing you, headphones with a mic.
- Expect: a recruiter screen, a skills interview or test, a final interview, sometimes a paid trial task.
- Prepare STAR stories (Situation, Task, Action, Result) for common questions: a difficult customer, a mistake you fixed, working without supervision.
- Ask good questions: "How does the team communicate?", "What does success look like in the first 90 days?"

## Contracts, payment and tax

- Get a written contract before starting: role, pay, currency, payment schedule, hours, notice, equipment, confidentiality.
- Payment methods: local bank transfer, Wise, Payoneer, Deel/Remote payouts, PayPal (see the getting-paid lesson).
- As a contractor you must declare income to KRA yourself (see the taxes lesson).
- **A legitimate employer never asks you to pay** for training, equipment, "application processing" or a work permit for a remote job.

## Your remote setup

| Need | Practical options |
|---|---|
| Internet | Home fibre plus a mobile data backup (a second network) |
| Power | UPS for the router, power bank, or a small inverter/solar if outages are common |
| Workspace | A table, a supportive chair, a quiet corner |
| Equipment | Laptop with enough RAM, headset with mic, webcam |
| Security | Strong passwords, password manager, 2-step verification, screen lock |

## Working well remotely

- Over-communicate: daily updates in the team channel, say when you're online and offline.
- Respect time zones; put your hours in your profile ("Available 9am–6pm EAT").
- Write clearly; remote work is mostly written.
- Deliver on time; if you'll be late, say so early.
- Set boundaries to avoid burnout: a start time, breaks, an end time.

## Fake remote job red flags

- You must pay for training, a "starter kit", equipment or registration.
- Interviews only on Telegram/WhatsApp chat with no video and no company email.
- Salary far above the market for very little work ("KSh 5,000 per hour typing").
- Requests for your M-Pesa PIN, ID photos with selfies before any contract, or bank login.
- "Task" jobs where you deposit money to "unlock" higher-paying tasks.

:::think A company emails: "Congratulations! You've been hired as a remote data entry clerk at $40/hour. To begin, buy our approved laptop from our vendor and we'll reimburse you." What do you do?
This is a classic fake-cheque/equipment scam. Real employers send equipment or reimburse through payroll after proper hiring. Don't pay, verify the company and recruiter independently (official website, LinkedIn employees), and report the message.
:::

## Summary

- Remote jobs give one employer and regular pay while you work from home; roles span support, sales, admin, content, tech, finance, AI data and education.
- Know the difference between employee and contractor arrangements; read contracts.
- Find jobs on LinkedIn, remote boards, Kenyan job sites, company pages and through referrals; "EMEA" roles often suit Kenya's time zone.
- Use a tailored, results-focused CV, a strong LinkedIn, a portfolio, careful tests and STAR interview stories.
- Prepare internet and power backup, communicate a lot, and never pay to get a job.

```quiz
Q: What does the A in the STAR interview method stand for?
A: Action
Q: Which region abbreviation (four letters) often covers Europe, the Middle East and Africa in job posts?
A: EMEA
Q: Should a real employer ask you to pay for training before you start? (yes/no)
A: no
Q: What do companies call the software that scans CVs for keywords? (abbreviation)
A: ATS | applicant tracking system
Q: As a contractor, who handles declaring your income to KRA?
A: you | me | myself | the contractor
```

lessons.title: Working as a virtual assistant or online admin support
lessons.body:
# Working as a virtual assistant or online admin support

A **virtual assistant (VA)** helps businesses and busy professionals with admin, customer support, scheduling, research and social media, remotely. It's one of the most accessible online jobs: you need reliable internet, a laptop, good communication and organisation, and everyday digital skills taught on this learning hub.

## What VAs do

| Area | Tasks |
|---|---|
| **Admin** | Email inbox management, calendar scheduling, data entry, filing documents |
| **Customer support** | Replying to emails, chats and WhatsApp messages; handling orders |
| **Research** | Finding suppliers, leads, prices, travel options; summarising findings |
| **Social media** | Scheduling posts, replying to comments, simple Canva graphics |
| **E-commerce support** | Uploading products, updating stock, processing orders |
| **Bookkeeping support** | Recording receipts and invoices in spreadsheets or tools like QuickBooks |
| **Content** | Transcription, proofreading, formatting documents and presentations |

## Skills and tools to learn

| Skill | Where to learn here |
|---|---|
| Professional email and Google Workspace | Email & Google Drive, Calendar & Meet lessons |
| Spreadsheets | Excel & Google Sheets tutorial |
| Documents and presentations | Word, PowerPoint lessons |
| Graphics | Canva tutorial |
| Typing speed (40+ wpm) | Keyboard & typing lesson |
| AI assistants for drafting and research | AI tools tutorial |
| Common tools | Trello/Asana, Slack, Zoom, Calendly, Canva, Google Workspace, Notion |

Soft skills matter as much: clear written English, reliability, confidentiality, time management, and asking good questions.

## Build proof before you apply

1. **Pick a focus**: e.g. "Email and calendar management for real estate agents" or "Customer support for online shops".
2. **Create sample work**: an organised inbox system with labels, a cleaned-up spreadsheet, a social media calendar, a research report. Put them in a simple portfolio (Google Drive folder or website).
3. **Take free certificates**: Google's free courses, HubSpot Academy (customer service, social media), and others.
4. **Practise locally**: help a local business, church or school with admin for a testimonial.

## Where to find work

- Freelance platforms: **Upwork**, Fiverr, OnlineJobs.ph-style boards, LinkedIn Jobs (filter "remote").
- Remote job boards: We Work Remotely, Remote OK, and company career pages.
- **Direct outreach**: offer help to local businesses, agencies and entrepreneurs on LinkedIn.
- Referrals from satisfied clients (the best source long-term).

See the *Freelancing platforms* and *Profile and proposals* lessons for writing winning proposals.

## Pricing

Start with an hourly rate or a monthly package ("20 hours per month of inbox and calendar support"). Use the rate calculator in the *Pricing your work* lesson, factor in internet and power costs, platform fees and taxes, and raise your rates as you gain reviews and experience.

## Working professionally

- Agree on the **scope, hours, communication channel and response times** in writing.
- Use a password manager or the client's shared-access tools; **never ask clients to send passwords in plain messages**.
- Keep client information **confidential** (and follow data protection rules).
- Send a short **weekly report**: what you did, what's pending, questions.
- Track your time (Toggl, Clockify) if billing hourly.
- Have backup power and internet (a power bank, a mobile data bundle) for reliability.

## Getting paid in Kenya

Common options include payment through the platform to your bank or **M-Pesa** (via supported withdrawal methods), **Payoneer**, **PayPal** (withdrawal to M-Pesa is available), and direct bank transfers. Compare fees and exchange rates, and keep records for tax purposes.

## Avoid VA scams

- No legitimate job asks you to **pay** to get hired or to buy "training materials" first.
- Be careful with "clients" who want you to receive money and forward it, or to buy gift cards.
- Keep communication and payment on the platform until trust is established.

```quiz
Q: What does VA stand for? (two words)
A: virtual assistant
Q: Name a free tool for tracking time spent on client work.
A: Toggl | Clockify
Q: Should a legitimate employer ask you to pay before hiring you? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: What should you send clients each week to show your progress? (two words)
A: weekly report | report | a report
Q: Should clients send you passwords in plain chat messages? (yes or no)
A: no
```

lessons.title: Virtual assistance, customer support and remote jobs
lessons.body:
# Virtual assistance, customer support and remote jobs

Businesses everywhere need people to **answer customers, manage inboxes and calendars, update spreadsheets and handle admin**. This work can be done from home in Kenya, and our good English, time zone (close to Europe and the Middle East) and growing BPO industry make Kenyans popular hires.

This lesson complements [Working as a virtual assistant](./?track=make-money-online&lesson=virtual-assistant-work) with **where to find the jobs**.

## Types of roles

| Role | What you do | Skills |
|---|---|---|
| **Virtual assistant (VA)** | Email, calendar, bookings, research, documents | Google Workspace, organisation, clear writing |
| **Customer support (chat/email)** | Answer customer questions, solve problems | Typing speed, patience, product knowledge |
| **Call centre agent** | Phone support or sales | Clear speaking, calm under pressure |
| **Social media support** | Reply to comments and DMs for brands | Tone, speed |
| **Data entry and admin** | Updating CRMs, spreadsheets, catalogues | Accuracy, Excel/Sheets |
| **Online bookkeeping assistant** | Recording invoices and receipts | Excel, QuickBooks/Xero basics |
| **Executive / real-estate / e-commerce VA** | Specialist support for one industry | Industry tools |

## Where to find these jobs

| Platform | What it is |
|---|---|
| [Upwork](https://www.upwork.com) | Freelance VA and support contracts |
| [Fiverr](https://www.fiverr.com) | Package VA services ("10 hours of admin support") |
| [LinkedIn Jobs](https://www.linkedin.com/jobs/) | Remote and local roles; set location to "Remote" |
| [We Work Remotely](https://weworkremotely.com) | Remote jobs, including customer support |
| [Remote OK](https://remoteok.com) | Remote jobs; filter by "worldwide" |
| [Remote.co](https://remote.co) | Curated remote job listings |
| [Working Nomads](https://www.workingnomads.com) | Remote job listings by category |
| [BrighterMonday](https://www.brightermonday.co.ke) | Kenyan jobs, including BPO and remote roles |
| [Fuzu](https://www.fuzu.com) | Kenyan and East African jobs and courses |
| [MyJobMag Kenya](https://www.myjobmag.co.ke) | Kenyan job listings |

**BPOs (business process outsourcing companies) in Kenya** hire agents for international clients, often with training, a salary and benefits. Look up the careers pages of large contact-centre companies operating in Nairobi, Mombasa and other towns, and check the **Ajira Digital** and **Jitume** programmes for partner opportunities.

## Getting hired

1. **Set up properly**: a laptop, a headset with a microphone, and backup internet (a Safaricom/Airtel hotspot besides home Wi-Fi). Many jobs test your speed.
2. **Learn the tools**: Google Workspace (Gmail, Calendar, Docs, Sheets), Microsoft 365, Zoom, Slack, Trello/Asana, a help-desk tool (Zendesk, Freshdesk, HubSpot: most have free trials or courses). This hub covers Google Workspace, Word and Excel.
3. **Record a 1-minute introduction video** (clear voice, good light, quiet background). Clients love it.
4. **Create a one-page CV for remote work**: typing speed, tools, availability in **their** time zone, and results ("handled 60 customer chats a day with 95% satisfaction").
5. **Apply consistently**: 5 tailored applications a day.

## Interview questions to prepare

- "Tell me about a time you dealt with an angry customer."
- "How do you prioritise when everything is urgent?"
- "What would you do if you didn't know the answer to a customer's question?"
- "Show us your typing speed" (aim for 50+ words per minute, accurately).

Answer with the **STAR method**: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

## Customer support writing: practise

Good support replies **thank, solve and confirm**:

> Hi Amina, thank you for reaching out, and sorry your order is late. I've checked: it left our Nairobi warehouse this morning and the rider will deliver by 4 pm today. I've also added free delivery to your next order for the trouble. Is there anything else I can help with?

```quiz
Q: What does BPO stand for? Write the three words.
A: business process outsourcing
Q: Which interview answer method uses Situation, Task, Action, Result?
A: STAR | STAR method
Q: What should you have besides home Wi-Fi for remote work?
A: backup internet | a hotspot | a backup connection
Q: A good support reply should thank, solve and ...?
A: confirm
Q: Name one help-desk tool used in customer support.
A: Zendesk | Freshdesk | HubSpot
```

lessons.title: Online tutoring and small online tasks: teaching platforms, lesson setup, micro-task sites and realistic earnings
lessons.body:
# Online tutoring and small online tasks: teaching platforms, lesson setup, micro-task sites and realistic earnings

Two very different ways to earn online share this unit:

- **Online tutoring** uses what you already know (a school subject, English, coding, music, Excel) to teach learners by video call or recorded lessons. Pay can be good and it grows with your reputation.
- **Micro-tasks** are tiny jobs done online (tagging images, short surveys, testing an app, recording your voice) that pay small amounts each. They need little skill but pay little, so they're best as a side income or a stepping stone.

This unit explains both in detail so you can choose wisely and avoid the many fake "earn by clicking" sites.

:::note What you will learn
- Who uses online tutoring and what subjects are in demand
- Tutoring platforms vs finding your own students
- Setting up lessons: tools, lesson plans, pricing and payments
- Child safety and professionalism
- Types of micro-tasks and legitimate sites
- Realistic earnings and how to spot fake task sites
:::

---

## Part 1: Online tutoring

### Who needs tutors?

| Learner | Typical needs |
|---|---|
| Kenyan pupils and students (CBC, KCSE, IGCSE) | Maths, sciences, languages, revision, homework help |
| Diaspora families | Swahili lessons for children, Kenyan curriculum support |
| International learners | English conversation, exam prep (IELTS/TOEFL), coding, Swahili for travel/work |
| University students | Statistics, programming, research methods |
| Adults and professionals | Excel, computer basics, digital marketing, public speaking |

### Platforms vs your own students

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **Tutoring platforms** (e.g. Preply, italki for languages, Superprof, and local platforms) | Students find you; payments handled | Commission (often high at first), competition, platform rules and country support vary |
| **Your own students** (WhatsApp, Facebook groups, schools, referrals, your website) | You keep everything, set your own rates | You must market yourself and collect payments |

Most tutors start on a platform or with referrals, then build their own client base.

### Step 1: Choose your offer

Be specific: "KCSE Chemistry revision for Form 3–4", "Swahili for diaspora kids aged 6–12", "Excel for job seekers in 4 sessions". A specific offer is easier to market than "I teach anything".

### Step 2: Set up your tools

- **Video call**: Google Meet, Zoom, Microsoft Teams.
- **Whiteboard**: Google Jamboard alternatives such as Microsoft Whiteboard, Miro, or a pen tablet; a phone pointed at paper also works.
- **Materials**: Google Docs/Slides, past papers you're allowed to use, worksheets you created.
- **Scheduling**: Google Calendar or Calendly (free plan).
- **Setup**: stable internet, headset, good light, quiet room, plain background.

### Step 3: Plan a lesson

A 60-minute lesson plan:

```
1. Warm-up (5 min): quick recap questions from last lesson
2. Teach (15 min): one concept with clear examples
3. Guided practice (15 min): solve problems together
4. Independent practice (15 min): learner solves, you watch and correct
5. Wrap-up (5 min): summarise, assign homework
6. After the lesson (5 min): send notes and progress update to learner/parent
```

### Step 4: Price and get paid

| Type | Example rates |
|---|---|
| Local primary/secondary tutoring | KSh 500–2,000 per hour |
| Exam prep and specialist subjects | KSh 1,500–3,500+ per hour |
| International learners | $8–30+ per hour depending on subject and experience |

Sell **packages** (e.g. 8 lessons paid upfront at a small discount). Collect payment before lessons via M-Pesa, bank or the platform. Have a cancellation policy (e.g. 12 hours' notice or the lesson is charged).

### Child safety and professionalism

:::warning Protect children and yourself
- Communicate with parents, not directly with minors on private apps.
- Keep sessions professional, in a visible space; consider recording only with parental consent.
- Never ask for personal photos or information unrelated to lessons.
- Follow platform child-protection rules.
:::

### Growing as a tutor

- Collect reviews and results ("improved from D+ to B in 2 terms").
- Run group classes (5–10 learners at a lower price each) to earn more per hour.
- Turn your best lessons into recorded courses or revision packs (see the digital products lesson).

---

## Part 2: Micro-tasks

### Types of micro-tasks

| Task | What you do | Example platforms to research |
|---|---|---|
| **Surveys and research studies** | Answer questions for academic or market research | Prolific (availability depends on country), research panels |
| **Website and app testing** | Record yourself using a site and speak your thoughts | User-testing platforms |
| **Data labelling** | Tag images, classify text, check AI answers | Annotation platforms (see the AI annotation lesson) |
| **Voice and video recording** | Read sentences for speech datasets | Data collection platforms, sometimes project-based |
| **Search and ads evaluation** | Rate search results for relevance | Rater roles through large vendors |
| **Small gigs** | Quick tasks on Microworkers-style sites | Low pay; check reviews |

Country availability changes often; many platforms accept or pause Kenyan workers depending on project needs.

### Realistic earnings

Micro-tasks pay small amounts per task: a few cents to a few dollars. Many people earn a little pocket money; some with consistent access and high accuracy earn more. Treat it as:
- A way to earn while learning a bigger skill
- Practice with online payments (PayPal, Payoneer)
- An introduction to AI data work, which can lead to better-paid specialist projects

### How to do well

- Complete your profile honestly; many sites screen by demographics and skills.
- Read instructions fully; accuracy scores decide whether you keep getting work.
- Work at the times tasks are released (often US/Europe working hours).
- Track your hourly earnings; drop sites that pay less than your time is worth.

### Fake task sites: red flags

- "Earn KSh 2,000 a day by liking videos" or "rating products"
- You must **pay a registration fee** or "upgrade to VIP" to withdraw
- You must **recharge/deposit** to unlock bigger tasks (a well-known task scam)
- Earnings grow only when you recruit friends
- No clear company, address or real reviews

:::think A site shows you "earned" KSh 4,800 in a week of tasks, but says you must pay KSh 1,500 "withdrawal activation" first. What's happening?
It's a scam: the balance is fake, created to make you pay. Legitimate platforms never charge to withdraw your earnings. Don't pay; stop using it and warn others.
:::

## Summary

- Online tutoring uses your knowledge to teach local, diaspora and international learners; specific offers sell best.
- Use platforms or find your own students; set up video, whiteboard, scheduling and a clear lesson plan.
- Charge per hour or by package, collect payment upfront, have a cancellation policy, and protect children.
- Micro-tasks (surveys, testing, labelling, recording) pay small amounts; good for side income and learning.
- Never pay to register, unlock tasks or withdraw: those are scams.

```quiz
Q: Which part of a lesson plan has the learner solve problems while you watch? (two words)
A: independent practice
Q: When tutoring a child, should you communicate with the parent or only with the child?
A: parent | the parent | parents
Q: A site asks for a fee before you can withdraw your task earnings. Real or scam?
A: scam
Q: Is it usually better to sell single lessons or packages paid upfront?
A: packages | package
Q: Name one type of micro-task.
A: survey | surveys | app testing | website testing | data labelling | data labeling | voice recording | testing | labelling | labeling
```

lessons.title: Micro-tasks, surveys and testing websites
lessons.body:
# Micro-tasks, surveys and testing websites

**Micro-tasks** are small online jobs that take seconds or minutes: tagging an image, checking a search result, answering a survey, testing a website and saying what confused you. They need almost no skill, which is exactly why they **pay little**. They're useful for learning how online work and payments work, earning small amounts in spare time, and moving towards better-paid work like testing or annotation.

## Honest expectations

- Most people earn **a few hundred to a few thousand shillings a month** from micro-tasks and surveys.
- You may be screened out of many surveys (they want specific age groups or countries).
- **Website and app testing** pays the best in this category, but tests are limited.
- Use it as a **side income or a stepping stone**, not a main income.

## Platforms

> Availability depends on country and changes often. Check the official site, and never pay to join.

| Platform | What you do | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [Clickworker](https://www.clickworker.com) | Short text, categorisation and data tasks | Assessments unlock more tasks; paid via PayPal. |
| [Toloka](https://toloka.ai) | Label images, rate search results, simple AI tasks | Many short tasks; good practice for annotation work. |
| [Prolific](https://www.prolific.com) | Academic research surveys and studies | Fair pay per study when available; eligibility varies by country. |
| [Microworkers](https://www.microworkers.com) | Varied small tasks from many employers | Choose tasks carefully. |
| [ySense](https://www.ysense.com) | Surveys, tasks and offers | Long-running; payouts via PayPal and others. |
| [UserTesting](https://www.usertesting.com) | Record yourself using websites and apps and say what you think | Better pay per test; needs clear spoken English and a microphone. |
| [Userlytics](https://www.userlytics.com) | Website and app usability tests | Paid per completed test. |
| [Test IO](https://test.io) | Find bugs in apps and websites (crowdtesting) | Learn basic software testing; paid per accepted bug. |
| [uTest](https://www.utest.com) | Crowdtesting community | Free training academy for testers. |

## Turning micro-tasks into a skill

Website and app **testing** can grow into a real career:

1. Join **uTest** and finish their free academy courses.
2. Learn how to write a **good bug report**: steps to reproduce, expected result, actual result, device and screenshots.
3. Practise on websites you use. Write bug reports in a Google Doc as a portfolio.
4. Learn the basics of **QA (quality assurance)**: test cases, regression testing, and later automation with tools like Selenium or Playwright (learn JavaScript or Python first in this hub).

A good bug report looks like this:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Title | Checkout button does nothing after entering M-Pesa number |
| Steps | 1. Add any product to cart 2. Go to checkout 3. Enter 0712345678 4. Tap "Pay" |
| Expected | M-Pesa PIN prompt is sent to the phone |
| Actual | Nothing happens; no error shown |
| Device | Tecno Spark 10, Android 13, Chrome 129 |
| Evidence | Screenshot and screen recording attached |

## Scams that pretend to be micro-tasks

These are **not** real jobs:

- **"Like videos / follow accounts and earn"** apps where you must **deposit money** to "upgrade" or "unlock withdrawals". These are pyramid and task scams. Many Kenyans have lost savings to them.
- **"Watch ads and earn KSh 1,000 a day"** apps: the money comes from new members' "registration fees", not ads.
- **Telegram "tasks"** that start by paying small amounts, then ask you to "invest" to continue.
- Anyone asking for your **M-Pesa PIN**, OTP code or to "send a small fee to receive your payment".

**Rule:** if you must pay money to earn money from simple tasks, it's a scam. See [Avoiding online money scams](./?track=make-money-online&lesson=avoid-scams).

```quiz
Q: Do micro-tasks usually pay a lot or a little?
A: a little | little
Q: Which type of micro-work pays best: surveys or website testing?
A: website testing | testing
Q: Which crowdtesting community offers a free academy for testers?
A: uTest
Q: A bug report lists steps, expected result, actual result and the ...?
A: device | device details
Q: An app asks you to deposit KSh 1,000 to unlock withdrawals from "liking videos". Is it legitimate? (yes or no)
A: no
```

lessons.title: Online tutoring, teaching and selling courses
lessons.body:
# Online tutoring, teaching and selling courses

If you can explain something well (a language, maths, coding, music, Excel, exam preparation), people will pay you to teach them. You can tutor **live, one to one**, teach **classes**, or record a **course once and sell it many times**.

## Live tutoring and language platforms

| Platform | What you teach | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [Preply](https://preply.com) | Languages and school subjects, one to one | You set your price; the platform takes a commission (higher on trial lessons). Kiswahili tutors are in demand. |
| [italki](https://www.italki.com) | Languages (community tutor or professional teacher) | Teach English, Kiswahili or other languages you speak well. |
| [Cambly](https://www.cambly.com) | English conversation practice | Requirements for tutors change; check the tutor page. |
