| [Wyzant](https://www.wyzant.com) | School and university subjects | Mainly US students; check eligibility. |
| [Superprof](https://www.superprof.com) | Any subject, online or in person | Students contact you through your profile. |
| [Outschool](https://outschool.com) | Small live classes for children | Check teacher requirements for your country. |
| Local (WhatsApp, Google Meet) | KCSE/CBC revision, computer classes, coding for kids | Often the fastest start: parents pay by M-Pesa. |

**Teach Kiswahili to the world**: diplomats, NGO staff, missionaries, tourists and the diaspora's children all want lessons. A good Kiswahili tutor profile with a friendly video can fill a schedule.

## Sell recorded courses

| Platform | How it works |
|---|---|
| [Udemy](https://www.udemy.com/teaching/) | Upload video courses; Udemy markets them and shares revenue. Big audience, but prices are often discounted. |
| [Teachable](https://teachable.com) | Your own course website; you keep more of the price and do your own marketing. |
| [Thinkific](https://www.thinkific.com) | Similar to Teachable, with a free plan. |
| [Gumroad](https://gumroad.com) | Sell courses, e-books and downloads simply. |
| [Skillshare](https://www.skillshare.com/teach) | Paid by minutes watched by members. |
| [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com) | Free lessons build an audience; earn from ads and sell a full course. |
| Your own website with M-Pesa | Best for Kenyan buyers who prefer M-Pesa over cards. |

## What makes a good online teacher

1. **Clear audio** matters more than video quality (use a cheap clip-on microphone).
2. **Short lessons** (5 to 15 minutes per video) with one goal each.
3. **Practice**: exercises, quizzes and real examples (like this hub).
4. **A friendly intro video** on your profile: who you are, who you help, how lessons work.
5. **Reviews**: ask your first students to leave one.

## Course idea checklist

- Is it a skill people pay for? (Search the topic on Udemy and YouTube: lots of content = demand.)
- Can you teach it better for a specific audience? ("Excel for Kenyan SACCO accountants", "Kiswahili for medical volunteers")
- Can you show a result? ("Build your first website in a weekend")



## Selling photos, videos and music (stock media)

If you take good photos or videos, or make music, you can license them to businesses, bloggers and video makers worldwide through **stock agencies**. Every download earns you a royalty. Authentic **African** photos and videos (everyday life, business, farming, cities, nature) are in demand because there are too few of them.

| Platform | Sell | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [Shutterstock Contributor](https://submit.shutterstock.com) | Photos, vectors, videos, music | Huge buyer base; review for quality. |
| [Adobe Stock Contributor](https://contributor.stock.adobe.com) | Photos, vectors, videos, 3D | Built into Adobe apps, so many designers buy here. |
| [Alamy](https://www.alamy.com/contributor/) | Photos | Good share of each sale. |
| [Getty Images / iStock](https://esp.gettyimages.com) | Photos and videos | Contributor app for submissions. |
| [Pond5](https://www.pond5.com) | Stock video, music, sound effects | Video footage of Africa sells well. |
| [Envato (AudioJungle, VideoHive)](https://author.envato.com) | Music, video templates | Large creator marketplace. |

Rules to know:

- **Model releases**: if a person can be recognised, you need their signed permission for commercial use.
- **No logos or brands** in commercial images (blur or avoid them).
- **Keywords matter**: describe what's in the image (who, what, where, mood) so buyers find it.
- Upload consistently: portfolios with hundreds of good images earn steadily; a few images earn little.

```quiz
Q: Which platform lets you teach languages one to one and set your own price?
A: Preply | italki
Q: Which platform shares revenue from recorded video courses and markets them for you?
A: Udemy
Q: What do you need from a recognisable person in a stock photo?
A: a model release | model release | permission
Q: Which platform is known for stock video, music and sound effects?
A: Pond5
Q: About how long should each lesson video be, in minutes? Give a number from 5 to 15.
A: 5 | 10 | 15 | 8 | 12
```

lessons.title: Avoiding online money scams: the 15 most common traps in Kenya, how they work and how to protect yourself
lessons.body:
# Avoiding online money scams: the 15 most common traps in Kenya, how they work and how to protect yourself

Wherever people look for money online, scammers follow. Kenyans lose money every day to fake jobs, "investment" groups, forex signal sellers, task apps, SIM swaps and fake buyers. Scammers are organised, patient and good at psychology. The best protection is understanding **how** each scam works, so you recognise the pattern even when the story changes.

This unit is one of the most important in the subject. Read it fully, and share it with friends and family.

:::note What you will learn
- The psychology scammers use
- 15 common scams, how each works and the warning signs
- Checking whether a company or offer is real
- Protecting your M-Pesa, accounts and identity
- What to do if you've been scammed, and where to report
:::

## How scammers think

Almost every scam uses some of these levers:

| Lever | What it sounds like |
|---|---|
| **Greed / big returns** | "Double your money in 7 days" |
| **Urgency** | "Offer ends tonight", "Pay now or lose the job" |
| **Authority** | Fake Safaricom, KRA, bank or police staff |
| **Social proof** | Screenshots of "payouts", fake testimonials, groups full of fake members |
| **Fear** | "Your account will be blocked", "There's a warrant for your arrest" |
| **Small first win** | Paying you small amounts at first to win trust before the big ask |

:::warning The golden rule
If you have to **pay money to receive money** (a fee to get a job, to withdraw earnings, to unlock tasks, to release a prize or loan), it's almost certainly a scam.
:::

## The 15 common scams

### 1. Fake job offers
"Hiring data entry clerks, KSh 3,000 per day, work from home." You pay for "registration", "training" or "a starter kit" and never hear from them again. **Signs**: pay to apply, chat-only interviews, salary far too high, Gmail addresses for a "big company".

### 2. Task / "like and earn" apps
You're paid to like videos or rate products. Small payouts arrive, then you're told to deposit money to unlock higher tasks or "complete a combination order". The deposits grow until you can't withdraw anything. **Signs**: deposits required, "VIP levels", Telegram groups with "mentors".

### 3. Ponzi and pyramid "investments"
Returns are paid from new members' money, not real business. They collapse, and most people lose. **Signs**: guaranteed high returns, rewards for recruiting, no clear product, pressure to reinvest.

### 4. Forex and crypto signal scams
"Account managers" promise to trade for you with 30% weekly profits, or sell "100% accurate signals". Fake dashboards show profits until you try to withdraw. **Signs**: guaranteed profits, unlicensed brokers, requests to send money to personal M-Pesa numbers. Check whether a forex broker is licensed by the **Capital Markets Authority (CMA)**.

### 5. Fake loan apps
You're asked to pay an "insurance" or "processing" fee before a loan is released. **Signs**: upfront fees, apps outside official stores, unrealistic approval. Licensed digital lenders are listed by the **Central Bank of Kenya**.

### 6. "Wrong number" M-Pesa reversal
You receive an SMS that looks like an M-Pesa credit, then a call: "I sent money to you by mistake, please send it back." No money actually arrived. **Protection**: always check your actual M-Pesa balance or statement. Genuine reversals are handled by Safaricom (via 456), not by sending money back to a stranger.

### 7. SIM swap and impersonation
Scammers call pretending to be Safaricom or a bank, ask for your PIN or a code sent to your phone, then take over your line or account. **Protection**: Safaricom and banks never ask for your PIN. Never share one-time codes.

### 8. Fake buyers and overpayment
A "buyer" sends a fake payment confirmation (or overpays) and asks you to send the "balance" back. **Protection**: confirm payments in your actual statement before releasing goods.

### 9. Fake sellers
Cheap phones, cars or land advertised online; you pay a deposit and the seller disappears. **Protection**: meet in safe public places, use pay-on-delivery, verify land at the registry with official searches, never pay large deposits to strangers.

### 10. Account recovery and "verification" scams
Messages say your Facebook/Instagram/WhatsApp will be disabled unless you "verify" through a link. The link steals your password. **Protection**: never log in through links in messages; turn on 2-step verification.

### 11. Freelance platform scams
A "client" asks you to move off Upwork/Fiverr to Telegram, pay for "software" to do the job, or do large unpaid "tests". **Protection**: keep communication and payment on the platform until you know the client well.

### 12. Fake scholarship, visa and overseas job agents
Fees for guaranteed visas, overseas jobs or scholarships. **Protection**: verify agencies with the **National Employment Authority (NEA)** for overseas jobs; real scholarships don't charge application fees in most cases.

### 13. Prize and promotion scams
"You've won KSh 50,000 in a Safaricom promotion, send KSh 1,000 to release it." **Protection**: you can't win a competition you didn't enter; real promotions don't ask for fees.

### 14. Romance scams
Someone builds an online relationship over weeks, then has an emergency: hospital fees, customs charges for a "gift". **Protection**: be very cautious with anyone who asks for money and avoids video calls.

### 15. Fake "courses" and "mentorship"
Gurus sell expensive programmes promising guaranteed income, mostly teaching you to recruit others into the same programme. **Protection**: look for real, verifiable results, free previews and refund policies.

## How to check if something is real

1. **Search** the company name + "scam", "reviews", "Kenya".
2. **Verify registration**: business registration via eCitizen/BRS; CMA for investment and forex; CBK for lenders and banks; NEA for recruitment agencies.
3. **Check contact details**: official website, physical address, company email domain, LinkedIn employees.
4. **Ask someone you trust** before paying. Scammers rush you because they know a second opinion stops them.
5. **Test with no money**: a real job or platform lets you start without paying.

## Protect your money and identity

- Never share your **M-Pesa PIN**, bank PIN, passwords or one-time codes.
- Use **2-step verification** on email, social media and freelance accounts.
- Use a **password manager** and unique passwords.
- Don't send ID photos and selfies to unverified "employers".
- Set an **M-Pesa** or bank transaction limit that fits your needs.
- Check your phone line works normally; if you suddenly lose network, contact your provider quickly (possible SIM swap).

## If you've been scammed

1. **Act fast**: call your bank or Safaricom (for M-Pesa, call 100/200 or use official channels) to request a hold or reversal if possible.
2. **Collect evidence**: screenshots, phone numbers, transaction codes, links, chat history.
3. **Report**: to the **DCI** (Directorate of Criminal Investigations) or your nearest police station; forward scam SMS to **333** (Safaricom's scam reporting short code); report fake accounts to the platform.
4. **Secure accounts**: change passwords, enable 2-step verification, check linked devices.
5. **Warn others** and don't be ashamed: scammers target everyone, including educated and experienced people.
6. **Beware "recovery" scammers** who promise to get your money back for a fee. They're another scam.

:::think A WhatsApp group shows daily screenshots of members earning KSh 10,000 from "AI trading robots". The admin says: "Deposit KSh 5,000 today, earn 20% daily, offer closes at midnight." Which levers and warning signs can you spot?
Greed (20% daily), urgency (closes at midnight), social proof (screenshots, group members) and probably authority ("AI robot"). Guaranteed daily returns are impossible in real trading. It's an investment scam or Ponzi; check CMA licensing and don't deposit.
:::

## Summary

- Scammers use greed, urgency, authority, social proof, fear and small first wins.
- If you must pay to receive money, it's almost certainly a scam.
- Learn the 15 common patterns: fake jobs, task apps, Ponzi schemes, forex/crypto signals, loan apps, M-Pesa reversal tricks, SIM swap, fake buyers and sellers, phishing, freelance, visa, prize, romance and guru scams.
- Verify with eCitizen/BRS, CMA, CBK and NEA; never share PINs or codes; use 2-step verification.
- If scammed: act fast, collect evidence, report to DCI and 333, secure accounts and ignore "recovery" offers.

```quiz
Q: If you must pay money to receive money (fees to withdraw or get a job), it is probably a what?
A: scam | a scam
Q: Which Kenyan body licenses forex brokers? (abbreviation)
A: CMA | Capital Markets Authority
Q: To which short code do you forward scam SMS on Safaricom?
A: 333
Q: Should you ever share your M-Pesa PIN with Safaricom staff who call you? (yes/no)
A: no
Q: Which body verifies overseas recruitment agencies in Kenya? (abbreviation)
A: NEA | National Employment Authority
Q: Investments paid from new members' money instead of real profit are called what kind of scheme?
A: Ponzi | Ponzi scheme | pyramid | pyramid scheme
```

lessons.title: Taxes, records and managing money: KRA PIN, filing returns, turnover tax, record keeping and saving for online earners
lessons.body:
# Taxes, records and managing money: KRA PIN, filing returns, turnover tax, record keeping and saving for online earners

Online income is real income. Whether you're paid through M-Pesa, PayPal, Payoneer or a bank, the money you earn freelancing, creating content or selling products is generally taxable in Kenya. Many online earners ignore this until KRA writes to them or a bank, visa or tender asks for a **tax compliance certificate**. Others earn well but have nothing saved because irregular income is hard to manage.

This unit explains the basics of tax for online earners, how to keep records, and how to manage irregular income so you build real wealth.

:::warning General education, not tax advice
Tax rules change with each Finance Act. Always confirm current rates and rules on **kra.go.ke** or with a qualified tax adviser before filing, especially as your income grows.
:::

:::note What you will learn
- Why online earners should be tax compliant
- Getting a KRA PIN and using iTax
- Which taxes may apply: income tax, turnover tax, and others
- Filing your annual return step by step
- eTIMS invoices and what they mean for you
- Simple record keeping
- Managing irregular income: budgeting, emergency fund, saving and investing
- Pension and health cover when you're self-employed
:::

## Why be tax compliant?

- It's the law, and penalties and interest for late filing add up.
- A **Tax Compliance Certificate (TCC)** is needed for government tenders, some jobs, and is often asked for in business deals.
- Records of declared income help with **loans, visas and mortgages**: banks want proof of income.
- Some international platforms and payment providers report or request tax information.

## Step 1: Get a KRA PIN

1. Go to **itax.kra.go.ke**.
2. Choose *New PIN Registration* → *Individual* → *Online form*.
3. Enter your ID details, contact information and income sources (you can select employment and/or business income).
4. Submit; your PIN certificate is sent to your email.

If you already have a PIN (for example from employment), update your income sources to include business income if you're freelancing.

## Which taxes might apply?

| Situation | Possible tax | How it works (check current rules) |
|---|---|---|
| Employed, with side freelancing | **Income tax** on total income | Salary is taxed through PAYE; side income is declared in your annual return |
| Self-employed freelancer/creator | **Income tax** on profit (income minus allowable expenses) | Graduated rates apply; declared in your annual return |
| Small business with sales between the turnover tax bands | **Turnover Tax (TOT)** | A flat percentage of gross sales (1.5% under recent law for annual turnover of KSh 1–25 million), filed monthly; eligible businesses may choose it instead of income tax on profit |
| Large turnover businesses | **VAT** registration | Required above the VAT threshold (KSh 5 million annual taxable turnover under current law) |
| Paying for professional services as a business | **Withholding tax** | Some clients deduct it and give you a certificate you can claim |

### Individual income tax bands (monthly, as at recent years)

| Monthly taxable income (KSh) | Rate |
|---|---|
| First 24,000 | 10% |
| Next 8,333 | 25% |
| Next 467,667 (up to 500,000) | 30% |
| Next 300,000 (up to 800,000) | 32.5% |
| Above 800,000 | 35% |

Residents get a **personal relief** of KSh 2,400 per month (KSh 28,800 per year). Here's an example of how bands work:

```try-python
bands = [(24000, 0.10), (8333, 0.25), (467667, 0.30), (300000, 0.325), (float("inf"), 0.35)]
def monthly_tax(income):
    tax, left = 0, income
    for size, rate in bands:
        part = min(left, size)
        tax += part * rate
        left -= part
        if left <= 0:
            break
    return max(tax - 2400, 0)   # personal relief

for income in [20000, 50000, 100000]:
    print("Profit KSh %d/month -> tax about KSh %.0f" % (income, monthly_tax(income)))
```

This is a simplified calculation for learning: it ignores deductions, reliefs and levies such as SHIF and the housing levy.

## Step 2: Allowable expenses (for income tax on profit)

If you pay income tax on profit, you're taxed on **income minus expenses wholly and exclusively incurred** to earn it. For online workers these can include:
- Internet and phone costs used for work (the business share)
- Software subscriptions, hosting, domain names
- Equipment (laptop, camera, microphone) through capital allowances
- Platform fees and payment charges
- Co-working space rent, training directly related to your work

Keep receipts. Under eTIMS rules, many expenses must be backed by **eTIMS invoices** from the supplier to be deductible.

## Step 3: File your annual return

- Annual individual returns are due by **30 June** for the previous year (January–December).
- If you had no income at all, file a **nil return**. Not filing at all attracts penalties.
- Log in to iTax → *Returns* → *File Return* → select *Income Tax – Resident Individual*.
- Download the Excel or use the online form (simpler cases), enter employment income (from your P9 form if employed), business income and expenses.
- Submit and pay any tax due via **M-Pesa Paybill 572572** using the payment registration number generated (check the current details on iTax).

## eTIMS (electronic Tax Invoice Management System)

Businesses are required to issue electronic tax invoices through eTIMS, including small businesses and service providers. Options include the eTIMS web portal, the eTIMS mobile app and USSD (*222#). If you invoice businesses for your services, expect some to ask for an eTIMS invoice. Check KRA's eTIMS guidance for current requirements.

## Step 4: Keep simple records

A sheet with these columns is enough to start:

| Date | Description | Client/Supplier | Income (KSh) | Expense (KSh) | Category | Payment ref | Receipt/invoice link |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Tips:
- Separate business and personal money: a separate M-Pesa line, Till, or bank account for business.
- Record foreign income in KSh using the rate on the day received.
- Save invoices, platform statements (Upwork, Fiverr, PayPal, Payoneer) and receipts in a dated folder.
- Review monthly: total income, total expenses, profit.

## Managing irregular income

Online income often goes up and down. A system:

1. **Pay yourself a fixed "salary"**: put all earnings into a business account, then transfer the same amount to yourself every month.
2. **Set aside tax**: move a percentage (e.g. 10–20%) of each payment into a separate savings account for tax.
3. **Emergency fund**: build 3–6 months of essential expenses in a money market fund (MMF) or savings account you can access quickly.
4. **Budget**: needs first (rent, food, transport, internet), then savings, then wants. The 50/30/20 rule is a simple guide.
5. **Invest for the long term** only after the emergency fund: MMFs, government bonds and Treasury bills, SACCOs. Avoid "investments" that promise guaranteed high returns.
6. **Reinvest in skills and equipment** that increase your earnings.

## Pension and health cover

Self-employed people don't get employer contributions, so:
- Register and contribute to the **Social Health Authority (SHA)** scheme as required for self-employed persons.
- Consider **NSSF** voluntary contributions and/or a registered **personal pension scheme** or income drawdown fund; contributions to registered schemes may also attract tax benefits within limits.
- Consider private health or life insurance if you support a family.

:::think A freelancer earns KSh 120,000 one month and KSh 20,000 the next. In good months they spend everything, and in bad months they borrow. What system would fix this?
Put all income into a business account, pay themselves a fixed monthly amount based on their average income, set aside a tax percentage from every payment, build a 3–6 month emergency fund in an MMF, and only spend from the fixed salary.
:::

## Summary

- Online income is generally taxable; compliance unlocks TCCs, loans, visas and peace of mind.
- Register on iTax for a KRA PIN and include business income as a source.
- Possible taxes: income tax on profit (graduated rates, KSh 2,400 monthly relief), turnover tax for eligible small businesses, VAT above the threshold, withholding tax.
- File annual returns by 30 June (nil returns if no income); keep records and eTIMS invoices for expenses.
- Manage irregular income with a fixed salary, a tax pot, an emergency fund, a budget, safe long-term investing and your own pension and health cover.

```quiz
Q: What is the deadline each year for filing individual annual returns in Kenya?
A: 30 June | 30th June | June 30 | june 30th
Q: What is the online portal for KRA PINs and returns called?
A: iTax | itax.kra.go.ke
Q: If you had no income in a year, what kind of return do you file? (two words)
A: nil return | a nil return
Q: What is the monthly personal relief for a resident individual (KSh)?
A: 2400 | 2,400 | ksh 2400
Q: How many months of essential expenses should an emergency fund cover? (give a range like 3-6)
A: 3-6 | 3 to 6 | 3–6 | three to six
Q: What KRA system issues electronic tax invoices? (abbreviation)
A: eTIMS | etims
```

lessons.title: Your 30-day action plan: from zero to your first online income, week by week
lessons.body:
# Your 30-day action plan: from zero to your first online income, week by week

You've learned about many ways to earn online. Knowledge alone doesn't pay; **action** does. This final unit turns everything into a practical 30-day plan with daily tasks. It won't make you rich in a month (nobody honest can promise that), but if you follow it, by day 30 you'll have a skill direction, a portfolio, profiles, a pipeline of applications or content, and very possibly your first paid work.

:::note What you will build in 30 days
- A clear choice of one main earning path
- A basic skill level and 3 portfolio samples
- Professional profiles (LinkedIn + one platform)
- A payment setup (M-Pesa, PayPal/Payoneer or bank)
- 30+ applications, pitches or published pieces of content
- A simple tracker and weekly review habit
:::

## Before you start: your setup

| Need | Minimum |
|---|---|
| Device | A smartphone (a laptop is better for most skills; a cyber café or shared laptop can work at first) |
| Internet | A data bundle or Wi-Fi you can rely on daily |
| Time | 2–3 focused hours a day (adjust if you're working or studying) |
| Accounts | Gmail, LinkedIn, M-Pesa; later PayPal/Payoneer |
| Tracker | A Google Sheet with tabs: Learning, Portfolio, Applications/Content, Income |

## Choose one path

Pick **one** main path for these 30 days. Switching every week is the number one reason people never earn.

| If you... | Consider |
|---|---|
| Write well | Content writing, copywriting, transcription, blogging |
| Like design | Graphic design, social media content, printables |
| Like tech/logic | Web design, coding, IT support, data entry, Excel |
| Are good with people | Virtual assistant, customer support, sales, tutoring |
| Like being on camera | Content creation (YouTube/TikTok), UGC, tutoring |
| Have products or a trade | E-commerce, social media selling |
| Are detail-oriented | Data annotation, QA testing, bookkeeping |

---

## Week 1: Choose, learn and set up (days 1–7)

| Day | Tasks |
|---|---|
| 1 | Write down your goal (e.g. "earn my first KSh 5,000 online by day 30"). Choose your path. Create your tracker. |
| 2 | Find one free course for your skill (Ajira Digital, Google, freeCodeCamp, HubSpot, YouTube or this learning hub). Study 2 hours. |
| 3 | Study 2 hours. List 10 people/companies who pay for this skill and how much (search job boards and Fiverr gigs). |
| 4 | Study 2 hours. Practise: create your first rough sample. |
| 5 | Set up LinkedIn properly: photo, headline, about, skills. Connect with 20 people in your field. |
| 6 | Set up payments: confirm M-Pesa details; open PayPal and/or Payoneer if you'll work internationally (use your real details). |
| 7 | **Review**: what did you learn? Adjust your study plan. Rest a bit. |

## Week 2: Build your portfolio (days 8–14)

| Day | Tasks |
|---|---|
| 8 | Study the work of top people in your field. Note what makes it good. |
| 9 | Create portfolio sample 1 (a real-looking project: a blog post, a logo, a landing page, a spreadsheet, a short video). |
| 10 | Get feedback from someone experienced (a community, a friend, a mentor). Improve it. |
| 11 | Create sample 2. |
| 12 | Create sample 3. |
| 13 | Put your samples in one place: Google Drive folder, Behance, GitHub, Canva PDF or a simple website. |
| 14 | **Review**: are your samples good enough that you'd pay for them? Fix the weakest one. |

:::tip Real projects beat imaginary ones
Offer to do one small project for a local business, church, chama or friend at a low price or free in exchange for a testimonial. A real client name on your portfolio builds trust fast.
:::

## Week 3: Go to market (days 15–21)

| Day | Tasks |
|---|---|
| 15 | Create a profile on one platform (Upwork, Fiverr, a tutoring site or a local job board) or set up your content channel. Use the profile lesson's templates. |
| 16 | Send 5 tailored applications/pitches or publish 1 piece of content. |
| 17 | Send 5 more / publish 1 more. Tell your network what you offer (WhatsApp status, LinkedIn post). |
| 18 | Approach 5 local businesses directly with a specific offer. |
| 19 | Send 5 more / publish 1 more. Follow up on earlier messages politely. |
| 20 | Improve your profile based on what you've learned (headline, gig images, pricing). |
| 21 | **Review**: how many replies? What's working? Adjust your pitch. |

A simple pitch template:

```
Hi [Name], I saw [specific thing about their business/job post].
I [do X] for [type of client] – here's a similar sample: [link].
For you, I'd [specific idea: e.g. redesign your menu / write 4 blog posts a month].
Would you like me to send a quick quote? – [Name]
```

## Week 4: Deliver, follow up and grow (days 22–30)

| Day | Tasks |
|---|---|
| 22 | Keep sending 5 applications or publishing daily. Reply to every enquiry within hours. |
| 23 | If you get a job: confirm scope, price, deadline and deposit in writing. Deliver early and well. |
| 24 | Ask satisfied clients for a review/testimonial and referrals. |
| 25 | Learn one advanced topic in your skill. |
| 26 | Create sample 4 based on the type of work clients ask for most. |
| 27 | Record all income and expenses in your tracker; set aside a share for tax and savings. |
| 28 | Follow up with every warm lead. |
| 29 | Plan your next 30 days: income goal, skills to learn, number of pitches. |
| 30 | **Big review**: total applications, replies, clients, income. Celebrate progress. |

---

## Tracking your progress

Your numbers tell you what to fix:

| Metric | If it's low... |
|---|---|
| Applications sent | Send more: aim for 5+ a day |
| Reply rate | Improve targeting and personalise your pitch |
| Interviews/calls → jobs | Improve portfolio and how you explain your process |
| Repeat clients | Improve quality, communication and deadlines |

```try-python
applications = 60
replies = 9
jobs = 3
income = 14500
print("Reply rate: %.0f%%" % (replies / applications * 100))
print("Job rate from replies: %.0f%%" % (jobs / replies * 100))
print("Average per job: KSh %.0f" % (income / jobs))
```

## Common reasons people quit (and how to push through)

- **"No one is replying."** Normal at the start. Improve one thing at a time and keep volume up.
- **"I'm not good enough yet."** Start with simpler jobs; you improve by doing paid work.
- **"Everyone is doing it."** Be specific: a niche, a local market or a better service beats competing on everything.
- **"I spent money on a course and got nothing."** Use free learning first; avoid guaranteed-income programmes.
- **"I earned, then nothing."** Build a pipeline: keep pitching and creating even when busy.

:::think After 30 days, Wanjiru has sent 70 applications, got 6 replies, 1 small job worth KSh 3,000 and a good review. Should she switch to a new skill?
No. One job and a review is real progress. Her reply rate (about 9%) suggests her pitch is working somewhat; she should keep the same skill, improve her portfolio with the job, specialise further, and keep the volume up. Switching resets her progress to zero.
:::

## Summary

- Choose one path for 30 days and track everything in a simple sheet.
- Week 1: learn and set up profiles and payments. Week 2: build 3 portfolio samples. Week 3: go to market with 5 pitches or content pieces daily. Week 4: deliver, ask for reviews, follow up and plan the next month.
- Use metrics (applications, reply rate, job rate, average per job) to know what to fix.
- Expect slow starts; consistency and specialisation beat switching skills.

```quiz
Q: How many main earning paths should you focus on in your first 30 days?
A: 1 | one
Q: How many portfolio samples does the plan build in week 2?
A: 3 | three
Q: 50 applications bring 5 replies. What is the reply rate in percent?
A: 10 | 10% | 10 percent
Q: After your first job, what should you ask a happy client for? (one word)
A: review | testimonial | referral | referrals | a review
Q: Should you stop pitching once you are busy with one client? (yes/no)
A: no
```
