lessons.title: Formatting documents like a pro: fonts, paragraphs, spacing, lists and consistent design
lessons.body:
# Formatting documents like a pro: fonts, paragraphs, spacing, lists and consistent design

A well-formatted document is easier to read, looks professional and earns trust, whether it's a CV, a business proposal, a school report or meeting minutes. Poor formatting (random fonts, uneven spacing, text pushed around with spaces and Enter keys) looks careless and breaks when someone else opens the file. This unit teaches professional formatting in **Microsoft Word** step by step, with the equivalent in **Google Docs**.

:::note What you will learn
- Character formatting: fonts, sizes, emphasis, colour, case
- Choosing fonts that look professional
- Paragraph formatting: alignment, line and paragraph spacing, indents
- Bullets and numbering, multilevel lists
- Tabs, borders, shading and columns
- Format Painter and clearing formatting
- Show/hide formatting marks and why "spaces for alignment" is a mistake
- A consistent formatting checklist
:::

## Character formatting

Select text first (double-click a word, triple-click a paragraph, `Ctrl+A` for everything), then use **Home → Font** (Word) or the toolbar (Docs).

| Format | Word | Google Docs | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bold | `Ctrl+B` | `Ctrl+B` | Headings, key terms |
| Italic | `Ctrl+I` | `Ctrl+I` | Titles of works, foreign words, emphasis |
| Underline | `Ctrl+U` | `Ctrl+U` | Rarely (looks like a link) |
| Strikethrough | Home → abc | `Alt+Shift+5` | Showing deletions |
| Superscript / subscript | `Ctrl+Shift+=` / `Ctrl+=` | `Ctrl+.` / `Ctrl+,` | 1st, m², H₂O |
| Change case | `Shift+F3` | Format → Text → Capitalisation | UPPER, lower, Title |
| Increase/decrease size | `Ctrl+]` / `Ctrl+[` | `Ctrl+Shift+.` / `,` | |
| Font dialog | `Ctrl+D` | | All options in one place |

### Choosing fonts

| Use | Good choices | Size |
|---|---|---|
| Body text (reports, letters) | Calibri, Arial, Aptos, Times New Roman, Georgia | 11–12 pt |
| Headings | The same font in bold, or a complementary font | 14–20 pt |
| CVs | Calibri, Arial, Cambria, Garamond | 10.5–12 pt |
| Posters/flyers | Bold sans-serif for headlines | Large |

Rules:
- Use **one or two fonts** per document.
- Avoid decorative fonts (Comic Sans, Algerian) in formal documents.
- **Serif** fonts (Times New Roman, Georgia) have small strokes on letters and suit printed long text; **sans-serif** (Arial, Calibri) look clean on screens. Both are fine; be consistent.
- Check institution requirements: many universities require Times New Roman 12, double or 1.5 spacing.

### Colour and highlight

Keep body text black or very dark grey. Use colour sparingly for headings or one brand colour. Highlighting is for drafts and review, not final documents.

## Paragraph formatting

A **paragraph** in Word is everything up to where you pressed Enter (shown as ¶ when formatting marks are visible). Paragraph settings are in **Home → Paragraph** and **Layout → Paragraph**.

### Alignment

| Alignment | Shortcut | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Left | `Ctrl+L` | Most body text (easiest to read) |
| Centre | `Ctrl+E` | Titles, cover pages |
| Right | `Ctrl+R` | Dates in some letters, numbers |
| Justify | `Ctrl+J` | Newspaper-style even edges; can create big gaps between words |

### Line spacing

Space between lines **within** a paragraph: Home → Line and Paragraph Spacing (or `Ctrl+1` single, `Ctrl+5` 1.5, `Ctrl+2` double). 1.15 is a comfortable default; 1.5 or double for assignments if required.

### Paragraph spacing (before and after)

Space **between** paragraphs. Set it (e.g. 6 pt before, 8 pt after) in Layout → Spacing, instead of pressing Enter twice. Benefits: consistent gaps, no empty paragraphs that shift when editing.

### Indents

| Indent | Use | How |
|---|---|---|
| Left/right indent | Quotations, notes | Layout → Indent, or drag the ruler markers |
| First-line indent | Traditional paragraphs | Paragraph dialog → Special → First line |
| Hanging indent | Reference lists (APA style), numbered lists | Paragraph dialog → Special → Hanging |

Turn on the ruler: **View → Ruler**.

## Formatting marks: see what's really there

Click **¶** (Home → Show/Hide, `Ctrl+Shift+8`) to show hidden marks:

| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `¶` | Paragraph end (Enter) |
| `·` | Space |
| `→` | Tab |
| `↵` | Line break (`Shift+Enter`) |
| `......Page Break......` | Manual page break |

:::warning Don't align with spaces or Enter
Pressing the spacebar many times to line text up, or Enter many times to move to a new page, creates documents that break as soon as fonts, printers or content change. Use **tabs**, **alignment**, **paragraph spacing**, **page breaks** (`Ctrl+Enter`) and **tables** instead. Showing formatting marks reveals these problems.
:::

## Lists

### Bullets and numbering

Home → **Bullets** or **Numbering**. Tips:
- Use bullets when order doesn't matter; numbers for steps.
- Press **Enter twice** to end a list, or click the button again.
- **Tab** demotes an item (sub-point); **Shift+Tab** promotes it.
- Right-click a number → **Restart at 1** or **Continue numbering**.
- Typing `1.` and a space (or `*` and a space) starts a list automatically (AutoFormat).

### Multilevel lists

Home → **Multilevel List** for outlines like 1, 1.1, 1.1.1 (great for policies, reports and legal documents). Linking multilevel lists to heading styles numbers headings automatically.

## Tabs

**Tab stops** line text up precisely, for example in letters, forms and simple lists with prices:

1. Click the tab selector at the left end of the ruler to choose left, centre, right or **decimal** tab.
2. Click on the ruler where you want the stop.
3. Press `Tab` in your text to jump to it.
4. **Leaders** (dotted lines) are set in Paragraph → Tabs (e.g. `Unga ........ KSh 180`).

For anything with many rows, a **table** (borders hidden if needed) is usually easier.

## Borders, shading and columns

- **Borders and shading:** Home → Borders → Borders and Shading: a box around a note, a line under a letterhead, shaded headings.
- **Page borders:** Design → Page Borders (certificates, invitations; avoid in formal reports).
- **Columns:** Layout → Columns (newsletters, brochures); insert a **column break** (Layout → Breaks) to control where text moves to the next column.

## Format Painter and clearing formatting

- **Format Painter** (paintbrush on Home): select formatted text → click the brush → click/drag over other text to copy the formatting. **Double-click** the brush to apply to several places; press `Esc` to stop.
- **Clear All Formatting** (Home → eraser icon, or `Ctrl+Space` for character formatting): removes formatting, useful for text pasted from websites.
- **Paste options:** after pasting, choose **Keep Text Only** to drop strange website formatting (or `Ctrl+Shift+V` in Google Docs).

## Professional formatting checklist

- [ ] One or two fonts; consistent sizes for body and each heading level
- [ ] Headings using **Styles** (next lesson), not manual bold + size
- [ ] Consistent line and paragraph spacing; no double Enters
- [ ] No spaces/Enters used for alignment; tabs, tables and page breaks used instead
- [ ] Lists formatted with bullets/numbering; consistent punctuation in list items
- [ ] Left-aligned body text (or justified if required)
- [ ] Page numbers, headers/footers where appropriate
- [ ] Spell check done; formatting marks checked
- [ ] Saved as PDF for sharing final versions

:::think A document looks perfect on your computer, but when your lecturer opens it, the text on page 3 has moved to the top of page 4 and the cover page is split. What likely caused this?
The document probably used many Enter presses and spaces to position text, and different fonts/printer settings on the lecturer's computer changed line lengths, pushing everything down. Using page breaks, paragraph spacing, styles and sending a **PDF** prevents this.
:::

## Practice tasks

1. Format a one-page letter: Calibri 11, 1.15 line spacing, 8 pt after paragraphs, no empty paragraphs.
2. Turn on formatting marks in a document someone else made and fix any spaces/Enters used for alignment.
3. Create a multilevel list for a club constitution (1, 1.1, 1.1.1).
4. Make a price list with right tabs and dot leaders.
5. Paste text from a website, then clean it with Keep Text Only and Format Painter.

## Summary

- Character formatting: fonts, sizes, bold/italic, super/subscript, case; choose one or two professional fonts.
- Paragraph formatting: alignment, line spacing, spacing before/after, indents (first-line, hanging).
- Show formatting marks (¶) and never align with spaces or Enters; use tabs, tables, page breaks.
- Lists: bullets, numbering, multilevel lists; Tab/Shift+Tab to change levels.
- Borders, shading, columns, Format Painter, Clear Formatting and paste options keep documents clean and consistent.

```quiz
Q: Which shortcut centres text in Word? Write like Ctrl+E.
A: Ctrl+E | ctrl e
Q: Which button shows hidden formatting marks? (one character)
A: ¶ | pilcrow | show/hide
Q: Which shortcut changes text case in Word? Write like Shift+F3.
A: Shift+F3 | shift f3
Q: Which tool copies formatting from one place to another? (two words)
A: Format Painter
Q: Which indent is used in APA reference lists?
A: hanging | hanging indent
Q: Which key demotes a list item to a sub-point?
A: Tab
Q: How many fonts should a professional document normally use? Write a range like 1-2.
A: 1-2 | one or two | 2 | 1 to 2
```

lessons.title: Styles, headings and an automatic table of contents: the secret to long documents
lessons.body:
# Styles, headings and an automatic table of contents: the secret to long documents

Reports, projects, proposals, theses, policies and manuals can run to dozens or hundreds of pages. Formatting each heading by hand and typing a table of contents manually wastes hours and creates errors whenever pages change. **Styles** solve this: you tag text as "Heading 1", "Heading 2" or "Normal", and Word handles consistent formatting, navigation, numbering and an automatic **table of contents**. This is the single most valuable Word skill for students and professionals.

:::note What you will learn
- What styles are and why they matter
- Applying built-in styles (Heading 1–3, Title, Normal)
- Modifying styles so the whole document updates at once
- The Navigation Pane for moving and reorganising sections
- Creating and updating an automatic table of contents
- Numbered headings, captions, and tables of figures
- Section breaks for different page numbering (roman numerals, then 1, 2, 3)
- Equivalent steps in Google Docs
:::

## What are styles?

:::define Style
A saved set of formatting (font, size, colour, spacing, indentation, numbering) with a name, such as "Heading 1" or "Normal". Applying a style applies all of that formatting at once, and marks the text's role in the document.
:::

Benefits:
1. **Consistency:** every Heading 1 looks identical.
2. **Speed:** one click instead of five formatting steps.
3. **Global changes:** change the Heading 1 style once, and every Heading 1 in a 100-page document updates.
4. **Navigation:** the Navigation Pane lists headings so you can jump to and drag sections.
5. **Automatic table of contents**, numbering and cross-references.
6. **Accessibility:** screen readers use heading styles to navigate (and exported PDFs keep headings as bookmarks).

## Applying styles

**Word:** Home → **Styles** gallery. Click in a paragraph (no need to select it all) and click a style.

| Style | Use | Shortcut (Word) |
|---|---|---|
| **Title** | The document's title (cover) | |
| **Heading 1** | Chapters / main sections | `Ctrl+Alt+1` |
| **Heading 2** | Sub-sections | `Ctrl+Alt+2` |
| **Heading 3** | Sub-sub-sections | `Ctrl+Alt+3` |
| **Normal** | Body text | `Ctrl+Shift+N` |
| **List Paragraph, Quote, Caption** | Lists, quotations, figure captions | |

**Google Docs:** the dropdown next to the font (Normal text, Title, Heading 1, 2, 3), or `Ctrl+Alt+1/2/3`.

### Heading hierarchy

Use headings in order, like an outline:

```
Heading 1: Chapter 1 Introduction
  Heading 2: 1.1 Background
  Heading 2: 1.2 Problem statement
    Heading 3: 1.2.1 Specific objectives
Heading 1: Chapter 2 Literature review
```

Don't skip levels (Heading 1 straight to Heading 3), and don't use headings just to make text big.

## Modifying a style

Want all Heading 1s in Times New Roman 16, bold, navy, with 12 pt space before?

1. Right-click **Heading 1** in the Styles gallery → **Modify**.
2. Set font, size, colour, bold.
3. **Format → Paragraph** for spacing (e.g. 12 pt before, 6 pt after) and "Keep with next" (keeps the heading on the same page as the following text).
4. Choose **New documents based on this template** if you want it as your default (optional).
5. Click OK: every Heading 1 updates instantly.

Alternative: format one heading the way you want, then right-click the style → **Update Heading 1 to Match Selection**.

**Google Docs:** format a heading, then Format → Paragraph styles → Heading 1 → **Update 'Heading 1' to match**.

### Setting the Normal style

Modify **Normal** to set the default body font, size and spacing (e.g. Calibri 11, 1.15 line spacing, 8 pt after). Most other styles are based on Normal, so this sets the overall look.

## The Navigation Pane

**View → Navigation Pane** (`Ctrl+F` and click "Headings"): shows all headings as a clickable outline.

- Click a heading to jump there.
- **Drag headings** to move whole sections (with all their text) up or down.
- Right-click to promote/demote or delete sections.
- Collapse levels to see the big picture.

Google Docs shows a similar **document outline** (View → Show outline).

## Automatic table of contents

1. Apply heading styles throughout the document.
2. Place the cursor where the table of contents should go (usually after the title page; insert a page break first).
3. **References → Table of Contents** → choose an automatic style.
4. Word lists headings with page numbers and clickable links.

### Updating it

When headings or page numbers change: click the table → **Update Table** (or right-click → Update Field, or `F9`) → **Update entire table**. Always update before printing or exporting to PDF.

### Customising

References → Table of Contents → **Custom Table of Contents**: choose how many levels to show (e.g. 3), tab leaders (dots), and formats. Modify the "TOC 1", "TOC 2" styles to change how entries look.

**Google Docs:** Insert → Table of contents (with page numbers or with blue links); click the refresh icon to update.

:::think A student types their table of contents by hand. Two days before submission, their supervisor asks them to add a new section in Chapter 2. What problems will they face, and how would styles have helped?
Adding a section shifts many page numbers, so the manual table becomes wrong and must be retyped and checked line by line (and mistakes are likely). With heading styles and an automatic table, they'd add the heading, click **Update Table**, and every entry and page number would be correct in seconds.
:::

## Numbered headings

For reports that need "1, 1.1, 1.1.1" numbering:
1. Click in a Heading 1.
2. Home → **Multilevel List** → choose the style showing "1 Heading 1, 1.1 Heading 2, 1.1.1 Heading 3".
3. All headings number automatically and renumber when you move sections.

## Captions, figures and tables

- Right-click an image or table → **Insert Caption** → "Figure 1: Map of Nakuru County" or "Table 1: Survey results". Numbers update automatically.
- **References → Insert Table of Figures** creates a list of figures/tables (common in projects and theses).
- **Cross-references** (References → Cross-reference) let you write "see Figure 3" that updates if numbering changes.

## Sections: different page numbering in one document

Academic documents often need: **no number** on the cover, **roman numerals** (i, ii, iii) for preliminary pages (declaration, abstract, table of contents), then **1, 2, 3** from Chapter 1.

1. Put the cursor at the end of the cover page → **Layout → Breaks → Section Break (Next Page)**.
2. Do the same after the preliminary pages, before Chapter 1.
3. Double-click the footer in section 2 → turn off **Link to Previous** (Header & Footer tab).
4. Insert → Page Number → Bottom of Page; then **Format Page Numbers** → choose i, ii, iii and **Start at i**.
5. In section 3's footer, turn off Link to Previous again, insert page numbers, format as 1, 2, 3 and **Start at 1**.
6. In section 1 (cover), delete the page number (or tick **Different First Page**).

Section breaks also allow **landscape pages** in a portrait document (for a wide table): add section breaks before and after, then set that section's orientation to landscape.

## Templates and the Styles Pane

- **Styles Pane** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S` or the small arrow in the Styles group) lists all styles and lets you create new ones (e.g. "Code", "Kiswahili quote").
- Save a document with your styles as a **template** (`.dotx`) for future reports: File → Save As → Word Template.
- Design → **Themes** and **Style Sets** change the look of all styles at once.

## Practice tasks

1. Open a long document (or create one with 3 chapters and subsections) and apply Title, Heading 1–3 and Normal styles.
2. Modify Heading 1 and Normal; watch the whole document update.
3. Insert an automatic table of contents; add a new section and update the table.
4. Add numbered headings with a multilevel list.
5. Set up a project with no number on the cover, roman numerals for preliminary pages and arabic numbers from Chapter 1.

## Summary

- Styles store formatting and meaning; use Title, Heading 1–3 and Normal consistently.
- Modify a style once to update the whole document; set Normal for the base look.
- The Navigation Pane lets you jump to and drag sections.
- Insert an automatic table of contents (References → Table of Contents) and update it before printing.
- Add numbered headings, captions, tables of figures and cross-references.
- Use section breaks for different page numbering and landscape pages; save templates for reuse.

```quiz
Q: Which style should chapter titles use?
A: Heading 1 | heading 1
Q: Which tab in Word has the Table of Contents command?
A: References
Q: Which key updates fields like the table of contents?
A: F9
Q: Which pane lists headings so you can drag sections around? (two words)
A: Navigation Pane | navigation
Q: Which break lets you change page numbering style in one document? (two words)
A: section break | Section Break (Next Page)
Q: Which footer option must you turn off to number sections differently? (three words)
A: Link to Previous | link to previous
Q: What numbering style is usually used for preliminary pages? (two words)
A: roman numerals | roman | i ii iii
```

lessons.title: Academic documents in Word: citations, references (APA/Harvard), footnotes, captions and formatting a project
lessons.body:
# Academic documents in Word: citations, references (APA/Harvard), footnotes, captions and formatting a project

Research proposals, projects, theses, reports and assignments at college and university follow strict formatting rules: title pages, preliminary pages, chapters, citations, reference lists, footnotes, figure captions, page numbering and plagiarism checks. Word has tools that automate most of this. This unit shows how to format a complete academic document professionally and ethically.

:::note What you will learn
- The structure of a typical research project/proposal
- Why and when to cite; avoiding plagiarism (including AI misuse)
- Citation styles: APA and Harvard basics
- Word's Citations & Bibliography tools; reference managers (Zotero, Mendeley)
- Footnotes and endnotes
- Captions, lists of figures/tables, cross-references
- Page setup and numbering for academic work
- Final checks before submission
:::

## Typical structure of a research project

| Part | Contents |
|---|---|
| **Title page** | Title, your name and registration number, institution, department, "A research project submitted in partial fulfilment...", month and year |
| **Declaration** | Statement that the work is yours, signatures (student and supervisor) |
| **Dedication / Acknowledgements** | Optional thanks |
| **Abstract** | 250–350 word summary: problem, objectives, methods, key findings, conclusion |
| **Table of contents, list of tables, list of figures, abbreviations** | Generated automatically |
| **Chapter 1: Introduction** | Background, problem statement, objectives, research questions, justification, scope, limitations |
| **Chapter 2: Literature review** | What others have found; theoretical framework; research gap |
| **Chapter 3: Methodology** | Research design, population, sampling, data collection instruments, analysis, ethics |
| **Chapter 4: Findings/results and discussion** | Data presentation (tables, charts) and interpretation |
| **Chapter 5: Summary, conclusions and recommendations** | |
| **References** | All sources cited |
| **Appendices** | Questionnaires, interview guides, budget, work plan, letters |

Always follow **your institution's guidelines**, which override general advice (fonts, spacing, margins, citation style).

Typical requirements: Times New Roman 12 pt, 1.5 or double line spacing, margins of about 2.5–3 cm (larger left margin for binding), justified or left-aligned text, roman numerals for preliminary pages and arabic numbers from Chapter 1.

## Citing sources and avoiding plagiarism

**Citing** means acknowledging the sources of ideas, data, quotations and images you use.

Why:
- **Honesty:** presenting others' work as yours is plagiarism, a serious academic offence (can lead to failing or discontinuation).
- **Credibility:** shows your work is based on evidence.
- **Traceability:** readers can find your sources.

What needs citing: direct quotes, paraphrased ideas, statistics, theories, images, tables and diagrams from others. Common knowledge (e.g. "Nairobi is the capital of Kenya") doesn't.

### Paraphrasing properly

Rewrite the idea **in your own words and structure**, then cite. Changing a few words is still plagiarism.

### AI tools and academic integrity

Using AI to write sections you submit as your own work is generally treated as academic misconduct unless your institution explicitly allows it (and requires disclosure). AI can also invent fake references ("hallucinated" citations). If allowed, use AI for brainstorming or checking grammar, verify every fact and source yourself, and disclose use as your institution requires.

### Plagiarism checkers

Institutions use tools like **Turnitin** to compare your work against published sources and other submissions. A similarity score isn't automatically "plagiarism" (quotes and references match too), but large unreferenced matches are a problem.

## Citation styles: APA and Harvard basics

### APA (7th edition) in-text citations

- Paraphrase: (Wanjiru, 2023) or Wanjiru (2023) found that...
- Two authors: (Otieno & Kamau, 2022)
- Three or more authors: (Mwangi et al., 2021)
- Direct quote with page: (Wanjiru, 2023, p. 45)
- Organisation: (Kenya National Bureau of Statistics [KNBS], 2024), then (KNBS, 2024)

### APA reference list examples

```
Book:
Wanjiru, M. (2023). Digital entrepreneurship in East Africa. Nairobi University Press.

Journal article:
Otieno, P., & Kamau, J. (2022). Mobile money adoption among small traders in Kisumu.
    African Journal of Business Studies, 14(2), 45–62. https://doi.org/10.xxxx/xxxxx

Report by an organisation:
Kenya National Bureau of Statistics. (2024). Economic survey 2024. KNBS.

Web page:
Communications Authority of Kenya. (2025, March 10). Sector statistics report.
    https://www.ca.go.ke/...
```

Rules: alphabetical by author surname; **hanging indent** (first line at the margin, following lines indented); italicise book and journal titles as the style requires; include DOIs or URLs for online sources.

### Harvard (author-date)

Similar to APA; details vary by institution:
- In-text: (Wanjiru 2023) or (Wanjiru 2023, p. 45)
- Reference: Wanjiru, M. (2023) *Digital entrepreneurship in East Africa*. Nairobi: Nairobi University Press.

Other styles: **MLA** (humanities), **Chicago** (history, uses footnotes), **IEEE** (engineering, numbered [1]).

## Word's citation tools

**References** tab → **Citations & Bibliography**:

1. **Style:** choose APA (7th, if available), Harvard, MLA, Chicago, IEEE.
2. **Insert Citation → Add New Source:** choose type (book, journal article, website, report) and fill fields (author, title, year, publisher, URL).
3. Word inserts the in-text citation in the chosen style.
4. Reuse sources: Insert Citation shows your saved sources.
5. **Manage Sources:** edit or add details.
6. **Bibliography → References/Works Cited:** generates the list automatically at the cursor; update it when you add citations (click the list → Update Citations and Bibliography).

Check generated references carefully against your institution's style guide: Word's styles don't always match the latest editions exactly.

### Reference managers (recommended for big projects)

**Zotero** (free) and **Mendeley** (free) collect sources from browsers and PDFs, store them in libraries, and insert citations and bibliographies into Word/Google Docs via plugins. They save huge time for theses and journal articles.

## Footnotes and endnotes

- **Footnote:** a note at the bottom of the page; **endnote:** at the end of the document/chapter.
- References → **Insert Footnote** (`Ctrl+Alt+F`) / **Insert Endnote** (`Ctrl+Alt+D`).
- Numbers update automatically when you add or delete notes.
- Use for explanations, definitions or (in Chicago style) citations.

## Captions, lists and cross-references

- Right-click a table or figure → **Insert Caption**:
  - Tables: caption **above** ("Table 4.1: Respondents by age").
  - Figures: caption **below** ("Figure 4.2: Monthly sales trend").
- Include chapter numbers in captions: Caption → Numbering → Include chapter number (requires numbered Heading 1).
- References → **Insert Table of Figures**: generate the List of Tables and List of Figures.
- References → **Cross-reference**: "as shown in Table 4.1" stays correct if numbers change; update with `F9`.
- Always cite sources for figures/tables you didn't create ("Source: KNBS (2024)").

## Page setup and numbering

1. **Layout → Margins → Custom:** e.g. left 3.5 cm (binding), others 2.5 cm (follow your guidelines).
2. **Line spacing:** select all → 1.5 or 2.0 as required.
3. **Section breaks** (Layout → Breaks → Next Page) after the title page and after preliminary pages.
4. **Page numbers:** roman (i, ii) for preliminaries, arabic (1, 2) from Chapter 1, unlinked footers (see the Styles and table of contents lesson).
5. **Headings with styles** and an automatic table of contents.
6. Each chapter starting on a new page: Heading 1 style → Paragraph → Line and Page Breaks → **Page break before**.

## Final checks before submission

- [ ] Follows the institution's guidelines (fonts, spacing, margins, structure)
- [ ] Table of contents, lists of tables/figures updated (`Ctrl+A`, then `F9`)
- [ ] Every in-text citation appears in the references, and vice versa
- [ ] Reference list in the correct style, alphabetical, hanging indents
- [ ] Captions numbered correctly; sources cited for borrowed figures/tables
- [ ] Page numbering correct in each section
- [ ] Spelling and grammar checked (set the correct English variant); consistent tense and terminology
- [ ] Abstract within word limit
- [ ] Plagiarism/similarity check if required
- [ ] Exported to **PDF** (File → Save As → PDF, with "Create bookmarks using headings" option) and opened to verify

:::think A student's reference list contains a journal article the AI chatbot suggested, but they can't find it anywhere online. What should they do?
Remove it. AI tools sometimes generate convincing but non-existent references. Only cite sources you have actually found and read (through Google Scholar, library databases, journal websites or official reports). Citing fake sources is academic misconduct.
:::

## Practice tasks

1. Set up a project template with a title page, declaration, abstract, table of contents and five chapter headings.
2. Add five sources (book, journal article, report, website, thesis) with Word's citation tool in APA style and generate a reference list.
3. Insert two tables and two figures with captions, then generate lists of tables and figures.
4. Add a footnote and a cross-reference.
5. Set roman numerals for preliminary pages and arabic numbers from Chapter 1.

## Summary

- Academic documents follow a standard structure and your institution's specific guidelines.
- Cite all borrowed ideas, data, quotes and images; paraphrase properly; plagiarism (including misuse of AI) is serious.
- APA/Harvard use author–date citations and alphabetical reference lists with hanging indents.
- Word's Citations & Bibliography tools and reference managers (Zotero, Mendeley) automate citations.
- Use footnotes/endnotes, captions, lists of figures/tables and cross-references.
- Set margins, spacing, section breaks and page numbering correctly; check everything and submit as PDF.

```quiz
Q: In APA style, how do you cite a source with three or more authors in text? Write the Latin abbreviation used.
A: et al. | et al
Q: Which indent is used in APA reference lists?
A: hanging | hanging indent
Q: Do table captions go above or below the table?
A: above
Q: Which Word tab contains Citations & Bibliography?
A: References
Q: Which shortcut inserts a footnote? Write like Ctrl+Alt+F.
A: Ctrl+Alt+F | ctrl alt f
Q: Name one free reference manager.
A: Zotero | Mendeley
Q: Should you cite a reference you cannot find or verify? (yes or no)
A: no
```

lessons.title: Page layout, headers, page numbers and printing
lessons.body:
# Page layout, headers, page numbers and printing

Reports, proposals, project documents and CVs are judged partly on how they **look on the page**. This lesson covers the layout tools that make documents look professional in Microsoft Word (and the same ideas in Google Docs and LibreOffice Writer).

## Page setup (Layout tab)

| Setting | Typical choice | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Paper size** | A4 (standard in Kenya), not Letter | Layout → Size |
| **Orientation** | Portrait; Landscape for wide tables | Layout → Orientation |
| **Margins** | Normal (2.54 cm) or as your college requires | Layout → Margins |
| **Columns** | 1; 2–3 for newsletters | Layout → Columns |

> Documents downloaded from the internet are often set to **Letter** size, which prints with odd gaps on A4 paper. Always check Size → A4 before printing.

## Headers, footers and page numbers

- **Insert → Header / Footer**: text that repeats on every page (document title, organisation name, confidentiality notice).
- **Insert → Page Number**: choose position (e.g. bottom centre). Use **Format Page Numbers** for "Page 1 of 10" or roman numerals.
- **Different first page** (in Header & Footer tools): no header on a cover page.

## Section breaks: different layouts in one document

A report often needs a cover page with no number, preliminary pages numbered i, ii, iii, then chapters numbered 1, 2, 3, and maybe one landscape page for a big table.

1. Put the cursor where the new part starts.
2. **Layout → Breaks → Section Break (Next Page)**.
3. In the new section's header/footer, turn off **Link to Previous**.
4. Change page number format or orientation for just that section.

| Break | Does |
|---|---|
| Page break (**Ctrl + Enter**) | Starts a new page, same section |
| Section break (Next Page) | New page and a new section with its own settings |
| Column break | Moves text to the next column |

> Never press Enter many times to reach a new page: when you edit earlier text, everything shifts. Use Ctrl + Enter.

## Paragraph spacing and line spacing

**Home → Paragraph** dialog:

- **Line spacing**: 1.15 or 1.5 is comfortable; many colleges require 1.5 or double for assignments.
- **Spacing before/after**: e.g. 6 pt after each paragraph instead of pressing Enter twice.
- **Indentation**: first-line indent or hanging indent (for references).
- **Keep with next**: stops a heading being left alone at the bottom of a page.

## Professional touches

| Feature | Where |
|---|---|
| **Cover page** | Insert → Cover Page |
| **Footnotes** | References → Insert Footnote (Alt + Ctrl + F) |
| **Captions** for figures and tables | References → Insert Caption, then Insert Table of Figures |
| **Watermark** ("DRAFT", "CONFIDENTIAL") | Design → Watermark |
| **Page borders** | Design → Page Borders (use rarely) |
| **Citations and bibliography** | References → Insert Citation, Bibliography (APA, Harvard...) |

## Printing and PDFs

1. **File → Print** (Ctrl + P) shows a **preview**: check every page before printing.
2. Choose pages (e.g. `1-3, 5`), copies, one-sided or **double-sided**, and pages per sheet.
3. To share a document that must look the same everywhere, **File → Save As → PDF** (or Export → Create PDF).

PDFs keep fonts and layout fixed and can't be casually edited, which makes them right for CVs, invoices, reports and applications.

## Checklist before submitting a report

- [ ] A4, correct margins
- [ ] Consistent heading styles and an automatic table of contents
- [ ] Page numbers (none on the cover)
- [ ] Figures and tables captioned
- [ ] Spell check done (F7), names and figures double-checked
- [ ] Saved as PDF if submitting online

```quiz
Q: Which paper size is standard in Kenya?
A: A4
Q: Which shortcut inserts a page break?
A: Ctrl + Enter | ctrl+enter
Q: What must you turn off in a new section's header to give it different page numbers? (three words)
A: Link to Previous | link to previous
Q: Which file format keeps a document looking the same on every device?
A: PDF
Q: Which break lets one page be landscape while others are portrait? (two words)
A: section break
```

lessons.title: Writing a CV, cover letter and formal letters: layout, content and examples
lessons.body:
# Writing a CV, cover letter and formal letters: layout, content and examples

Your CV and cover letter are often the only things an employer sees before deciding whether to call you. Formal letters are still used for applications, complaints, requests to schools, banks, county offices and employers. This unit shows you exactly how to write and format a modern CV, a strong cover letter and standard formal letters in Word or Google Docs, with examples tailored to the Kenyan job market.

:::note What you will learn
- What a CV is for and how employers read it (seconds, and sometimes software)
- CV sections in order, with examples of strong wording
- Formatting a clean, ATS-friendly CV in Word/Docs
- Mistakes that get CVs rejected
- Writing a targeted cover letter
- Formal letter layout (block format), with an example
- Saving, naming and sending applications
:::

## How employers read CVs

- Recruiters often scan a CV in **seconds** at first, looking for relevant job titles, skills, education and achievements.
- Many organisations use **Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS)**: software that reads CVs and filters them by keywords. Complicated layouts (text boxes, columns, images, tables for layout) can confuse ATS and lose information.
- So a good CV is **clear, relevant, easy to scan and simple to parse**.

## CV sections (in order)

### 1. Contact details (top)

```
WANJIKU KAMAU
Nairobi, Kenya · 0712 345 678 · wanjiku.kamau@gmail.com · linkedin.com/in/wanjikukamau
```

- Name in larger bold text.
- Phone (in a format employers can call), professional email, town (full address not needed), LinkedIn/portfolio link.
- **Don't include:** ID number, date of birth, marital status, religion, tribe, photo (unless specifically requested). This protects your privacy and avoids bias.

### 2. Professional summary (3–4 lines)

Who you are, your key skills and what you offer, tailored to the job:

> Accounting graduate (BCom, Finance) with internship experience in M-Pesa reconciliation, invoicing and QuickBooks. Skilled in Excel (pivot tables, XLOOKUP) and detail-oriented reporting. Seeking an accounts assistant role in a growing SME.

### 3. Skills

Group relevant skills; match words from the job advert (truthfully):

```
Technical: QuickBooks, Excel (pivot tables, XLOOKUP, charts), iTax filing, Google Workspace
Professional: financial reporting, reconciliation, customer service, time management
Languages: English (fluent), Kiswahili (fluent)
```

### 4. Work experience (most recent first)

For each role: job title, organisation, location, dates, then **3–5 bullet points of achievements**, not just duties.

```
Accounts Intern · Mavuno Hardware Ltd, Thika · Jan 2026 – Jun 2026
- Reconciled daily M-Pesa and bank transactions for 3 branches, reducing month-end errors.
- Prepared 120+ customer invoices monthly in QuickBooks.
- Built an Excel stock report that cut weekly reporting time from 3 hours to 45 minutes.
```

**Weak:** "Responsible for invoices." **Strong:** "Prepared 120+ invoices monthly in QuickBooks with 99% accuracy."

Use action verbs: *prepared, managed, organised, built, improved, reduced, trained, led, analysed, designed, sold, resolved*. Add numbers where possible (how many, how much, how fast).

No formal experience? Include **internships, attachments, volunteering, church/community roles, freelance work, school leadership, projects** (e.g. "Built a website for a local salon").

### 5. Education

```
Bachelor of Commerce (Finance) · Kenyatta University · 2022 – 2025 · Second Class Upper
Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) · Moi Forces Academy · 2021 · B+
```

Most recent first. For experienced professionals, education can come after experience; for fresh graduates, it can come before.

### 6. Certifications and training

Short courses, professional exams (CPA sections), Google/Microsoft certificates, Ajira Digital/Jitume training, first aid.

### 7. Optional sections

Projects, achievements/awards, volunteer work, publications, interests (only if relevant or interesting, e.g. "Captain, university chess club").

### 8. Referees

Two or three people who can confirm your work or character (supervisors, lecturers), with title, organisation, phone and email. **Ask permission first.** If space is tight, "Referees available on request" is acceptable unless the advert asks for referees.

## Formatting a clean CV in Word or Google Docs

| Element | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Length | **1 page** for students/graduates; **2 pages** for experienced professionals |
| Font | Calibri, Arial, Cambria or similar, 10.5–12 pt; headings 13–16 pt |
| Margins | 1.5–2.5 cm |
| Headings | Bold, maybe a thin line below (Borders → Bottom border) |
| Layout | Single column; avoid text boxes, images, icons for key information, and complicated tables (ATS-friendly) |
| Spacing | Consistent space between sections; use paragraph spacing, not empty lines |
| Bullets | Simple round bullets; consistent punctuation |
| Dates | Consistent format ("Jan 2026 – Jun 2026"), right-aligned with a right tab |
| File | Save as **PDF** unless the employer asks for Word; name it `CV-Wanjiku-Kamau.pdf` |

### Right-aligning dates with a tab

1. Type the job title and organisation.
2. Set a **right tab stop** at the right margin (click the tab selector on the ruler until it shows the right tab, then click near the right edge).
3. Press `Tab` and type the dates: they line up neatly on every line.

### Templates

Word (File → New → search "resume") and Google Docs (Template gallery) have CV templates. Choose simple ones; heavily designed templates with columns and graphics may not pass ATS.

## Common CV mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Spelling and grammar errors | Spell check + read aloud + ask someone to proofread |
| Unprofessional email | `firstname.lastname@...` |
| Generic CV for every job | Tailor the summary and skills to each advert |
| Duties instead of achievements | Action verbs + results + numbers |
| Too long (4+ pages) or crowded | 1–2 pages, white space |
| Personal details (ID, tribe, religion) | Remove them |
| Lying or exaggerating | Never: background checks and interviews expose it |
| Photos and fancy graphics | Simple, readable layout (unless photos are requested) |
| Sending `.docx` that looks broken on other devices | Send PDF |

## The cover letter

A cover letter (or application letter) explains **why you want this job** and **why you're a good fit**. Keep it to **one page**, 3–4 paragraphs.

```
Wanjiku Kamau
Nairobi · 0712 345 678 · wanjiku.kamau@gmail.com

2 October 2026

The Human Resources Manager
Mavuno Hardware Ltd
P.O. Box 1234-01000, Thika

Dear Hiring Manager,

RE: APPLICATION FOR ACCOUNTS ASSISTANT POSITION (REF: AA/2026/04)

I am writing to apply for the Accounts Assistant position advertised on
your website on 28 September 2026. As a Finance graduate with hands-on
experience in M-Pesa reconciliation and QuickBooks, I am confident I can
support your finance team from day one.

During my internship at a three-branch hardware business, I reconciled
daily M-Pesa and bank transactions, prepared over 120 invoices monthly,
and built an Excel stock report that reduced reporting time by 75%.
I enjoy accurate, organised work and solving problems with data.

I am particularly drawn to Mavuno Hardware's growth across Kiambu County,
and I would welcome the opportunity to contribute to efficient financial
operations as you expand.

My CV is attached for your consideration. I am available for an interview
at your convenience and can be reached on 0712 345 678.

Yours faithfully,

Wanjiku Kamau
```

Tips:
- **Address a person** if you can find the name ("Dear Ms. Wambui"); then close with "Yours sincerely". If you use "Dear Sir/Madam" or "Dear Hiring Manager", close with "Yours faithfully" (British convention common in Kenya).
- Reference the specific job and where you saw it.
- Show you researched the organisation.
- Match 2–3 of their requirements with evidence.
- Don't repeat your whole CV.

## Formal letters (block format)

Used for requests, complaints, resignations, applications to institutions and official communication.

```
[Your address]
P.O. Box 5678-00100
Nairobi

[Date]
2 October 2026

[Recipient's title and address]
The Principal
Highway Secondary School
P.O. Box 910-00200
Nairobi

[Salutation]
Dear Sir/Madam,

[Subject line, bold or underlined]
RE: REQUEST FOR TRANSFER LETTER FOR JOHN KAMAU (ADM. NO. 4521)

[Body: purpose first, details, request/action]
I am writing to request a transfer letter for my son, John Kamau, Form 2B,
Admission Number 4521, as our family is relocating to Eldoret in November.

I would be grateful if the letter, together with his academic report
for Term 2, could be ready by 25 October 2026.

Thank you for your assistance.

[Complimentary close]
Yours faithfully,

[Signature]

[Name]
Mary Wanjiru (Parent)
0722 000 000
```

Formatting: everything left-aligned (block format), one blank line (or paragraph spacing) between parts, a clear subject line, and a polite, concise tone.

### Common formal letter types

| Letter | Key content |
|---|---|
| Request | What you need, why, by when |
| Complaint | What happened (facts, dates, reference numbers), impact, what resolution you want |
| Resignation | Position, last working day (per notice period), thanks, handover offer |
| Recommendation request | Who you are, what it's for, deadline, attach CV/details |
| Internship/attachment application | Course, institution, period required, skills, attach introduction letter |

:::think A graduate sends the same CV and letter starting "Dear Sir" to 50 companies without changing anything. Why might they get few responses, and what would improve them?
Generic applications don't show fit for the specific role, often miss keywords that ATS and recruiters look for, and "Dear Sir" can seem careless. Tailoring the summary, skills and cover letter to each advert (keywords, the company's needs, the exact job title and reference) significantly improves the chances.
:::

## Sending applications

- Follow instructions exactly (email subject format, file type, reference number, deadline, portal).
- Name files clearly: `CV-Wanjiku-Kamau.pdf`, `Cover-Letter-Wanjiku-Kamau-AA-2026-04.pdf`.
- Email body: short and professional (see the email lesson); mention the attachments.
- Keep a spreadsheet of where you applied, dates and follow-ups.
- Beware of job scams: never pay to apply (see the scams lesson).

## Practice tasks

1. Write your professional summary (3–4 lines) for a job you want.
2. Rewrite three duties from your experience as achievements with action verbs and numbers.
3. Build a one-page ATS-friendly CV with right-aligned dates using a right tab.
4. Write a tailored cover letter for a real job advert.
5. Write a formal complaint letter about a delayed delivery, with a reference number and requested resolution.

## Summary

- A CV must be clear, relevant, scannable and ATS-friendly: contacts, summary, skills, experience (achievements), education, certifications, referees.
- Use action verbs and numbers; tailor to each job; remove personal details like ID and tribe; keep 1–2 pages; send as PDF.
- Cover letters are one page: the job and where you saw it, why you fit (evidence), why this organisation, and a polite close.
- Formal letters use block format: addresses, date, salutation, subject line, concise body, complimentary close and name.
- Follow application instructions, name files clearly and avoid job scams.

```quiz
Q: How long should a graduate's CV usually be? (pages)
A: 1 | one | 1 page
Q: What does ATS stand for? Write the first word.
A: Applicant
Q: Should you include your ID number and tribe on a CV? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: Which file format should you usually send your CV in?
A: PDF | pdf
Q: If a letter starts "Dear Sir/Madam", how should it close (British convention)? (two words)
A: Yours faithfully
Q: Which tab stop aligns dates to the right margin on a CV?
A: right | right tab
Q: Should CV bullet points list duties or achievements?
A: achievements
```

lessons.title: Tables and mail merge: organising information and sending personalised letters in bulk
lessons.body:
# Tables and mail merge: organising information and sending personalised letters in bulk

Tables organise information clearly in documents: timetables, price lists, invoices, schedules, comparison charts and forms. **Mail merge** is a powerful time-saver: write one letter and automatically produce hundreds of personalised copies (invitations, fee reminders, certificates, offer letters, labels and envelopes) using names and details from a spreadsheet. This unit teaches both step by step in Microsoft Word, with notes for Google Docs.

:::note What you will learn
- Inserting and drawing tables; adding and deleting rows and columns
- Formatting tables: styles, borders, shading, alignment, widths
- Merging and splitting cells; repeating header rows
- Converting text to tables; simple formulas and sorting in Word tables
- What mail merge is and where it's used
- Preparing the data source in Excel
- Running a mail merge: letters, emails, labels and certificates
- Rules and fields (IF...THEN...ELSE), formatting merged numbers and dates
:::

## Part 1: Tables

### Inserting a table

1. **Insert → Table** → drag across the grid to choose columns × rows, or **Insert Table** to type exact numbers.
2. Type in the first cell; press **Tab** to move to the next cell (Tab in the last cell adds a new row); **Shift+Tab** moves back.

**Google Docs:** Insert → Table → choose size.

### Changing the structure

Click in the table: Word shows **Table Design** and **Layout** tabs.

| Task | How (Layout tab or right-click) |
|---|---|
| Insert rows/columns | Insert Above/Below/Left/Right (or hover at the edge and click the ⊕) |
| Delete rows/columns/table | Delete → Rows/Columns/Table |
| Merge cells | Select cells → Merge Cells (e.g. a title across the top) |
| Split cells | Split Cells → choose columns/rows |
| Column width | Drag borders, or AutoFit → AutoFit Contents / AutoFit Window |
| Distribute evenly | Distribute Rows / Distribute Columns |
| Cell alignment | Alignment group (e.g. align centre vertically) |
| Text direction | Text Direction (vertical headers) |

### Formatting tables

- **Table Design → Table Styles:** professional colour schemes in one click; tick **Header Row**, **Banded Rows** (alternating shading) and **Total Row** options.
- **Borders and shading:** select cells → Borders/Shading.
- **Repeat header rows:** select the header row → Layout → **Repeat Header Rows**, so long tables show headers on every page.
- **Prevent rows breaking across pages:** Table Properties → Row → untick "Allow row to break across pages".
- **Numbers:** right-align number columns; decimal tabs can line up decimals.

### Converting text to a table (and back)

If you have text separated by tabs or commas (e.g. pasted from elsewhere):
1. Select it → **Insert → Table → Convert Text to Table**.
2. Choose the separator (tabs, commas).

Layout → **Convert to Text** does the reverse.

### Sorting and simple formulas

- **Sort:** Layout → **Sort** (by a column, ascending/descending; tick "Header row").
- **Formula:** Layout → **Formula** → `=SUM(ABOVE)` totals a column; `=SUM(LEFT)` totals a row. Word formulas don't update automatically: select and press **F9**. For serious calculations, use Excel and paste/link the table.

### Example: an invoice table

| Item | Qty | Unit price (KSh) | Amount (KSh) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Website design (5 pages) | 1 | 25,000 | 25,000 |
| Domain (.co.ke, 1 year) | 1 | 1,200 | 1,200 |
| Hosting (1 year) | 1 | 6,000 | 6,000 |
| **Total** | | | **32,200** |

Format: header row shaded, numbers right-aligned, total row bold, borders light.

:::tip Tables for layout vs data
In Word, tables are also useful for layout (e.g. a form with label and answer columns, or a signature block), with borders hidden. On websites, layout tables are bad practice, but in documents they're fine.
:::

## Part 2: Mail merge

### What is mail merge?

:::define Mail merge
A feature that combines a **main document** (a letter, email, label or certificate template) with a **data source** (a list of names and details, usually in Excel) to produce many personalised documents automatically.
:::

| Use | Example |
|---|---|
| Schools | Fee balance letters to 600 parents with each student's name, class and balance |
| Businesses | Personalised offers or statements to customers |
| Events | Invitations, name badges, certificates of attendance |
| HR | Offer letters, payslip notices |
| Churches/chamas | Contribution statements, meeting invitations |
| Shipping | Address labels and envelopes |

Without mail merge, you'd type or edit each letter manually: slow and error-prone.

### Step 1: Prepare the data source (Excel)

| FirstName | LastName | Class | Balance | Phone |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Amina | Hassan | Grade 9A | 12500 | 0712000001 |
| Brian | Otieno | Grade 8B | 0 | 0712000002 |
| Chebet | Kiprono | Grade 9A | 4200 | 0712000003 |

Rules:
- **One header row** with simple names (no spaces is easiest: `FirstName`, `Balance`).
- One record per row; no blank rows or merged cells.
- Keep numbers as numbers; format phone numbers as text to keep leading zeros.
- Save and **close** the Excel file before merging.

### Step 2: Write the main document

Write the letter normally, leaving places for personal details:

```
Dear Parent/Guardian of ______,

Our records show a fee balance of KSh ______ for ______ (Class ______)...
```

### Step 3: Run the merge in Word

1. **Mailings → Start Mail Merge → Letters** (or E-mail Messages, Envelopes, Labels).
2. **Select Recipients → Use an Existing List** → choose the Excel file → choose the sheet (tick "First row of data contains column headers").
3. Optional: **Edit Recipient List** to filter (e.g. only students with Balance > 0) or sort.
4. Place the cursor where a detail goes → **Insert Merge Field** → choose `FirstName`, etc. Fields appear as «FirstName».
5. **Preview Results** to see real data; use the arrows to check several records.
6. **Finish & Merge:**
   - **Edit Individual Documents** → creates one new document with all letters (review, save or print).
   - **Print Documents** → print directly.
   - **Send Email Messages** → sends personalised emails (requires Outlook set up, choose the email field and subject).

Your merged letter:

```
Dear Parent/Guardian of «FirstName» «LastName»,

Our records show a fee balance of KSh «Balance» for «FirstName» (Class «Class»)
as at 2 October 2026. Kindly clear the balance by 31 October 2026 through
the school paybill.
```

### Rules: personalise further

**Mailings → Rules** adds logic:
- **If...Then...Else:** e.g. if `Balance` = 0, print "Thank you for clearing all fees."; otherwise, print the balance reminder.
- **Skip Record If:** don't produce letters for some records (e.g. Balance equals 0).
- **Fill-in / Ask:** prompt for a value at merge time.

### Formatting numbers and dates in merges

Merged numbers sometimes lose formatting (12500 instead of 12,500). Fix with field codes:
1. Right-click the field → **Toggle Field Codes** → you'll see `{ MERGEFIELD Balance }`.
2. Change it to `{ MERGEFIELD Balance \# "#,##0" }` for thousands separators (or `\# "#,##0.00"` for decimals).
3. For dates: `{ MERGEFIELD DueDate \@ "d MMMM yyyy" }` shows "31 October 2026".
4. Right-click → Update Field, then Toggle Field Codes back.

### Labels and certificates

- **Labels:** Mailings → Start Mail Merge → **Labels** → choose the label brand/size (matching your label sheets) → select recipients → insert fields in the first label → **Update Labels** (copies the layout to all labels) → Finish & Merge.
- **Certificates:** design one certificate (landscape, borders, logo), insert «FullName» and «Course» fields, merge to individual documents, then export to PDF.

### Google Docs alternatives

Google Docs doesn't have built-in mail merge for letters in the free version; options include Google Workspace mail merge features in Gmail (for some editions), or add-ons/extensions for Docs and Sheets. Many people do mail merges in Word with an Excel or Google Sheets (downloaded) data source.

:::think A school merges fee letters but every balance shows as "12500" without commas, and some parents with zero balance still get reminder letters. How would you fix both problems?
Add a number format switch to the field (`\# "#,##0"`) so balances show as 12,500. Use **Edit Recipient List** to filter out records where Balance equals 0, or a **Skip Record If** rule, or an **If...Then...Else** rule that prints a thank-you message instead of a reminder.
:::

### Privacy and accuracy

- Mail merges often use personal data (names, phones, balances): store the data securely and use it only for the intended purpose (Data Protection Act).
- **Preview and spot-check** before printing or emailing hundreds of documents; a mistake repeated 500 times is embarrassing and costly.
- For emails, send a **test** to yourself first.

## Practice tasks

1. Create a weekly timetable table with merged header cells, repeated header row and banded rows.
2. Build an invoice table with a `=SUM(ABOVE)` total and right-aligned numbers.
3. Create an Excel list of 10 people and mail merge personalised event invitations.
4. Add an If...Then...Else rule that changes the message based on a value.
5. Make a page of address labels from the same list.

## Summary

- Tables: insert, add/delete rows and columns, merge/split cells, table styles, repeat header rows, convert text to tables, sort and simple formulas (F9 to update).
- Mail merge combines a template with a data source to create personalised letters, emails, labels and certificates.
- Prepare clean Excel data (one header row, no blanks), then Mailings → Start Mail Merge → Select Recipients → Insert Merge Fields → Preview → Finish & Merge.
- Use Rules (If...Then...Else, Skip Record If) and field switches for number/date formats.
- Protect personal data and preview before printing or sending.

```quiz
Q: Which key moves to the next cell in a Word table?
A: Tab
Q: Which option shows the header row on every page of a long table? (three words)
A: Repeat Header Rows
Q: Which Word table formula totals the numbers above?
A: =SUM(ABOVE) | SUM(ABOVE)
Q: In mail merge, what is the list of names and details called? (two words)
A: data source
Q: Which Word tab contains mail merge commands?
A: Mailings
Q: Which mail merge rule prints different text depending on a value?
A: If...Then...Else | If Then Else | IF
Q: Which field switch adds thousands separators? Write it like \# "#,##0".
A: \# "#,##0" | #,##0
```

lessons.title: Track changes, comments and working on documents together
lessons.body:
# Track changes, comments and working on documents together

In offices, NGOs and group assignments, documents pass between several people. **Track Changes** and **Comments** show who changed what, so nothing is lost and the final version is agreed.

## Track Changes (Review tab)

1. **Review → Track Changes** (Ctrl + Shift + E) to turn it on.
2. Every insertion, deletion and formatting change is now marked, in a different colour for each person.
3. Choose the view in **Display for Review**:
   - **All Markup**: see every change
   - **Simple Markup**: clean text with a red line where changes are
   - **No Markup**: preview the final result
   - **Original**: the document before changes

## Accepting and rejecting changes

- **Review → Next / Previous** to move between changes.
- **Accept** or **Reject** each one, or use the arrow under Accept for **Accept All Changes**.
- The final version should have **no remaining tracked changes or comments** before you send it outside the organisation, otherwise readers can see all earlier edits.

> Before sending a document to a client or an employer, use **File → Info → Check for Issues → Inspect Document** to find hidden comments, tracked changes and personal information.

## Comments

- Select text → **Review → New Comment** (Ctrl + Alt + M).
- Use **@mention** (e.g. @Wanjiku) in Microsoft 365 to notify a colleague by email.
- **Reply** to discuss, and **Resolve** when done.

Good comments are specific: "Please add the 2025 enrolment figures here" is better than "incomplete".

## Compare two versions

Someone edited a copy without Track Changes? **Review → Compare → Compare** shows the differences between the original and the revised document as tracked changes.

## Real-time co-authoring

When the file is saved in **OneDrive** or **SharePoint** (Microsoft 365), or when you use **Google Docs**, several people can edit at the same time. You see their cursors, and changes save automatically.

| Tool | Share | Version history |
|---|---|---|
| Word + OneDrive | Share button → people or link | File → Info → Version History |
| Google Docs | Share → add emails, set Viewer/Commenter/Editor | File → Version history |

Permission levels:

- **Viewer**: can only read.
- **Commenter**: can add comments and suggestions.
- **Editor**: can change everything.

Google Docs' **Suggesting mode** (pencil icon → Suggesting) works like Track Changes.

## Protecting a document

- **Review → Restrict Editing**: allow only comments or form filling.
- **File → Info → Protect Document → Encrypt with Password**: needed to open it. Don't lose the password: it can't be recovered.
- Mark as Final to discourage casual edits.

## A simple team workflow

1. One person creates the document from a template and shares it.
2. Everyone writes in their assigned section, with Track Changes on (or in Suggesting mode).
3. The lead reviews, accepts or rejects changes, and resolves comments.
4. Final check: Inspect Document, spell check, page numbers, table of contents update.
5. Export to PDF for submission; keep the Word file as the editable master.

Name versions clearly: `Proposal_v3_2026-09-28.docx`, not `final final 2.docx`.

```quiz
Q: Which keyboard shortcut turns Track Changes on or off in Word?
A: Ctrl + Shift + E | ctrl+shift+e
Q: Which view shows the document as if all changes were accepted? (two words)
A: No Markup | no markup
Q: Which Word feature finds hidden comments and personal information? (two words)
A: Inspect Document | inspect document
Q: Which Google Docs mode works like Track Changes?
A: Suggesting | suggesting mode
Q: Which permission level lets someone comment but not edit?
A: Commenter
```

lessons.title: Excel and Google Sheets basics: the interface, data entry, formatting and working efficiently
lessons.body:
# Excel and Google Sheets basics: the interface, data entry, formatting and working efficiently

Excel is the computer skill employers in Kenya ask for most often, from banks, SACCOs and NGOs to supermarkets, schools and county offices. It's used for records, budgets, reports, payroll, stock, marks, data analysis and dashboards. This first unit builds a solid foundation: the interface, entering and editing data efficiently, formatting numbers properly, managing sheets, and keyboard shortcuts that make you fast. Everything works in Google Sheets too (differences are noted).

:::note What you will learn
- Why Excel matters and who uses it
- The interface: ribbon, Name Box, formula bar, sheets, status bar
- Entering, editing and filling data quickly (AutoFill, Flash Fill)
- Data types: text, numbers, dates, and why "numbers stored as text" break formulas
- Number formats: currency, comma, percentage, dates, custom formats
- Rows, columns, sheets: inserting, deleting, hiding, freezing
- Navigation and selection shortcuts
- Good spreadsheet design habits
:::

## Why Excel?

- **Universal:** almost every organisation uses spreadsheets.
- **Powerful:** from simple totals to analysing hundreds of thousands of rows.
- **Valuable on a CV:** "Advanced Excel" (formulas, lookups, pivot tables, charts) is a frequent requirement for accounting, admin, data, HR, procurement, M&E and sales roles.
- **Freelance demand:** data cleaning, dashboards and spreadsheet automation are common paid jobs online.

| Who | Uses Excel for |
|---|---|
| Accountants, bookkeepers | Ledgers, reconciliations (bank and M-Pesa), financial statements |
| Shop and business owners | Sales, stock, expenses, profit |
| Teachers and school admins | Marks, rankings, fee balances, timetables |
| HR officers | Staff records, leave, payroll calculations |
| NGOs and researchers | Survey data, M&E indicators, reports |
| Chama officials | Contributions, loans, interest, dividends |
| Analysts | Dashboards, forecasts, pivot tables |

## The interface

| Part | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Ribbon** | Tabs: Home (formatting), Insert (charts, tables), Page Layout, Formulas, Data (sort, filter, validation), Review, View |
| **Name Box** | Shows the selected cell address (e.g. `C5`); type an address and press Enter to jump there |
| **Formula bar** | Shows/edits the cell's real content (formula or value) |
| **Grid** | Columns A, B, C... (up to XFD: 16,384 columns) and rows 1, 2, 3... (over 1 million rows) |
| **Sheet tabs** | Worksheets at the bottom: rename, colour, move, add (+) |
| **Status bar** | Shows **Sum, Average, Count** of selected cells instantly |

:::tip Quick totals without formulas
Select a range of numbers and look at the **status bar**: Excel shows the Sum, Average and Count immediately. Right-click the status bar to add Min and Max.
:::

## Entering and editing data

| Action | How |
|---|---|
| Confirm and move down / right | `Enter` / `Tab` |
| Edit a cell | Double-click, `F2`, or the formula bar |
| Cancel editing | `Esc` |
| New line inside a cell | `Alt+Enter` |
| Fill the same value into many cells | Select cells, type, press `Ctrl+Enter` |
| Copy cell above | `Ctrl+D` (fill down); `Ctrl+R` fills right |
| Undo / redo | `Ctrl+Z` / `Ctrl+Y` |
| Today's date / current time | `Ctrl+;` / `Ctrl+Shift+;` |

### AutoFill

Drag the **fill handle** (small square at the bottom-right of the selection) to continue patterns:
- `Mon` → Tue, Wed...; `January` → February...; `Term 1` → Term 2...
- `1, 2` (select both) → 3, 4, 5...; `5, 10` → 15, 20...
- Formulas copy with adjusted references.
- **Double-click** the fill handle to fill down as far as the adjacent column has data.

### Flash Fill (Excel)

Excel learns a pattern from your example (`Ctrl+E`):

| Full name | First name |
|---|---|
| Wanjiku Kamau | **Wanjiku** (type this one) |
| Brian Otieno | → Ctrl+E fills "Brian" |
| Amina Hassan | → "Amina" |

Great for splitting names, extracting codes, combining columns or reformatting phone numbers. (Google Sheets offers "Smart Fill" suggestions.)

## Data types

| Type | Default alignment | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Text** | Left | `Unga 2kg`, `0712345678` (as text) |
| **Number** | Right | `180`, `0.16`, `1250.5` |
| **Date/time** | Right | `02/10/2026`, `14:30` (stored as numbers behind the scenes) |
| **Boolean** | Centre | `TRUE`, `FALSE` |
| **Error** | Centre | `#DIV/0!`, `#N/A` |

### Numbers stored as text (a very common problem)

Data copied from websites, systems or CSV files often contains numbers stored as **text**: they align left, show a small green triangle, and `SUM` ignores them.

Fixes:
- Select → click the warning icon → **Convert to Number**.
- **Data → Text to Columns → Finish** (converts a whole column).
- Multiply by 1 or use `=VALUE(A2)`.
- Remove spaces or "KSh" text with Find & Replace (`Ctrl+H`).

### Dates are numbers

Excel stores dates as serial numbers (days since 1 January 1900), which is why you can subtract them (`=B2-A2` gives days between dates). If a date shows as a number like `46297`, apply a date format. Make sure dates are recognised as dates (right-aligned) and use your regional format consistently (day/month/year in Kenya).

## Number formatting

Formatting changes how a value **looks**, not the value itself. **Home → Number** group, or `Ctrl+1` (Format Cells).

| Format | Shows | Shortcut |
|---|---|---|
| General | As typed | `Ctrl+Shift+~` |
| Number with comma | 1,250.00 | `Ctrl+Shift+!` |
| Currency/Accounting | KSh 1,250.00 (choose the KES symbol) | |
| Percentage | 16% | `Ctrl+Shift+%` |
| Short/long date | 02/10/2026 / Friday, 2 October 2026 | `Ctrl+Shift+#` |
| Text | Keeps leading zeros (phone numbers, IDs) | |

### Custom formats

Format Cells → **Custom**:
- `"KSh "#,##0` → KSh 12,500
- `#,##0.00;[Red]-#,##0.00` → negatives in red
- `0000` → 0045 (fixed digits for codes)
- `dd-mmm-yyyy` → 02-Oct-2026

:::warning Don't type units into numbers
Typing `KSh 180` or `180/-` makes the cell **text** and breaks formulas. Type `180` and use a currency or custom format.
:::

## Formatting for readability

- **Bold header row** with fill colour; **wrap text** for long headers.
- **AutoFit** columns: double-click the boundary between column letters (or select all and double-click).
- **Borders** for printed tables.
- **Alignment:** text left, numbers right, headers centred.
- **Cell styles** (Home → Cell Styles) for consistent headings, totals, inputs.
- **Format as Table** (`Ctrl+T`): instant banded rows, filters and structured references (covered in the Tables lesson).

## Rows, columns and sheets

| Task | How |
|---|---|
| Select a column/row | Click its letter/number; `Ctrl+Space` / `Shift+Space` |
| Insert row/column | Right-click header → Insert; `Ctrl+Shift++` |
| Delete row/column | Right-click → Delete; `Ctrl+-` |
| Hide/unhide | Right-click → Hide / Unhide |
| Resize | Drag the boundary, or AutoFit |
| Freeze headers | View → Freeze Panes → Freeze Top Row (or freeze at a selected cell for rows and columns) |
| New sheet | `+` beside the tabs; `Shift+F11` |
| Rename sheet | Double-click the tab |
| Move/copy sheet | Drag the tab (hold `Ctrl` to copy), or right-click → Move or Copy |
| Switch sheets | `Ctrl+PgUp` / `Ctrl+PgDn` |

## Navigation and selection shortcuts

| Shortcut | Does |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl+Arrow` | Jump to the edge of the data |
| `Ctrl+Shift+Arrow` | Select to the edge of the data |
| `Ctrl+Home` / `Ctrl+End` | Go to A1 / the last used cell |
| `Ctrl+A` | Select the current data region (press again for the whole sheet) |
| `Ctrl+G` or `F5` | Go To (a cell or named range) |
| `Ctrl+F` / `Ctrl+H` | Find / Replace |
| `Ctrl+1` | Format Cells |
| `Alt` | Shows key tips for every ribbon command |

Using these daily is what makes people "fast in Excel".

## Good spreadsheet design habits

1. **One table per sheet** (or clearly separated), starting at A1, with **one header row**.
2. **One record per row, one type of data per column** (don't mix dates and text in a column).
3. **No blank rows or columns** inside data; no merged cells in data tables (they break sorting and filtering).
4. **Inputs separate from calculations:** put rates (VAT 16%, commission 5%) in labelled cells and reference them.
5. **Consistent formats** (dates, currency).
6. **Name sheets clearly** ("Sales Jan 2026", "Summary").
7. **Document assumptions** with notes or a "Read me" sheet.
8. **Save versions** and back up (OneDrive/Google Drive).

:::think A colleague's sales sheet has the title in merged cells across A1:F1, blank rows between each week, and prices typed like "KSh 1,500". Why will sorting, filtering and SUM give problems, and how would you fix it?
Merged cells and blank rows stop Excel from recognising the table as one continuous range, so sorting/filtering break or miss rows. Prices typed with "KSh" are text, so SUM ignores them. Fix: put the title above (or remove the merge), delete blank rows, make one header row, convert prices to real numbers (Find & Replace "KSh " with nothing, then Convert to Number) and apply a currency format.
:::

## Excel vs Google Sheets: quick differences

| Feature | Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Works offline | Yes | Limited (offline mode) |
| Collaboration | Via OneDrive/SharePoint | Excellent, real-time, free |
| Saving | Manual/AutoSave | Automatic |
| Advanced features | Power Query, Power Pivot, more chart types | Simpler, some unique functions (`GOOGLEFINANCE`, `IMPORTRANGE`, `QUERY`) |
| Cost | Paid (Microsoft 365) | Free |

## Practice tasks

1. Create a sheet of 15 products with columns: Code, Product, Category, Price, Stock. Format prices as KSh with commas.
2. Use AutoFill to create a list of 12 months and a numbered list 1–50.
3. Use Flash Fill to split 10 full names into first and last names.
4. Paste numbers stored as text (e.g. from a website) and convert them to real numbers.
5. Freeze the header row, rename the sheet, and practise `Ctrl+Arrow` navigation.

## Summary

- Excel is essential for records, analysis and reports across Kenyan workplaces; Google Sheets is a free, collaborative alternative.
- Know the interface: ribbon, Name Box, formula bar, sheet tabs, status bar (quick Sum/Average/Count).
- Enter data quickly with Enter/Tab, `Ctrl+Enter`, AutoFill and Flash Fill (`Ctrl+E`).
- Understand data types; fix numbers stored as text; dates are numbers.
- Format numbers (comma, currency, percentage, dates, custom) without typing units.
- Manage rows, columns and sheets; freeze panes; use navigation shortcuts.
- Design clean tables: one header row, no blank rows or merged cells, inputs separate from calculations.

```quiz
Q: Which shortcut opens the Format Cells dialog?
A: Ctrl+1 | ctrl 1
Q: Which shortcut triggers Flash Fill in Excel?
A: Ctrl+E | ctrl e
Q: Which shortcut adds a new line inside a cell?
A: Alt+Enter | alt enter
Q: Where can you see the sum of selected cells without a formula? (two words)
A: status bar
Q: Numbers stored as text align to which side by default?
A: left
Q: Which shortcut enters today's date? Write like Ctrl+;.
A: Ctrl+; | ctrl ;
Q: Which View option keeps the header row visible when scrolling? (two words)
A: Freeze Panes | freeze top row
Q: Should you merge cells inside a data table you want to sort? (yes or no)
A: no
```

lessons.title: Formulas and cell references: relative, absolute and mixed
lessons.body:
# Formulas and cell references: relative, absolute and mixed

The real power of a spreadsheet is that one formula can be copied down hundreds of rows. To do that correctly you must understand **cell references**, the most important concept in Excel and Google Sheets.

## Formulas recap

Every formula starts with `=`:

| Formula | Result |
|---|---|
| `=B2*C2` | Multiply two cells |
| `=SUM(D2:D10)` | Add a range |
| `=D11*16%` | 16% of a cell |
| `=(B2+C2)/2` | Brackets control the order |

Order of operations: brackets, then `^` (power), then `*` and `/`, then `+` and `-`.

## Relative references (the default)

In this price list, D2 has `=B2*C2`:

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Item | Price | Qty | Total |
| 2 | Unga | 180 | 3 | `=B2*C2` → 540 |
| 3 | Sugar | 160 | 2 | `=B3*C3` → 320 |
| 4 | Oil | 350 | 1 | `=B4*C4` → 350 |

When you copy D2 down (drag the **fill handle**, the small square at the cell's corner, or double-click it), Excel **adjusts** the references: row 3 gets `=B3*C3`. That's a **relative** reference: it means "the cell two to the left, on my row".

## Absolute references: $ locks a cell

Now add VAT using a rate stored in one cell, **F1 = 16%**. In E2 you type `=D2*F1` and copy down... row 3 becomes `=D3*F2`, which is empty. Wrong!

Lock the rate with dollar signs: `=D2*$F$1`. Now every row uses F1.

| | D | E (VAT) | | F |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Total | VAT | | **16%** |
| 2 | 540 | `=D2*$F$1` → 86.40 | | |
| 3 | 320 | `=D3*$F$1` → 51.20 | | |

> Shortcut: after typing a reference, press **F4** to cycle through `F1` → `$F$1` → `F$1` → `$F1`.

## Mixed references

| Reference | Column | Row | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `B2` | changes | changes | Normal row-by-row formulas |
| `$B$2` | fixed | fixed | One constant cell (rate, target) |
| `$B2` | fixed | changes | Always read column B, any row |
| `B$2` | changes | fixed | Always read row 2, any column |

Classic example: a **multiplication table** or a **price grid**. In B2, `=$A2*B$1` copied across and down multiplies each row header by each column header.

## Referencing other sheets

```
=Prices!B2                (cell B2 on the sheet called Prices)
=SUM('Term 1'!C2:C40)     (quote sheet names that contain spaces)
```

## Named ranges: easier to read

Select F1, type a name like `VAT` in the **Name Box** (left of the formula bar) and press Enter. Now write `=D2*VAT`: clear, and automatically absolute.

## Common errors and what they mean

| Error | Meaning | Usual fix |
|---|---|---|
| `#DIV/0!` | Dividing by zero or an empty cell | `=IFERROR(A2/B2, 0)` or check B2 |
| `#VALUE!` | Text where a number is expected | Remove spaces/letters from numbers |
| `#REF!` | A referenced cell was deleted | Undo, or fix the formula |
| `#NAME?` | Misspelled function or name | Check spelling: `=SUM`, not `=SUMM` |
| `#N/A` | Lookup value not found | See the Lookups lesson |
| `######` | Column too narrow | Widen the column |

Show all formulas at once with **Ctrl + `** (the key left of 1), great for checking a sheet.

## Practice

Build a fee sheet: columns Name, Fee, Paid, Balance (`=B2-C2`), and a **% paid** column `=C2/B2` formatted as a percentage. Add a cell with a late-payment penalty rate and a Penalty column that uses it with an absolute reference.

```quiz
Q: What symbol locks a column or row in a cell reference?
A: $ | dollar sign
Q: Which key cycles through $F$1, F$1 and $F1 after typing a reference?
A: F4
Q: You copy =B2*C2 down one row. What does it become?
A: =B3*C3 | B3*C3
Q: Which error appears when dividing by zero?
A: #DIV/0! | DIV/0
Q: Which reference always reads column B but lets the row change: $B2 or B$2?
A: $B2
```

lessons.title: Essential functions: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MIN, MAX, ROUND, IF, COUNTIF and SUMIF
lessons.body:
# Essential functions: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MIN, MAX, ROUND, IF, COUNTIF and SUMIF

Functions are what make spreadsheets powerful. Instead of adding 200 numbers by hand, you write `=SUM(B2:B201)`. Instead of checking each student's result, `=IF(C2>=50,"Pass","Fail")` decides for you. This unit teaches the essential functions every Excel user needs, how function syntax works, and practical examples from shops, schools, chamas and offices.

:::note What you will learn
- How functions work: name, brackets, arguments, ranges
- Inserting functions (typing, AutoSum, Insert Function)
- SUM, AVERAGE, MEDIAN, MIN, MAX, LARGE, SMALL
- COUNT, COUNTA, COUNTBLANK
- ROUND, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN, INT
- IF basics and nested IF
- COUNTIF, SUMIF, AVERAGEIF and their -IFS versions
- RANK and percentage calculations
- Common errors and how to read them
:::

## How functions work

```
=SUM(B2:B10)
 │   │
 │   └ argument: the range B2 to B10
 └ function name
```

- Start with `=`, then the function name, then **arguments** in brackets.
- Separate arguments with **commas** (some regional settings use semicolons `;`).
- A **range** like `B2:B10` means "B2 through B10"; `B2:D10` is a rectangle.
- Non-adjacent ranges: `=SUM(B2:B10, D2:D10)`.

### Ways to insert functions

1. **Type** it: Excel suggests functions as you type and shows a tooltip with the arguments.
2. **AutoSum** (Home → Σ, or `Alt+=`): inserts SUM; its dropdown has Average, Count, Max, Min.
3. **Insert Function** (`fx` button or `Shift+F3`): search for a function and fill arguments in a dialog with explanations.

## Totals and averages

| Function | Does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `SUM` | Adds numbers | `=SUM(D2:D31)` monthly sales |
| `AVERAGE` | Mean | `=AVERAGE(C2:C41)` class average |
| `MEDIAN` | Middle value (less affected by extremes) | `=MEDIAN(E2:E100)` typical salary |
| `MIN` / `MAX` | Smallest / largest | `=MAX(D2:D31)` best day |
| `LARGE(range, k)` | k-th largest | `=LARGE(C2:C41, 3)` third-highest mark |
| `SMALL(range, k)` | k-th smallest | `=SMALL(D2:D31, 1)` same as MIN |

Example: daily sales in `B2:B8`.

| | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Day | Sales (KSh) |
| 2 | Mon | 12,400 |
| 3 | Tue | 9,850 |
| 4 | Wed | 15,200 |
| 5 | Thu | 11,000 |
| 6 | Fri | 18,600 |
| 7 | Sat | 22,300 |
| 8 | Sun | 7,500 |
| 10 | Total | `=SUM(B2:B8)` → 96,850 |
| 11 | Average | `=AVERAGE(B2:B8)` → 13,835.71 |
| 12 | Best day | `=MAX(B2:B8)` → 22,300 |
| 13 | Worst day | `=MIN(B2:B8)` → 7,500 |

:::tip AVERAGE ignores blanks but counts zeros
An empty cell is skipped by `AVERAGE`; a cell containing 0 is included. If a day had no sales recorded, decide whether to leave it blank (not included) or enter 0 (included and lowers the average).
:::

## Counting

| Function | Counts | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `COUNT` | Cells containing **numbers** | `=COUNT(C2:C41)` students with marks entered |
| `COUNTA` | **Non-empty** cells (any type) | `=COUNTA(A2:A41)` number of students listed |
| `COUNTBLANK` | Empty cells | `=COUNTBLANK(C2:C41)` missing marks |

## Rounding

| Function | Does | Example (A2 = 1234.567) |
|---|---|---|
| `ROUND(x, n)` | Rounds normally to n decimals | `=ROUND(A2, 2)` → 1234.57; `=ROUND(A2, 0)` → 1235; `=ROUND(A2, -2)` → 1200 |
| `ROUNDUP(x, n)` | Always up | `=ROUNDUP(A2, 0)` → 1235 |
| `ROUNDDOWN(x, n)` | Always down | `=ROUNDDOWN(A2, 0)` → 1234 |
| `INT(x)` | Down to the whole number | `=INT(A2)` → 1234 |
| `MROUND(x, m)` | To the nearest multiple | `=MROUND(1237, 5)` → 1235 |

Formatting a cell to show 2 decimals only changes the **display**; `ROUND` changes the **value** (important for totals that must match receipts).

Example: number of buses needed for 130 people with 33 seats: `=ROUNDUP(130/33, 0)` → 4.

## IF: making decisions

```
=IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false)
=IF(C2>=50, "Pass", "Fail")
```
