# AI for business, study and earning

## Business

- **Marketing**: captions, product descriptions, ad copy, blog outlines, content calendars.
- **Customer service**: draft replies to common questions; FAQ pages; WhatsApp message templates.
- **Admin**: meeting summaries, letters, quotations, simple contracts to review with a lawyer.

## Study

- Ask for explanations at your level, then ask it to **quiz you**.
- Turn notes into flashcards and practice questions.
- Get feedback on your essay's structure (but write it yourself).
- Learn to code: paste an error message and ask what it means.

## Earning with AI skills

- Offer social media management for small businesses, using AI to work faster.
- Writing and editing services (always edit AI drafts to be accurate and natural).
- Data entry and cleaning with AI-assisted Excel.
- Building simple websites and chatbots.

## Responsible use checklist

- ✔ Check facts, numbers and names.
- ✔ Keep private and client data out of public tools.
- ✔ Be honest when work is AI-assisted if your school, client or employer requires it.
- ✔ Add your own knowledge, local context and voice. That's what clients pay for.

```quiz
Q: Which Canva feature set includes AI image and design tools? (two words)
A: Magic Studio
Q: Should you check facts and numbers in AI answers? (yes or no)
A: yes
Q: What is the main thing clients pay for that AI can't replace? (your own knowledge, context and …)

```

lessons.title: AI safety, ethics, privacy and your career
lessons.body:
# AI safety, ethics, privacy and your career

AI is changing how people work, learn and get information. Using it responsibly protects you, the people you work with, and your future career. This lesson covers the risks, the ethics, and how to stay valuable in an AI world.

## How AI chatbots work (in one paragraph)

Large language models (LLMs) learn patterns from huge amounts of text and predict likely next words. That's why they're fluent and helpful, and also why they can be **confidently wrong**: they generate plausible text, which isn't the same as checked facts. Newer tools can search the web, read files or run code, but you're still responsible for the result.

## Main risks and what to do

| Risk | What it looks like | Protect yourself |
|---|---|---|
| **Wrong information** | Invented facts, laws, fees, references | Verify with official or primary sources |
| **Privacy leaks** | Pasting ID numbers, client data, passwords | Don't share personal or confidential data; check privacy settings |
| **Bias** | Unfair assumptions about gender, ethnicity, age | Question outputs; review decisions affecting people |
| **Deepfakes** | Fake voices and videos of real people | Verify unusual requests by calling back on a known number |
| **AI-powered scams** | Perfectly written phishing, cloned voices of relatives | Use a family "safe word"; never send money on a voice note alone |
| **Over-reliance** | Can't do the work without AI | Keep practising core skills |
| **Copyright** | Copying protected text, images, code | Use your own work and properly licensed material |

## Deepfakes and voice cloning

Scammers can clone a voice from a short clip and call pretending to be a child, parent or boss asking for urgent M-Pesa. Defences:

- Hang up and **call back** on the number you already have.
- Agree a **family code word** for emergencies.
- Be suspicious of urgency and secrecy.
- Remember video and audio can be faked; check with other sources.

## Ethics: using AI fairly

1. **Be honest** about AI use in school and work where it matters.
2. **Don't harm or deceive**: no fake reviews, impersonation, harassment or misinformation.
3. **Respect privacy and consent**, including other people's photos and data (Kenya Data Protection Act).
4. **Keep humans in charge** of important decisions about people: hiring, loans, grades, medical care.
5. **Credit sources** and respect creators.

## Using AI at work

- Check your employer's AI policy before using tools with company data.
- Use approved/business versions for confidential work where available.
- You are accountable for anything you send, publish or deploy, even if AI drafted it.
- Keep records of important AI-assisted decisions.

## Your career in an AI world

AI is best at **tasks**; people are still needed for **judgement, relationships, context and responsibility**. To stay valuable:

| Build | Why |
|---|---|
| Strong fundamentals (maths, writing, coding, networking) | You can check and improve AI output |
| Domain knowledge (agriculture, health, finance, education) | AI needs someone who understands the real problem |
| Communication and teamwork | Clients and managers trust people |
| AI skills: prompting, automation, evaluating outputs | Makes you much more productive |
| Ethics and good judgement | Increasingly valued as AI spreads |

Jobs growing with AI include AI-assisted content and design, data labelling and quality review, automation for small businesses, AI trainers and prompt/workflow specialists, and developers building AI into apps.

## A personal AI checklist

- [ ] I verify important facts and test code.
- [ ] I don't paste private or confidential data.
- [ ] I follow my school's or employer's AI rules.
- [ ] I label or disclose AI use where it matters.
- [ ] I practise core skills without AI too.

```quiz
Q: What does LLM stand for? (three words)
A: large language model | large language models
Q: A relative calls with a strange voice asking for urgent M-Pesa. What should you do first? (two words)
A: call back | hang up | verify
Q: Should AI make final decisions about hiring people without human review? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: Who is responsible for work you publish that AI helped draft?
A: me | you | I am | the person | yourself
Q: What is a fake video or voice of a real person made with AI called?
A: deepfake | a deepfake | deepfakes
```

lessons.title: eCitizen: creating an account and applying for government services online, step by step
lessons.body:
# eCitizen: creating an account and applying for government services online, step by step

**eCitizen** is the Government of Kenya's main online portal for public services: passports, good conduct certificates, business name registration, birth certificates, driving licence services, land searches and many more, with payment by M-Pesa or card. Using eCitizen confidently saves you queues, travel and middlemen, and helping others with it is a common cyber café and digital services business. This unit explains how eCitizen works, how to create and secure an account, and how to apply for common services safely.

:::warning Menus and fees change
Government portals are updated regularly. The steps and fees described here are a guide; always follow what the **official** site shows on the day, and confirm fees on the payment page. Use only official addresses ending in **.go.ke**.
:::

:::note What you will learn
- What eCitizen is and which agencies use it
- Creating an account and logging in securely
- Navigating services and the dashboard
- Paying with M-Pesa and getting receipts
- Step-by-step: good conduct certificate, passport, business name search/registration, birth certificate
- Tracking applications and downloading documents
- Avoiding fake sites and middleman scams
- Offering eCitizen help as a service (ethically)
:::

## What is eCitizen?

:::define eCitizen
The official Kenyan government digital services platform (ecitizen.go.ke) where citizens, residents, businesses and visitors access services from many government agencies through one account and pay online.
:::

Examples of services available through eCitizen (availability changes):

| Agency | Example services |
|---|---|
| **Directorate of Immigration** | Passport applications and renewals, visas and permits |
| **Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI)** | Police clearance (certificate of good conduct) |
| **Business Registration Service (BRS)** | Business name search and registration, company registration, annual returns |
| **Civil Registration** | Birth and death certificate applications |
| **NTSA** | Driving licence renewals, smart DL, vehicle transfers and searches |
| **Ministry of Lands** | Land searches and related services |
| **Many ministries and counties** | Licences, permits and fees |

## Creating an eCitizen account

You'll need: your **ID number** (or passport/alien ID), a **phone number** registered in your name, and an **email address**.

1. Go to **ecitizen.go.ke** (type it yourself) and choose **Create account / Sign up**.
2. Choose your account type (e.g. Kenyan citizen).
3. Enter your ID details as on the ID card, phone number and email.
4. Verify your phone/email with the code sent to you.
5. Set a **strong password** you don't use elsewhere.
6. Log in and complete your profile.

Tips:
- Use **your own** phone number and email: they're used for verification codes and notifications.
- Write down your login email/ID safely; enable any extra security options offered.

## Navigating eCitizen

After logging in, you'll typically see a **dashboard** listing agencies/services, your applications and payments. Choose an agency (e.g. DCI, Immigration, BRS), then the service. Many services open in that agency's section of the portal, using the same eCitizen login.

## Paying for services

1. After filling an application, you'll get an **invoice/payment page** showing the amount (includes any convenience fee).
2. Choose **M-Pesa** (usually via a paybill and account number/bill reference shown, or an STK push prompt to your phone) or a card.
3. Pay **exactly** as instructed: correct paybill and the bill reference/account number shown.
4. Wait for confirmation; the application status changes to paid.
5. **Download/print the receipt** and keep the M-Pesa confirmation SMS.

:::tip Keep records
Save PDFs of applications, invoices and receipts in a folder (e.g. `Documents/Government/2026`). If something goes wrong, the bill reference and M-Pesa code help support staff trace your payment.
:::

## Step by step: certificate of good conduct (police clearance)

Often required for jobs, further studies and travel.

1. Log in to eCitizen → choose **DCI** (Directorate of Criminal Investigations).
2. Select **Police Clearance Certificate** → apply (choose the purpose if asked).
3. Fill or confirm your details; submit.
4. **Pay** the fee shown via M-Pesa.
5. **Download the invoice/application form** if required and follow instructions for **fingerprint capture**: typically at a DCI office or designated centre (bring your ID and the printed form). Some processes have been updated over time; follow the latest instructions shown.
6. **Track** the status in your eCitizen account; when ready, download the certificate (and verify its authenticity using the method provided by the DCI, such as a QR code/serial).

## Step by step: passport application (overview)

1. Log in → **Directorate of Immigration** (or the immigration services section).
2. Choose the passport type (ordinary passport; number of pages) and **new application** or **renewal/replacement**.
3. Fill the form carefully: personal details, parents' details, contacts, previous passport (if any).
4. Upload required documents and photos as specified (e.g. ID copies, birth certificate for some applicants, recommender details or guarantor requirements, passport-size photos in the correct format).
5. **Pay** the fee shown.
6. **Book an appointment** (if required) at an immigration office/Huduma centre for biometrics (photo, fingerprints) and bring originals.
7. **Track** the status; collect the passport when notified (bring ID and the old passport for renewals).

Requirements differ for minors, renewals and lost passports; read the requirements list on the portal before starting.

## Step by step: business name search and registration (BRS)

1. Log in → **Business Registration Service**.
2. **Name search/reservation:** propose one or more names; pay the search fee; wait for approval (rejected if too similar to existing names or restricted words).
3. **Register:** choose business name registration (sole proprietor/partnership) or company registration; fill owners' details (ID, KRA PIN, contacts, address), nature of business.
4. Pay the registration fee; submit.
5. **Download the certificate** when approved. Then register for relevant **KRA obligations**, county business permits and other licences for your sector.

(The **Registering a business online** lesson covers this in depth.)

## Step by step: birth certificate (late/first registration or copies)

1. Log in → **Civil Registration Services** (or the relevant department).
2. Choose the service: application for a birth certificate (using the birth notification number from the hospital/registration), replacement, or correction.
3. Fill details exactly as in the birth notification; upload required documents (parents' IDs, notification).
4. Pay; track; collect from the designated registry or as instructed.

## Tracking applications

- Use the **dashboard/applications** section to see status: submitted, paid, under review, approved, ready for collection.
- Watch your **email and SMS** for notifications.
- If stuck for long: use the agency's official support channels (contact pages, Huduma Centres) with your application reference and M-Pesa code.

## Avoiding scams and mistakes

| Risk | Protection |
|---|---|
| **Fake websites** copying eCitizen | Type `ecitizen.go.ke` yourself; check the `.go.ke` ending |
| **Middlemen** who "fast-track" for extra money | Apply yourself; official fees are on the portal; extra "speed" payments may be bribery |
| **Sharing your login** with strangers | Never share your password/OTP; if a cyber café helps, type the password yourself and change it after |
| **Wrong details** (typos in names, ID numbers) | Double-check before paying; corrections cost time and money |
| **Paying the wrong paybill/reference** | Copy exactly from the invoice page |
| **Lost documents** | Download and back up receipts and certificates |

:::think A person on Facebook offers to get your good conduct certificate "in 24 hours without fingerprints" for KSh 3,000. What should you do?
Decline. It's either a scam (you lose the money) or a fake/irregular certificate that can be detected and get you into serious trouble with employers and the law. Apply through the official eCitizen DCI service and follow the official process.
:::

## Offering eCitizen services ethically (cyber cafés and digital agents)

Many people earn by helping others use eCitizen. Do it professionally:
- Display **official fees** and your **service fee** separately.
- Get the client's consent; let them enter passwords and OTPs, or help them change passwords afterwards.
- Never keep copies of clients' IDs and documents longer than needed; delete downloads from the computer.
- Never falsify information or documents.
- Know the processes well and keep up with changes.

## Practice tasks

1. Create (or review) your eCitizen account; update your password and contact details.
2. Explore the list of agencies on eCitizen and note five services relevant to you or your family.
3. Write down the steps and documents required for a good conduct certificate as currently shown on the portal.
4. Create a folder system for government documents and receipts.
5. Make a simple price list (official fee + service fee) for three services if you plan to offer help to others.

## Summary

- eCitizen (ecitizen.go.ke) provides many government services online through one account: immigration, DCI, BRS, civil registration, NTSA, lands and more.
- Create an account with your ID, phone and email; use a strong, unique password; never share OTPs.
- Fill forms carefully, pay the exact amount to the shown paybill/reference, and save receipts.
- Common services: good conduct (DCI), passports (Immigration), business names (BRS), birth certificates (civil registration).
- Track applications on the dashboard; use official support channels.
- Avoid fake sites, middlemen and falsification; offer help ethically.

```quiz
Q: What is the official eCitizen web address?
A: ecitizen.go.ke | www.ecitizen.go.ke
Q: Which agency issues the certificate of good conduct? (abbreviation)
A: DCI
Q: Which agency handles business name registration? (abbreviation)
A: BRS
Q: Which payment method is most commonly used on eCitizen?
A: M-Pesa | mpesa
Q: Should you pay a middleman to get a good conduct certificate without fingerprints? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: What should you save after paying for a service? (one word)
A: receipt | receipts
```

lessons.title: KRA PIN and iTax returns: registering, filing nil and employment returns, and staying compliant
lessons.body:
# KRA PIN and iTax returns: registering, filing nil and employment returns, and staying compliant

Almost every adult in Kenya with an ID needs a **KRA PIN**: for jobs, bank accounts, SIM-related services, business registration, buying land or vehicles, and tenders. And every PIN holder is generally required to **file an annual income tax return** by **30 June**, even if they had no income (a "nil return"). Missing the deadline attracts penalties. This unit explains KRA, the PIN, iTax, how to file nil and employment returns step by step, and how freelancers and small businesses should think about tax.

:::warning Rules and menus change
Tax laws, rates, deadlines and the iTax interface change. This lesson explains the general process; always confirm current requirements on **kra.go.ke** / **itax.kra.go.ke**, or consult KRA or a tax professional for your situation.
:::

:::note What you will learn
- What KRA is and why taxes matter
- What a KRA PIN is and how to register for one
- Logging in to iTax and resetting your password
- Tax obligations: what they are
- Filing a nil return step by step
- Filing an employment income return with a P9 form
- Deadlines, penalties and compliance certificates
- Freelancers, side hustles and small businesses: what to know
:::

## KRA and why taxes matter

The **Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA)** collects taxes on behalf of the government. Taxes fund roads, schools, hospitals, security and public services. Main taxes you'll hear about:

| Tax | Who pays |
|---|---|
| **PAYE** (Pay As You Earn) | Employees (deducted from salary by the employer) |
| **Income tax** (individuals, companies) | People and businesses with taxable income |
| **Turnover Tax (TOT)** | Small businesses within a set turnover range (check current thresholds and rate) |
| **VAT** (Value Added Tax, standard 16%) | VAT-registered businesses charge it on sales |
| **Withholding tax** | Deducted at source on certain payments (e.g. some professional/consultancy fees) |
| **Rental income tax** | Landlords with residential rental income |
| **Excise duty, customs duty** | On specific goods and imports |

## The KRA PIN

:::define KRA PIN
A unique Personal Identification Number (letter + 9 digits + letter, e.g. A012345678Z) that identifies you or your business for all tax matters.
:::

You need it for employment, opening certain bank accounts, business registration, land and vehicle transactions, tenders and more.

### Registering for a KRA PIN (individual)

1. Go to **itax.kra.go.ke** (type it yourself).
2. Choose **New PIN Registration**.
3. Select **Taxpayer type: Individual** and **Mode: Online form**.
4. Enter your ID details (ID number, date of birth), contacts (email, phone) and address details as requested.
5. Choose **obligations** if asked (for most employed people: Income Tax - Resident Individual).
6. Submit; your PIN certificate is sent to your **email**. Download and keep it safely.

Tips: use **your own** active email (iTax sends passwords and certificates there). If you already have a PIN (many people were registered by employers or banks), don't create a second one: retrieve it instead.

## Logging in to iTax

1. Go to **itax.kra.go.ke**.
2. Enter your **KRA PIN** → Continue.
3. Enter your **password** and the security stamp (arithmetic question) → Log in.

**Forgot password:** click "Forgot Password/Unlock Account", enter your PIN, answer the security stamp; a new password is sent to your registered email. If you no longer have access to that email, you'll need to update it through KRA's support process.

Change the default password to a strong, unique one after logging in.

## Tax obligations

An **obligation** is a type of tax you're registered for, for example:
- **Income Tax - Resident Individual** (most individuals)
- **Income Tax - PAYE** (employers)
- **VAT**, **Turnover Tax**, **Residential Rental Income**

You file returns for each obligation you have. Wrong obligations cause confusion (e.g. a VAT obligation means monthly VAT returns are expected). If you have obligations you don't need, contact KRA about amending them.

## Filing a nil return (no income)

A **nil return** declares that you had no taxable income in the year (for example, students or unemployed people with a PIN). It must still be filed by **30 June** for the previous year (January–December).

Steps (typical flow):
1. Log in to iTax.
2. Go to **Returns** → **File Nil Return**.
3. Select the **Tax Obligation**: Income Tax - Resident Individual → Next.
4. The **return period** is shown (e.g. 01/01/2025 – 31/12/2025); confirm.
5. **Submit**.
6. Download the **e-Return Acknowledgement Receipt** and keep it.

:::warning Only file nil if you truly had no income
If you earned salary, business income, rent or other taxable income, filing a nil return is incorrect and can lead to penalties. Employees must file their employment income using their **P9** form.
:::

## Filing an employment income return (salaried employees)

If you're employed, your employer deducts PAYE monthly, but you still file an annual return to declare your income and the tax already deducted.

### What you need

- Your **P9 form** from each employer for the year (shows your gross pay, deductions, taxable pay and PAYE).
- Details of reliefs/exemptions if applicable (e.g. insurance relief, disability exemption certificate, pension contributions).
- Your iTax login.

### Steps (typical flow)

1. Log in → **Returns** → **File Return**.
2. Select **Income Tax - Resident Individual** → Next.
3. Choose the online form for employment income (KRA provides a simplified online form for employment-only income; others use the downloadable Excel form).
4. Enter the **return period**.
5. Enter **employer details and amounts from your P9**: employer PIN, gross pay, taxable pay, tax paid (PAYE). iTax may pre-fill data submitted by employers; **check it carefully against your P9**.
6. Add any reliefs/exemptions you qualify for (with supporting details).
7. Review the computation: tax due vs tax paid. Often the result is zero (PAYE already covered it); sometimes there's tax payable or a refund claim.
8. **Submit** and download the acknowledgement receipt.
9. If tax is payable, generate a **payment slip** and pay (via M-Pesa paybill or bank) using the payment registration number before the deadline.

Multiple employers in a year? Include all P9s. Side income (business, freelance, rent) needs additional sections or a different form; get guidance.

## Deadlines and penalties

| Item | Usual rule (confirm current law) |
|---|---|
| Individual income tax return | By **30 June** for the previous calendar year |
| Late filing | Penalties apply (KRA sets the amounts; for individuals, a fixed minimum or a percentage of tax due, whichever is higher) |
| Late payment | Penalty and interest on unpaid tax |
| Monthly returns (VAT, PAYE for employers, TOT) | Usually by the 20th of the following month |

File early: iTax gets very busy in the last days of June.

## Tax Compliance Certificate (TCC)

A **TCC** shows you've filed returns and paid taxes; it's required for many jobs (especially public service), tenders and licences. Apply on iTax (Certificates → Apply for Tax Compliance Certificate). It's issued if your returns and payments are up to date.

## Freelancers, side hustles and small businesses

Online income (Upwork, Fiverr, YouTube, transcription, design clients) and small business income are **taxable** like other income.

- **Keep records:** invoices, platform statements, M-Pesa statements, receipts for business expenses (data, equipment, rent).
- **Declare** income in your annual return under the appropriate section (business income), or register for the relevant regime (such as Turnover Tax for eligible small businesses), as advised.
- **Business registration:** register a business name (BRS via eCitizen) as you grow; open a separate business account/line.
- **eTIMS:** KRA has introduced electronic invoicing requirements (eTIMS) for many businesses; check whether they apply to you.
- **Get advice:** a qualified accountant or KRA's taxpayer support can confirm which taxes apply to your situation.

:::think A university student registered a KRA PIN to apply for an internship but never earned income. Do they need to file returns?
Generally yes: PIN holders are required to file an annual return by 30 June, and someone with no income files a **nil return**. Not filing can lead to penalties. If they start earning (internship stipend, freelance income), they must declare that income instead of filing nil.
:::

## Avoiding iTax scams

- KRA won't ask for your iTax password, M-Pesa PIN or OTPs by phone, SMS or email.
- "Tax refund" messages with links are common phishing: log in to iTax yourself to check.
- Use only `itax.kra.go.ke` and `kra.go.ke`.
- If a cyber café files for you, let them guide you but enter your password yourself, and change it afterwards.

## Practice tasks

1. Log in to iTax (or retrieve your PIN/password) and download your PIN certificate.
2. Check which obligations are on your PIN.
3. If you have no income, walk through filing a nil return and save the receipt.
4. If employed, request your P9 from your employer and identify gross pay, taxable pay and PAYE on it.
5. Set up a simple income and expense record for any side hustle.

## Summary

- KRA collects taxes; main taxes include PAYE, income tax, Turnover Tax, VAT and withholding tax.
- A KRA PIN (letter + 9 digits + letter) is needed for jobs, banking, business and property; register on itax.kra.go.ke.
- Log in with your PIN and password; reset via registered email.
- Obligations define which returns you file; most individuals have Income Tax - Resident Individual.
- Nil returns are for no income; employees file with their P9; deadline **30 June** for the previous year.
- Late filing and payment attract penalties; a TCC proves compliance.
- Freelancers and small businesses must keep records and declare income; get professional advice when unsure.

```quiz
Q: What is the official iTax website?
A: itax.kra.go.ke | https://itax.kra.go.ke
Q: By what date must individual income tax returns be filed? Write day and month.
A: 30 June | June 30 | 30th June
Q: What return do you file if you had no income?
A: nil return | nil | a nil return
Q: Which form from your employer shows your annual pay and PAYE?
A: P9 | P9 form
Q: What is Kenya's standard VAT rate? Write as a percentage.
A: 16% | 16
Q: Which certificate proves you are tax compliant? (abbreviation)
A: TCC
Q: Will KRA ask for your iTax password by phone? (yes or no)
A: no
```

lessons.title: Registering a business online and getting it ready to trade
lessons.body:
# Registering a business online and getting it ready to trade

Registering your hustle as a business makes it easier to open a business bank account, get a Till number, apply for tenders and LPOs, work with corporate clients and build trust. In Kenya most steps are done online through **eCitizen**. Requirements and fees change, so always confirm on the official sites before paying.

> Only pay through the official eCitizen payment page. Never send "registration fees" to an individual's phone number, and beware of fake "agents" and websites.

## 1. Choose a business type

| Type | In short | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **Business name** (sole proprietorship or partnership) | Registers the trading name; you and the business are legally the same | Small hustles, freelancers, shops |
| **Private limited company (Ltd)** | A separate legal entity; owners' personal assets are protected | Growing businesses, investors, tenders |
| **Limited Liability Partnership (LLP)** | Partners with limited liability | Professional firms |
| **Community group / CBO / chama** | Registered through the relevant government office | Self-help groups |

Get advice (e.g. from an accountant or a Huduma Centre) if you're unsure.

## 2. Register on eCitizen (Business Registration Service)

The general steps:

1. Log in at **ecitizen.go.ke** (create an account with your ID if you don't have one).
2. Go to the **Business Registration Service (BRS)**.
3. **Name search and reservation**: propose a few names; approval takes some time. Unique, simple names get approved faster.
4. Fill in the registration form: owners' details, business address, nature of business.
5. Upload the required documents (e.g. ID copies, passport photos, KRA PINs of owners).
6. **Pay** through eCitizen (M-Pesa is accepted).
7. Download your **certificate** once approved.

Companies also get a **CR12** (list of directors and shareholders), often requested by banks and clients.

## 3. KRA PIN and tax obligations

- The business (for companies) needs its own **KRA PIN**; sole proprietors use their personal PIN.
- Know which taxes apply: many small businesses fall under **Turnover Tax**; others under income tax; **VAT** registration is required above a turnover threshold.
- File returns on **iTax** on time, even NIL returns, to avoid penalties.

(See the *KRA iTax* lesson. Rules and thresholds change: check KRA's website or ask an accountant.)

## 4. County permits and licences

Most businesses need a **county single business permit** from their county government (many counties now apply online). Some sectors need extra licences: food handling, health, pharmacies, transport, liquor, etc.

## 5. Get paid professionally

- Open a **business bank account** (you'll need the certificate and KRA PIN).
- Apply for an M-Pesa **Till number** (Buy Goods) or **Paybill** for your business.
- Create simple **invoices and receipts** with your registered name and PIN.
- Keep records of all income and expenses (a spreadsheet is fine to start).

## 6. Get online

- A **Google Business Profile** so customers find you on Google Maps (see the Digital marketing tutorial).
- **WhatsApp Business** with a catalogue.
- A simple **website** and a professional email (`info@yourbusiness.co.ke`).

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Better |
|---|---|
| Paying "agents" outside eCitizen | Pay only through official channels |
| Not filing iTax returns because "there was no income" | File NIL returns |
| Mixing personal and business money | Separate accounts and records |
| Ignoring county permits | Check your county's requirements early |

```quiz
Q: Which government portal is used to register a business name or company online?
A: eCitizen | ecitizen.go.ke
Q: Which business type makes the business a separate legal entity: business name or limited company?
A: limited company | private limited company | Ltd
Q: Which document lists a company's directors and shareholders? (letters and numbers)
A: CR12
Q: Should you file tax returns even when there was no income? (yes or no)
A: yes
Q: Which county document do most businesses need to operate? (three words)
A: single business permit | business permit
```

lessons.title: KUCCPS, higher education funding (HELB/HEF), KNEC and other education services online
lessons.body:
# KUCCPS, higher education funding (HELB/HEF), KNEC and other education services online

Every year, hundreds of thousands of Kenyan students and parents navigate online systems for university and college placement, student funding, exam registration and results, and certificates. Mistakes (wrong course choices, missed deadlines, fake portals) can cost a year. This unit explains the main education services and how to use them carefully, with practical tips for students, parents and cyber café attendants who help them.

:::warning Policies change often
Placement rules, funding models, portals and deadlines have changed several times in recent years. Use this lesson as a guide to **what to look for**, and always confirm details on the **official** websites and announcements from the Ministry of Education and the relevant bodies.
:::

:::note What you will learn
- The education bodies and what each does
- KUCCPS: placement, course selection, cluster points, revision and inter-institution transfers
- Higher education funding: HELB loans, scholarships and the Higher Education Financing (HEF) portal
- KNEC: exam registration, results and certificate services
- TVET and other services
- Protecting student accounts and avoiding scams
:::

## The main bodies

| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| **Ministry of Education** | Policy for basic education, TVET and higher education |
| **KNEC** (Kenya National Examinations Council) | National exams (e.g. KCSE, KPSEA/KJSEA under CBC), results, certificates |
| **KUCCPS** (Kenya Universities and Colleges Central Placement Service) | Placing government-sponsored students into universities and TVET colleges |
| **HELB** (Higher Education Loans Board) | Student loans (and loan repayment for past beneficiaries) |
| **Universities Fund / scholarship bodies** | Scholarships and funding under current models |
| **TVETA**, **KNQA** and others | TVET accreditation, qualifications frameworks |
| **CUE** (Commission for University Education) | Accrediting universities and programmes (check that a programme is accredited before enrolling) |

## KUCCPS: university and college placement

### How placement works (overview)

1. After KCSE results, KUCCPS opens its **student portal** for course application/selection (dates are announced publicly).
2. Students log in, choose programmes (degree, diploma, certificate, artisan) in order of preference, based on their grades and each programme's requirements.
3. KUCCPS places students using merit (grades/cluster points), programme requirements, capacity and choices.
4. Results are published; students download **admission/placement letters** from the institution or portal and report as instructed.
5. A **revision** window often allows unplaced students or those wanting changes to re-apply for programmes with remaining slots.
6. **Inter-institution transfers** can be requested within set periods, with reasons.

### Logging in

- Use the official KUCCPS student portal (find it from **kuccps.ac.ke**, the official site).
- Typical login details include your **KCSE index number**, **year**, and a password (for first-time login, instructions are on the portal, sometimes using your birth certificate number or KCPE details).
- Pay any application fee only through the official method shown on the portal.

### Choosing courses wisely

1. **Check minimum requirements** (overall grade and subject grades) for each programme.
2. **Understand cluster points/cut-offs:** competitive programmes (medicine, engineering, law) have high cut-off points that vary each year; past cut-offs give an idea, not a guarantee.
3. **Spread your choices:** include realistic options (not only the most competitive programmes).
4. **Research careers:** job prospects, professional bodies (e.g. engineering and nursing registration require accredited programmes), and your interests.
5. **Consider TVET:** diplomas and certificates in technical fields (electrical, ICT, plumbing, hospitality, agriculture) lead to practical skills and jobs, and can progress to degrees.
6. **Check accreditation** (CUE for universities, TVETA for colleges).
7. **Location and costs:** accommodation, transport and fees.

:::think A student with a B- chooses only medicine and pharmacy at the most competitive universities. What's the risk, and what's a better strategy?
These programmes usually have very high cut-offs, so the student may not be placed in any choice and lose time. A better strategy is to include a mix: one or two ambitious choices, several programmes where their grades comfortably meet past cut-offs (e.g. related health sciences or diplomas leading to progression), and courses they'd genuinely be happy to study.
:::

## Higher education funding

Kenya's funding approach for university and TVET students changed in 2023 to a **student-centred funding model**, combining **government scholarships**, **HELB loans** and **household contributions**, based on a needs assessment. Students have applied through the **Higher Education Financing (HEF)** portal for this model. The model has faced legal and policy debates, so check the latest official guidance.

### General steps (typical)

1. Confirm your placement and admission.
2. Create an account on the official funding portal (HEF/HELB as directed for your cohort).
3. Fill in personal, family, income and education details **truthfully**; the needs assessment uses this information.
4. Upload required documents (ID, admission letter, parents' IDs or death certificates where applicable, etc.).
5. Submit before the deadline and track status.
6. Accept the award terms (loan agreement) and provide bank details as instructed.
7. Continuing students may need to apply again each year (subsequent loans).

### HELB loans: responsibilities

- Loans are repayable after studies (with interest and repayment terms set by HELB).
- Graduates should register and start repaying as required; defaulting leads to penalties and can affect credit records.
- Keep your contact details updated.

### Other funding sources

- County bursaries and ward development funds (application windows announced locally).
- NG-CDF bursaries (constituency).
- University and private scholarships (Equity Wings to Fly/Elimu, Mastercard Foundation partners, KCB, county government and others: check current programmes and eligibility).
- Never pay "agents" to get scholarships.

## KNEC services

| Service | How (typical) |
|---|---|
| **Exam registration** | Schools register candidates through KNEC systems; private candidates follow KNEC's published process |
| **Results** | Official results portal and SMS service announced each year (e.g. sending an index number to a KNEC short code) |
| **Certificates and replacements** | Through schools and KNEC procedures; replacements and confirmations follow formal processes with fees |
| **Verification of results** | Employers and institutions can verify through KNEC's official channels |

When results are released, the official channels are announced by the Ministry/KNEC; avoid links shared randomly on WhatsApp claiming to show "early results".

## Other student services

- **University portals:** fee statements, unit registration, timetables, exam cards, results. Change default passwords.
- **NHIF/SHA:** student health cover arrangements have changed with the transition from NHIF to the **Social Health Authority (SHA)** in 2024; follow your institution's guidance.
- **Student IDs and eCitizen services:** good conduct certificates for attachments, birth certificates, passports.
- **Attachment/internship placements:** institution portals, county and national internship programmes (apply only through official sites).

## Protecting student accounts and avoiding scams

| Scam | Reality |
|---|---|
| "Pay KSh 2,000 to change your course to medicine" | Placement changes happen only through official KUCCPS processes, not agents |
| "Guaranteed HELB/scholarship approval for a fee" | Funding decisions follow official assessments; agents can't buy approvals |
| Fake results websites | Use only official KNEC channels |
| Fake admission letters / fake universities | Verify with the institution, KUCCPS and CUE |
| Cyber café keeping your login | Change passwords after someone helps you |

Tips:
- Use **official websites** (`.go.ke`, `.ac.ke`, and the bodies' known domains).
- Keep **logins private**; use a strong password.
- **Download and save** placement letters, application confirmations and receipts.
- **Note deadlines** in your phone calendar.

## Helping students as a cyber café or digital agent

- Learn each process from official guides each year (they change).
- Explain options; let students make their own choices (don't push courses).
- Charge transparent service fees; never promise placement or funding outcomes.
- Protect personal data; log out and delete downloads.

## Practice tasks

1. Visit the official KUCCPS website and find the latest announcements and student portal link.
2. List five programmes you're interested in, with their minimum requirements and past cut-offs.
3. Find the current official guidance on higher education funding (HEF/HELB) for your cohort.
4. Write down the official channel for receiving national exam results this year.
5. Make a checklist of documents a student needs for funding applications.

## Summary

- KNEC runs exams and results; KUCCPS places government-sponsored students; HELB and the HEF portal handle loans and scholarships under the current funding model; CUE and TVETA accredit institutions.
- Choose courses using requirements, past cut-offs, accreditation, career prospects and a mix of ambitious and realistic options; consider TVET.
- Apply for funding truthfully, before deadlines, and repay loans responsibly.
- Use only official channels for placement, funding and results; save documents; never pay agents for guaranteed outcomes.

```quiz
Q: Which body places government-sponsored students in universities and colleges? (abbreviation)
A: KUCCPS
Q: Which body runs national examinations like KCSE? (abbreviation)
A: KNEC
Q: Which board provides student loans? (abbreviation)
A: HELB
Q: Which commission accredits universities? (abbreviation)
A: CUE
Q: Can an agent change your KUCCPS placement for a fee? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: In which year did Kenya introduce the student-centred university funding model?
A: 2023
```

lessons.title: SHA health cover, NSSF, NTSA and Huduma services: registering, paying and checking statements
lessons.body:
# SHA health cover, NSSF, NTSA and Huduma services: registering, paying and checking statements

Beyond eCitizen and KRA, Kenyans regularly deal with health insurance, retirement savings, driving licences, vehicle records and in-person government services. These systems have changed significantly in recent years (for example, **NHIF was replaced by the Social Health Authority (SHA)** in October 2024). This unit explains what each body does, how to register and check your status online, and how to avoid scams.

:::warning Always confirm current details
Registration channels, contribution rates and procedures for SHA, NSSF and NTSA have changed recently and may change again. Use this lesson to understand the services, then confirm current requirements on the official websites or offices.
:::

:::note What you will learn
- SHA: what it is, who must register, contributions and checking cover
- NSSF: retirement savings, statements and benefits
- NTSA: driving licences, vehicle searches and transfers through eCitizen
- Huduma Centres and other in-person services
- Keeping records and avoiding scams
:::

## Social Health Authority (SHA)

In **October 2024**, the **National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF)** was replaced by the **Social Health Authority (SHA)** under new health laws. SHA manages funds including the **Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF)**, a **Primary Healthcare Fund** and an **Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund**.

### Who registers

Kenyan residents are expected to register, including household members (spouse, children). Employees' contributions are typically deducted by employers; people in informal work contribute based on assessed income through the official process.

### How to register and check (typical channels)

- The official SHA website (**sha.go.ke**) and its registration portal.
- USSD (the official short code announced by SHA, e.g. *147#).
- Assistance at health facilities, Huduma Centres and SHA offices.

You'll typically need your ID number, phone number and dependants' details (birth certificate numbers for children). After registering, you can check your membership and contribution status through the official channels.

### Using cover

- Visit SHA-contracted facilities; you may need to verify your identity (and sometimes an OTP to your phone).
- Ask the facility which services are covered under SHA packages and whether any amount is payable by you.
- Keep receipts and records of treatment.

:::tip Keep your contributions up to date
Cover can depend on being registered and up to date with contributions. Check your status before planned treatment, and update dependants when your family changes.
:::

## National Social Security Fund (NSSF)

**NSSF** is a statutory retirement savings scheme: employees and employers contribute monthly, and members receive benefits on retirement (and in certain situations such as permanent disability, emigration or to survivors).

- Contributions are calculated under the **NSSF Act, 2013**, with rates and upper limits phased in over several years (amounts have increased in stages since 2024; check the current tier limits).
- Employers deduct and remit employee contributions.
- **Check your statement:** register on the NSSF self-service portal or use the official USSD/SMS services to confirm that your employer has remitted contributions. Missing contributions should be raised with your employer and NSSF.
- **Self-employed people** can register and contribute voluntarily.
- Consider additional retirement savings (registered personal pension schemes, employer pension schemes, SACCOs, money market funds) because NSSF alone may not be enough.

## National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA)

NTSA services are accessed through **eCitizen** (NTSA section), replacing the older TIMS system.

| Service | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Driving licence renewal** | Online through eCitizen; pay; the smart driving licence (DL) has replaced old red booklets for many drivers |
| **Smart DL application** | Apply online, pay, then visit an NTSA office/centre for biometrics and collection as instructed |
| **Provisional driving licence (PDL)** | For learners, through accredited driving schools |
| **Vehicle search** | Check ownership and details before buying a vehicle (pay a small fee) |
| **Vehicle transfer** | Seller initiates transfer; buyer accepts; fees paid online; requires both parties' accounts and documents |
| **Logbook services** | Duplicate logbooks, changes of particulars |
| **Inspection bookings** | For certain vehicle categories |

:::warning Before buying a used vehicle
Do an **official vehicle search** on eCitizen/NTSA to confirm the owner, logbook details and any caveats (e.g. financing by a bank). Do the transfer through the official system, and never pay the full amount before confirming the seller's identity and the vehicle's records.
:::

## Huduma Centres and other in-person services

**Huduma Centres** (in counties across Kenya) offer many government services under one roof: ID applications and replacements, birth certificates, NSSF/SHA/KRA help, good conduct fingerprinting (as designated), business services and more. Useful when you need help with online processes or in-person verification.

Other important services:
- **National ID** (Registration of Persons): new IDs at 18, replacements for lost IDs; Kenya has been rolling out the **Maisha Namba**/digital ID system, so check current procedures.
- **Civil registration:** births and deaths.
- **County services:** business permits, land rates, parking (often through county portals and M-Pesa paybills).

## Keeping records

| Document | Why |
|---|---|
| SHA registration confirmation and contribution statements | Proof of cover |
| NSSF statements | Proof of contributions for retirement and claims |
| Driving licence, logbook, NTSA search results | Vehicle ownership and legal driving |
| Receipts for all payments (M-Pesa messages, eCitizen receipts) | Disputes and audits |

Store digital copies in a secure cloud folder (with 2-Step Verification) and originals safely at home.

## Avoiding scams

- Use only official websites (`.go.ke` and the known official domains) and official short codes.
- No agent can "speed up" your SHA cover, NSSF benefits or driving licence for extra money outside official fees.
- Calls/SMS claiming your "SHA cover will be cancelled unless you pay to this number" are likely scams: check your status yourself through official channels.
- Don't share OTPs sent during SHA verification at hospitals with anyone except the facility system process you initiated.
- For vehicle purchases, beware of fake logbooks and "too cheap" deals.

:::think Your employer deducts NSSF from your payslip every month, but your NSSF statement shows no contributions for the last six months. What should you do?
Raise it with your employer's HR/payroll department first, with your payslips as evidence. If it isn't resolved, report it to NSSF (employers are legally required to remit deductions). Keep checking your statement regularly so problems are caught early.
:::

## Practice tasks

1. Check your SHA registration status through the official channel and confirm your dependants are listed.
2. Register on the NSSF self-service portal (or use the official USSD) and download or view your statement.
3. Log in to eCitizen and find the NTSA services list.
4. Write down the steps to do an official vehicle search before buying a car.
5. Create a secure folder for your health, pension, licence and vehicle documents.

## Summary

- SHA replaced NHIF in October 2024; register yourself and dependants, keep contributions up to date and check status through official channels before treatment.
- NSSF is statutory retirement savings; check statements regularly to confirm employer remittances; consider additional savings.
- NTSA services (licences, vehicle searches and transfers) run through eCitizen; always search vehicles before buying.
- Huduma Centres provide many services in person.
- Keep records, use official channels, and avoid agents and scam messages.

```quiz
Q: Which body replaced NHIF in October 2024? (abbreviation)
A: SHA
Q: Which body manages statutory retirement savings? (abbreviation)
A: NSSF
Q: Through which portal are NTSA services like licence renewal accessed?
A: eCitizen | ecitizen
Q: What should you do before buying a used vehicle? (two words: an official ...)
A: vehicle search | search
Q: Where can you get many government services under one roof? (two words)
A: Huduma Centre | Huduma Centres | Huduma
Q: If your employer deducts NSSF but your statement shows nothing, who should you contact first?
A: employer | your employer | HR
```

lessons.title: Online applications: documents, good conduct and avoiding mistakes
lessons.body:
# Online applications: documents, good conduct and avoiding mistakes

Jobs, scholarships, HELB loans, KUCCPS placement, passports, the Certificate of Good Conduct, business permits: more and more applications happen online. Most rejections and delays come from avoidable mistakes. This lesson is a practical guide to doing them right the first time.

## Prepare a digital document folder

Create a folder on Google Drive (and a copy on your phone) with clear, **scanned** copies:

| Document | Tips |
|---|---|
| National ID (both sides) | Clear, all corners visible |
| KRA PIN certificate | Download from iTax |
| Passport photo | Plain light background, recent, as a JPG |
| Academic certificates and transcripts | KCSE, college, university |
| Birth certificate | For some applications |
| CV (PDF) | Updated, one to two pages |
| Certificate of Good Conduct | If you have one: note its date, many employers want a recent one |

Name files clearly: `Amina_Hassan_KCSE_Certificate.pdf`, not `IMG_20260912_0045.jpg`.

### Scanning well with a phone

Use **Google Drive → Scan**, Adobe Scan or Microsoft Lens: they crop, straighten and produce readable PDFs. Scan in good light, and check that every word can be read when zoomed in.

### File size and format

Portals often limit size (e.g. 1–2 MB) and format (PDF or JPG). To reduce size: scan in greyscale, lower the resolution slightly, or use a free PDF compressor. Combine pages into **one PDF** when a portal allows only one upload.

## Certificate of Good Conduct (police clearance)

Issued by the DCI, applied for through **eCitizen**. The general process is: apply and pay online, then complete **fingerprinting** at an approved DCI location or Huduma Centre, and download the certificate when ready. Check the current steps on eCitizen before you start, and apply early: processing takes time.

## Filling in forms: avoid these mistakes

1. **Names exactly as on your ID**, in the same order.
2. **Correct ID number, phone and email**: you'll receive codes and results there. Use an email you check.
3. Don't wait for the **deadline day**: portals slow down and crash.
4. Read the instructions twice; answer every required field.
5. **Save and screenshot** confirmation pages, reference numbers and M-Pesa payment messages.
6. **Log out** afterwards, especially at cyber cafés.

## Staying safe with applications

- Use only official sites (they usually end in **.go.ke** for government, or the organisation's known domain).
- **Never pay for a "guaranteed" job, placement or loan approval**: that's a scam.
- Don't share your eCitizen, iTax or email password with cyber café attendants. If someone helps you, type the password yourself, then change it later.
- Beware of WhatsApp messages with "application links": check the address carefully.
- Verify job adverts with the employer's official website or phone number.

## Writing short answers and cover letters

Many applications ask "Why do you want this?" or "Describe your experience":

- Keep it specific and honest; give **examples with results**: "I built a website for my college's ICT club that 300 students use."
- Match the requirements listed in the advert.
- Check spelling and grammar (and have someone else read it).
- Write it first in a document, then paste it: portals sometimes time out and lose what you typed.

## After applying

- Note deadlines and expected response dates in your calendar.
- Check email (including **Spam**) and SMS regularly.
- Follow up politely if a date passes with no response.
- Keep improving: every application teaches you something.

```quiz
Q: What should your name on a form match exactly?
A: ID | national ID | my ID | your ID
Q: Which Google Drive feature turns paper documents into PDFs?
A: Scan | scan
Q: Government websites in Kenya usually end in what? (write the ending)
A: .go.ke | go.ke
Q: Should you pay someone for a guaranteed job placement? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: What should you save after submitting an application? (one word)
A: confirmation | screenshot | reference number
```

tracks.title: Computer hardware & maintenance
tracks.summary: Know the parts inside a computer, buy the right laptop, install Windows, fix common problems and keep computers fast and virus-free.

lessons.title: Inside the computer: every hardware component, how it works and how to identify it
lessons.body:
# Inside the computer: every hardware component, how it works and how to identify it

To repair, upgrade or build computers (or simply buy the right one and explain problems to a technician), you need to know what's inside the box. This unit opens up a desktop and laptop, explaining each component's job, how it connects, how to identify it, the common specifications, and the failures technicians see most often. It's the foundation for the troubleshooting, upgrade and Windows installation lessons in this subject.

:::note What you will learn
- Safety before opening a computer (power and static electricity)
- Motherboard: form factors, sockets, slots, chipsets and BIOS/UEFI
- CPU, cooling and thermal paste
- RAM types (DDR4/DDR5, SO-DIMM) and capacity
- Storage: HDD, SATA SSD, NVMe SSD, interfaces
- Graphics cards, power supplies, cases and cables
- Laptop internals vs desktops
- Identifying components with software (Task Manager, System Information, CPU-Z)
- Common hardware failures and symptoms
:::

## Safety first

1. **Shut down and unplug** the power cable; for laptops, disconnect the charger and, if possible, the battery.
2. Press the power button for a few seconds after unplugging to drain residual power.
3. **Static electricity (ESD)** can damage components: touch a grounded metal object first, or use an **anti-static wrist strap**; work on a non-carpeted surface; handle cards by the edges.
4. **Never open the power supply unit (PSU)**: capacitors inside can hold dangerous charge even when unplugged.
5. Keep screws organised (a magnetic tray or labelled containers); take photos before disconnecting cables.
6. Laptops: some have warranty stickers; opening may void warranty.

## The motherboard

:::define Motherboard
The main circuit board connecting all components: CPU, memory, storage, expansion cards, ports and power. Also called the mainboard or system board.
:::

### Form factors (sizes)

| Form factor | Size | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **ATX** | Full size (about 30.5 × 24.4 cm) | Standard desktops, more slots |
| **Micro-ATX** | Smaller | Common office PCs |
| **Mini-ITX** | Very small | Compact PCs |
| Laptop boards | Custom shapes | Specific to each model |

### Key parts of the motherboard

| Part | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **CPU socket** | Holds the processor; must match the CPU (e.g. Intel LGA1700, AMD AM4/AM5) |
| **RAM slots (DIMM)** | Memory modules; dual-channel works best with matching pairs in the right slots |
| **PCIe slots** | Expansion cards: graphics, network, NVMe adapters (x16 for graphics, x1 for small cards) |
| **M.2 slots** | NVMe/SATA SSDs (and some Wi-Fi cards) |
| **SATA ports** | Hard drives, SATA SSDs, DVD drives |
| **Chipset** | Controls communication between CPU and devices; determines features |
| **Power connectors** | 24-pin main power, 4/8-pin CPU power |
| **Front panel headers** | Power button, LEDs, USB and audio from the case front |
| **CMOS battery** (CR2032 coin cell) | Keeps BIOS settings and the clock when unplugged |
| **Rear I/O panel** | USB, display outputs, Ethernet, audio |
| **VRMs** | Regulate power to the CPU |

### BIOS/UEFI

The **firmware** that runs first when you power on: checks hardware (POST), then starts the operating system from a boot drive. **UEFI** is the modern replacement for BIOS, with mouse support, secure boot and support for large drives. Enter setup by pressing a key at startup (often `F2`, `Del`, `F10`, `F12` for boot menu, or `Esc`, depending on the manufacturer).

Common settings: **boot order** (USB first to install Windows), date/time, **Secure Boot**, virtualization (needed for some software), enabling/disabling devices.

A dead CMOS battery causes symptoms like the clock resetting and "CMOS checksum error" messages.

## The CPU (processor)

- Executes instructions; speed affected by **cores/threads**, **clock speed (GHz)**, **cache**, and **generation/architecture**.
- **Intel:** Core i3/i5/i7/i9 and Core Ultra; suffixes matter (U = low-power laptop, H/HX = high-performance laptop, K = unlocked desktop, F = no integrated graphics).
- **AMD:** Ryzen 3/5/7/9; suffixes (U, H/HS, X, G = with graphics).
- Desktop CPUs can be replaced (matching socket/chipset); most laptop CPUs are **soldered**.

### Cooling

CPUs produce heat and need a **heat sink and fan** (or liquid cooler). **Thermal paste** fills tiny gaps between the CPU and cooler to transfer heat. Old dried paste plus dust causes overheating; technicians clean and re-apply paste during servicing.

Symptoms of overheating: loud fans, the PC slowing down (thermal throttling), sudden shutdowns.

## RAM (memory)

| Type | Used in |
|---|---|
| **DDR3** | Older PCs (around 2010–2015) |
| **DDR4** | Most PCs from about 2015–2022 |
| **DDR5** | Newer PCs |
| **DIMM** | Desktop modules (long) |
| **SO-DIMM** | Laptop modules (short) |
| **Soldered (LPDDR)** | Many thin laptops: can't be upgraded |

Types aren't interchangeable (different notches). Speed (e.g. 3200 MHz) and capacity (8 GB, 16 GB) matter. RAM problems cause random crashes, blue screens and failure to boot (often with beep codes).

## Storage

| Type | Interface | Speed | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HDD** (3.5" desktop, 2.5" laptop) | SATA | Slow (spinning platters) | Cheap, large; vulnerable to drops; clicking noise = failing |
| **SATA SSD** (2.5") | SATA | Fast (several times faster than HDD in everyday use) | Easy upgrade for old laptops/desktops |
| **M.2 SATA SSD** | M.2 slot, SATA protocol | Same as SATA SSD | Check the slot supports SATA |
| **M.2 NVMe SSD** | M.2 slot, PCIe protocol | Fastest | Check slot type (M key, PCIe generation) |
| **eMMC** | Soldered | Slow-ish | Budget laptops/tablets; can't upgrade |

Identifying: an M.2 drive is a small stick; check the keying (notches) and the motherboard manual for NVMe vs SATA support.

## Graphics (GPU)

- **Integrated graphics** (in the CPU): fine for office, video and light editing.
- **Dedicated graphics cards** (NVIDIA GeForce/RTX, AMD Radeon): gaming, 3D, video editing, AI. Desktop cards use a PCIe x16 slot and often extra power cables from the PSU.

## Power supply unit (PSU)

Converts AC mains power to DC voltages (12V, 5V, 3.3V) for components.
- **Wattage:** enough for the system plus headroom (a basic office PC needs little; gaming PCs with graphics cards need more).
- **Efficiency ratings:** 80 PLUS Bronze/Gold etc.
- Cheap, poor-quality PSUs fail and can damage other parts; use reputable brands.
- Laptops use an external **adapter**: correct voltage/wattage and connector matter.

Use a **UPS** or surge protector where power is unstable; voltage surges and outages damage PSUs and drives.

## Cases, fans and cables

- **Case:** holds and cools components; airflow front-to-back/bottom-to-top; dust filters help.
- **Cables:** SATA data and power, 24-pin and 8-pin power, PCIe power, front panel.
- **Fans:** intake and exhaust; clean dust regularly (dusty environments clog them quickly).

## Laptop internals

Laptops pack components tightly:
- Bottom panel removal (screws, sometimes clips).
- Common **upgradeable** parts on many models: SSD/HDD, RAM (if not soldered), Wi-Fi card, battery.
- **Not usually upgradeable:** CPU, GPU, soldered RAM.
- Delicate ribbon cables (keyboard, display, touchpad): open connectors carefully.
- Keyboards, screens, hinges and charging ports are common repair parts.

Before buying parts, check the exact model's specifications (manufacturer's website, service manual, or tools like Crucial's System Scanner for RAM compatibility).

## Identifying components with software

| Tool | Shows |
|---|---|
| **Task Manager → Performance** (`Ctrl+Shift+Esc`) | CPU model, RAM amount/speed/slots used, disk type (SSD/HDD), GPU |
| **System Information** (`msinfo32`) | Detailed system summary, BIOS version, motherboard |
| **Settings → System → About** | CPU, RAM, Windows edition, device name |
| **Device Manager** | All devices and driver problems (yellow warnings) |
| **CPU-Z** (free) | CPU, motherboard, RAM type and timings |
| **CrystalDiskInfo** (free) | Drive health (SMART status) |
| **dxdiag** | Graphics and DirectX information |

:::think A customer wants more RAM for a laptop. What would you check before buying a RAM stick?
Whether the laptop's RAM is upgradeable or soldered, how many slots it has and how many are free, the RAM type (DDR4/DDR5, SO-DIMM), supported speed, and maximum supported capacity. Use Task Manager/CPU-Z and the manufacturer's specifications or a compatibility tool before buying.
:::

## Common hardware failures and symptoms

| Symptom | Possible cause |
|---|---|
| No power at all, no lights | PSU/adapter failure, power button, socket, motherboard |
| Fans spin but no display | RAM not seated, GPU/display issue, motherboard, CPU |
| Beeps at startup | POST error codes (RAM, GPU); check the manufacturer's beep code list |
| Clicking or grinding noise | Failing HDD: **back up immediately** |
| Random shutdowns | Overheating, failing PSU, battery |
| Blue screens | Faulty RAM, drivers, failing drive |
| Slow, freezing, files corrupt | Failing drive, malware, low RAM |
| Clock resets | Dead CMOS battery |
| Laptop won't charge | Adapter, charging port, battery, motherboard charging circuit |
| Swollen battery (case bulging, touchpad lifting) | **Stop using; replace safely** (fire risk) |

## Practice tasks

1. Open Task Manager → Performance and write down your CPU, RAM (amount, speed, slots) and disk type.
2. Run `msinfo32` and find your motherboard model and BIOS version.
3. Install CrystalDiskInfo (or check SMART status) and note your drive's health.
4. Find your laptop/desktop model's specifications online and list which parts are upgradeable.
5. With supervision and safety steps, open a desktop and identify the motherboard, CPU cooler, RAM, storage, PSU and cables.

## Summary

- Work safely: unplug, discharge, prevent static, never open PSUs.
- The motherboard connects everything (sockets, RAM slots, PCIe, M.2, SATA, chipset, BIOS/UEFI, CMOS battery).
- CPUs need proper cooling and thermal paste; RAM types (DDR4/DDR5, DIMM/SO-DIMM) aren't interchangeable.
- Storage ranges from HDD (slow) to SATA SSD and NVMe (fastest); check slot compatibility.
- GPUs, PSUs (quality and wattage), cases, fans and cables complete a desktop; laptops have fewer upgradeable parts.
- Identify parts with Task Manager, msinfo32, Device Manager, CPU-Z and CrystalDiskInfo; learn common failure symptoms.

```quiz
Q: What should you never open because of dangerous stored charge? (three letters)
A: PSU | power supply
Q: What small battery keeps BIOS settings and the clock? (one word)
A: CMOS | CMOS battery | CR2032
Q: What laptop RAM module type is shorter than desktop DIMMs?
A: SO-DIMM | sodimm
Q: Which SSD type is fastest: SATA or NVMe?
A: NVMe | nvme
Q: What material helps transfer heat between the CPU and cooler? (two words)
A: thermal paste
Q: What should you do immediately if a hard disk starts clicking? (two words)
A: back up | backup
Q: Which Windows command opens System Information?
A: msinfo32
```

lessons.title: Speeding up an old computer: SSD and RAM upgrades
lessons.body:
# Speeding up an old computer: SSD and RAM upgrades

A slow laptop is often not "dead". The two upgrades that make the biggest difference are replacing a hard disk (HDD) with a **solid-state drive (SSD)** and adding **RAM**. For a few thousand shillings a 5-year-old laptop can feel new, and upgrade work is a good income stream for technicians.

## Diagnose first

Open **Task Manager** (Ctrl + Shift + Esc) → **Performance**:

| What you see | Likely bottleneck | Upgrade |
|---|---|---|
| **Disk** at 100% for long periods, slow start-up | Old hard disk (HDD) | **SSD** |
| **Memory** above ~85% with a few apps open | Not enough RAM | **More RAM** |
| CPU at 100% on simple tasks | Very old processor, or malware | Check for malware first; the CPU usually can't be upgraded on laptops |

Also check what's installed: Task Manager → Performance → Disk shows **HDD** or **SSD**; Memory shows total RAM, **slots used** and speed (e.g. DDR4-2666).

## SSD: the biggest speed boost

| Type | Looks like | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **2.5" SATA SSD** | Same size as a laptop hard disk | Fits most laptops from ~2010–2018 that have a 2.5" HDD |
| **M.2 SATA** | A small stick | Check whether your M.2 slot supports SATA |
| **M.2 NVMe** | A small stick | Fastest; needs an NVMe-compatible M.2 slot |

Find the right one: search your laptop's exact **model number** (on the sticker underneath, or in Settings → System → About) plus "SSD upgrade", or use Crucial's system scanner.

### Moving to the SSD

Two options:

1. **Clean install** (recommended if the system is messy): back up files, fit the SSD, install Windows from a USB made with Microsoft's **Media Creation Tool**, then install drivers and restore files.
2. **Clone** the old disk to the SSD with a USB-to-SATA adapter and cloning software (e.g. Macrium Reflect, or the SSD maker's tool), then swap the drives.

After installing, check the SSD's health with its maker's tool or CrystalDiskInfo.

## RAM upgrades

- Find the **type** (DDR3, DDR4, DDR5; laptops use **SO-DIMM** sticks), speed and maximum supported RAM for your model.
- Check free slots. Some laptops have RAM **soldered** on the board with one free slot, or none.
- Match the speed and type; for best performance use **two identical sticks** (dual channel).
- 8 GB is the practical minimum for Windows 11 today; 16 GB for programming, design and many browser tabs.

## Safety and good practice

1. **Back up** the customer's data before any work.
2. Shut down fully, unplug the charger and, if possible, disconnect the battery.
3. Touch a metal part first (or use an **anti-static wrist strap**) to discharge static electricity.
4. Use the right screwdriver; keep screws organised (a magnetic mat or labelled cups).
5. Handle RAM and SSDs by the edges; never force connectors.
6. Test before closing the case completely.

## Other cheap speed-ups (no hardware)

- Uninstall unused programs and disable unnecessary **start-up apps** (Task Manager → Startup).
- Run a malware scan (Microsoft Defender full scan).
- Keep at least 15–20% of the disk free.
- Install updates and drivers.
- Clean dust from fans and vents: overheating slows the CPU.

## Pricing upgrade jobs

Quote **parts + labour** separately, test the machine in front of the customer, return the old disk (with their data) or offer to wipe it, and give a short warranty on your labour.

```quiz
Q: Which upgrade usually gives the biggest speed boost to an old laptop with a hard disk?
A: SSD | an SSD | solid state drive
Q: What type of RAM stick do most laptops use? (hyphenated or not)
A: SO-DIMM | SODIMM
Q: Which Windows tool shows whether Disk or Memory is the bottleneck? (two words)
A: Task Manager
Q: What should you always do before opening a customer's computer? (two words)
A: back up | backup | back up data
Q: What protects components from static electricity? (three words)
A: anti-static wrist strap | wrist strap | antistatic wrist strap
```

lessons.title: Installing Windows and software: bootable USB, clean install, drivers, activation and setup checklist
lessons.body:
# Installing Windows and software: bootable USB, clean install, drivers, activation and setup checklist

Installing (or reinstalling) Windows is one of the most useful skills for anyone who maintains computers: it fixes badly infected or very slow systems, sets up new SSDs, and prepares computers for school labs and offices. Technicians charge for it, and doing it correctly (with backups, the right drivers and genuine licences) separates professionals from amateurs. This unit walks through the whole process step by step.

:::warning Back up first
A clean install **erases** the drive you install to. Back up documents, photos, browser bookmarks/passwords, email data and licence keys before starting. Confirm the backup opens on another device.
:::

:::note What you will learn
- When to reinstall vs repair
- Windows editions, versions and system requirements (Windows 11 TPM/Secure Boot)
- Creating a bootable USB with the official Media Creation Tool
- BIOS/UEFI boot settings and the boot menu
- Clean installation step by step (partitions, local vs Microsoft account)
- Drivers: what they are and how to install the right ones
- Activation and genuine licensing
- Post-install setup checklist and essential software
- Restoring data and user settings
:::

## Reinstall or repair?

Try simpler fixes first:

| Option | What it does | When |
|---|---|---|
| **Troubleshooters / malware scan / updates** | Fix specific problems | First steps |
| **System Restore** | Rolls system files and settings back to an earlier point (keeps personal files) | After a bad update or driver |
| **Reset this PC → Keep my files** | Reinstalls Windows, keeps personal files (removes apps) | Persistent problems, slowness |
| **Reset this PC → Remove everything** | Fresh Windows from within Windows | Selling/donating, severe problems |
| **Clean install from USB** | Erases the drive and installs fresh | New SSD, heavily infected systems, upgrades, when Reset fails |

## Editions and requirements

| Edition | For |
|---|---|
| **Windows 11 Home** | Personal use |
| **Windows 11 Pro** | Business features (BitLocker, Remote Desktop host, domain join, policies) |
| **Education/Enterprise** | Institutions (volume licensing) |

**Windows 11 minimum requirements** include a compatible 64-bit CPU (roughly Intel 8th gen / AMD Ryzen 2000 series or newer), **4 GB RAM**, **64 GB storage**, **UEFI with Secure Boot**, and **TPM 2.0**. Use Microsoft's **PC Health Check** app to test. Practically, aim for 8 GB RAM and an SSD.

Windows 10 support ended in **October 2025** (except for paid extended security updates), so new installations should use Windows 11 where hardware supports it. Older unsupported hardware might be better with a lightweight Linux distribution for basic use (see the Linux subject).

## Step 1: Create a bootable USB (official method)

You need a USB flash drive of **8 GB or more** (it will be erased) and a working Windows PC with internet.

1. On a working PC, download the **Media Creation Tool** from Microsoft's official Windows download page (microsoft.com/software-download).
2. Run it, accept the licence, choose **Create installation media (USB flash drive)**.
3. Choose language, edition and 64-bit.
4. Select the USB drive; the tool downloads Windows (several GB) and makes the USB bootable.

Alternative: download the ISO file and use **Rufus** (rufus.ie) to write it to USB. Never download Windows from unofficial sites: modified images can contain malware.

## Step 2: Boot from the USB

1. Plug the USB into the target computer.
2. Restart and press the **boot menu key** repeatedly at startup: commonly `F12` (Dell, Lenovo), `F9` (HP), `Esc` (some HP/Asus), `F11` (MSI), `F8`... (check the brand). Or enter **BIOS/UEFI setup** (`F2`, `Del`, `F10`) and set the USB first in **boot order**.
3. Choose the USB drive (often listed as "UEFI: [USB name]").
4. If it won't boot: check **Secure Boot**/UEFI settings (Windows 11 media boots in UEFI mode), try another USB port, or remake the USB.

## Step 3: Install Windows (clean install)

1. **Language, time and keyboard** → Next → **Install now**.
2. **Product key:** enter it, or choose "I don't have a product key" (if the PC previously had activated Windows of the same edition, it often activates automatically with a **digital licence** once online).
3. Choose the **edition** matching your licence (Home or Pro).
4. Accept terms → choose **Custom: Install Windows only (advanced)** for a clean install.
5. **Partitions:** select the drive. For a clean install on the system drive, delete the old Windows partitions on that drive (**this erases data**), leaving **Unallocated space**, then select it and click Next; Windows creates the needed partitions automatically. **Be careful not to delete data partitions/drives you want to keep** (check sizes and labels).
6. Windows copies files and restarts several times (remove the USB when it restarts to setup, or set the SSD first in boot order).
7. **Out-of-box setup (OOBE):** region, keyboard, network, then sign in with a **Microsoft account** (default for Windows 11 Home) or set up as required by the organisation; create a PIN; choose privacy settings (turn off unnecessary tracking/ads options).

:::tip Name the PC and user sensibly
Use a clear device name (e.g. `LAB-PC-07`, `KAMAU-LAPTOP`) and a user account in the owner's name. In labs and offices, use consistent naming so computers are easy to manage.
:::

## Step 4: Drivers

:::define Driver
Software that lets Windows communicate with a hardware device (graphics, Wi-Fi, audio, touchpad, chipset, printer). Without the right driver, the device may not work or may work poorly.
:::

1. **Connect to the internet** (Wi-Fi or Ethernet; if Wi-Fi doesn't work, use Ethernet, USB tethering from a phone, or install the Wi-Fi driver from a USB).
2. Run **Windows Update** (Settings → Windows Update → Check for updates; also **Advanced options → Optional updates** for drivers).
3. Open **Device Manager** (right-click Start → Device Manager): devices with yellow warning icons need drivers.
4. Download missing drivers from the **manufacturer's support site** using the exact model or serial number (Dell, HP, Lenovo, etc.; many have support assistant apps), or from component makers (Intel, AMD, NVIDIA, Realtek).
5. Restart after installing chipset and graphics drivers.

Avoid "driver updater" utilities from unknown websites: many bundle adware.

## Step 5: Activation and licensing

- Check: Settings → System → **Activation**.
- **Digital licence:** linked to the hardware (and your Microsoft account), activates automatically after reinstalling the same edition.
- **Product key:** entered during or after setup.
- Organisations use **volume licences**.

Use **genuine** Windows. Activators and cracked copies from the internet often contain malware, can stop working, and are illegal (they violate copyright). If a computer has no licence, buy a genuine one from Microsoft or authorised resellers, or consider free alternatives (Linux) where suitable.

## Step 6: Post-install checklist

| Task | Notes |
|---|---|
| Windows Update until no more updates | Restart as needed |
| All drivers installed | Device Manager has no warnings |
| Windows Security on | Real-time protection; run a quick scan |
| Browser | Edge/Chrome/Firefox; sign in to restore bookmarks/passwords if wanted |
| Office suite | Microsoft 365 (licence), or LibreOffice (free) |
| PDF reader | Built-in browser viewer or Adobe Reader |
| Compression | Built-in ZIP; 7-Zip for other formats |
| Media player | VLC |
| Communication | Zoom/Teams/WhatsApp Desktop as needed |
| Backups | OneDrive/Google Drive sync; File History to an external drive |
| Power settings | Sleep times; battery mode |
| Restore point | Create one after setup (System Protection → Create) |
| Remove bloatware | Uninstall trial software that came with the PC |
| User data restored | Copy documents back from the backup |

Install software from **official websites or the Microsoft Store**; watch installers for bundled offers (untick extra toolbars/apps).

### Installing software safely

1. Download from the official site or Microsoft Store (or `winget` for advanced users: `winget install VideoLAN.VLC`).
2. Check the publisher in the installer's security prompt.
3. Choose **Custom** install when offered to untick unwanted extras.
4. Keep software updated; uninstall what you don't use.

## Mass setups (labs and offices)

For many identical computers, technicians use imaging and management tools (e.g. creating a configured image and deploying it, or Windows Autopilot/Intune in organisations). For a small school lab, a consistent checklist and the same software list on every PC already saves lots of time.

:::think After a clean install, a laptop's Wi-Fi doesn't work and there's no Ethernet port. How can you get it online to download drivers?
Use **USB tethering** from an Android phone (Settings → Hotspot & tethering → USB tethering), which Windows usually recognises without extra drivers, or download the Wi-Fi driver on another computer from the manufacturer's site and copy it via USB. Then run Windows Update for remaining drivers.
:::

## Common installation problems

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
