lessons.body:
# Data: Retrofit for APIs and Room for the local database

Most Android apps load data from a server and keep a local copy for speed and offline use. The standard tools are **Retrofit** (HTTP APIs) and **Room** (a database on the phone, built on SQLite).

## Permissions

Add internet permission to `AndroidManifest.xml` (above `<application>`):

```xml
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
```

## Retrofit: calling a REST API

Dependencies (check the latest versions): `com.squareup.retrofit2:retrofit`, a JSON converter (for example `com.squareup.retrofit2:converter-gson` or kotlinx.serialization), and optionally `com.squareup.okhttp3:logging-interceptor`.

### 1. Model classes for the JSON

```kotlin
data class ProductDto(
    val id: Int,
    val name: String,
    val price: Int,
    val stock: Int,
)

data class CreateOrderRequest(val productId: Int, val qty: Int, val phone: String)
data class OrderResponse(val orderId: Int, val total: Int, val status: String)
```

### 2. The API interface

```kotlin
import retrofit2.http.*

interface DukaApi {
    @GET("products")
    suspend fun products(@Query("q") search: String? = null): List<ProductDto>

    @GET("products/{id}")
    suspend fun product(@Path("id") id: Int): ProductDto

    @POST("orders")
    suspend fun createOrder(@Body body: CreateOrderRequest): OrderResponse
}
```

`suspend` functions run on a background thread automatically and return the parsed result.

### 3. Build the client (once)

```kotlin
import okhttp3.OkHttpClient
import retrofit2.Retrofit
import retrofit2.converter.gson.GsonConverterFactory
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit

object Network {
    private val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
        .connectTimeout(15, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
        .readTimeout(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
        .addInterceptor { chain ->                       // add the login token to every request
            val token = TokenStore.token
            val request = chain.request().newBuilder()
                .apply { if (token != null) header("Authorization", "Bearer $token") }
                .build()
            chain.proceed(request)
        }
        .build()

    val api: DukaApi = Retrofit.Builder()
        .baseUrl("https://api.example.co.ke/v1/")       // must end with /
        .client(client)
        .addConverterFactory(GsonConverterFactory.create())
        .build()
        .create(DukaApi::class.java)
}

object TokenStore { var token: String? = null }        // in a real app: encrypted storage
```

### 4. Handle errors

```kotlin
import java.io.IOException
import retrofit2.HttpException

suspend fun <T> safeCall(block: suspend () -> T): Result<T> = try {
    Result.success(block())
} catch (e: IOException) {
    Result.failure(Exception("No internet connection"))
} catch (e: HttpException) {
    Result.failure(Exception(if (e.code() == 401) "Please sign in again" else "Server error (${e.code()})"))
}
```

> **Testing with a server on your laptop:** the emulator reaches your computer at `http://10.0.2.2:PORT`. Plain `http://` is blocked by default, so use HTTPS for real servers (and only allow cleartext for local testing via a network security config).

## Room: the local database

Dependencies: `androidx.room:room-runtime`, `androidx.room:room-ktx` and the Room compiler via **KSP**.

### Entity (a table)

```kotlin
import androidx.room.*

@Entity(tableName = "products")
data class ProductEntity(
    @PrimaryKey val id: Int,
    val name: String,
    val price: Int,
    val stock: Int,
    val updatedAt: Long = System.currentTimeMillis(),
)
```

### DAO (queries)

```kotlin
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow

@Dao
interface ProductDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY name")
    fun observeAll(): Flow<List<ProductEntity>>           // emits again whenever the table changes

    @Query("SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%' || :q || '%' ORDER BY name")
    fun search(q: String): Flow<List<ProductEntity>>

    @Upsert
    suspend fun upsertAll(items: List<ProductEntity>)    // insert or update

    @Query("UPDATE products SET stock = stock - :qty WHERE id = :id")
    suspend fun reduceStock(id: Int, qty: Int)
}
```

### Database

```kotlin
@Database(entities = [ProductEntity::class], version = 1)
abstract class DukaDatabase : RoomDatabase() {
    abstract fun productDao(): ProductDao
}

// create once (e.g. in your Application class or with Hilt):
// val db = Room.databaseBuilder(context, DukaDatabase::class.java, "duka.db").build()
```

When you change tables in a new version, write a **Migration** (`version = 2` plus `addMigrations(...)`) so users keep their data.

## The repository: offline-first

```kotlin
class ProductRepositoryImpl(
    private val api: DukaApi,
    private val dao: ProductDao,
) {
    // The UI always reads the local database: instant, works offline
    fun products(): Flow<List<ProductEntity>> = dao.observeAll()

    // Refresh from the server when possible; the Flow above updates the UI automatically
    suspend fun refresh(): Result<Unit> = safeCall {
        val remote = api.products()
        dao.upsertAll(remote.map { ProductEntity(it.id, it.name, it.price, it.stock) })
    }
}
```

The ViewModel exposes `repository.products()` as state, calls `refresh()` on start and on pull-to-refresh, and shows an error message only if refreshing fails, while still showing the cached list.

## Other storage

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Small settings (theme, onboarding done) | **DataStore** (Preferences) |
| Tokens and secrets | Encrypted storage backed by the **Android Keystore** |
| Files (photos, PDFs) | App-specific storage (`context.filesDir`) |
| Background sync even when the app is closed | **WorkManager** |

```quiz
Q: Which library calls REST APIs in Android?
A: Retrofit
Q: Which library is Android's local database layer on top of SQLite?
A: Room
Q: In Room, which annotation marks a table class?
A: @Entity | Entity
Q: In Room, what is the interface with your queries called?
A: DAO | Dao | data access object
Q: Which permission does an app need to use the network?
A: INTERNET | android.permission.INTERNET
Q: Which Jetpack library runs background sync even when the app is closed?
A: WorkManager
```

lessons.title: Testing, signing and releasing your Android app
lessons.body:
# Testing, signing and releasing your Android app

Your app works on your phone. Now make it reliable on everyone's phone and publish it on Google Play.

## Unit tests (plain Kotlin)

Logic in ViewModels, repositories and helper functions can be tested on your computer in milliseconds. Tests live in `app/src/test/`.

```kotlin
import org.junit.Assert.assertEquals
import org.junit.Assert.assertNull
import org.junit.Test

fun normalisePhone(input: String): String? {
    val d = input.filter { it.isDigit() }
    return when {
        Regex("^0[17]\\d{8}$").matches(d) -> "254" + d.drop(1)
        Regex("^254[17]\\d{8}$").matches(d) -> d
        else -> null
    }
}

class PhoneTest {
    @Test fun acceptsLocalFormat() = assertEquals("254712345678", normalisePhone("0712 345 678"))
    @Test fun acceptsInternational() = assertEquals("254112345678", normalisePhone("+254 112 345 678"))
    @Test fun rejectsShortNumbers() = assertNull(normalisePhone("12345"))
}
```

Run with the green ▶ beside the test, or `./gradlew test`.

To test ViewModels with coroutines, use `kotlinx-coroutines-test` (`runTest`) and a fake repository that returns fixed data.

## Compose UI tests

UI tests in `app/src/androidTest/` drive the real screens:

```kotlin
class CounterScreenTest {
    @get:Rule val compose = createComposeRule()

    @Test fun tappingAddIncreasesQuantity() {
        compose.setContent { QuantityPicker(item = "Unga") }
        compose.onNodeWithText("1").assertExists()
        compose.onNodeWithContentDescription("More").performClick()
        compose.onNodeWithText("2").assertExists()
    }
}
```

## Before release: the checklist

- [ ] Test on a cheap, older phone (2 GB RAM, Android 8 to 10) and a small screen.
- [ ] Turn on airplane mode mid-request: the app must show a friendly message, not crash.
- [ ] Rotate the phone on every screen: no lost input (ViewModel / `rememberSaveable`).
- [ ] Dark mode and large font size.
- [ ] Remove unused permissions and debug logs of personal data.
- [ ] Crash reporting added (Firebase Crashlytics).
- [ ] Privacy policy ready (required on Google Play).

## Shrinking and obfuscation

In `app/build.gradle.kts`, release builds should enable **R8**:

```kotlin
android {
    buildTypes {
        release {
            isMinifyEnabled = true          // removes unused code, shortens names
            isShrinkResources = true        // removes unused resources
            proguardFiles(getDefaultProguardFile("proguard-android-optimize.txt"), "proguard-rules.pro")
        }
    }
}
```

This makes the app smaller and harder to reverse-engineer. Test the release build: some libraries need keep rules.

## Versioning

```kotlin
defaultConfig {
    applicationId = "ke.co.marzley.duka"   // never changes after publishing
    versionCode = 3                        // must increase with every upload
    versionName = "1.1.0"                  // what users see
    minSdk = 24
    targetSdk = 35                         // keep up with Google Play's yearly requirement
}
```

## Signing and building the bundle

1. **Build → Generate Signed App Bundle / APK → Android App Bundle**.
2. Create a new **upload keystore** (`.jks`), with strong passwords. **Back it up** and never commit it to Git.
3. Choose the **release** build and finish. The `.aab` file appears under `app/release/`.
4. In Play Console, use **Play App Signing** (Google manages the final signing key; your upload key can be reset if lost).

## Publishing on Google Play (summary)

1. Play Console account (US$25 once).
2. Create the app, fill **store listing** (descriptions, icon, screenshots, feature graphic).
3. **App content**: privacy policy, data safety, content rating, target audience, ads.
4. **Testing**: internal and closed testing. New personal accounts need a **closed test with at least 12 testers for 14 days** before production (check the current rule).
5. **Production release** with release notes; consider a **staged rollout**.

Full details: **App development fundamentals → Testing and publishing**.

## Project ideas to build next

1. **Duka stock and sales app** with Room, offline-first, and a daily report.
2. **Chama contributions app**: members, contributions, loans, M-Pesa payment through your backend.
3. **School notices app**: news feed from an API, push notifications with Firebase Cloud Messaging.
4. **Field data collection**: forms with GPS location and photos, synced with WorkManager.

Publish one, put the code on GitHub with a README and demo video, and you have a strong Android portfolio.

```quiz
Q: Which folder holds plain Kotlin unit tests in an Android project?
A: src/test | app/src/test | test
Q: Which Gradle command runs unit tests?
A: ./gradlew test | gradlew test
Q: Which tool shrinks and obfuscates release builds?
A: R8
Q: Which number must increase with every upload to Google Play?
A: versionCode
Q: What file holds your upload signing key?
A: keystore | .jks | jks | a keystore
Q: Which service lets Google manage the final signing key?
A: Play App Signing
```

# React Native and Expo: setup and your first app **React Native** lets you build real Android and iPhone apps with **JavaScript** (or TypeScript) and **React**. Unlike a website in a wrapper, React Native draws **native** buttons, lists and text, so apps feel at home on each phone. Apps built with it include parts of Facebook, Instagram, Shopify, Discord and many fintech apps. **Expo** is the recommended way to start: it handles the native tooling for you, lets you run the app on your phone instantly with the **Expo Go** app, and builds store-ready apps in the cloud. > **Before you start:** learn **JavaScript** and the **React** subject in this hub (components, props, state, effects). React Native uses exactly the same React ideas. ## Setup (about 15 minutes) 1. Install **Node.js LTS** from nodejs.org. 2. Install **Expo Go** on your Android phone from the Play Store. 3. Create and start a project: ```bash npx create-expo-app@latest duka cd duka npx expo start ``` 4. A QR code appears in the terminal. **Scan it with Expo Go**: the app opens on your phone. Save a file and it reloads in about a second. Your phone and computer must be on the **same Wi-Fi**. If not, run `npx expo start --tunnel`. No computer at all yet? Use **snack.expo.dev**: write React Native in the browser and run it on your phone through Expo Go. ## Project structure (Expo Router template) ``` duka/ ├── app/ ← screens: each file is a route (Expo Router) │ ├── _layout.tsx ← navigation layout (stack, tabs) │ └── index.tsx ← the first screen ├── assets/ ← images, fonts, icon, splash screen ├── components/ ← your reusable components ├── app.json ← app name, icon, package id, permissions └── package.json ``` New templates use **TypeScript** (`.tsx`). Plain JavaScript works too; the examples here are JavaScript so they're easy to read. ## Your first screen ```jsx import { View, Text, Pressable, StyleSheet } from "react-native"; import { useState } from "react"; export default function Home() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ( Karibu Duka 🛒 Items in your cart: {count} setCount(count + 1)}> Add item ); } const styles = StyleSheet.create({ screen: { flex: 1, alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center", padding: 24, backgroundColor: "#fff" }, title: { fontSize: 28, fontWeight: "800", color: "#0b1b35" }, subtitle: { fontSize: 16, marginVertical: 12, color: "#475569" }, button: { backgroundColor: "#ffb800", paddingVertical: 14, paddingHorizontal: 28, borderRadius: 999 }, buttonText: { fontWeight: "700", color: "#0b1b35", fontSize: 16 }, }); ``` ## React vs React Native | React (web) | React Native | |---|---| | `

lessons.title: Core components, styling and Flexbox layouts
lessons.body:
# Core components, styling and Flexbox layouts

React Native gives you a small set of **core components** that map to native views on Android and iPhone. Layout uses **Flexbox**, like CSS, with a few differences.

## The core components

| Component | Use |
|---|---|
| `View` | A box: layout container |
| `Text` | Any text |
| `Image` | Local or remote images |
| `ScrollView` | Scrollable content (short lists, forms) |
| `FlatList` / `SectionList` | Long, efficient lists (next lesson) |
| `TextInput` | Text entry |
| `Pressable` | Anything tappable, with pressed feedback |
| `Switch` | On/off toggle |
| `ActivityIndicator` | Loading spinner |
| `Modal` | A pop-up screen |
| `KeyboardAvoidingView` | Moves content up when the keyboard opens |
| `SafeAreaView` (from `react-native-safe-area-context`) | Keeps content away from the notch and system bars |

## Styling

Styles are JavaScript objects. Property names are **camelCase** and numbers are **density-independent pixels** (no `px`):

```jsx
import { View, Text, Image, StyleSheet } from "react-native";

export function ProductCard({ name, price, imageUrl, inStock }) {
  return (
    <View style={styles.card}>
      <Image source={{ uri: imageUrl }} style={styles.image} resizeMode="cover" />
      <View style={styles.info}>
        <Text style={styles.name} numberOfLines={1}>{name}</Text>
        <Text style={styles.price}>KSh {price.toLocaleString()}</Text>
        <Text style={[styles.badge, !inStock && styles.soldOut]}>{inStock ? "In stock" : "Sold out"}</Text>
      </View>
    </View>
  );
}

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  card: {
    flexDirection: "row",
    backgroundColor: "#fff",
    borderRadius: 14,
    padding: 12,
    marginHorizontal: 16,
    marginVertical: 6,
    elevation: 2,                                   // Android shadow
    shadowColor: "#000", shadowOpacity: 0.08, shadowRadius: 8, shadowOffset: { width: 0, height: 3 },   // iPhone shadow
  },
  image: { width: 72, height: 72, borderRadius: 10, backgroundColor: "#f1f5f9" },
  info: { flex: 1, marginLeft: 12, justifyContent: "center" },
  name: { fontSize: 16, fontWeight: "700", color: "#0b1b35" },
  price: { fontSize: 15, color: "#0b7a5a", marginTop: 2 },
  badge: { marginTop: 6, alignSelf: "flex-start", fontSize: 12, color: "#166534", backgroundColor: "#dcfce7", paddingHorizontal: 8, paddingVertical: 2, borderRadius: 999, overflow: "hidden" },
  soldOut: { color: "#991b1b", backgroundColor: "#fee2e2" },
});
```

- Combine styles with an array: `style={[styles.badge, !inStock && styles.soldOut]}` (later styles win).
- **Remote images need a width and height**.
- `numberOfLines={1}` cuts long text with "…".

## Flexbox in React Native

Differences from web CSS:

| Property | React Native default | Web default |
|---|---|---|
| `flexDirection` | **column** | row |
| `alignContent` | flex-start | stretch |
| `flex: 1` | Takes the available space | Similar |

```jsx
import { View, Text, StyleSheet } from "react-native";

export default function Dashboard() {
  return (
    <View style={s.screen}>
      <Text style={s.title}>Today</Text>
      <View style={s.row}>
        <View style={[s.tile, { backgroundColor: "#dcfce7" }]}>
          <Text style={s.value}>KSh 8,640</Text>
          <Text>Sales</Text>
        </View>
        <View style={[s.tile, { backgroundColor: "#fef3c7" }]}>
          <Text style={s.value}>3</Text>
          <Text>Low stock</Text>
        </View>
      </View>
      <View style={s.spacer} />
      <Text style={s.footer}>Synced 2 minutes ago</Text>
    </View>
  );
}

const s = StyleSheet.create({
  screen: { flex: 1, padding: 16, backgroundColor: "#f8fafc" },
  title: { fontSize: 24, fontWeight: "800", marginBottom: 12 },
  row: { flexDirection: "row", gap: 12 },                 // gap works in recent React Native versions
  tile: { flex: 1, padding: 16, borderRadius: 14 },        // two tiles share the row equally
  value: { fontSize: 22, fontWeight: "800" },
  spacer: { flex: 1 },                                      // pushes the footer to the bottom
  footer: { textAlign: "center", color: "#64748b" },
});
```

## Text input and the keyboard

```jsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { View, Text, TextInput, Pressable, KeyboardAvoidingView, Platform, StyleSheet } from "react-native";

export default function PhoneForm() {
  const [phone, setPhone] = useState("");
  const digits = phone.replace(/\D/g, "");
  const valid = /^(0[17]\d{8}|254[17]\d{8})$/.test(digits);

  return (
    <KeyboardAvoidingView behavior={Platform.OS === "ios" ? "padding" : undefined} style={st.screen}>
      <Text style={st.label}>M-Pesa number</Text>
      <TextInput
        value={phone}
        onChangeText={setPhone}                 // gives the text directly (not an event)
        placeholder="0712 345 678"
        keyboardType="phone-pad"
        maxLength={16}
        style={[st.input, phone && !valid && st.inputError]}
      />
      {phone !== "" && !valid && <Text style={st.error}>Enter a Safaricom or Airtel number</Text>}
      <Pressable
        disabled={!valid}
        onPress={() => alert("We'd now send an M-Pesa prompt (through our server)")}
        style={({ pressed }) => [st.button, !valid && { opacity: 0.4 }, pressed && { opacity: 0.8 }]}
      >
        <Text style={st.buttonText}>Pay</Text>
      </Pressable>
    </KeyboardAvoidingView>
  );
}

const st = StyleSheet.create({
  screen: { flex: 1, padding: 20, justifyContent: "center" },
  label: { fontWeight: "700", marginBottom: 6 },
  input: { borderWidth: 1, borderColor: "#cbd5e1", borderRadius: 12, padding: 14, fontSize: 18 },
  inputError: { borderColor: "#dc2626" },
  error: { color: "#dc2626", marginTop: 6 },
  button: { marginTop: 16, backgroundColor: "#0b7a5a", padding: 16, borderRadius: 12, alignItems: "center" },
  buttonText: { color: "white", fontWeight: "700", fontSize: 16 },
});
```

## Platform differences

```js
import { Platform } from "react-native";

const fontFamily = Platform.select({ ios: "System", android: "Roboto" });
if (Platform.OS === "android") {
  // Android-only behaviour
}
```

Most code works on both; use `Platform` only for small differences.

## UI libraries

**React Native Paper** (Material Design), **Tamagui** and **NativeWind** (Tailwind-style classes) give you ready components and theming. Start with core components so you understand what they do.

```quiz
Q: What is the default flexDirection in React Native?
A: column
Q: Which component makes anything tappable with pressed feedback?
A: Pressable
Q: Which TextInput prop gives the typed text directly?
A: onChangeText
Q: Which keyboardType shows a number pad for phone numbers?
A: phone-pad
Q: How do you combine two styles on one component?
A: an array | with an array | style={[a, b]} | array
Q: Which module tells you whether the app runs on Android or iOS?
A: Platform
```

lessons.title: Start here: how to earn online from Kenya safely (and the full list of 130+ ways)
lessons.body:
# Start here: how to earn online from Kenya safely (and the full list of 130+ ways)

Thousands of Kenyans earn real money online every month: writers, transcribers, designers, developers, virtual assistants, AI trainers, content creators, online sellers and tutors. Thousands of others lose money to fake "online jobs", pyramid schemes and trading scams. The difference is usually **knowledge**: knowing which work is real, what skills it needs, how to start, how to get paid and how to spot a scam.

This subject explains **more than 130 ways to earn online**, grouped into 13 families. Each method has: what it is, who it suits, step-by-step instructions to start, where to find work, honest pay expectations and the risks. Read this first unit fully before choosing a method.

:::warning The honest truth first
- **There is no "easy money" online.** Real online income is payment for **work, skills or products** that someone values.
- **Nobody legitimate asks you to pay to get a job.** "Registration fees", "activation fees" and "starter kits" for online jobs are the number one scam in Kenya.
- **Most beginners earn little in the first 1–3 months.** Income grows with skills, reviews and consistency.
- **Trading (forex, Deriv, crypto) is not a job or salary.** Most retail traders lose money. Treat it as a high-risk activity to study carefully, never as a way to pay rent.
:::

## Who this subject is for

- Students and graduates looking for income while studying or job hunting
- Employed people wanting a side income
- Parents and caregivers who need flexible work from home
- People with a phone only (several methods work on a phone), and people with a laptop (more options)
- Anyone in Ajira Digital or Jitume programmes wanting more detail

## What you need to start

| Need | Why | Minimum |
|---|---|---|
| **A device** | To do the work | A smartphone works for some methods (social media, selling, some microtasks); a **laptop** opens most freelance work |
| **Reliable internet** | Deadlines and video calls | Mobile data bundles or home Wi-Fi; a backup (hotspot) |
| **Email address** | All platforms use it | A professional Gmail: `firstname.lastname@gmail.com` |
| **National ID / passport** | Identity verification (KYC) on platforms and payment services | Your real ID; never use someone else's account |
| **M-Pesa** | Receiving local payments and withdrawals | Registered in your own name |
| **PayPal, Payoneer, Wise or a bank account** | Receiving international payments | See "Getting paid" below |
| **KRA PIN** | Tax compliance, some clients ask | Free on iTax |
| **Basic computer skills** | Typing, files, Google Docs/Word | See the IT basics and Word subjects |
| **English writing** | Most international work is in English | Clear, correct sentences |

:::tip Phone-only? Start here
If you only have a phone: social media management for local businesses, selling on WhatsApp/Facebook Marketplace, content creation, some AI and microtask apps, customer support on chat, and tutoring by WhatsApp or Google Meet. Save part of your first income towards a used laptop (good refurbished laptops are available from around KSh 20,000–35,000).
:::

## The 13 families of online work

| # | Family | Examples | Lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Writing and language | Articles, copywriting, editing, translation, CVs | Writing and language work |
| B | Transcription and audio | Transcription, captions, voice-over, podcast editing | Transcription and audio |
| C | AI training and data | Annotation, AI rating, coding for AI, data entry | AI training and data work |
| D | Microtasks and testing | Surveys, usability testing, beta testing, studies | Microtasks, surveys and testing |
| E | Graphics and design | Logos, social graphics, templates, stock photos | Graphics and design |
| F | Content creation | YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, podcasts, UGC | Content creation |
| G | Marketing services | Social media management, ads, SEO, affiliate | Marketing services |
| H | Tech and programming | Websites, apps, M-Pesa integration, automation | Tech and programming |
| I | Teaching and expertise | Tutoring, courses, coaching, communities | Teaching and expertise |
| J | Selling online | Jumia, WhatsApp selling, digital products, crafts | Selling online |
| K | Virtual assistance and remote jobs | VA, customer support, bookkeeping | Remote work |
| L | Trading and investing (high risk / long term) | Forex, Deriv, crypto, NSE, T-bills, MMFs | Trading and investing: honest guide |
| M | Local services powered by online | Cyber services, photography, delivery apps, hotspots | Local services sold online |

## The full list (130+ ways)

**A. Writing and language:** 1 Blog and article writing · 2 SEO content writing · 3 Copywriting · 4 Ghostwriting · 5 Technical writing · 6 Proofreading and editing · 7 Translation · 8 CV, cover letter and LinkedIn writing · 9 Grant and proposal writing · 10 Product descriptions · 11 Email newsletters · 12 Scriptwriting

**B. Transcription and audio:** 13 General transcription · 14 Captioning and subtitling · 15 Specialist (medical/legal) transcription · 16 Kiswahili and local-language transcription · 17 Voice-over · 18 Audiobook narration · 19 Podcast editing · 20 Voice data recording for AI · 21 Audio cleanup and music services

**C. AI training and data:** 22 Image and video annotation · 23 Text labelling · 24 AI response rating (RLHF) · 25 AI writing evaluation and prompt writing · 26 Coding tasks for AI · 27 Expert AI training · 28 Search and ads evaluation · 29 Content moderation · 30 Data entry · 31 Web research and lead lists · 32 Local-language data for AI

**D. Microtasks and testing:** 33 Microtask platforms · 34 Paid surveys · 35 Usability testing · 36 Crowdtesting (beta testing) · 37 Research studies and focus groups · 38 Mystery shopping · 39 Game testing · 40 Cashback and referrals · 41 Contests and bounties

**E. Graphics and design:** 42 Logos · 43 Social media graphics · 44 Flyers, posters and event branding · 45 Brand identity kits · 46 UI/UX design · 47 Canva templates · 48 Print-on-demand designs · 49 Stock photos and videos · 50 Illustration · 51 Presentation design · 52 Photo editing · 53 Thumbnails · 54 Infographics · 55 Motion graphics and animation

**F. Content creation:** 56 YouTube long videos · 57 YouTube Shorts · 58 TikTok · 59 Facebook · 60 Instagram · 61 Podcasting · 62 Blogging with ads · 63 UGC creator · 64 Brand deals · 65 Live streaming and gifts · 66 Video editing for creators · 67 Faceless channels

**G. Marketing services:** 68 Social media management · 69 Facebook/Instagram ads · 70 Google Ads · 71 SEO for local businesses · 72 Google Business Profile setup · 73 Email marketing · 74 Affiliate marketing · 75 WhatsApp Business setup · 76 Community management · 77 Lead generation and appointment setting · 78 Influencer marketing management

**H. Tech and programming:** 79 Business websites · 80 WordPress · 81 Online shops · 82 Mobile apps · 83 M-Pesa integration · 84 Website maintenance and bug fixing · 85 Automation · 86 Data analysis and dashboards · 87 Remote IT support · 88 Bug bounties · 89 Selling code and themes · 90 No-code apps and chatbots · 91 Hosting and domain reselling

**I. Teaching and expertise:** 92 Online tutoring · 93 Teaching English · 94 Teaching Kiswahili and other languages · 95 Online courses · 96 Live workshops · 97 Coaching and consulting · 98 Selling your own notes and study guides · 99 Interview and exam preparation services · 100 Paid communities

**J. Selling online:** 101 Jumia · 102 Kilimall and other marketplaces · 103 WhatsApp, Facebook Marketplace and Instagram · 104 Your own online shop · 105 Local dropshipping · 106 Digital products · 107 Print-on-demand merchandise · 108 Kenyan crafts to the world · 109 Reselling and thrift (mitumba) online · 110 Farm produce online

**K. Virtual assistance and remote work:** 111 Virtual assistant · 112 Customer support · 113 Chat and email support · 114 Bookkeeping · 115 E-commerce store assistant · 116 Recruitment sourcing · 117 Project coordination · 118 Remote full-time jobs

**L. Trading and investing:** 119 Forex trading · 120 Deriv synthetic indices and options · 121 Crypto trading · 122 NSE shares · 123 Treasury bills and bonds · 124 Money market funds · 125 Copy trading · 126 Introducing broker / trading affiliate (with ethics)

**M. Local services sold online:** 127 Cyber and e-services (KRA, eCitizen, KUCCPS) · 128 Photography and videography · 129 Phone and computer repair · 130 Delivery and ride apps · 131 Home tutoring booked online · 132 Wi-Fi hotspot business

## Getting paid in Kenya

| Method | Used for | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **M-Pesa** | Local clients, some platforms, withdrawals | Instant; keep business and personal records separate |
| **PayPal** | Many international clients and platforms | In Kenya you can withdraw PayPal balance to M-Pesa via the PayPal option in the M-Pesa app, or to a bank |
| **Payoneer** | Upwork, Fiverr and many marketplaces | Withdraw to a Kenyan bank account |
| **Wise** | Receiving from clients abroad | Withdraw to bank or M-Pesa where supported |
| **Bank transfer (SWIFT)** | YouTube AdSense, big clients, salaries | Fees per transfer; ask your bank about USD accounts |
| **Platform wallets** | Upwork, Fiverr, Jumia, etc. | Each has its own withdrawal options and fees |

Always use accounts **in your own name**. "Account renting" (using someone else's Upwork or AI-platform account, or letting someone use yours) breaks platform rules, gets accounts banned and often ends with the worker not being paid.

## Ten rules for staying safe

1. **Never pay to get a job.** No real employer charges registration or activation fees.
2. **Too good to be true is false.** "Earn KSh 5,000 daily by liking posts" is a scam.
3. **No guaranteed returns.** Anyone promising fixed weekly profits from forex, crypto or "investment" is running a scam or a Ponzi scheme.
4. **Keep payments on the platform.** Clients asking to pay "outside Upwork/Fiverr" often disappear, and it breaks the rules.
5. **Verify companies:** check their website, reviews, and LinkedIn; search "[company] scam".
6. **Protect your data.** Don't send copies of your ID to random WhatsApp recruiters.
7. **Beware of fake cheques and overpayments.** "I sent too much, refund the difference" is a classic trick.
8. **Never share OTP codes, PINs or passwords.**
9. **Check licences** for anything involving your money: the **CMA** (Capital Markets Authority) lists licensed brokers and fund managers; the **CBK** regulates banks and payment providers.
10. **When in doubt, ask** in trusted communities (Ajira Digital clubs, your college, experienced freelancers) before acting.

## Taxes and records (the short version)

- Online income is taxable in Kenya like any other income. As a freelancer you are generally responsible for declaring it and filing your **annual return on iTax by 30 June**.
- Keep a simple record: date, client, amount, fees, and what you spent on work (data, equipment).
- Rules and rates (income tax bands, turnover tax, withholding tax) change; check **kra.go.ke** or ask a tax adviser. The **Taxes, records and managing money** lesson in the Make Money Online subject goes deeper.

## How to choose your first method

Answer honestly:

1. **What skills do I already have?** (Typing, writing, design, a language, teaching, selling, coding, a profession like nursing or accounting.)
2. **What device do I have?** (Phone only, or laptop.)
3. **How much time per week?** (5 hours, 20 hours, full time.)
4. **Do I want quick small income or slower, bigger income?** Microtasks pay quickly but little; skills like design, development and marketing take months to learn but pay far more.
5. **What do I enjoy?** You'll quit work you hate.

| Your situation | Good first methods |
|---|---|
| Phone only, little experience | WhatsApp/Facebook selling, social media help for local businesses, microtask apps, UGC videos |
| Good English and typing | Transcription, proofreading, writing, AI rating, VA work |
| Creative | Canva graphics, thumbnails, short videos, photography |
| Teacher or strong student | Online tutoring, notes, YouTube lessons |
| Technical | Websites, WordPress, IT support, data analysis, coding for AI |
| Professional (nurse, lawyer, accountant, engineer) | Expert AI training, consulting, specialist writing |
| Have stock or a business | Jumia, own shop, WhatsApp catalogue |

:::think Why do microtasks and surveys usually pay less than skills like web development?
Because almost anyone can do them, so there are many workers competing for the same small tasks, and each task creates little value for the client. Skills like web development take months to learn, fewer people can do them well, and the result (a website that brings customers) is worth a lot to a business. Pay follows **value** and **scarcity** of skill.
:::

## How to use this subject

- Read each family's lesson, then pick **one or two** methods (not ten).
- Follow the step-by-step instructions for 30 days.
- Use the related skill subjects on this hub (writing, Excel, Canva/graphic design, web development, AI tools) to build the skill.
- Track your hours and income; adjust after a month.

## Summary

- Online income is payment for work, skills or products; there is no easy money.
- You need a device, internet, email, your own ID, M-Pesa and an international payment method.
- 13 families and 132 methods are covered in this subject.
- Never pay for a job, never trust guaranteed returns, keep payments on platforms, verify everything.
- Declare your income and keep records.
- Choose one or two methods based on your skills, device, time and goals.

```quiz
Q: Should you pay a registration fee to get an online job? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: By what date are annual tax returns filed on iTax? Write day and month.
A: 30 June | June 30 | 30th June
Q: Which Kenyan regulator lists licensed forex brokers? Write the abbreviation.
A: CMA
Q: Is "account renting" allowed on platforms like Upwork? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: Which service lets you move PayPal money to M-Pesa? (the mobile money service)
A: M-Pesa | mpesa
Q: Is forex trading a reliable salary for beginners? (yes or no)
A: no
```

lessons.title: A. Writing and language work (ways 1–12): articles, copywriting, editing, translation and more
lessons.body:
# A. Writing and language work (ways 1–12): articles, copywriting, editing, translation and more

Every website, app, advert, email, product page and video script starts as **words**. Businesses worldwide pay for clear, persuasive writing, and Kenyans have an advantage: strong English education, often a second or third language (Kiswahili and mother tongues), and time zones that overlap with Europe and partly with the US. This unit explains 12 writing and language methods step by step.

:::note Before you start
- **Skills needed for all writing work:** correct grammar and spelling, clear sentences, research skills, meeting deadlines, and taking feedback without getting upset.
- **Tools (free):** Google Docs, Grammarly or LanguageTool (free versions), Hemingway Editor (readability), Google Search for research.
- **AI tools:** ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini can help you brainstorm and edit, but clients pay for **your** judgement, accuracy and voice. Never submit unedited AI text as original work if the client expects human writing; many clients check, and trust is your business.
:::

## How to build a writing portfolio (do this first)

Clients hire writers by reading samples. You need 3–5 strong samples before applying anywhere.

1. **Choose 2–3 niches** you know or can learn: technology, personal finance, health and fitness, travel in Kenya, agriculture, education, real estate, e-commerce.
2. **Write samples** (800–1,500 words each) as if for a real client: "How to start poultry farming in Kenya: costs and profits", "10 budget phones under KSh 20,000 compared".
3. **Publish them** free on **Medium**, **LinkedIn articles**, a free **Google Sites** or **WordPress.com** blog, or a Google Drive folder with view-only links.
4. **Make a one-page portfolio**: your photo, niches, links to samples, contacts (email, LinkedIn, WhatsApp).

:::tip Quality beats quantity
Three excellent, well-researched samples with clear headings, sources and no errors beat twenty rushed ones. Read each sample aloud before publishing.
:::

---

### 1. Blog and article writing

**What it is.** Writing informative articles for company blogs, websites and online magazines: guides, how-tos, lists, news explainers.

**Who it suits.** Good English, curious researchers, people who enjoy explaining things.

**How to start, step by step:**
1. Build your portfolio as above in 2–3 niches.
2. Create profiles on **Upwork** (upwork.com), **Fiverr** (fiverr.com) and **PeopleperHour** (peopleperhour.com). Write a clear headline: "Tech and personal finance writer: clear, researched blog posts".
3. Check job boards: **ProBlogger job board** (problogger.com/jobs), LinkedIn Jobs ("content writer remote"), and Kenyan agencies and digital marketing firms that hire freelance writers.
4. Pitch Kenyan businesses directly: many SMEs, schools and SACCOs need blog posts but have no writer. Email them a short pitch with a sample and a suggested topic list.
5. Deliver on time, with headings, short paragraphs, sources and an attractive title. Ask satisfied clients for a review and repeat work.

**Pay (honest).** Beginners on marketplaces often start low (a few dollars per 500 words). Writers with good samples and niches commonly earn far more per article; specialists in finance, tech or health can earn several times beginner rates. Long-term clients matter more than one-off jobs.

**Watch out.** Avoid "content mills" that pay extremely little for huge volume, and "test articles" demanded unpaid by unknown clients (scammers collect free articles this way). A short test of 200–300 words is reasonable; a full unpaid article isn't.

---

### 2. SEO content writing

**What it is.** Writing articles designed to rank on Google for specific searches (keywords), so the client gets free traffic.

**Skills.** Normal writing skills plus SEO basics: keyword research, search intent, headings, internal links, meta titles and descriptions.

**How to start:**
1. Learn SEO basics (the Marketing subject on this hub, Google's free SEO Starter Guide, HubSpot Academy's free SEO course).
2. Practise with free tools: Google's "People also ask", Google Trends, Ubersuggest/AnswerThePublic free tiers, Google Search Console on your own blog.
3. Write a sample targeting a real keyword, e.g. "how to apply for a KRA PIN", and explain your keyword choice in your portfolio.
4. Offer "SEO blog posts" on Fiverr/Upwork and to local businesses; show results (e.g. "this post reached page 1 for X") when you have them.

**Pay.** Higher than general writing because results bring customers. Bundle services: keyword research + article + meta description.

---

### 3. Copywriting

**What it is.** Writing words that **sell**: website pages, adverts, product launch emails, sales pages, social media ads, brochure text, slogans.

**Skills.** Understanding customers, persuasion, short punchy writing, testing what works.

**How to start:**
1. Study classic copywriting principles: **AIDA** (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action), benefits over features, clear calls to action.
2. Rewrite real examples for practice: take a weak Kenyan business website and rewrite its home page (don't publish their brand as your client, just show "before/after" as a practice piece).
3. Offer services: "website copy", "Facebook ad copy", "product descriptions", "sales emails".
4. Partner with web designers (they often need someone to write their clients' website text).

**Pay.** One of the best-paid writing skills because it directly makes money for clients; experienced copywriters charge per project rather than per word.

:::example Features vs benefits
- Feature: "Our phones have a 5,000 mAh battery."
- Benefit: "Go two full days without charging, even with WhatsApp and YouTube."
Copywriting turns features into benefits the customer cares about.
:::

---

### 4. Ghostwriting

**What it is.** Writing content that is published under someone else's name: books, LinkedIn posts for executives, speeches, blog posts for founders, memoirs.

**How to start:**
1. Get comfortable writing in other people's voices: interview someone and write a post as them.
2. Offer "LinkedIn ghostwriting" to busy professionals, coaches and CEOs (a monthly package of posts).
3. For books: start with short e-books, interview the client, create an outline they approve, then write chapter by chapter.
4. Use contracts: agree on deadlines, number of revisions, confidentiality and payment milestones (e.g. 30% upfront).

**Ethics.** Ghostwriting for businesses and individuals is a normal profession. **Writing school or university assignments, theses or exams for students to submit as their own is academic dishonesty**: it can get the student expelled, it harms education, and many "academic writing" arrangements in Kenya leave writers unpaid with no legal protection. Build your career on legitimate writing.

---

### 5. Technical writing

**What it is.** Writing instructions and documentation: user manuals, help centre articles, software documentation, API docs, standard operating procedures (SOPs), training guides.

**Who it suits.** People with technical or IT knowledge who can explain clearly; engineers, IT graduates, developers, health workers (for medical device manuals).

**How to start:**
1. Learn the basics: plain language, numbered steps, screenshots, consistent terms. Google's free **Technical Writing courses** (developers.google.com/tech-writing) are excellent.
2. Create samples: a "How to set up M-Pesa Till on a POS" guide with screenshots, or documentation for an open-source project on GitHub.
3. Learn tools: Markdown, Google Docs, basic HTML, screenshots and annotations, and documentation sites (GitBook, Docusaurus).
4. Apply to software companies, SaaS startups and documentation agencies; contribute to open-source docs to get visible experience.

**Pay.** Technical writing is generally among the better-paid writing fields, especially for software documentation.

---

### 6. Proofreading and editing

**What it is.** Finding and fixing errors (proofreading) or improving clarity, structure and flow (editing) in documents, books, websites, reports and CVs.

**How to start:**
1. Test yourself honestly: can you spot errors in grammar, punctuation, consistency (e.g. "KSh" vs "Kshs"), and style?
2. Learn a style guide basics (e.g. British vs American spelling; clients specify which).
3. Learn **Track Changes** in Word and **Suggesting mode** in Google Docs; clients expect it.
4. Offer services to: authors self-publishing books, students (proofreading their own work is fine; rewriting it is not), businesses, NGOs, and non-native English speakers abroad.
5. Price per word or per page; give a quick sample edit of one page to win clients.

**Tip.** Specialise: academic proofreading (language only), business documents, fiction, website copy.

---

### 7. Translation

**What it is.** Converting written text from one language to another: English ↔ Kiswahili is in steady demand (NGO materials, apps, health information, marketing for East Africa), plus French, Arabic, Somali, Amharic and local languages.

**Who it suits.** Truly fluent in both languages, careful with meaning and culture.

**How to start:**
1. Choose your language pairs and specialities (health, legal, marketing, software).
2. Create samples (translate a public-domain text and show both versions).
3. Join translation platforms and agencies: **ProZ** (proz.com, the largest translator directory), **TranslatorsCafe**, **Gengo**, **Smartling/agency** roles, and localisation jobs on Upwork.
4. Learn a CAT tool (Computer-Assisted Translation) such as the free version of **Matecat** or **OmegaT**.
5. For Kiswahili, offer **localisation** (adapting apps and websites, not just word-for-word translation) and **reviewing machine translation** (post-editing), a growing service.

**Watch out.** Machine translation (Google Translate) is fast but makes meaning errors; clients pay for accuracy. Never deliver raw machine translation as human work.

---

### 8. CV, cover letter and LinkedIn writing

**What it is.** Writing professional CVs, cover letters and LinkedIn profiles for job seekers, a strong local market (graduates, people applying abroad, public service applicants).

**How to start:**
1. Learn modern CV standards: 1–2 pages, achievements with numbers, ATS-friendly format (simple layout, standard headings, no text in images).
2. Create 3 sample CVs (with fictional names) for different levels: graduate, mid-career, executive.
3. Offer services on Fiverr, LinkedIn, Facebook groups for job seekers, and campuses.
4. Package: CV + cover letter + LinkedIn update. Add an interview prep call as an upsell (method 99).

**Pay.** Locally, CV writing is often priced from a few hundred to a few thousand shillings; international clients pay more.

**Ethics.** Never invent qualifications or experience. Present real achievements well.

---

### 9. Grant and proposal writing

**What it is.** Writing funding applications for NGOs, community groups, startups, researchers and schools; and business proposals and tenders for companies.

**Who it suits.** Strong writers who understand projects, budgets and logical frameworks; people with NGO or business experience.

**How to start:**
1. Learn grant structure: problem statement, objectives, activities, logframe, monitoring and evaluation, budget, sustainability.
2. Study real open calls (foundations, embassies, development agencies) and their requirements.
3. Volunteer to write one proposal for a community group or youth group to build a sample (with permission).
4. Market to NGOs, CBOs, startups and consultants; network on LinkedIn.

**Pay.** Usually per proposal. Avoid "success fee only" arrangements as a beginner (you work for free if the grant isn't won), and never promise that a grant will be won.

---

### 10. Product descriptions

**What it is.** Writing the text for products in online shops: Jumia and Kilimall sellers, Shopify stores, supermarkets going online, Amazon sellers abroad.

**How to start:**
1. Write samples for 10 products in one category (phones, beauty, kitchen): title, 3–5 benefit bullets, specifications, and a short paragraph.
2. Learn marketplace rules (title length, keywords, banned claims).
3. Offer bulk packages to online sellers: "50 product descriptions".
4. Find clients: Kenyan sellers on Jumia/Kilimall, Instagram shops, e-commerce agencies.

---

### 11. Email newsletter writing

**What it is.** Writing regular emails for businesses and creators: newsletters, welcome sequences, promotions.

**How to start:**
1. Learn email basics: subject lines, one main message, clear call to action, mobile-friendly.
2. Learn a tool: **Mailchimp**, **MailerLite** or **Brevo** (free tiers).
3. Start your own small newsletter (e.g. weekly tech tips) as proof.
4. Offer monthly packages ("4 newsletters per month") to businesses, schools and coaches; combine with method 73 (email marketing).

---

### 12. Scriptwriting

**What it is.** Writing scripts for YouTube videos, adverts, explainer videos, podcasts, radio ads and TikTok content.

**How to start:**
1. Study successful videos: write down how they hook viewers in the first 10 seconds, structure, and end with a call to action.
2. Write sample scripts: a 60-second advert, a 7-minute YouTube explainer, a 30-second TikTok.
3. Offer to YouTubers (many need scripts for faceless channels), agencies and businesses making video ads.
4. Learn the format: two-column scripts (visuals | audio) for video.

---

## Turning writing into a stable income

1. **Niche down:** "fintech writer" earns more than "general writer".
2. **Raise prices gradually** as reviews grow.
3. **Retainers:** offer monthly packages (e.g. 8 blog posts a month) for predictable income.
4. **Upsell:** writing + images + publishing on WordPress; copy + design via a designer partner.
5. **Keep learning:** SEO, marketing, a speciality subject.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Applying without samples | Build 3–5 samples first |
| Copying from other websites | Plagiarism ends careers; always write originally and cite sources |
| Submitting unedited AI text | Use AI as an assistant only; fact-check and rewrite |
| Missing deadlines | Promise realistic dates; communicate early if delayed |
| Writing assignments for students | Choose legitimate writing work |
| Accepting long unpaid "tests" | Offer a short paid test or your samples |

## Practice tasks

1. Choose two niches and write one 1,000-word sample in each.
2. Rewrite the home page of a small business website (as practice) using AIDA.
3. Translate a 300-word health notice from English to Kiswahili (or another language you know).
4. Write a CV for a fictional graduate using ATS-friendly formatting.
5. Create an Upwork or Fiverr profile draft: headline, overview, three portfolio items.

## Summary

- Writing work includes articles, SEO content, copywriting, ghostwriting, technical writing, editing, translation, CVs, grants, product descriptions, newsletters and scripts.
- Build 3–5 excellent samples first; publish them in a simple portfolio.
- Find work on Upwork, Fiverr, PeopleperHour, ProBlogger, ProZ, LinkedIn and by pitching Kenyan businesses directly.
- Avoid plagiarism, unedited AI text, unpaid long tests and academic cheating.
- Grow income by specialising, retainers and upselling.

```quiz
Q: How many writing samples should you prepare before applying, at minimum?
A: 3 | three | 3-5
Q: What does the A at the start of AIDA stand for?
A: Attention
Q: Which type of writing is designed to rank on Google?
A: SEO | SEO writing | SEO content writing | SEO content
Q: Which website is the largest directory for translators?
A: ProZ | proz.com | proz
Q: Is writing students' assignments for them to submit legitimate work? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: Which Word feature shows edits for the client to accept or reject? (two words)
A: Track Changes | track changes
```

lessons.title: B. Transcription and audio work (ways 13–21): transcription, captions, voice-over and podcast editing
lessons.body:
# B. Transcription and audio work (ways 13–21): transcription, captions, voice-over and podcast editing

Every day, millions of hours of audio and video are recorded: interviews, meetings, lectures, court sessions, podcasts, YouTube videos, doctor's notes and customer calls. Much of it needs to become **text** (transcripts and captions), or needs a **human voice** (voice-overs, narration). This unit covers nine audio-related ways to earn, from beginner-friendly transcription to skilled voice work.

:::note What all audio work needs
- **Good headphones** (over-ear or quality earphones): you can't transcribe accurately from phone speakers.
- **A quiet place** and patience.
- **Fast, accurate typing** (aim for 50+ words per minute with high accuracy; free practice on typing.com, monkeytype.com, 10fastfingers.com).
- **Excellent listening and English spelling**, including names, places and technical terms (research them).
- A laptop (most transcription is impractical on a phone).
:::

---

### 13. General transcription

**What it is.** Listening to audio or video and typing exactly what is said, following the platform's **style guide** (how to mark speakers, unclear words, timestamps, filler words).

**Two styles you'll meet:**
- **Clean verbatim:** remove "um", "uh", false starts and repetitions; fix stutters. The most common.
- **Full (true) verbatim:** type everything exactly, including "um", laughter [laughs], pauses and false starts. Used in research and legal work.

**How to start, step by step:**
1. **Practise first:** transcribe 5–10 minutes of a podcast or YouTube interview and compare with its captions. Note your mistakes.
2. **Learn the tools:** a free transcription player like **oTranscribe** (otranscribe.com) lets you pause, rewind and slow audio with keyboard shortcuts while typing.
3. **Read the style guide carefully** before any test. Most failures are style guide mistakes, not hearing mistakes.
4. **Apply to platforms** (each has an entry test; availability for Kenyan applicants changes, so check the current application page):
   - **GoTranscript** (gotranscript.com): popular with Kenyan transcribers; strict tests.
   - **TranscribeMe** (transcribeme.com): short audio clips; pathways to specialised teams.
   - **Rev** (rev.com/freelancers): transcription and captions.
   - **Scribie** (scribie.com): short files, a good place to practise.
   - **Upwork/Fiverr**: direct clients (researchers, podcasters, journalists).
5. **Start with short, clear files**, build your accuracy score, then take longer and harder files (accents, poor audio) that pay more per minute.
6. **Find direct clients:** university researchers (interview transcripts), journalists, NGOs (focus group discussions), churches (sermon transcripts), YouTubers.

**Pay (honest).** Platforms usually pay **per audio minute**. Beginners often find it slow at first: one hour of audio can take 3–5 hours to transcribe until you get faster. Income improves with speed, accuracy, specialisation and direct clients. Work availability on platforms goes up and down.

:::warning Transcription scams
"Pay KSh 1,500 to activate your transcription account" or "buy a transcription account" are scams. Real platforms are free to join. Buying or renting accounts breaks rules and can get you banned without payment.
:::

---

### 14. Captioning and subtitling

**What it is.** Creating **captions** (same-language text synchronised with video, including sound cues like [music]) and **subtitles** (translations) for YouTube videos, films, online courses, TV and events.

**How to start:**
1. Learn caption rules: maximum characters per line (often around 32–42), 1–2 lines, reading speed, timing to speech, speaker identification.
2. Learn free tools: **Subtitle Edit** (Windows, free), **Aegisub**, or YouTube Studio's subtitle editor. Understand formats: **SRT** and **WebVTT**.
3. Make samples: caption a 3-minute public-domain or your own video in SRT.
4. Apply to captioning platforms (Rev captions, Verbit, 3Play Media, subtitle agencies) and offer YouTubers captioning; many Kenyan creators and churches want Kiswahili or English captions.
5. Offer **subtitle translation** (English ↔ Kiswahili) for films and NGO videos.

**Why it pays well.** Captions require timing skills as well as transcription; accessibility laws in many countries require captions on public videos, so demand is steady.

---

### 15. Specialist transcription (medical and legal)

**What it is.** Transcribing doctors' dictations, medical reports (medical transcription), court proceedings, depositions and legal interviews (legal transcription).

**Who it suits.** People with medical or legal training (nurses, clinical officers, paralegals, law graduates) or anyone willing to study the terminology seriously.

**How to start:**
1. Learn the terminology (medical: anatomy, drugs, abbreviations; legal: court procedures, Latin terms).
2. Take a reputable course if needed; some employers require certification.
3. Understand **confidentiality**: medical and legal records are highly sensitive; follow data protection rules strictly.
4. Apply to specialist teams on transcription platforms, or medical transcription/BPO companies (some operate in Kenya, serving international hospitals).

**Pay.** Higher than general transcription because errors can be dangerous (a wrong drug dose) and expertise is scarce.

**Note.** AI speech recognition now does much of the first draft in medicine, so many jobs are now **editing AI transcripts** for accuracy. The skill of checking carefully remains valuable.

---

### 16. Kiswahili and local-language transcription

**What it is.** Transcribing and translating audio in Kiswahili, Sheng, Kikuyu, Dholuo, Luhya, Kalenjin, Kamba, Somali and other languages, for researchers, NGOs, media monitoring, market research and AI companies.

**Why it's an opportunity.** Fewer people can do it, and there is far less automatic transcription for African languages, so human transcribers are needed.

**How to start:**
1. Practise transcribing local radio interviews or vernacular sermons, then translating them to English.
2. Contact research firms, universities and NGOs that run surveys and focus groups (they need transcripts and translations).
3. Watch for language projects on AI data platforms (method 32) and translation agencies.
4. Keep your spelling consistent (agree on a spelling standard with the client).

---

### 17. Voice-over work

**What it is.** Recording your voice for adverts, explainer videos, e-learning courses, YouTube videos, phone systems (IVR: "Press 1 for..."), radio and TV, animations and audiobooks.

**Who it suits.** Clear, pleasant voices; people who can read naturally and take direction. Kenyan English, Kiswahili and African accents are increasingly requested for local and pan-African campaigns.

**How to start, step by step:**
1. **Set up a home studio** cheaply: a quiet room with soft furnishings (curtains, a mattress, blankets reduce echo; many beginners record in a wardrobe full of clothes), a USB microphone (e.g. entry-level condenser mics), a pop filter, and free **Audacity** software.
2. **Learn basic audio editing** in Audacity: noise reduction, cutting breaths and mistakes, normalising volume, exporting MP3/WAV.
3. **Record a demo reel**: 60–90 seconds with short clips in different styles (commercial, corporate, e-learning, character, Kiswahili).
4. **Create profiles** on **Fiverr**, **Voices.com**, **Voice123** and **Upwork**; send your demo to Kenyan production houses, radio stations, ad agencies and e-learning companies.
5. **Deliver professionally:** clean audio, on time, with one free revision for mistakes.

**Pay.** Varies hugely: short Fiverr gigs pay little; commercial ads (especially TV/radio) pay well and sometimes include usage fees.

---

### 18. Audiobook narration

**What it is.** Reading whole books aloud for audiobook platforms.

**How to start:**
1. Build voice-over basics (method 17) and stamina (narrating one finished hour typically takes several hours of recording and editing).
2. Learn audiobook standards (consistent volume, room tone, chapter files, noise floor).
3. Find work: **ACX** (Audible's marketplace) is limited to certain countries (mainly US, UK, Canada and Ireland residents), so from Kenya look at Upwork/Fiverr narration jobs, publishers of African literature, and authors self-publishing directly.
4. Record a sample chapter of a public-domain book (e.g. from Project Gutenberg) for your portfolio.

---

### 19. Podcast editing

**What it is.** Editing podcast recordings: removing mistakes and long pauses, balancing volume between speakers, adding intro music, cleaning noise, creating show notes and short clips.

**How to start:**
1. Learn **Audacity** (free) or **Reaper** (affordable) or **Descript** (edits audio by editing the transcript).
2. Practise on free raw podcast files or record your own conversation.
3. Offer packages: "Edit + show notes + 3 short clips for social media".
4. Find clients: Kenyan podcasters (a growing scene), churches, companies starting podcasts, and international podcasters on Upwork/Fiverr.
5. Add video podcast editing (most podcasts now publish on YouTube) to earn more.

---

### 20. Voice data recording for AI

**What it is.** Recording yourself reading sentences or having conversations to train speech recognition and voice AI, often for under-served languages and accents (Kenyan English, Kiswahili, local languages).

**How to start:**
1. Look for **speech data projects** on AI data platforms (Appen, OneForma, and others) and on research project announcements from universities.
2. Follow instructions exactly (quiet room, specific microphone distance, reading exactly as written).
3. Understand that these are usually **short projects**, not continuous work.

**Watch out.** Read consent terms: you're giving permission to use your voice to train AI. Never pay to join a "voice project". Note that some valuable language projects (like Mozilla Common Voice) are **volunteer** and unpaid; contributing is good for your language, but it isn't income.

---

### 21. Audio cleanup and music services

**What it is.** Cleaning noisy recordings (interviews, church services, wedding videos), mixing and mastering songs for local artists, producing jingles and radio adverts, making beats.

**How to start:**
1. Learn a DAW (digital audio workstation): **Audacity** for cleanup; **Reaper**, **FL Studio** or **Cakewalk** (free on Windows) for music.
2. Learn mixing basics: EQ, compression, noise reduction, loudness standards for streaming.
3. Build a portfolio: before/after cleanup samples; jingles for imaginary businesses.
4. Clients: local musicians, churches, radio stations, small businesses needing jingles; online, beat-selling on platforms like BeatStars and services on Fiverr.

**Copyright.** Only use samples and loops you have the rights to; register your own music with Kenya's collective management organisations if you release songs.

---

## A typical first month in transcription

| Week | Focus |
|---|---|
| 1 | Typing practice daily; learn oTranscribe; transcribe 3 practice files and compare with captions |
| 2 | Study two platforms' style guides; take their tests |
| 3 | Start with short files; track accuracy feedback |
| 4 | Contact 10 local researchers, NGOs or podcasters with an offer |

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Ignoring the style guide | Read it twice; keep it open while working |
| Guessing unclear words | Use the platform's [inaudible] tag correctly, research names |
| Phone speakers instead of headphones | Use headphones |
| Echoey voice recordings | Record in a room with soft furnishings |
| Paying to "activate" an account | Real platforms are free; it's a scam |
| Sharing confidential audio | Follow confidentiality and data protection rules |

## Practice tasks

1. Take a typing test and record your words per minute and accuracy; practise 15 minutes daily for two weeks.
2. Transcribe 5 minutes of a podcast in clean verbatim, then the same in full verbatim.
3. Make an SRT caption file for a 2-minute video.
4. Record a 60-second voice demo in Audacity with noise reduction applied.
5. Write an email offering transcription and translation to a university research team.

## Summary

- Audio work: general, specialist and local-language transcription; captioning/subtitling; voice-over; narration; podcast editing; voice data for AI; audio cleanup and music.
- You need headphones, a quiet space, fast accurate typing (or a good voice and a simple home studio), and attention to style guides.
- Platforms include GoTranscript, TranscribeMe, Rev, Scribie, Voices.com, Voice123, Upwork and Fiverr; local researchers, NGOs, churches and podcasters are strong direct clients.
- Kiswahili and local-language skills are a real advantage.
- Never pay to join; protect confidential recordings.

```quiz
Q: Which transcription style removes "um" and false starts? (two words)
A: clean verbatim
Q: Which free web tool helps you control audio while transcribing?
A: oTranscribe | otranscribe
Q: Which caption file format starts with numbered blocks and timestamps? Write its extension letters.
A: SRT | srt
Q: Which free software is commonly used to record and edit voice-overs?
A: Audacity
Q: Is Mozilla Common Voice a paid job? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: Should you pay to activate a transcription account? (yes or no)
A: no
```

lessons.title: C. AI training and data work (ways 22–32): annotation, AI rating, Remotasks-style tasks and data entry
lessons.body:
# C. AI training and data work (ways 22–32): annotation, AI rating, Remotasks-style tasks and data entry

Artificial intelligence learns from examples prepared by humans: photos with every car outlined, sentences labelled as positive or negative, chatbot answers ranked from best to worst. This human work is called **data annotation** or **AI training**, and Kenya has been one of the world's important hubs for it, with companies like **Sama** and **CloudFactory** employing data workers in Nairobi, and thousands of Kenyans working on platforms such as Remotasks before it left the country. This unit explains the eleven main types of AI and data work, how to get in, and the realities of pay, availability and working conditions.

:::warning What happened to Remotasks in Kenya
**Remotasks** (owned by Scale AI) was very popular with Kenyan workers. In **March 2024 it stopped offering work in Kenya** (and some other countries), leaving many workers without access. Lessons from that:
1. **Never depend on one platform.** Projects and whole platforms can end suddenly.
2. **Never buy or rent accounts** from others to get around country restrictions; accounts get banned and earnings are lost.
3. **Build transferable skills** (accuracy, a subject speciality, coding, languages) that work on many platforms and in full-time jobs.
:::

## How AI training work works

1. You **apply** to a platform or company and pass qualification tests.
2. You're added to **projects** (each with its own guidelines, often 10–50 pages).
3. You complete **tasks** in the platform's tool; reviewers check quality.
4. Pay is per task or per hour; your **quality score** decides how much work you get.
5. Projects end; you qualify for new ones.

:::tip The two keys to success
**Read guidelines completely** (most people skim and fail), and **choose quality over speed**. Accurate workers get promoted to reviewer roles and better projects; fast careless workers get removed.
:::

## Platforms and companies to know

Availability by country changes often, so always check each platform's current application page:

| Company / platform | Type of work | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Sama** (sama.com) | Data annotation (employed roles, Nairobi) | Employer, not a gig app; check careers page |
| **CloudFactory** (cloudfactory.com) | Data work with a managed workforce, Nairobi presence | Check open roles |
| **Appen** (appen.com) | Search evaluation, data collection, annotation | Many short projects; worldwide |
| **TELUS Digital** (formerly TELUS International AI) | Search and ads rating, annotation | Rater roles by country and language |
| **OneForma** (oneforma.com) | Language data, transcription, annotation | Many language projects |
| **Toloka** (toloka.ai) | Microtasks and AI data | Open in many countries |
| **Clickworker** (clickworker.com) | Microtasks, data, AI training | Pays via PayPal/Payoneer |
| **Outlier** (outlier.ai) | Expert AI training (writing, coding, STEM) | Owned by Scale AI; check if your country is accepted |
| **DataAnnotation.tech** | AI writing and coding evaluation | Country list is limited; check |
| **Upwork / LinkedIn** | Annotation contracts, AI trainer jobs | Search "data annotation", "AI trainer", "RLHF" |

---

### 22. Image and video annotation

**What it is.** Labelling images and video frames: drawing **bounding boxes** around objects (cars, people, products), tracing exact outlines (**polygons / segmentation**), marking points (**keypoints** on faces or bodies), tracking objects across video frames, and labelling road scenes for self-driving cars.

**Skills.** Patience, precision, a good screen and mouse (a laptop or desktop; a mouse is much more accurate than a touchpad).

**How to start:**
1. Learn the tool types with free software: **CVAT** (cvat.ai) and **Label Studio** (labelstud.io) let you practise annotation on your own images.
2. Apply to annotation companies and platforms above; take the qualification tests carefully.
3. Build speed only after your accuracy is consistently high.

---

### 23. Text labelling and classification

**What it is.** Reading text and labelling it: sentiment (positive/negative), topic, intent ("wants a refund"), named entities (marking names, places, amounts), spam detection, and checking machine translations.

**How to start:** apply to Appen, OneForma, Toloka and Clickworker projects; practise with Label Studio. Language skills (Kiswahili and others) open extra projects.

---

### 24. AI response rating (RLHF)

**What it is.** Chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini improve partly through **RLHF** (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback): humans compare AI answers and rate which is more helpful, correct, safe and well written, and explain why.

**Skills.** Excellent English reading and writing, careful fact-checking, clear explanations of your ratings.

**How to start:**
1. Use AI chatbots a lot and notice their mistakes: wrong facts, missed instructions, unsafe advice, poor formatting.
2. Learn the common rating dimensions: helpfulness, honesty/accuracy, harmlessness, instruction following, writing quality.
3. Apply to AI trainer roles (platforms above; search "AI trainer" and "AI writing evaluator" on LinkedIn and Upwork).
4. In tests, **justify your ratings specifically**: "Response B is better because it answers both parts of the question and correctly states the KRA deadline, while A ignores the second part."

---

### 25. AI writing evaluation and prompt writing

**What it is.** Writing prompts (questions and instructions) that challenge AI models, writing ideal "gold" responses, and **red-teaming** (trying to make AI produce harmful content, so developers can fix it, under strict guidelines).

**How to start:** strong writing samples (method 1), practise writing complex prompts with clear constraints, and apply to AI training projects. Red-teaming projects require following safety rules strictly and handling disturbing content professionally.

---

### 26. Coding tasks for AI training

**What it is.** Writing, reviewing and rating code produced by AI; creating coding problems and solutions; explaining bugs. Languages commonly requested: Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, C++, SQL, Go.

**Who it suits.** Developers and strong programming students. Pay is usually much higher than general annotation.

**How to start:**
1. Get solid at one or two languages (Python and JavaScript subjects on this hub).
2. Practise on coding challenge sites (LeetCode, HackerRank, Exercism) and review AI-generated code critically.
3. Apply for "AI coding trainer" or "software engineer, AI training" roles; tests usually involve finding bugs and explaining fixes.

---

### 27. Expert AI training (maths, science, medicine, law, finance)

**What it is.** AI companies hire **subject experts** to write hard questions, check AI reasoning step by step and correct errors in specialised fields.

**Who it suits.** Graduates and professionals: maths, physics, chemistry, biology, medicine, nursing, pharmacy, law, accounting, engineering, economics. Often a degree is required, sometimes a master's or PhD for top projects.

**How to start:** apply to expert AI trainer programmes (e.g. Outlier and similar, where available, plus LinkedIn listings), highlight your degree and specialism, and prepare for subject tests.

:::kenya
Kenya has many well-qualified graduates in sciences, health and engineering who struggle to find jobs locally. Expert AI training is one of the few online fields where a degree in, say, chemistry or nursing directly leads to well-paid remote work, though availability depends on projects and country eligibility.
:::

---

### 28. Search engine and ads evaluation (rater jobs)

**What it is.** Rating how relevant search results, ads, maps results or recommendations are for a query in your country and language, following detailed guidelines (Google publishes its own Search Quality Rater Guidelines publicly).

**How to start:** apply to rater roles at TELUS Digital, Appen and similar companies when they open for Kenya/English or Kiswahili; study the public rater guidelines before the exam. These are often part-time with set weekly hours.

---

### 29. Content moderation

**What it is.** Reviewing posts, images and videos against platform rules and removing harmful content, for social media companies and apps, usually through outsourcing companies (BPOs).

**The reality.** Content moderation can expose workers to violent and disturbing content. In Kenya, former moderators brought widely reported legal cases about working conditions and mental health support. If you consider this work:
- Ask about **psychological support**, exposure limits, breaks and contracts **before** accepting.
- Know your rights under Kenyan labour law.
- It's fine to decide this work isn't for you.

---

### 30. Data entry

**What it is.** Typing or copying information into spreadsheets, databases, CRMs or online stores: product catalogues, survey results, invoices, contact lists.

**How to start:**
1. Master **Excel/Google Sheets** basics (the Excel subject on this hub): formatting, sorting, filters, data validation, removing duplicates.
2. Offer data entry on Upwork/Fiverr and to local businesses (stock lists, school records).
3. Prove accuracy with a small sample task.

**Watch out.** "Data entry jobs" advertised on WhatsApp/Telegram that ask for a "registration fee" or ask you to "buy software" are scams. Real data entry is often low-paid; add Excel skills to move into better-paid data analysis (method 86).

---

### 31. Web research and lead lists

**What it is.** Finding information online for clients: building lists of potential customers (business names, websites, emails) for sales teams, researching competitors, collecting prices, verifying addresses.

**How to start:** learn advanced Google search operators (`site:`, quotes, `filetype:`), LinkedIn search, Google Maps business research, and spreadsheet organisation. Offer "lead generation lists" on Upwork/Fiverr. Follow data protection rules: use publicly available business information, not personal data scraped without permission.

---

### 32. Local-language data for AI

**What it is.** Creating and checking data in African languages: translating sentences, writing natural sentences, rating translations, transcribing local-language audio (method 16), recording speech (method 20).

**How to start:** list all languages you speak fluently on platform profiles (OneForma, Appen, Toloka, and others), watch for language projects, and join African language technology communities (such as Masakhane, a research community for African languages) to hear about projects and research.

---

## A realistic plan to get into AI work

1. **Week 1:** create accounts on 3–4 platforms that accept Kenya; complete profiles honestly (languages, education, skills).
2. **Week 1–2:** take qualification tests slowly; read every guideline.
3. **Ongoing:** keep a notebook of each project's rules; ask questions in project forums.
4. **Parallel:** build a stronger skill (coding, a subject speciality, Excel) for higher-paying AI training and jobs.
5. **Always:** keep other income options; projects end without warning.

## Rights and red flags

| Red flag | What to do |
|---|---|
| "Pay to get a Remotasks/Outlier account" | Scam; never buy or rent accounts |
| Recruiter on WhatsApp asking for ID photos and fees | Verify on the company's official website first |
| No contract, unclear pay | Ask for written terms |
| Harmful content without support | Ask about wellbeing support; you can decline |
| Payment through someone else's account | Use only accounts in your own name |

## Practice tasks

1. Install Label Studio or use CVAT online and annotate 20 images with bounding boxes.
2. Ask two AI chatbots the same tricky question and write a rating explaining which answer is better and why.
3. List your languages and subject strengths; find two AI projects that match them.
4. Clean a messy spreadsheet of 100 contacts (remove duplicates, fix formatting).
5. Read the first chapter of Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines.

## Summary

- AI training work: image/video annotation, text labelling, AI rating (RLHF), prompt writing and red-teaming, coding and expert training, search rating, moderation, data entry, research and local-language data.
- Kenya is a hub (Sama, CloudFactory and many platform workers), but platforms change: Remotasks stopped serving Kenya in March 2024.
- Success = reading guidelines fully and prioritising accuracy.
- Higher pay comes from coding, subject expertise and languages.
- Never buy/rent accounts or pay to join; know your rights, especially in content moderation.

```quiz
Q: In which year did Remotasks stop offering work in Kenya?
A: 2024
Q: What does RLHF stand for? Write the first word.
A: Reinforcement
Q: What is drawing a rectangle around an object in an image called? (two words)
A: bounding box | bounding boxes
Q: Should you buy or rent an AI platform account from someone else? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: Name the free annotation tool whose name starts with "Label".
A: Label Studio
Q: What matters more in annotation work: speed or quality?
A: quality | accuracy
```

lessons.title: D. Microtasks, surveys and testing (ways 33–41): small online tasks, usability tests and bounties
lessons.body:
# D. Microtasks, surveys and testing (ways 33–41): small online tasks, usability tests and bounties

These are the easiest online tasks to start: answering surveys, completing small tasks, testing websites and apps, joining research studies. They need few skills, which is exactly why they usually **pay little** and work isn't always available. Used well, they're a way to earn your first dollars, learn how online platforms work and fund data or a laptop while you build a bigger skill. This unit explains nine methods honestly, including which ones are worth your time.

:::warning Set your expectations
- Microtasks and surveys are **pocket money**, not a salary for most people in Kenya.
- Many survey sites screen you out after several minutes, or have few surveys for Kenya.
- **Usability testing and crowdtesting** pay better per hour and build real skills.
- Countless fake "earn by watching ads / liking posts / typing captchas" apps are scams or pay almost nothing. If an app pays you to do something useless, ask who is paying, and why.
:::

---

### 33. Microtask platforms

**What it is.** Tiny tasks of seconds to minutes: categorising images, checking if a search result matches, verifying business details, short transcriptions, writing a sentence, tagging products.
