**Where:** **Clickworker** (clickworker.com), **Toloka** (toloka.ai), **Amazon Mechanical Turk** (mturk.com; acceptance outside the US is limited and often closed), **Appen** short projects, **OneForma**.

**How to start:**
1. Sign up with your real details; complete qualification tests (they unlock better-paid tasks).
2. Start early in the day and check regularly; tasks appear and disappear.
3. Track your effective hourly earnings; drop task types that pay too little.
4. Withdraw regularly via PayPal/Payoneer.

---

### 34. Paid surveys (honest view)

**What it is.** Answering market research questionnaires for points or small cash.

**How to start:** reputable panels that accept Kenyan members change over time; look for long-established market research panels and read recent reviews from Kenyan users before signing up.

**Honest view.** Expect frequent disqualification, small rewards and high payout thresholds. Never pay to join a survey site; never give ID or banking passwords. Surveys can be an occasional extra, not a strategy.

---

### 35. Website and app usability testing

**What it is.** Companies pay ordinary people to use their website or app while **speaking their thoughts aloud** and recording the screen, so designers see where users get confused.

**Where:** **UserTesting** (usertesting.com), **Userlytics** (userlytics.com), **Testbirds** (testbirds.com), **Trymata**, **Userfeel**. Availability varies by country and demographic.

**How to start, step by step:**
1. Sign up and take the **practice test** seriously: think aloud clearly, describe what you expect and what confuses you.
2. Install any required screen recorder and test your microphone.
3. Answer screener questions **honestly** (lying gets you banned and wastes the client's money).
4. Check for tests several times a day; good testers get more invitations.
5. Speak continuously: "I'm looking for the sign-up button... I expected it at the top right... this text is too small on my phone."

**Pay.** Per test (often 10–20 minutes); better than surveys per minute, but tests are limited.

**Bonus skill.** This is real **UX research** experience. Combined with design learning, it leads towards UX research and design roles (method 46).

---

### 36. Crowdtesting (software and app beta testing)

**What it is.** Finding bugs in apps and websites on your own devices and reporting them clearly; companies pay per valid bug and for test cycles.

**Where:** **uTest** (utest.com, part of Applause), **Testbirds**, **Test IO**, **Testlio** (more selective, for experienced testers).

**How to start:**
1. Join uTest Academy (free courses on testing basics and writing bug reports).
2. Learn to write a perfect bug report: title, steps to reproduce, expected vs actual result, device/OS/browser, screenshots or screen recording.
3. Join test cycles; follow scope rules exactly (out-of-scope bugs don't pay).
4. Build reputation, then move to paid test cycles and better platforms.

**Career path.** Software testing (QA) is a real profession: crowdtesting experience plus learning test automation (Selenium, Playwright) can lead to QA jobs.

:::example A good bug report
**Title:** Checkout button does nothing on Android Chrome after entering an M-Pesa number
**Steps:** 1. Add any item to cart. 2. Go to checkout. 3. Choose M-Pesa, enter 0712345678. 4. Tap "Pay now".
**Expected:** STK push prompt appears.
**Actual:** Button shows a spinner for 2 seconds, then nothing happens. No error message.
**Device:** Samsung A14, Android 14, Chrome 129. **Attachment:** screen recording.
:::

---

### 37. Paid research studies and focus groups

**What it is.** Taking part in academic and market research studies online (questionnaires, experiments, interviews, focus group calls).

**Where:** **Prolific** (prolific.com) is a well-known platform for academic studies; country eligibility is limited and changes, so check. Locally, market research firms recruit participants for focus groups in Nairobi and other towns, sometimes paying participants for their time.

**Tips.** Be honest in screeners, pay attention (studies include attention checks), and only join firms you can verify.

---

### 38. Mystery shopping

**What it is.** Visiting shops, restaurants, banks or calling customer care as a normal customer, then reporting on service quality using a detailed form. Increasingly includes online mystery shopping (testing a company's website, chat or delivery).

**How to start:** register with established mystery shopping/market research companies operating in Kenya; complete assignments exactly as briefed and submit detailed, timely reports.

:::warning The classic mystery shopping scam
"You've been selected as a mystery shopper. We'll send you money; send part of it to evaluate an M-Pesa agent / money transfer service and keep the rest." This is a fraud: the money is stolen or fake, and you end up liable. Real mystery shopping never asks you to forward money.
:::

---

### 39. Game testing

**What it is.** Playing unreleased games to find bugs and give feedback on fun and difficulty.

**Reality.** It's mostly a QA job (repetitive, detailed bug reporting), not "getting paid to play". Paid opportunities come through crowdtesting platforms and game QA studios. Mobile game studios in Kenya and Africa also hire testers occasionally.

---

### 40. Cashback and referral bonuses

**What it is.** Getting a percentage back on purchases through cashback programmes, or earning bonuses for referring new users to legitimate services (some banks, apps and online services run referral programmes).

**Honest view.** Small amounts, useful only if you were buying anyway. **Never** join "referral" schemes where your earnings come mainly from recruiting people who pay to join: that's a **pyramid scheme**, illegal in Kenya, and most participants lose money.

---

### 41. Contests and bounties

**What it is.** Competing for prizes or rewards:
- **Design contests** (e.g. 99designs, logo contests): many designers compete, one winner is paid.
- **Data science competitions** on **Kaggle** (kaggle.com) and **Zindi** (zindi.africa, an African data science competition platform with prizes and job opportunities).
- **Bug bounties** (method 88): rewards for security vulnerabilities.
- **Writing and essay competitions**, hackathons and innovation challenges.

**Honest view.** Winning is uncertain, but contests build portfolios and visibility. Zindi and Kaggle results are respected on CVs for data science jobs.

---

## Which of these are worth your time?

| Method | Effort | Pay per hour | Builds a skill? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Microtasks | Low | Low | A little (attention to detail) |
| Surveys | Low | Very low | No |
| Usability testing | Low–medium | Medium (when available) | Yes (UX) |
| Crowdtesting | Medium | Low–medium, grows with reputation | Yes (QA career) |
| Research studies | Low | Low–medium | No |
| Mystery shopping | Medium | Low–medium | Some (reporting) |
| Contests (Zindi, Kaggle) | High | Uncertain | Yes (data science, design) |

Use low-skill methods as a **bridge**, and spend most of your time building a skill from the other families.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Joining dozens of survey sites | Pick a few reputable ones; track hourly earnings |
| Lying in screeners | Answer honestly; bans are permanent |
| Paying for "task apps" or "VIP levels" | Scam; never pay |
| Forwarding money in "mystery shopping" | Fraud; refuse |
| Treating microtasks as a career | Use them to fund learning a real skill |

## Practice tasks

1. Sign up on one microtask platform and one usability platform; complete the qualification or practice test.
2. Write a perfect bug report for a real bug you've noticed in an app or website.
3. Record yourself (screen + voice) testing a Kenyan e-commerce website for 10 minutes while thinking aloud.
4. Create a Zindi account and read one beginner competition's description.
5. Track a week of microtask work: hours, earnings, effective hourly rate.

## Summary

- Microtasks, surveys and studies are easy to start but pay little and availability varies.
- Usability testing and crowdtesting pay better and build real UX and QA skills.
- Contests (design, Kaggle, Zindi, bug bounties) build portfolios and visibility.
- Avoid pay-to-join task apps, pyramid "referral" schemes and money-forwarding "mystery shopping".

```quiz
Q: In usability testing, what should you do continuously while using the site? (two words)
A: think aloud | speak thoughts | talk aloud
Q: Which African data science competition platform has prizes? (one word)
A: Zindi
Q: In a bug report, what list lets someone recreate the bug? (three words: steps to ...)
A: steps to reproduce | reproduce
Q: Is a scheme where earnings come mainly from recruiting paying members legal in Kenya? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: Should a mystery shopper ever forward money to someone? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: Which platform's free Academy teaches crowdtesting basics? (one word)
A: uTest | utest
```

lessons.title: E. Graphics and design (ways 42–55): logos, social graphics, templates, stock photos and more
lessons.body:
# E. Graphics and design (ways 42–55): logos, social graphics, templates, stock photos and more

Every business needs visuals: a logo, social media posts, flyers, a website, product photos, presentations. Design is one of the most popular online skills in Kenya because tools like **Canva** made starting easy, while professional tools (Adobe Illustrator, Photoshop, Figma) let skilled designers charge much more. This unit explains 14 design-based ways to earn, step by step, with honest notes on where beginners get stuck.

:::note The design skills ladder
1. **Beginner (weeks):** Canva templates, simple social posts, flyers. Learn on this hub's Graphic design subject and Canva's free Design School.
2. **Intermediate (months):** design principles (hierarchy, alignment, contrast, spacing), typography, colour theory, Adobe Express/Photoshop basics, Figma.
3. **Professional (6–18 months of practice):** branding, Illustrator vector work, UI/UX, motion, a strong portfolio and client process.
Pay rises with every step.
:::

## Your design portfolio (do this first)

- Create a **Behance** (behance.net) and/or **Dribbble** (dribbble.com) profile; post 6–12 of your best pieces.
- Make **concept projects** for imaginary or real local businesses ("rebrand concept for a Kisumu bakery"), clearly labelled as concepts.
- Show your **process**: sketches, options, final, mockups (the logo on a shop sign, T-shirt, phone screen).
- Post work on Instagram, LinkedIn and TikTok (time-lapse "design with me" videos attract clients).

---

### 42. Logo design

**What it is.** Designing logos (symbols, wordmarks) for businesses, churches, schools, events and startups.

**How to start:**
1. Learn logo principles: simple, memorable, works in one colour and at tiny sizes (favicon) and large (signboard).
2. Learn **vector** design (Illustrator, or free alternatives **Inkscape** and **Figma**); logos must be vectors (SVG, AI, EPS, PDF) so they scale without blurring.
3. Design 5 concept logos for local businesses; present them on mockups.
4. Offer packages on Fiverr/Upwork and locally: logo + colour palette + fonts + files for print and web.

**Process clients appreciate:** short questionnaire (business, audience, style, competitors) → 2–3 concepts → revisions (agree how many) → final files (PNG, SVG, PDF; colour, black, white versions).

**Watch out.** Never copy or lightly modify existing logos or use paid stock icons without a licence; trademark problems land on your client and your reputation.

---

### 43. Social media graphics

**What it is.** Designing posts, stories, carousels, banners and ads for businesses' Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn and WhatsApp status.

**How to start:**
1. Master Canva sizes: 1080×1080 (square post), 1080×1350 (portrait post), 1080×1920 (stories/status/reels covers).
2. Create a consistent template set for a sample brand: colours, fonts, logo placement.
3. Offer **monthly packages** to local businesses (e.g. 12 posts/month), often combined with social media management (method 68).
4. Sell to salons, restaurants, churches, schools, real estate agents, boutiques: they post every week and need content.

---

### 44. Flyers, posters and event branding

**What it is.** Flyers, posters, banners, roll-up banners, event programmes, church event posters, wedding stationery, menus and business cards.

**How to start:**
1. Learn print basics: **CMYK** colour, **bleed** (extra margin, usually 3 mm), **300 DPI** resolution, safe areas, exporting print-ready PDFs.
2. Partner with **printers** in your town: many get customers who need design.
3. Market on WhatsApp status, Facebook groups and campuses; events (graduations, weddings, harambees, conferences) need designs constantly.

---

### 45. Brand identity kits

**What it is.** A complete brand system: logo variations, colour palette, typography, patterns, business cards, letterhead, social templates and a **brand guidelines** PDF explaining how to use them.

**Why it pays more.** It's a bigger project solving a bigger problem (looking professional everywhere). Upsell logo clients into brand kits.

---

### 46. UI/UX design

**What it is.** Designing app and website interfaces (**UI**) and making them easy to use (**UX**): research, wireframes, prototypes and design systems, usually in **Figma**.

**How to start:**
1. Learn Figma (free) and UX basics: user research, user flows, wireframes, usability testing, accessibility.
2. Free courses: Google's UX Design certificate (paid via Coursera, with financial aid available), Figma's own learning resources, many YouTube courses.
3. Build 2–3 **case studies** showing the problem, research, wireframes, design and testing, e.g. "Redesigning a matatu booking app".
4. Apply for UI/UX roles and freelance projects; team up with developers.

**Pay.** Among the highest-paid design skills; strong demand from startups and app developers.

---

### 47. Canva templates

**What it is.** Designing reusable templates (social media packs, CVs, menus, planners, business cards, presentation decks, wedding invitations) and selling them to people who customise them in Canva.

**How to start:**
1. Join **Canva Creators** (Canva's programme where approved creators earn royalties when templates are used; apply with a portfolio and check current requirements).
2. Or sell template links yourself on **Etsy**-style marketplaces, **Creative Market**, **Gumroad**, **Payhip** or **Selar** (popular in Africa, accepts local payments), and your own website.
3. Make templates for specific audiences: "Kenyan restaurant menu templates", "church event poster pack", "CV templates for graduates".
4. Market with Pinterest, Instagram and TikTok demonstrations.

**Rules.** Follow Canva's licence for elements (some premium elements can't be resold in templates; check Canva's content licence).

---

### 48. Print-on-demand designs

**What it is.** Uploading designs to platforms that print them on T-shirts, mugs, phone cases and posters when someone orders; you earn a royalty or margin without holding stock.

**Where:** **Redbubble**, **Teepublic**, **Spreadshirt**, **Zazzle**, and locally, printing partners for your own online shop (method 107).

**How to start:** research niches (humour, professions like nurses and teachers, African culture and Swahili phrases, hobbies), create original designs, upload many, and promote on social media. Income is usually slow at first and builds with volume; never use trademarked characters, logos or slogans.

---

### 49. Stock photos and videos

**What it is.** Selling photos and videos through agencies that license them to businesses, media and designers worldwide.

**Where:** **Shutterstock** (submit.shutterstock.com), **Adobe Stock** (contributor.stock.adobe.com), **iStock/Getty**, **Alamy**, **Pond5** (video).

**How to start:**
1. Shoot in demand subjects with few existing images: **authentic African and Kenyan everyday life**, business, technology use, farming, education, healthcare, food, cities and landscapes.
2. Technical quality: sharp, well exposed, no noise; even good phones can work for some agencies, but a camera helps.
3. Get **model releases** signed for recognisable people and **property releases** where needed.
4. Keyword and caption every image accurately.
5. Upload consistently; income comes from a large portfolio over time.

:::kenya
Global buyers often struggle to find genuine, modern photos of African people using technology, running businesses, studying and working. Authentic Kenyan stock content fills a real gap.
:::

---

### 50. Illustration and digital art

**What it is.** Drawing for books (especially children's books), magazines, websites, games, brands, comics and stickers, digitally (Procreate on iPad, Krita and Photoshop on PC) or traditionally then scanned.

**How to start:** build a consistent style, post work on Instagram/Behance/ArtStation, offer commissions, contact authors and publishers (children's book illustration is a steady market), and sell prints and stickers.

---

### 51. Presentation design

**What it is.** Designing PowerPoint, Google Slides and Keynote decks: investor pitch decks, company profiles, conference talks, training materials.

**How to start:** master PowerPoint (the PowerPoint subject on this hub): slide masters, layouts, charts, animations, consistent design. Create sample decks (a startup pitch, a company profile, a school prize-giving presentation). Offer to startups, consultants, NGOs and corporates.

---

### 52. Photo editing and retouching

**What it is.** Editing photos: colour correction, retouching portraits, removing backgrounds, product photo cleanup for e-commerce, restoring old photos, wedding photo editing.

**How to start:** learn **Lightroom** (colour) and **Photoshop** or free **GIMP/Photopea** (retouching, background removal). Create before/after samples. Clients: photographers (who outsource editing), online shops (white-background product photos), and families (restoring old photos).

---

### 53. YouTube thumbnail design

**What it is.** Designing the clickable image for YouTube videos. Thumbnails strongly affect how many people click, so creators pay for good ones.

**How to start:** study top creators' thumbnails (big faces, emotion, 3–4 words maximum, high contrast), design 10 samples (1280×720), and offer to YouTubers in your niche, including Kenyan creators.

---

### 54. Infographics

**What it is.** Turning information and data into visual graphics for NGOs, health campaigns, reports, social media and education.

**How to start:** learn data visualisation basics, design samples (e.g. "How to register a business in Kenya in 5 steps"), and offer to NGOs, research organisations, schools and marketing agencies.

---

### 55. Motion graphics and animation

**What it is.** Animated logos, explainer videos, animated social posts, lower-thirds for YouTube, and 2D/3D animation.

**How to start:** start with **Canva** animations and **CapCut**, then learn **After Effects** (motion graphics), **Blender** (free 3D) or **Toon Boom/Moho** (2D animation). Build a showreel. Clients: businesses (explainer ads), YouTubers, agencies, churches and events.

---

## Pricing your design work

- **Per project** is better than per hour for most design (logo package, brand kit, 12-post bundle).
- Define **what's included** (number of concepts, revisions, file types) in writing.
- Take a **deposit** (often 50%) before starting for new clients.
- Raise prices as your portfolio improves; specialise (e.g. restaurant branding, church media, tech startups).

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Unlimited revisions | Agree on a number of revisions |
| Using images and fonts without licences | Use licensed or free-for-commercial-use resources |
| Copying other designers' work | Original work only; it's both unethical and risky |
| Sending low-resolution logos | Deliver vectors and print-ready files |
| No deposit | Take a deposit from new clients |
| Weak portfolio | 6–12 strong pieces beat 50 average ones |

## Practice tasks

1. Design a logo concept for a local business and present it on three mockups.
2. Create a 6-post Instagram template pack in Canva with a consistent brand.
3. Design a print-ready A5 flyer with 3 mm bleed and export a PDF.
4. Create a Behance profile and upload your best three pieces.
5. Take 20 authentic photos of everyday life in your town (with permission where people are recognisable) and pick the five best for stock.

## Summary

- Design earning paths: logos, social graphics, print, brand kits, UI/UX, Canva templates, print-on-demand, stock media, illustration, presentations, photo editing, thumbnails, infographics and motion.
- Start with Canva, then learn principles and professional tools (Figma, Illustrator/Inkscape, Photoshop/GIMP) to earn more.
- A focused portfolio on Behance/Dribbble wins clients; process and clear packages build trust.
- Respect licences and trademarks; take deposits; limit revisions.

```quiz
Q: Logos should be created as which type of graphic: raster or vector?
A: vector
Q: What size in pixels is a standard square Instagram post? Write as 1080x1080.
A: 1080x1080 | 1080 x 1080 | 1080×1080
Q: What extra margin around print designs is called? (one word)
A: bleed
Q: Which free tool is the most common for UI/UX design?
A: Figma
Q: What document must recognisable people sign for stock photos? (two words)
A: model release
Q: What size is a YouTube thumbnail? Write as 1280x720.
A: 1280x720 | 1280 x 720 | 1280×720
```

lessons.title: F. Content creation (ways 56–67): YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, podcasts, UGC and brand deals
lessons.body:
# F. Content creation (ways 56–67): YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, podcasts, UGC and brand deals

Kenyan creators now earn from YouTube ads, brand partnerships, sponsored TikToks, live gifts, affiliate links and their own products. Some have built real businesses. But for every creator who earns well, many post for months with little income. This unit explains twelve content-creation methods: how each platform pays, step-by-step setup, how to grow, and the honest timeline.

:::warning The honest timeline
Most creators earn **little or nothing for the first 6–12 months**. Platform payouts depend on audience location (advertisers pay more for viewers in the US and Europe than in Kenya), niche and watch time. In Kenya, the biggest creator income usually comes from **brand deals and selling your own products/services**, not platform payouts alone. Treat content as a long-term business.
:::

## The creator business model

| Income source | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Platform payouts** | Ad revenue share (YouTube, Facebook), creator programmes, bonuses |
| **Brand deals** | Companies pay you to feature products (sponsored posts, reviews, ambassadorships) |
| **Fan support** | Live gifts, channel memberships, Super Thanks, Stars, tips |
| **Affiliate marketing** | Commission when followers buy through your links (method 74) |
| **Your own products** | Courses, e-books, merchandise, services, events |
| **Services** | Being paid to create content for businesses (UGC, method 63) |

## Choosing a niche

A **niche** is a clear topic and audience. "Everything" channels rarely grow. Good niches combine **what you know or love**, **what people search for**, and **what brands pay for**.

| Niche | Who pays |
|---|---|
| Tech reviews (phones, laptops) | Phone brands, retailers, telcos |
| Personal finance, money and side hustles | Banks, fintechs, SACCOs, investment firms (careful: avoid promoting unlicensed schemes) |
| Farming and agribusiness | Agro-dealers, seed and feed companies, agri-fintech |
| Education and exam revision | Schools, edtech, publishers, your own courses |
| Food and cooking | Food brands, supermarkets, kitchen appliance shops |
| Beauty, hair and fashion | Cosmetics, salons, fashion brands |
| Travel and local tourism | Hotels, tour firms, airlines |
| Comedy and entertainment | Broad brands (large audiences needed) |
| Faith and motivation | Events, books |
| Fitness and health | Gyms, sports brands, health products |

---

### 56. YouTube (long videos)

**How YouTube pays.** Through the **YouTube Partner Program (YPP)**. Requirements (check YouTube's current page, as they change):
- **Fan funding features** (memberships, Super Thanks, Super Chat) open at **500 subscribers** with **3 public uploads in 90 days** and either **3,000 watch hours in 12 months** or **3 million Shorts views in 90 days**.
- **Ad revenue sharing** at **1,000 subscribers** plus **4,000 public watch hours in 12 months** or **10 million valid Shorts views in 90 days**.
- You also need to follow YouTube's monetisation policies, live in an eligible country (Kenya is eligible), and link an **AdSense** account (payments to your bank by wire transfer).

**How to start, step by step:**
1. Pick a niche and plan **10 video ideas** people actually search for (use YouTube search suggestions).
2. Equipment: a smartphone (rear camera, landscape), a cheap clip-on microphone (audio quality matters more than video), natural light from a window.
3. Script or outline every video: hook in the first 15 seconds, deliver value, call to action.
4. Edit with **CapCut** (free, phone and PC) or **DaVinci Resolve** (free, PC).
5. Create a strong thumbnail (method 53) and a searchable title ("How to apply for a KRA PIN in 2026: step by step").
6. Publish **consistently** (e.g. one video weekly) for at least 6 months; study YouTube Studio analytics (click-through rate, average view duration).
7. Reply to comments; collaborate with similar creators.

**Pay reality.** Revenue per 1,000 views varies widely by niche and audience country; finance, tech and business niches with international viewers earn more than entertainment watched mostly in Kenya. Many Kenyan YouTubers earn more from sponsorships than ads.

---

### 57. YouTube Shorts

**What it is.** Vertical videos up to 3 minutes. Shorts grow channels fast; Shorts ad revenue is shared from a pool and is usually much lower per view than long videos.

**Strategy.** Use Shorts to **attract subscribers** to your long videos and to your products/services; repurpose the same clips on TikTok, Reels and Facebook.

---

### 58. TikTok

**How TikTok earns for Kenyan creators.** TikTok's main creator payout programme (the **Creator Rewards Program**) has been available only in selected countries, and Kenya has not been on that list as of this writing (check TikTok's current eligibility). Kenyan TikTokers mainly earn through:
- **Brand deals** (often the biggest source), including via TikTok's **Creator Marketplace/TikTok One** where available.
- **LIVE gifts** (viewers send gifts that convert to "diamonds" and then money; you must meet age and follower requirements).
- **Selling your own products and services** and driving followers to WhatsApp or a shop.
- **Affiliate links** and promotions.

**How to start:**
1. Choose a niche; study 20 top videos in it (hook, length, sound, captions).
2. Post often (daily if possible at the start); the first 1–3 seconds decide whether people keep watching.
3. Use on-screen text and captions (many watch without sound).
4. Engage: reply to comments with videos, go LIVE when eligible.
5. Build a **media kit** (followers, average views, audience location, past brand work) to pitch brands.

---

### 59. Facebook

**How it pays.** Meta offers monetisation tools such as **in-stream ads**, **Stars** (fans send Stars during videos and lives), **subscriptions** and performance-based programmes, and has been expanding eligibility country by country. Check the **Monetisation** section in your Facebook **Professional Dashboard** to see what's available to your page.

**Why Facebook matters in Kenya.** It has a very large adult audience, Facebook groups are powerful for communities and selling, and many brands still advertise there.

**How to start:** create a **Page** or switch your profile to **professional mode**, post consistent video content (Reels plus longer videos), build community in groups, and follow Meta's monetisation and content policies (reposting others' content can disqualify you).

---

### 60. Instagram

**How it pays.** Mostly **brand partnerships** (sponsored posts, Reels and stories), affiliate links and driving followers to products/services. Instagram also offers tools like subscriptions and gifts in some regions.

**How to start:** strong visual niche (fashion, beauty, food, travel, design), consistent Reels, a clear bio with a link (WhatsApp or website), and **Highlights** for products, prices and reviews.

---

### 61. Podcasting

**What it is.** Audio (and increasingly video) shows on Spotify, Apple Podcasts and YouTube.

**How it pays.** Sponsorships (most common), listener support, premium episodes, and building authority that sells your services.

**How to start:**
1. Choose a format (solo, interviews, co-hosts) and a niche ("tech careers in Kenya", "farming business", "relationships").
2. Record with a USB mic or phone + clip mic; edit (method 19).
3. Host on a free podcast host (e.g. Spotify for Creators) that distributes to Spotify and Apple; publish video versions on YouTube.
4. Publish weekly; cut short clips for TikTok and Reels.

---

### 62. Blogging with ads

**What it is.** Writing helpful articles on your own website and earning from **Google AdSense** or ad networks, affiliate links and sponsored posts.

**How to start:** buy a domain and hosting (or start free), install WordPress, write in-depth articles answering real searches (SEO, method 2), apply for AdSense once you have quality content and traffic. Blogging is slow (often 6–12+ months to meaningful traffic), and AI-generated search answers are changing traffic, so focus on unique, experience-based content.

---

### 63. UGC (user-generated content) creator

**What it is.** Creating authentic-looking videos and photos **for brands to use in their own ads and pages**, like a customer testimonial or unboxing. You don't need a big following, because the brand posts the content, not you.

**How to start, step by step:**
1. Make 5–10 sample UGC videos with products you own: unboxing, "3 reasons I love...", before/after, tutorial. Natural lighting, clear voice, vertical format, 15–60 seconds.
2. Build a simple portfolio (Google Drive folder or a free website) and a rate card.
3. Pitch local brands (skincare, food, fashion, apps, fintechs) and global brands through UGC platforms and LinkedIn/Instagram DMs.
4. Agree on **usage rights** (how long and where the brand can use your content) and price accordingly.

**Why it's great for beginners.** Brands pay for the content itself; follower count matters much less.

---

### 64. Influencer brand deals

**How it works.** Brands pay creators to promote products to their audience: single posts, campaigns, ambassador contracts, event appearances.

**How to get deals:**
1. Build an engaged audience in a clear niche (engagement and audience fit matter more than raw follower count; micro-influencers with 5,000–50,000 engaged followers do get paid work).
2. Create a **media kit**: who you are, audience demographics and location, average views, engagement rate, past work, contacts, packages.
3. Pitch brands you already use, with a specific idea.
4. Use simple written agreements: deliverables, deadlines, payment terms (deposit), usage rights, exclusivity.
5. **Disclose sponsored content** ("#ad", "sponsored", or the platform's paid partnership label): it's required by platforms and builds trust.

**Ethics.** Never promote betting to minors, unlicensed investment schemes or "get rich quick" products. Your audience's trust is your business.

---

### 65. Live streaming and gifts

**What it is.** Earning from viewers' gifts and donations during live streams: TikTok LIVE gifts, YouTube Super Chat and memberships, Facebook Stars, and gaming streams on YouTube or Twitch.

**Tips.** Go live on a schedule, have a topic or activity (Q&A, tutorial, gaming, music), thank supporters by name, and moderate comments. Follow age rules; gifting features require you to be 18+.

---

### 66. Video editing for creators

**What it is.** Editing other people's videos: YouTube videos, Shorts/Reels/TikToks, podcasts, church services, adverts, weddings.

**How to start:** learn **CapCut** and then **DaVinci Resolve** or **Premiere Pro**; build a showreel; offer packages ("4 YouTube videos + 12 Shorts per month") to creators and businesses; find clients on Upwork, Fiverr, YouTube creator communities and locally. Editors with storytelling and retention skills are in high demand.

---

### 67. Faceless channels

**What it is.** Channels where the creator doesn't appear: voice-over with stock footage, screen recordings (software tutorials), animations, compilations, relaxing music, story narration.

**Honest notes:**
- Platforms demonetise **"reused" or mass-produced low-value content** (e.g. other people's clips, repetitive AI slideshows). YouTube's policies on inauthentic and repetitious content apply.
- Faceless channels succeed when they add **real value**: original scripts, research, good narration, useful tutorials.
- AI tools can help with scripts and voice, but disclose realistic altered or synthetic content where platforms require it, and check facts.

---

## A weekly creator routine

| Day | Task |
|---|---|
| Monday | Research ideas and write 2 scripts |
| Tuesday | Film |
| Wednesday | Edit main video |
| Thursday | Cut 3–5 short clips; design thumbnail |
| Friday | Publish; reply to comments |
| Weekend | Analyse stats; pitch 3 brands; learn one new skill |

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| No niche | Choose one topic and audience |
| Poor audio | Buy a cheap clip-on mic before a better camera |
| Inconsistent posting | Set a realistic schedule and keep it |
| Copying others' videos | Original content only; reuploads get demonetised |
| Buying followers | Destroys engagement and brand trust |
| Waiting for platform payouts only | Add brand deals, services and products |
| Promoting scams for money | Protect your audience's trust |

## Practice tasks

1. Write your niche statement: "I make [type of content] for [audience] to help them [result]."
2. Plan 10 video ideas with searchable titles.
3. Film and edit one 60-second video with captions in CapCut.
4. Make 3 UGC sample videos for products you own.
5. Draft a one-page media kit.

## Summary

- Content income comes from platform payouts, brand deals, fan support, affiliate links, products and services.
- YouTube's Partner Program has thresholds (500 subscribers for fan funding; 1,000 subscribers + 4,000 watch hours or 10M Shorts views for ads); Kenya is eligible.
- TikTok's main payout programme has been limited to certain countries; Kenyan TikTokers earn mainly from brand deals, LIVE gifts and selling.
- UGC lets beginners earn without a big audience.
- Choose a niche, post consistently, prioritise audio and value, disclose sponsorships, and expect a long build-up.

```quiz
Q: How many subscribers does YouTube's ad revenue sharing require?
A: 1000 | 1,000
Q: How many public watch hours in 12 months does YPP ad revenue require?
A: 4000 | 4,000
Q: What does UGC stand for? Write the first word.
A: User
Q: What should you add to sponsored posts so viewers know it's paid? (one word, e.g. #...)
A: ad | #ad | sponsored
Q: Which equipment should a new creator improve first: camera or microphone?
A: microphone | mic | audio
Q: What document summarises your audience and rates for brands? (two words)
A: media kit
```

lessons.title: G. Marketing services (ways 68–78): social media management, ads, SEO, affiliate and WhatsApp marketing
lessons.body:
# G. Marketing services (ways 68–78): social media management, ads, SEO, affiliate and WhatsApp marketing

Most small businesses know they should be online, but the owner is busy running the shop, clinic, school or farm. They'll pay someone who can bring them **customers**: posting consistently, running adverts, getting them onto Google Maps, managing WhatsApp enquiries. Marketing services are some of the most practical ways to earn in Kenya because the clients are all around you, and results are easy to explain.

:::note Core skills for all marketing services
- Understanding customers: who they are, what they want, where they spend time online
- Clear writing and basic design (Canva)
- Using analytics to show results (reach, clicks, messages, sales)
- Reliability and communication: clients want consistency more than genius
- Learn on this hub: the **Digital marketing** subject, **AI tools**, **Graphic design**. Free certifications: Google Skillshop, Meta Blueprint, HubSpot Academy.
:::

## How to get your first local clients

1. **Practise on 1–2 businesses free or cheap** for one month (a relative's shop, your church, a friend's salon) in exchange for a testimonial and results you can show.
2. **Create a simple offer** with a clear price: "12 posts a month + replies to messages: KSh X".
3. **Walk in and talk to businesses** near you: show a sample of what their page could look like.
4. **Report results monthly**: followers, reach, messages received, bookings. Results keep clients paying.

---

### 68. Social media management

**What it is.** Running a business's social media: planning content, designing posts, writing captions, posting on schedule, replying to comments and DMs, and reporting results.

**How to start, step by step:**
1. Learn each platform's basics: Facebook Pages and Meta Business Suite (schedule posts for Facebook and Instagram free), TikTok business accounts, LinkedIn pages.
2. Create a **content plan template**: monthly calendar with themes (product posts, tips, testimonials, behind-the-scenes, offers).
3. Get 1–2 practice clients; document before/after numbers.
4. Offer packages:
   - **Basic:** 8–12 posts/month on 2 platforms
   - **Standard:** + stories/Reels + replying to messages
   - **Premium:** + ad management (method 69) + monthly report
5. Use tools: Meta Business Suite, Canva (with Content Planner), Google Sheets for calendars, CapCut for Reels.

**Who pays:** salons, restaurants, schools, clinics, real estate agents, churches, hardware shops, hotels, boutiques, car yards, NGOs.

---

### 69. Facebook and Instagram ads manager

**What it is.** Creating and managing paid adverts on Meta (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp-click ads) to reach specific audiences: location, age, interests.

**How to start:**
1. Learn **Meta Ads Manager**: campaign objectives (awareness, traffic, engagement/messages, leads, sales), audiences, budgets, placements, the Meta Pixel.
2. Take **Meta Blueprint** free courses.
3. Run a small test campaign with your own money (e.g. KSh 500–1,000) for a practice business to learn.
4. Understand key numbers: reach, CPM (cost per 1,000 impressions), CTR (click-through rate), cost per message/lead, return on ad spend.
5. Charge a **management fee** separate from the client's ad budget (the client pays Meta directly with their card).

:::kenya Click-to-WhatsApp ads
"Click-to-WhatsApp" ads are very effective for Kenyan businesses: customers tap the ad and land in a WhatsApp chat with the business, where most local sales actually happen.
:::

---

### 70. Google Ads

**What it is.** Paid adverts on Google Search, YouTube and websites. Search ads catch people at the moment they're searching ("emergency plumber Nairobi").

**How to start:** take **Google Skillshop** courses and the Google Ads certifications (free); learn keyword match types, ad copy, landing pages and conversion tracking; start with small local search campaigns for clients with clear services (clinics, schools, lawyers, service businesses).

---

### 71. SEO for local businesses

**What it is.** Helping businesses rank higher on Google organically: website improvements, content, local listings, reviews and links.

**How to start:**
1. Learn SEO fundamentals (this hub's Marketing and HTML SEO lessons, Google's SEO Starter Guide).
2. Do an **SEO audit** for a business: page titles, descriptions, speed, mobile-friendliness, Google Business Profile, reviews, content gaps.
3. Offer an audit + fix package, then a monthly plan (content, profile updates, review requests, reports).
4. Show results with Google Search Console and Google Business Profile insights.

**Honesty rule.** Never promise "number one on Google guaranteed". Promise work and reports; results come over months.

---

### 72. Google Business Profile setup

**What it is.** Creating, verifying and optimising a business's free **Google Business Profile** so it appears on Google Maps and in "near me" searches with photos, hours, phone number and reviews.

**How to start, step by step:**
1. Learn the process on Google's help pages: create the profile, choose the right category, add accurate address/service area, hours, phone, website, photos, products/services.
2. Complete **verification** (Google chooses the method: video, phone/SMS, email, or postcard where applicable).
3. Optimise: 10+ quality photos, services with descriptions, regular posts, Q&A, and a system for getting genuine **reviews** from real customers (never fake reviews, which break Google's rules).
4. Offer this as a fixed-price service to every business on your street without one. It's quick to deliver and easy to understand.

**Pair it with:** a simple website (method 79) and WhatsApp Business setup (method 75).

---

### 73. Email marketing

**What it is.** Building email lists and sending newsletters, promotions and automated sequences (welcome series, abandoned cart reminders) for businesses.

**How to start:** learn **Mailchimp**, **MailerLite** or **Brevo** (free tiers); understand consent (only email people who signed up; Kenya's Data Protection Act applies), list building with sign-up forms, segmentation and automation. Offer to online shops, coaches, schools and event organisers.

---

### 74. Affiliate marketing

**What it is.** Earning a commission when people buy through your unique link.

**Programmes to know** (check current terms and whether they accept Kenyan affiliates):
- **Jumia's affiliate (KOL) programme**: earn commission on Jumia sales from your links.
- **Amazon Associates**: international products; check eligibility and payment options for Kenya.
- **Software and hosting affiliates**: many web hosting companies, website builders and online tools pay per sign-up.
- **Course platforms and digital products** (Udemy, Selar products, others).
- **Local brands and fintechs** running referral/affiliate programmes.

**How to start:**
1. Choose a niche where you can genuinely recommend products (e.g. "best budget phones", "tools for freelancers").
2. Create helpful content: reviews, comparisons, tutorials (blog, YouTube, TikTok, WhatsApp channel).
3. Place links naturally and **disclose** they're affiliate links.
4. Track which content earns; do more of it.

**Watch out.** Promoting forex "signal groups", unlicensed investment schemes or betting can harm your followers and may be illegal. Only promote products you'd recommend to family.

---

### 75. WhatsApp Business setup and marketing

**What it is.** Setting up **WhatsApp Business** for clients: business profile, catalogue with prices and photos, quick replies, greeting and away messages, labels for orders, broadcast lists, WhatsApp Channels, and click-to-chat links/QR codes.

**How to start:** master the free WhatsApp Business app features; create a setup checklist; offer setup + training as a fixed package to small businesses, plus monthly management (status updates, broadcasts, catalogue updates). For bigger businesses, learn about the **WhatsApp Business Platform (API)** via official providers for automated messages and chatbots.

**Rules.** Only message customers who agreed; spam gets numbers banned.

---

### 76. Community management

**What it is.** Managing online communities: Facebook groups, Telegram and WhatsApp communities, Discord servers, alumni and church groups, brand communities.

**Tasks:** welcoming members, moderating, starting discussions, organising events/lives, enforcing rules, reporting.

**How to start:** run your own community in a niche to learn, then offer services to brands, creators, crypto/tech projects (be careful with unregulated ones), NGOs and associations.

---

### 77. Lead generation and appointment setting

**What it is.** Finding potential customers for businesses and booking meetings or calls with them, by email, LinkedIn, phone or social media. Common for agencies, B2B companies, real estate and coaches abroad.

**How to start:** learn LinkedIn prospecting, writing short outreach messages, CRM tools (HubSpot free CRM, Google Sheets), and phone etiquette. Offer on Upwork ("appointment setter", "lead generation specialist"). Pay can include **commission per booked meeting or sale**; prefer a base fee plus commission.

---

### 78. Influencer marketing management

**What it is.** Connecting brands with creators: finding suitable influencers, negotiating, managing campaigns, ensuring disclosure, and reporting results. Or managing creators (talent management) by finding them brand deals for a percentage.

**How to start:** build relationships with micro-influencers in a niche, learn campaign planning and contracts, start with small local brand campaigns, and track results (reach, engagement, sales codes).

---

## Building a small marketing agency

Once you have several clients:

1. **Standardise packages** and an onboarding form (logins, brand assets, goals).
2. **Use contracts** with scope, payment terms (monthly in advance) and notice periods.
3. **Hire or partner**: a designer, a video editor, a writer.
4. **Monthly reports** with results and next month's plan.
5. **Register your business** (business name on eCitizen/BRS), get a KRA PIN for the business and keep records.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Selling "likes" instead of results | Focus on messages, calls, bookings and sales |
| Using the client's money on ads without a plan | Clear objective, budget and tracking |
| Fake reviews or bought followers | Never; they break rules and destroy trust |
| No contract or monthly prepayment | Use simple contracts; bill in advance |
| Promising guaranteed rankings | Promise work and transparent reports |
| Spamming WhatsApp contacts | Message only people who opted in |

## Practice tasks

1. Choose a local business and write a one-month content calendar with 12 post ideas.
2. Create a free Meta Business Suite account and schedule 3 posts for a practice page.
3. Audit a local business's Google presence (Maps listing, photos, reviews, website) and list 5 improvements.
4. Set up WhatsApp Business with a catalogue of 5 items for a practice business.
5. Complete one free certification (Google Skillshop, Meta Blueprint or HubSpot).

## Summary

- Marketing services: social media management, Meta ads, Google Ads, local SEO, Google Business Profile, email marketing, affiliate marketing, WhatsApp Business, community management, lead generation and influencer management.
- Local businesses everywhere need these services; start with practice clients and show results.
- Charge clear packages and management fees (ad budgets are separate).
- Be honest: no guaranteed rankings, fake reviews, spam or harmful promotions.

```quiz
Q: Which free Meta tool schedules Facebook and Instagram posts? (three words)
A: Meta Business Suite | business suite
Q: Which free Google listing puts a business on Google Maps? (three words)
A: Google Business Profile | business profile
Q: Should the client's ad budget and your management fee be separate? (yes or no)
A: yes
Q: What is Jumia's affiliate programme called? (three letters)
A: KOL
Q: Which ad type takes customers straight into a WhatsApp chat? (hyphenated, e.g. click-to-...)
A: click-to-WhatsApp | click to whatsapp
Q: Should you buy fake reviews for clients? (yes or no)
A: no
```

lessons.title: H. Tech and programming (ways 79–91): websites, apps, M-Pesa integration, automation and data
lessons.body:
# H. Tech and programming (ways 79–91): websites, apps, M-Pesa integration, automation and data

Technical skills take longer to learn than most online work, but they pay the most and are in demand worldwide. A Kenyan developer can build websites for local businesses, integrate M-Pesa payments, fix bugs for clients in Europe, analyse data for NGOs or work remotely for international companies. This unit covers 13 tech methods, with the learning path for each (most can be learned free on this hub).

:::note Learning paths on this hub
- **Websites:** HTML → CSS → JavaScript → (PHP & MySQL or WordPress) → Hosting
- **Apps:** App development fundamentals → Dart & Flutter or Kotlin or React Native → APIs & backends
- **Data:** Excel → SQL → Python → (Power BI / data visualisation)
- **IT support and security:** IT basics → Computer maintenance → Networking → Linux → Cybersecurity
Expect 3–6 months of consistent practice to reach paid beginner level in web development, longer for apps and data roles.
:::

## Your developer portfolio

- A **GitHub** account (github.com) with clean, documented projects.
- A **portfolio website** (built by you) listing 3–6 projects with screenshots, the problem solved, your role, technologies and live links.
- Real or realistic projects beat tutorial clones: "School fees payment system with M-Pesa", "Hardware shop inventory app", "Restaurant ordering website".

---

### 79. Business websites

**What it is.** Building websites for businesses, schools, churches, NGOs and professionals.

**How to start, step by step:**
1. Learn HTML, CSS and basic JavaScript (subjects on this hub); learn hosting (cPanel, domains, SSL, email).
2. Build 3 sample sites for different industries, deploy them online (GitHub Pages, Netlify or cheap hosting).
3. Create a clear offer: "5-page business website with WhatsApp button, contact form, Google Maps, SEO basics, hosting setup".
4. Find clients: local businesses without websites (many have only Facebook pages), referrals, Facebook groups, LinkedIn, and international clients on Upwork/Fiverr.
5. Use a process: discovery questionnaire → quote and deposit → design draft → build → client review → launch → training → maintenance plan.

**Pricing.** Local simple sites are often priced from about KSh 15,000 upward depending on pages and features; add yearly hosting and maintenance (recurring income).

---

### 80. WordPress development

**What it is.** WordPress powers a large share of all websites. Clients want WordPress sites they can edit themselves: blogs, business sites, school sites, news sites, membership sites.

**How to start:** learn WordPress installation on cPanel, themes, page builders (Elementor, Gutenberg blocks), essential plugins (SEO, security, backups, forms, caching), and basic PHP/CSS for customisation. Offer setup, customisation, speed optimisation, security hardening and maintenance.

---

### 81. Online shops (WooCommerce, Shopify and custom)

**What it is.** Building e-commerce stores with product catalogues, carts, delivery options and payments (M-Pesa, cards).

**How to start:** learn **WooCommerce** (WordPress) and/or **Shopify**; learn Kenyan payment integrations (M-Pesa plugins or gateways, card gateways licensed in Kenya); build a demo store; offer setup + product upload + training. Pair with product photography and product descriptions (methods 52, 10).

---

### 82. Mobile apps

**What it is.** Building Android and iOS apps for businesses, startups, SACCOs, schools and NGOs.

**How to start:** follow the App development path (Flutter is popular for building Android and iOS from one codebase); publish at least one real app on Google Play (a one-time developer registration fee applies); build portfolio apps that solve local problems; partner with designers (UI/UX) and backend developers.

**Pay.** App projects are larger (and riskier); always use milestones and contracts.

---

### 83. M-Pesa integration

**What it is.** Connecting websites, apps and systems to **Safaricom's Daraja API**: STK push (customer enters PIN on their phone), C2B (paybill/till payment notifications), B2C (paying customers), transaction status and balance queries.

**Why it's valuable.** Almost every Kenyan business system needs M-Pesa: school fees, rent collection, e-commerce, SACCO contributions, Wi-Fi hotspots, event tickets. Developers who do it reliably are in demand locally and with international companies entering Kenya.

**How to start:** study the **M-Pesa Daraja API** lesson in the APIs & backends subject on this hub; build in the **sandbox** (developer.safaricom.co.ke); handle callbacks, failures and duplicate payments correctly; keep credentials secret on the server; offer integration as a service to web developers and businesses.

---

### 84. Website maintenance and bug fixing

**What it is.** Keeping sites running: updates, backups, security fixes, uptime monitoring, content changes, fixing broken features and errors.

**Why it's great.** Recurring monthly income (care plans) and constant demand: many businesses have sites built by someone who disappeared.

**How to start:** offer monthly care plans (updates, backups, small edits, monitoring, reports); take bug-fixing jobs on Upwork ("fix my WordPress site", "PHP error", "website hacked"); learn debugging with browser DevTools and server logs.

---

### 85. Automation and scripts

**What it is.** Saving businesses time by automating repetitive work: Python scripts, Google Apps Script for Google Sheets, Excel macros, and no-code tools (**Zapier**, **Make**, **n8n**) connecting apps ("when a form is submitted, add to a spreadsheet, send an email and a WhatsApp notification").

**How to start:** learn Python basics (this hub), Google Apps Script, and one automation tool; offer "automate your reports/invoices/emails" services; show time saved.

---

### 86. Data analysis and dashboards

**What it is.** Cleaning data, analysing it and building reports and dashboards for businesses, NGOs, researchers and SACCOs, using **Excel**, **Google Sheets**, **SQL**, **Power BI**, **Tableau** or **Python**.

**How to start:**
1. Learn Excel deeply (pivot tables, XLOOKUP, charts), then SQL, then Power BI or Python (pandas).
2. Build portfolio dashboards using public data (Kenya National Bureau of Statistics, Kenya Open Data, Kaggle datasets): e.g. "County population and health facilities dashboard".
3. Offer services: survey data analysis for researchers and NGOs (common in Kenya), sales dashboards for businesses, monitoring and evaluation reports.
4. Compete on Zindi/Kaggle to build credibility (method 41).

---

### 87. Remote IT support

**What it is.** Helping people and small businesses with computer problems remotely (using tools like AnyDesk or TeamViewer), setting up Microsoft 365/Google Workspace, email, printers, networks, antivirus and backups; also helpdesk jobs for companies.

**How to start:** learn IT basics, computer maintenance, networking and Windows administration (this hub); consider certifications (CompTIA A+, Microsoft fundamentals); offer support contracts to small offices, schools and clinics; apply for remote helpdesk roles.

---

### 88. Bug bounties

**What it is.** Finding security vulnerabilities in companies' systems **with permission**, through official bug bounty programmes, and getting paid rewards.

**Where:** **HackerOne** (hackerone.com), **Bugcrowd** (bugcrowd.com), **Intigriti**, and companies' own responsible disclosure programmes.

**How to start:** learn web security (this hub's Cybersecurity subject, PortSwigger Web Security Academy (free), OWASP Top 10); practise legally on deliberately vulnerable labs; read programme scopes carefully and only test what's allowed.

:::warning Only hack with permission
Testing systems without authorisation is a crime under Kenya's **Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act**, even if you mean well. Bug bounty programmes give written permission and rules (scope). Stay inside them.
:::

**Honest view.** Bounties are competitive; beginners may go months without a valid finding. The skills lead to well-paid security jobs.

---

### 89. Selling code, themes and plugins

**What it is.** Creating reusable products: WordPress themes and plugins, website templates, app templates, scripts, UI kits, and selling them repeatedly.

**Where:** marketplaces like **CodeCanyon/ThemeForest** (Envato), your own website, Gumroad/Payhip/Selar; or the official WordPress plugin directory with a paid "pro" version.

**How to start:** solve a specific problem well (e.g. "M-Pesa payment plugin for a specific platform", "school website template"), document it, provide support, and update regularly. Passive-ish income, but support takes time.

---

### 90. No-code apps and chatbots

**What it is.** Building apps, websites and chatbots without much code using tools like **Glide**, **Bubble**, **Softr**, **FlutterFlow**, **Airtable**, and AI chatbot builders (website chatbots and WhatsApp bots via official API providers).

**How to start:** pick one tool, build 3 small useful apps (inventory tracker, booking app, FAQ chatbot for a school), and offer quick, affordable solutions to small businesses. Learn basic logic and data structure; no-code still needs clear thinking.

---

### 91. Hosting and domain reselling

**What it is.** Selling web hosting and domains (e.g. `.co.ke`) to clients through **reseller hosting** accounts or registrar reseller programmes, often bundled with website building and maintenance.

**How to start:** choose a reliable hosting provider's reseller plan, learn cPanel/WHM and DNS, offer support you can actually deliver (email setup, SSL, backups), and price clearly (yearly renewals). Reliability and quick support matter more than being cheapest.

---

## Finding tech clients and jobs

| Channel | Best for |
|---|---|
| Local businesses (walk-ins, referrals) | Websites, M-Pesa, IT support, maintenance |
| Upwork, Fiverr, Freelancer, Toptal (selective) | International projects |
| LinkedIn | Remote jobs, contracts, networking |
| GitHub and open source | Visibility, experience, credibility |
| Tech communities and events (meetups, hackathons, Google Developer Groups) | Jobs, partners, learning |
| Remote job boards (We Work Remotely, Remote OK, Wellfound) | Full-time remote roles |

## Contracts and protecting yourself

- **Written scope:** exactly what's included; extra features cost extra.
- **Milestones and deposits:** e.g. 40% to start, 30% at draft, 30% at launch.
- **Ownership:** transfer code ownership after full payment.
- **Hosting and accounts in the client's name** (domain especially), with your access, so there are no disputes later.
- **Never hold sites hostage** over disputes; it damages your reputation and may be illegal.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Endless tutorials without building | Build real projects from week 2 |
| No portfolio or GitHub | 3–6 documented projects |
| Underpricing and unlimited changes | Clear scope, milestones, change requests |
| Storing M-Pesa keys in front-end code | Keep secrets on the server only |
| Hacking without permission | Only authorised testing |
| No backups | Automated backups before any change |

## Practice tasks

1. Build and deploy a 3-page website for an imaginary business.
2. Complete the M-Pesa sandbox STK push from the APIs & backends subject.
3. Build an Excel or Power BI dashboard from a public Kenyan dataset.
4. Write a one-page website proposal with scope, timeline, price and milestones.
5. Automate one repetitive task (e.g. a Google Form that emails you each response).

## Summary

- Tech earning paths: websites, WordPress, online shops, apps, M-Pesa integration, maintenance, automation, data analysis, IT support, bug bounties, selling code, no-code apps and hosting reselling.
- They take longer to learn but pay the most; learn free on this hub and build a portfolio on GitHub.
- Use contracts, milestones and clear scope; keep domains in clients' names; keep secrets on servers.
- Security testing is only legal with permission.

```quiz
Q: What is Safaricom's M-Pesa developer API called?
A: Daraja | Daraja API
Q: In which environment should you build and test M-Pesa integration first?
A: sandbox | the sandbox
Q: Which Kenyan law makes unauthorised hacking a crime? Write the first two words.
A: Computer Misuse | Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act
Q: Which platform hosts code portfolios for developers?
A: GitHub | github
Q: Name the WordPress plugin used to build online shops.
A: WooCommerce | woocommerce
Q: Should a client's domain be registered in the developer's name or the client's name?
A: client | the client's name | client's name | the client
```

lessons.title: I. Teaching and expertise (ways 92–100): tutoring, teaching languages, courses, coaching and communities
lessons.body:
# I. Teaching and expertise (ways 92–100): tutoring, teaching languages, courses, coaching and communities

If you know something well, a school subject, a language, a profession, a software tool or a business skill, someone will pay to learn it from you. Online teaching ranges from one-on-one tutoring over Google Meet to selling recorded courses to thousands of people. Teachers, university students, professionals and skilled hobbyists can all earn this way. This unit covers nine methods.

:::note What makes a good online teacher
- Deep knowledge of the topic, **and** the patience to explain from the learner's level
- Clear structure: goals, small steps, practice, feedback
- Reliable setup: stable internet (with a backup), a headset, good lighting, a quiet space
- Tools: Google Meet/Zoom, a digital whiteboard (Google Jamboard alternatives, Miro, a drawing tablet or a phone as a document camera), Google Classroom or WhatsApp groups for materials
:::

---

### 92. Online tutoring (school, college and university)

**What it is.** One-on-one or small group lessons for CBC/CBE, KCSE, IGCSE/A-level, university units, and professional exams (CPA, ACCA modules).

**How to start, step by step:**
1. Choose subjects and levels you can teach confidently (e.g. Grade 7–9 Maths and Integrated Science, KCSE Chemistry).
2. Prepare a simple lesson structure: quick check of previous work → new concept → worked examples → practice → homework.
3. Find students: parents' WhatsApp and Facebook groups, your church and estate, schools (holiday tuition), referrals; international platforms like **Preply** and others for students abroad.
4. Price per hour or monthly packages (e.g. 8 lessons a month); take payment in advance (M-Pesa).
5. Report progress to parents monthly (topics covered, scores, areas to improve).

**Rules.** Follow child protection good practice: lessons with minors in visible settings, parents informed, professional communication only through parents' numbers where appropriate. Check current Ministry of Education rules on holiday tuition for school-going children.

---

### 93. Teaching English online

**What it is.** Teaching English to learners abroad (adults and children) who want conversation practice, business English or exam preparation (IELTS, TOEFL).

**How to start:**
1. Consider a **TEFL/TESOL certificate** (120-hour courses are common); many platforms and schools ask for one.
2. Join tutoring marketplaces such as **Preply** (preply.com) and **italki** (italki.com) as a tutor; some platforms prefer "native speakers" from specific countries, so check each platform's requirements honestly.
3. Record a strong **intro video**: clear voice, good light, smile, explain who you help and how.
4. Start with competitive rates to get first reviews, then raise them.
5. Specialise: business English, IELTS speaking, English for children, interview English.

---

### 94. Teaching Kiswahili and other languages

**What it is.** Teaching Kiswahili (and Kikuyu, Dholuo, Somali, Arabic, French, etc.) to foreigners: diplomats, NGO staff, missionaries, tourists, diaspora children and students of African languages.

**How to start:** list yourself on italki and Preply as a Kiswahili teacher; prepare a beginner curriculum (greetings, numbers, shopping, travel, grammar basics like noun classes); make short Kiswahili lessons on YouTube/TikTok to attract students; contact language schools and expatriate communities in Nairobi.

**Why it's an opportunity.** Kiswahili is spoken by tens of millions of people across East and Central Africa and is used by the African Union, so interest in learning it is real.

---

### 95. Selling online courses

**What it is.** Recording a course once and selling it many times.

**Where:** **Udemy** (huge marketplace, lower prices), **Teachable**, **Thinkific**, **Podia** (your own course site), **Selar** (popular in Africa with local payment options), or your own website/WhatsApp community + M-Pesa.

**How to start, step by step:**
1. **Validate demand:** ask your audience, check what people search and buy, run a free live class first.
2. **Outline:** clear outcome ("Build your first website in 30 days"), modules, short lessons (5–15 minutes), exercises.
3. **Record:** screen recordings (OBS Studio, free) for software topics, or phone video for practical skills; good audio is essential.
4. **Edit and upload** with worksheets and quizzes.
5. **Market:** free content on YouTube/TikTok/WhatsApp, email list, testimonials, launch discounts.
6. **Update** the course and support students.

**Good Kenyan course topics:** Excel for jobs, Canva design, digital marketing for small businesses, poultry farming business, Kenya tax filing (iTax) explained, coding, CV and interview skills, photography with a phone.

---

### 96. Live workshops and bootcamps

**What it is.** Paid live sessions or multi-week cohorts (Zoom/Google Meet or in person), e.g. "Weekend Excel bootcamp", "4-week freelancing class".

**How to start:** choose a practical topic with a clear result, plan sessions and assignments, set a price and a seat limit, collect payment via M-Pesa, record sessions for attendees, and gather testimonials. Cohorts create accountability, so students finish more often than with recorded courses.

---

### 97. Coaching and consulting

**What it is.** Selling your **expertise and judgement**: business consulting for SMEs, career coaching, fitness coaching, financial literacy, agribusiness advice, IT consulting, HR consulting, mentoring for students.

**How to start:** define a specific problem you solve for a specific client ("I help small restaurants cut food waste and increase profits"); publish helpful content to show expertise (LinkedIn, YouTube); offer a free 20-minute discovery call; sell packages (e.g. 4 sessions); collect testimonials.

**Rules.** Stay inside your qualifications. Medical, legal, financial investment and psychological advice are regulated professions in Kenya; don't present yourself as licensed if you aren't.

---

### 98. Selling your own notes, revision papers and study guides

**What it is.** Creating and selling **original** study materials: topic notes, revision guides, practice questions with marking schemes, past-paper walkthroughs you wrote yourself, flashcards.

**How to start:** create high-quality original materials, format them well (Word/Canva → PDF), sell via WhatsApp/M-Pesa, Selar, Payhip or your own site, and give free samples.

**Copyright and ethics.** Don't sell copyrighted textbooks or materials that belong to others (KNEC papers and publishers' books have rights holders), and never sell leaked exams: that's illegal and harms students. Your own original notes and questions are fine.

---

### 99. Interview and exam preparation services (ethical)

**What it is.** Mock interviews, aptitude test practice, public service interview preparation, preparing graduates for job assessments, exam technique coaching.

**How to start:** combine with CV writing (method 8); prepare question banks for common roles; run mock interviews by video with feedback. **Ethical line:** you help candidates prepare; you never sit exams or tests on their behalf.

---

### 100. Paid communities and memberships

**What it is.** A members-only group where people pay monthly for access to you, resources, accountability and each other: e.g. a freelancers' community, a farming club, a coding study group, a fitness group.

**Where:** WhatsApp Communities/Telegram (with M-Pesa subscriptions managed manually or via tools), Skool, Patreon, YouTube memberships, Discord.

**How to start:** build a free audience first; define what members get (weekly lives, resources, feedback, networking); start with a founding-member price; deliver consistently; keep the community safe and moderated.

---

## Pricing teaching and expertise

| Model | Example |
|---|---|
| Per hour | Tutoring, consulting calls |
| Package | 8 lessons/month; 4 coaching sessions |
| Per course | One-time course purchase |
| Cohort | 4-week bootcamp |
| Subscription | Monthly community membership |

Raise prices with results and testimonials. Specialists (exam board, profession, niche) earn more than generalists.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|
| Teaching without lesson plans | Outline goals and steps for every session |
| Poor audio/video setup | Headset, light facing you, stable internet |
| Not collecting payment in advance | Prepaid packages |
| Selling copyrighted or leaked materials | Only original materials |
| Overpromising results ("guaranteed A") | Promise effort and a clear method |
| Making a big course nobody asked for | Validate demand first |

## Practice tasks

1. Plan a 60-minute tutoring lesson for one topic you know, with practice questions.
2. Record a 60-second tutor intro video.
3. Outline a 6-module online course with lesson titles.
4. Create a 5-page original revision guide and export it as a PDF.
5. Write a one-paragraph offer for a coaching or consulting service.

## Summary

- Teaching and expertise: tutoring, teaching English, teaching Kiswahili and other languages, courses, workshops, coaching/consulting, original study materials, interview prep and paid communities.
- Good structure, reliable setup and results-based reputation are key.
- Use Preply/italki for language tutoring, Udemy/Teachable/Selar for courses, WhatsApp/Telegram/Skool for communities.
- Stay ethical: original materials, no leaked exams, no sitting tests for others, stay within your qualifications.

```quiz
Q: Which certificate is commonly required to teach English online? Write one acronym.
A: TEFL | TESOL
Q: Name a popular African course platform with local payment options.
A: Selar | selar.co
Q: Should you sell leaked exam papers? (yes or no)
A: no
Q: Which free software records your screen for courses? (three letters plus a word)
A: OBS | OBS Studio
Q: What should you do before building a big course? (one word: ... demand)
A: validate | validate demand
Q: Name one marketplace for language tutors.
A: Preply | italki
```

lessons.title: J. Selling online (ways 101–110): Jumia, Kilimall, WhatsApp, your own shop, digital products and crafts
lessons.body:
# J. Selling online (ways 101–110): Jumia, Kilimall, WhatsApp, your own shop, digital products and crafts

Kenyans buy online every day: phones and electronics on marketplaces, clothes on Instagram, food on WhatsApp, second-hand items on Facebook Marketplace, and digital products like e-books and templates. Selling online can be a full business or a side income. This unit explains ten selling methods with practical steps, costs and the logistics of delivery and payment in Kenya.

:::note The basics of any online selling business
1. **Product:** something people want, at a price that leaves profit after all costs.
2. **Trust:** real photos, reviews, clear prices, a physical location or reliable contacts, fair returns.
3. **Payment:** M-Pesa (Till or Paybill makes you look professional), cash on delivery, cards.
4. **Delivery:** riders (boda/courier apps), parcel services, matatu shuttles and courier companies for upcountry orders, or pickup points.
5. **Records:** stock, sales, costs, profit (a simple spreadsheet).
:::

## Calculate profit before selling anything

| Item | Example (KSh) |
|---|---|
| Selling price | 2,500 |
| Cost of product | 1,300 |
| Marketplace commission or ad cost per sale | 300 |
| Packaging | 50 |
| Delivery you pay (if free delivery) | 200 |
| M-Pesa charges / payment fees | 30 |
| **Profit per item** | **620** |

If you can't make a profit after all costs, change the product, price or channel.

---

### 101. Selling on Jumia

**What it is.** Listing products on **Jumia** (jumia.co.ke), Kenya's large online marketplace, which brings customers, handles payments and offers delivery options; you pay commissions and fees.

**How to start, step by step:**
1. Register as a seller on Jumia's seller centre (you'll need business details, ID, KRA PIN, and bank or payment details; check current requirements).
2. Complete seller training (Jumia provides guides and training).
3. List products with **excellent photos** (white background for the main image), accurate titles, specifications and competitive prices.
4. Understand commissions per category, fees, delivery and returns policies **before** pricing.
5. Fulfil orders fast; good ratings improve visibility. Use promotions (campaigns like Black Friday) carefully, keeping profit in mind.

**Best for:** electronics, accessories, beauty, fashion, home and kitchen products.

---

### 102. Kilimall and other marketplaces

**What it is.** **Kilimall** (kilimall.co.ke) and other marketplaces and classified sites (e.g. **Jiji** for classifieds) also let you list products.

**How to start:** compare commissions, traffic and categories; list your best products on two or three channels; keep stock levels synchronised to avoid selling what you don't have.

---

### 103. WhatsApp, Facebook Marketplace and Instagram selling

**What it is.** Selling directly through social media, the most common online selling method in Kenya.

**How to start, step by step:**
1. Set up **WhatsApp Business** with a catalogue (photos, prices, descriptions), greeting message and quick replies (method 75).
2. Post products on **WhatsApp Status** daily, in a **WhatsApp Channel**, and in relevant groups (follow group rules).
3. List on **Facebook Marketplace** (local buyers search it a lot) and in Facebook buy-and-sell groups.
4. Build an **Instagram** shop page with Highlights for categories, prices, delivery info and reviews.
5. Get an **M-Pesa Till** (Lipa na M-Pesa Buy Goods) for a professional payment experience.
6. Arrange reliable delivery: local riders, parcel services for upcountry.
7. Ask happy customers for photos and reviews; post them (with permission).

:::warning Protect yourself and your customers
- Common scams against sellers: fake M-Pesa SMS messages ("confirm the SMS by checking your actual M-Pesa balance or statement before releasing goods"), and buyers asking you to send money back after "overpaying".
- Don't ask customers to pay before delivery unless they trust you; consider pay-on-delivery for nearby orders or a deposit for custom items.
:::

---

### 104. Your own online shop

**What it is.** A website store you control (WooCommerce, Shopify, or simpler tools), with M-Pesa and card payments.

**Why.** No marketplace commissions, your own brand and customer list. **But** you must bring your own traffic (social media, ads, SEO).

**How to start:** start selling on social media first; when you have steady sales, build a store (method 81) or hire a developer; connect M-Pesa; drive traffic with content and ads.

---

### 105. Local dropshipping

**What it is.** Selling products you don't stock: you market them, the customer orders and pays, then you buy from a supplier (wholesaler in town, or a supplier who delivers) and arrange delivery, keeping the margin.

**How to start:**
1. Find reliable suppliers (wholesale shops, importers) who'll sell single items and can deliver or hold items for you.
2. Test products with low risk: post photos (with permission), take orders, then purchase.
3. Agree clearly with suppliers on stock confirmation, quality and returns.
4. Be honest with customers on delivery times.

**Risks.** Suppliers running out, quality problems and slow deliveries damage your reputation. International dropshipping into Kenya faces long shipping times and import duties; local suppliers usually work better.

---

### 106. Digital products

**What it is.** Products sold as downloads: e-books, guides, templates (Canva, Excel budget planners, CV templates), printables, presets, music beats, stock packs, courses (method 95).

**Where:** **Selar** (selar.co), **Payhip** (payhip.com), **Gumroad** (gumroad.com), Etsy-style marketplaces, your own site, or WhatsApp + M-Pesa with manual delivery.

**How to start:**
1. Solve a specific problem: "Excel budget template for Kenyan families", "Guide to starting a chicken business: costs and suppliers", "Wedding planning checklist".
2. Create it well (Canva, Google Docs, Excel), with clear instructions.
3. Set up a product page with a strong title, preview images and price.
4. Promote with free valuable content (TikTok, YouTube, WhatsApp Channel).

**Why it's attractive.** Create once, sell many times; no delivery costs.

---

### 107. Print-on-demand merchandise

**What it is.** Selling custom T-shirts, hoodies, mugs and caps with your designs, printed only when ordered: through international POD platforms (method 48) or **local printing partners** in Kenya for your own brand.

**How to start locally:** design a small collection (Swahili phrases, campus merchandise, church and event merch, profession-themed designs); partner with a local printer for per-order printing; take pre-orders with deposits; sell through social media and events.

---

### 108. Selling Kenyan crafts and products to the world

**What it is.** Selling handmade items (Maasai beadwork, kiondo baskets, soapstone carvings, kikoys, leather sandals, jewellery, art) and products like Kenyan tea and coffee to customers abroad.

**How to start:**
1. Source from artisans fairly (agree prices, quality and timelines; fair trade practices build lasting supply).
2. Photograph products beautifully; tell the story of the artisans.
3. Sell through international marketplaces that accept sellers from Kenya (check each platform's seller country list), your own website, Instagram and diaspora networks.
4. Learn **export basics**: packaging, courier costs (Posta EMS, international couriers), customs documents and any export requirements for your product category (e.g. food and wood products may need certificates).

---

### 109. Reselling and thrift (mitumba) online

**What it is.** Buying quality second-hand clothes (mitumba), shoes, bags, electronics or furniture, cleaning/repairing and photographing them, and reselling online.

**How to start:** learn to pick quality items in markets (Gikomba, Toi, local markets), clean and photograph them well, post consistently on Instagram/TikTok/WhatsApp, and offer delivery. "Thrift drops" at set times create excitement. For electronics, test thoroughly and be honest about condition.

---

### 110. Farm produce online

**What it is.** Selling eggs, vegetables, fruits, honey, milk products, chicken and other produce directly to households, restaurants and offices through WhatsApp, social media and delivery, or through agri-marketplace apps.
